items.title: ALMA Reveals a Dying Star's Final Breath, Encoded In a Giant Ring of Gas
items.subtitle: About 6,500 years ago, a dying star emitted its final thermal pulse.
items.feedText: That dying breath created a giant ring of gas detected by ALMA. Then only 700 years ago, the star formed an hourglass nebula. Theory predicted this, but this is the first direct evidence supporting it.
items.body:
# ALMA Reveals a Dying Star's Final Breath, Encoded In a Giant Ring of Gas

Stars transition through different stages as they evolve. Sun-like stars with low to intermediate masses (about 0.8 to 8 solar masses) begin as main-sequence stars, then transition sequentially to red giants, asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars, then post-AGB stars. By the end, they leave behind only a planetary nebula . Each of those transitions are detailed and complicated, and astrophysicists crave a more complete understanding of them.

Stars in their AGB phase have an important job. They spread heavy elements into the surrounding interstellar medium (ISM) and those elements are taken up in subsequent star and planet formation. As they transition from AGB phase to post-AGB phase, they experience thermal pulses that expel material. These events are like brief snapshots in the long life of a star, and catching one in the act is challenging.

Astronomers working with the Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA) have caught a star after what seems to be its final thermal pulse, leaving behing a planetary nebula. This is a rare opportunity to study this transition in detail.

> “We’ve caught, for the first time, a star’s final nuclear heartbeat, frozen in gas.” - Raghvendra Sahai, NASA/JPL.

Their observations are in new research titled " The Last Gasps of a Dying Star: ALMA Observations of the Preplanetary Nebula IRAS 06530–0213 ." It's published in The Astrophysical Journal, and the lead author is Raghvendra Sahai, senior research scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

IRAS 06530–0213 is a preplanetary nebula (PPN) about 12,000 light years away. Astronomers have been watching it for years as it takes shape. They know that the preplanetary nebula phase is a critical evolutionary stage in a star's transition from the asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stage to the planetary nebula (PN) stage. PPN structures contain critical insights that aren't available in any other way.

"These data show the presence of an extended circular ring—first evidence of the last thermal pulse preceding the post-asymptotic giant branch (AGB) phase in a carbon star—and a central bipolar nebula (CBN) and torus," the authors write. The outer ring came from the last thermal pulse about 6500 years ago, and is the first direct evidence of this type of thermal pulse that's emitted before a star like this begins its final phase.

This snapshot is all about the mass-loss stars experience as they die, and the authors explain that the AGB progenitor's mass-loss rate "decreased immediately after the thermal pulse, then rose again just before the post-AGB phase."

The mass-loss dropped off for about 2,000 years, then for about 1,000 years after that, it rose again. The filamentary structures around around the CBN are evidence of the star emitting a thick and lumpy shell of gas. An hourglass-shaped nebula with a torus is inside the filamentary arc region.

This ALMA image of IRAS 06530 show the PPN's structure. The outer molecular ring is from its progenitor star's final thermal pulse. The CBN is the central bipolar nebula, and the FAR is the filamentary arc region. The FAR is evidence of the progenitor's mass loss rate dropping immediately after the thermal pulse, then rising again just before the star's post-AGB phase. Image Credit: ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO); Sahai et al. (2026)

Based on the expansion ages of the torus and the CBN, Sahai and his co-researchers determined that the progenitor star transitioned to a post-AGB star around only 700 yrs ago, maybe a little less than that. That is a remarkably short amount of time to have lapsed since its transition, considering stellar ages.

In 2003 it was first identified as a carbon-rich PPN, and its envelope expansion velocity was measured. Subsequent research identified its s-process enrichment, where elements heavier than iron are synthesized. Then in 2025, this paper identified the PPN's spherical halo and central barrel-shaped torus.

Luck might not describe these most recent observations, because those prior observations were the primer, but good fortune might. The kind of good fortune that finds its way to people who spend their lives watching stars.

“Most of us think of stars as unchanging points of light, but this is a real-time snapshot of a star’s death throes,” said lead author Sahai, author and co-author of more than 140 published papers. “It’s the brief, violent transition between a bloated red giant and a glowing planetary nebula, frozen mid-action.”

There is something puzzling in this PPN and its filamentary arc region that still needs an explanation. "The arc stuctures are likely part of a 3D Archimedean spiral structure generally attributed to the presence of a binary companion," the authors write.

This image shows the central region of IRAS 06530, showing filamentary arc structures with dashed green, cyan, and white arcs. These arcs are typical signatures of a binary companion, but the researchers didn't fine one. Image Credit: ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO); Sahai et al. (2026)

Dying stars with companions not only have spiral structures, but they're normally found inside compact dust disks. The disks are evidence of mass-transfer with a close binary companion. The mass-transfer is usually the cause of the hourglass-shapes. But the researchers didn't find a dusty disk, the usual signature of a companion.

"However, we do not find a compact continuum source at the location of IRAS 06530’s central star, such as that associated with the compact dusty disks typically found in disk-prominent post-AGB objects known to have binary companions," the researchers explain.

“Dying stars so often have hidden companions that reshape their ejected material into intricate, bipolar or multipolar forms instead of simple spheres,” said Sahai. “IRAS 06530 shows that the story is more complicated than the tidy explanation we’ve been using.”

IRAS 06530 also has a chemical composition that's challenging to understand. It's significantly enriched in 13 C, 17 O, and modestly enriched in 15 N.

"Compared with solar values, the torus of IRAS 06530 appears to be significantly (modestly) enriched in 13C and 17O (15N), as well—a pattern of rare-isotope enrichment inconsistent with standard nucleosynthesis models," the authors write.

¹³C and ¹⁷O are expected, but ¹⁵N isn't. It should be destroyed and depleted to solar levels. Again, a binary companion could be one explanation for this anomaly, and future observations might find one. It's also possible that atypical bursts of nuclear burning are responsible, but that's beyond the scope of this work.

Finding the first direct evidence of a dying star's thermal pulse, something indicated by theory, is the kind of progress astrophysicists hope to make.

items.title: Recent sinking of Russian vessels abroad shows the Russia-Ukraine war has officially gone global
items.subtitle: Ukraine has been executing a series of successful strikes against Russian assets around the world.
items.feedText: Ukrainian forces disabled a Russian cargo vessel off the coast of Finland, and sunk a Russian corvette, the Merkury, along with damaging another cargo vessel, in Libyan waters. These attacks, in the aftermath of Ukraine’s severe damage to the Kerch Strait Bridge in Russian-occupied Crimea, have created hope among Ukraine’s allies. The year 2026 hasn’t advanced Ukraine’s goal of ending the war. A stagnant battlefront, increased Russian aerial attacks and a recalcitrant American president have increased the burden…
items.body:
Ukraine has been executing a series of successful strikes against Russian assets around the world. Ukrainian forces [disabled a Russian cargo vessel](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/world/article-russian-cargo-ship-still-burning-off-finland-after-suspected-ukrainian/) off the coast of Finland, and [sunk a Russian corvette](https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/articles/zelenskyy-confirms-ukrainian-naval-drones-072900157.html), the Merkury, along with damaging another cargo vessel, in Libyan waters.

These attacks, in the aftermath of Ukraine’s severe damage to the [Kerch Strait Bridge](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/17/ukraine-strikes-critical-damage-russia-kerch-bridge-crimea) in Russian-occupied Crimea, have created hope among Ukraine’s allies.

The year 2026 hasn’t advanced Ukraine’s goal of ending the war. A [stagnant battlefront](https://hfu.org/current-situation-in-ukraine-2026/), [increased Russian aerial attacks](https://www.cnn.com/2026/08/09/europe/russia-ukraine-escalation-aerial-strikes-intl-vis) and a [recalcitrant American president](https://apnews.com/article/russia-ukraine-war-trump-putin-diesel-228ccf74b2848c1ff0ac23f038b37512) have increased the burdens on Ukraine’s government and its people.

Russia hasn’t had a good year either. More than [400,000 Russians have been killed in the war](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/09/russians-killed-ukraine-war-leaked-data) — and potentially [as many as 700,000](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/23/world/europe/russia-ukraine-war-deaths.html).

For Ukraine to have any chance of winning, it must increase the pressure on Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s government. Making Russian assets vulnerable globally is one way to do it.

## The international dimension

Since its outset, the Russia-Ukraine conflict has had an international dimension. Ukraine’s allies, both [prior to](https://www.war.gov/News/Releases/Release/Article/3066864/fact-sheet-on-us-security-assistance-to-ukraine/) and [after](https://www.cfr.org/articles/how-much-us-aid-going-ukraine) Russia’s full-fledged invasion in 2022, rushed supplies to Ukraine in its moment of need.

Providing aid to Ukraine [has continued](https://www.defensenews.com/global/europe/2026/09/25/trump-administration-obligates-307m-for-military-aid-to-ukraine/) for the past four years, [despite disruptions](https://www.nytimes.com/live/2025/02/28/us/trump-news) caused by United States President Donald Trump’s involvement in the negotiation process.

The supplies provided by Ukraine’s allies are critical to its success. While the fighting is conducted by the Ukrainian people and Ukraine has increased [domestic arms production](https://thedefensepost.com/2026/07/03/ukraine-arms-exports/), outside supplies are crucial in a number of areas — notably, [air defence](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/22/zelenskyy-urges-us-to-release-patriot-missiles).

Equally important is the economic aid Ukraine’s allies [have and continue](https://www.kielinstitut.de/media/news/ukraine-aid-eu-support-is-crucial-but-harder-to-access/) to provide the country. Given the size differential between Russia and Ukraine and how hard the war [has hit the Ukrainian economy](https://ces.org.ua/en/tracker-economy-during-the-war/), economic aid allows Ukraine to provide basic services to its citizens.

Initially, Russia did not court outside support to the same extent as Ukraine, as it believed it would achieve a [rapid victory](https://www.rferl.org/a/russia-invasion-ukraine-intelligence-putin/31748594.html) over its adversary. Once the reality of the conflict became clear, Russia turned to the international community for support.

That support has taken many forms. [Iran and North Korea](https://thesoufancenter.org/intelbrief-2024-october-24/) have been among Russia’s top supporters, providing drones and soldiers.

Other countries, most notably China, have provided an [economic lifeline](https://www.dw.com/en/china-russia-economy-trade-sanctions-iran-strait-of-hormuz-technology-oil/a-77193402) to Russia, allowing it access to their markets in an effort to stave off the worst impacts of the economic sanctions Ukraine’s allies have imposed on the Russians.

Countries in [Central Asia](https://jamestown.org/central-asia-and-russia-sanctions/) and the [Middle East](https://www.reuters.com/world/us-allies-press-uae-over-russia-trade-sanctions-2024-05-01/) have also served Russia as important intermediaries for acquiring sanctioned materials.

## Targeting support

In a conflict that is increasingly [defined by attrition](https://doi.org/10.1080/13518046.2026.2714478), it’s been necessary for both Ukraine and Russia to rally their allies. The demands of [industrialized warfare](https://doi.org/10.1017/CHO9781139021203) and the production of necessary armaments means neither country can produce what’s needed on their own.

Because both sides are receiving critical support in this industrialized conflict, the war has [reached an equilibrium](https://www.newsweek.com/map-shows-how-ukraine-war-shifted-since-putin-said-its-coming-to-an-end-12700169). In their current states, neither side is likely to achieve a decisive breakthrough to rapidly end the fighting.

For both Ukraine and Russia, that means targeting their adversary’s international allies is necessary to win the conflict.

The least risky form of targeting enemy support, and among the most important, is [by constructing narratives while delegitimizing those of your opponent](https://doi.org/10.1080/03932729.2024.2327492).

Ukraine has [focused on Russia’s aggression and its violation of international norms and laws](https://www.chathamhouse.org/2022/02/ukraine-debunking-russias-legal-justifications). The focus on international law is particularly important for Ukraine given Russian accusations that [the West has flouted international norms](https://theconversation.com/western-countries-demand-russia-follows-international-law-so-why-dont-they-182659) for decades; Russia uses western association with Ukraine to gain support in the Global South.

Russia has put forward [several narratives](https://doi.org/10.1177/17506352241264436) to justify the war, ranging from defending itself from NATO imperialist expansion to its factually questionable [claims of the Ukrainian state’s genocide against ethnic Russians in Ukraine](https://www.themoscowtimes.com/2025/12/08/russian-prosecutors-accuse-dozens-of-top-ukrainian-officials-of-genocide-in-donbas-a91368).

Russia had some early successes from these narratives, making political gains [in Africa](https://www.cfr.org/backgrounders/russias-growing-footprint-africa) and earning support among [far-right](https://icct.nl/publication/russia-and-far-right-insights-ten-european-countries) European parties.

…

items.body:
[Via Marcin Wichary](https://unsung.aresluna.org/ive-spent-years-on-it-years-on-a-box/), who writes:

> Designer Pablo Stanley created [a really fun interactive exploration](https://composer.pablostanley.com/) of what it takes to create a seemingly simple
> “composer” (industry’s jargon for a more sophisticated input field
> or things like it). [...]
> Also, I am burying the lede: it’s a really enjoyable and
> well-crafted experience — don’t miss the sound and music! — and this unique way of talking about interface details could be
> inspiring in and of itself.
> You can also watch the entire thing [as a video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8q0pwh98qmU) with Stanley
> narrating, but I personally liked the interactive version more.

At first I enjoyed this a lot. I got maybe a quarter of the way through it before I thought it was too long — and then poked around and figured out that I wasn’t even halfway done with it yet. At first, yes, it brings to life just how many details a designer might have to think about. But after a bit it’s just interminable neuroticism. I drew this conclusion before I looked up [where Stanley works](https://www.linkedin.com/in/pablostanley1/), which I would have won a bet on. I wound up skipping over half of it, which makes this a rare exception — I almost never link to anything on DF which I skipped through.

At the point where I began wondering if this whole thing was a prank of some sort, all I could think was: this is why platforms need a HIG; why the HIG needs to be thorough, thoughtful, and good; and why designers ought to follow the platform’s HIG. It takes humility to defer to a standard platform reference, and humility is what is lacking in much of modern UI design in general, and Stanley’s interactive essay in particular.

And is it really industry jargon to call these “composers”? It’s a text box. It needs some buttons. It ought to look good. Its functionality ought to be obvious. It shouldn’t be needlessly distracting. Get to work. Build that. Move on. If you call these “composers” you might be in a segment of the industry where the life of a *designer* is so abstract and proudly navel-gazing that you don’t just lose the forest for the trees, but you lose the trees for endless rumination about the texture of bark. Real designers stay focused on helping users get through a delightful forest.

[★](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2026/11/25/the-life-of-a-composer)

items.body:
# Statement: ICIJ battles to protect source behind Pornhub documents story - ICIJ

- Skip to content After Aylo, Pornhub's parent company, sought to restrain us from publishing a story based on court records, ICIJ prevailed. Now a federal judge has ordered us to explain why we shouldn't be forced to reveal our source. By ICIJ Image: Leon Neal/Getty Images November 25, 2026 An age-restriction warning screen on the Pornhub website. When the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists asked Pornhub about its handling of child sexual abuse material and other nonconsensual content, the company’s parent, Aylo, went to court to stop the story. ICIJ fought back, arguing that the Alabama federal court where Aylo sought a temporary restraining order lacked jurisdiction over it and that the requested injunction would constitute an unconstitutional prior restraint under the First Amendment. The court denied Aylo’s motion on Nov. 16, and ICIJ immediately published the story Aylo didn’t want readers to see . But a separate question remains: whether ICIJ will be required to identify to the judge a confidential source who provided court records used in its investigation. U.S. District Judge Annemarie Carney Axon directed ICIJ to explain why it should not be required to disclose the source’s identity privately to the court. The judge’s inquiry concerns a specific court record identifying victims of child sexual abuse, which was among a larger collection of records provided to ICIJ by its source. In its response, filed on Nov. 23, ICIJ argued that the court has no authority to force it to identify its confidential source and that doing so would violate important First Amendment protections for journalists. Leak to us
- Contact ICIJ
## Do you have a story about corruption, fraud, or abuse of power?

The court said its goal was to prevent further circulation of the victims’ identifying information. ICIJ shares that concern. It has committed not to publish, disseminate or share that document and has restricted access to it. ICIJ’s story did not disclose any identifying information of victims.

Aylo sought the restraining order after ICIJ reporter David Kenner approached the company for comment about the records he obtained. The documents, which were filed in a class action lawsuit against Aylo-related companies alleging they knowingly and unlawfully profited from child sexual abuse material, were supposed to have been sealed, but were inadvertently made publicly available on the court’s electronic records system, where they remained for eight months. ICIJ later obtained copies from a confidential source.

Those records then formed the basis of an ICIJ investigation revealing how Aylo’s profits were built in part on allowing “some of the most heinous material on the internet” to remain on its platforms despite warnings from victims and law enforcement.

That investigation is now at the center of a legal dispute that threatens a fundamental principle of press freedom: journalists must be able to protect confidential sources while investigating powerful interests and exposing wrongdoing.

### GIVE TO HELP US INVESTIGATE!

Sources often take substantial personal risks to reveal information in the public interest. If they do not feel confident their identities will be protected, they may never come forward.

At ICIJ, protecting sources is fundamental to our ability to investigate wrongdoing and hold powerful institutions to account. Even disclosure solely to a judge would compromise source confidentiality and could set a dangerous precedent for journalists everywhere.

For nearly three decades, ICIJ has investigated powerful interests around the world despite legal threats, the detention of journalists and other efforts to obstruct our work. Even unsuccessful legal challenges impose substantial costs on nonprofit newsrooms like ours, diverting resources from investigations the public depends on.

We will vigorously defend the confidentiality of our sources and the principles of press freedom at stake in this case. The public’s right to know depends on journalists being able to protect those who help them uncover the truth.

## GIVE TO HELP US INVESTIGATE!

items.title: How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom
items.subtitle: Data centers are fueling a natural-gas surge: Natural gas has essentially become America's default electricity solution to meet rising demand, incl…
items.feedText: Nearly half the capacity of new proposals in the country's largest grid came from gas plants. Big tech's emissions are climbing fast: Meta's greenhouse-gas emissions jumped 45% in a single year — outpacing Google, Amazon, and Microsoft — and the company is quietly reconsidering its 2030 net-zero commitment. Companies are building their own power plants: Unable to wait for grid connections, data center developers have proposed over 100 off-grid gas facilities since early 2025, with combined capacity more than dou…
items.body:
In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a [feature story](https://www.technologyreview.com/2025/05/20/1116272/ai-natural-gas-data-centers-energy-power-plants/) describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right.

Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including renewables like wind and solar supported by batteries. But the reality in the US so far is that the data center boom is helping to fuel a massive natural-gas resurgence.

Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on in his story have expanded, and its power needs have too. The local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to [10](https://www.eenews.net/articles/meta-plans-7-new-gas-plants-to-power-massive-louisiana-data-center/). And as I wrote in a new story this week, data center developers are now looking beyond the grid and planning to build their own [off-grid gas power plants](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11/24/1149622/data-centers-natural-gas/). How did we get here?

If you want to understand the future of the grid, one way to do it is by looking at interconnection queues—lists of power plants that have requested a connection to the system. In recent years these queues have been dominated by renewables like wind and solar power, which are generally the cheapest way to build new energy capacity today.

But there’s been a shift in some places, particularly for PJM, the country’s largest power grid operator, which covers parts of 13 states in an area stretching from Illinois to Washington, DC. PJM has seen a major uptick in natural-gas proposals. In August, the operator [announced](https://insidelines.pjm.com/over-700-new-generation-projects-accepted-into-first-cycle-of-reformed-interconnection-process/) that it had accepted proposals for 715 total projects with a capacity of over 200 gigawatts to join its queue. Nearly half that total capacity represented natural-gas plants.

If all the projects in the queue were built, it would increase the fossil-fuel share on PJM’s grid from 61% to 67%, according to an [analysis by Kevin Kircher](https://kevinjkircher.com/what-energy-infrastructure-are-people-trying-to-build/), an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue.

PJM’s queue is reflective of a bigger trend across the US. Natural gas is already the single biggest source of electricity in the country, and it has basically become the default to meet exploding power demand.

This AI-driven rush is already affecting greenhouse-gas emissions for tech companies. Meta’s emissions are up 45% over last year’s, according to the company’s recently released [2026 Sustainability Report](https://sustainability.atmeta.com/blog/2026/11/19/meta-launches-2026-sustainability-report/). That’s even higher than the jumps from fellow hyperscalers Google ([18%](https://www.axios.com/2026/06/30/google-ai-boom-emissions-power-use)), Amazon ([16%](https://techcrunch.com/2026/07/02/a-warning-sign-about-ais-real-cost-courtesy-of-google-and-amazon/)), and Microsoft ([25%](https://www.esgdive.com/news/microsofts-data-center-expansion-drove-25-emissions-spike-2025-environmental-sustainability-report/825082/)). The company is also “reevaluating” its 2030 goal to reach net-zero emissions, according to the report, though there aren’t details about how or when it might reach a decision there.

And there’s another tidbit in that Meta report worth noting: The company said that when the grid can’t deliver power “on the necessary timeline,” it will look to other methods, including building its own on-site power generation.

This fits into a related and growing trend that I’ve been tracking recently: Data center developers are looking to bypass long wait times to hook up to the grid by building their own power plants instead.

It’s not new for large industrial facilities to supply their own power. Chemical plants often have natural-gas infrastructure on-site to generate electricity and heat, for example (though they’re generally connected to the grid as well). Mining operations are often remote, requiring an off-grid power source.

But the desire to come online quickly means there could be a massive boom in off-grid power plants for data centers. Over 100 such facilities have been proposed in the US, with a total capacity of 115 gigawatts (that’s more than double the entire peak power demand of California). The vast majority of these sites have been proposed since the beginning of 2025.

There are alternative ways to help meet growing electricity demand: Wind and solar are inexpensive options, and pairing them with batteries could improve their reliability, for example. I’ve also written before about [demand flexibility](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/06/03/1138350/virtual-power-plants-data-centers/)—efforts to limit power drawn from the grid when demand is high.

Right now, though, the evidence continues to stack up that the AI boom in the US is basically synonymous with a natural-gas boom.

*This article is from The Spark,* MIT Technology Review *’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday,* *[sign up here](https://forms.technologyreview.com/newsletters/climate-energy-the-spark/).*

items.body:
# The Small But Mighty Brains of Bumblebees - Nautilus

## The Small But Mighty Brains of Bumblebees

Sometimes the best thinkers come in tiny packages

11:00 AM CST on November 25, 2026

Bright macro shoot of the bumblebee sitting on the colourful flower. High quality photo

As humans, we credit our large brains, which contain upward of 86 million neurons , for our intelligence. But our superiority complex has been gradually dampened as other tiny-brained species, such as bumblebees , prove able to rival us on at least some cognitive tasks. In a recent commentary published in Science , biologists reviewed the brain capabilities of bumblebees (genus Bombus ), asking, “What are the minimal neural requirements for intelligence itself?”

The study authors, biologists Lars Chittka at Queen Mary University of London and Stanley Heinze at Lund University in Sweden, reviewed the cognitive feats that bees have been able to accomplish—for example, rolling a ball to climb up and reach nectar in an enclosure too cramped for flying and learning to move latches to open puzzle boxes.

Read more: “ Bumblebees Bounce to the Beat ”

At the same time, bumblebee brains contain fewer than a million nerve cells, a pittance of circuitry compared to our great network. So, their intelligence—defined in this study as “the ability to adapt to new situations by using cognition rather than instinct or trial and error”—stems from something else. The researchers explored aspects of bee brain architecture that might explain not only their problem-solving skills but also their “emotional contagion,” whereby bees transmit optimism about an anticipated food reward to nestmates.

Bumblebee brains contain a “mushroom body,” a region where associative memories are made in special neurons called Kenyon cells. It’s found in some other invertebrates as well, but bees have the monopoly with about 50 times more than, for instance, a fruit fly, a difference that could explain bees’ superior memory capacity. The study authors noted that the mushroom body architecture looks like the hippocampus in mammals, the area responsible for memories and recall. Maybe, they hypothesized, the “increased complexity of the mushroom body in bumblebees could have led to the evolution of additional, hippocampus-like circuits that conduct advanced com­putations such as pattern completion.”

Compared to fruit fly brains, bumblebees also have extra neural wiring associated with navigation, explaining how their brains calculate the optimal routes between multiple food sources—like a built-in GPS system. Plus, bumblebees have a more elaborate neuromodulatory system, which likely allows them to more subtly distinguish “between similar but not identical situations that might otherwise evoke the same action.”

It remains to be determined whether these special brain features evolved as neural wiring customizations on a simpler insect brain or just gradual boosts in computational abilities.

Regardless, it’s hard not to consider bumblebees as big-brained—no matter how tiny their physical brains might be.

items.title: Liebe in Zeiten der Rackets
items.subtitle: Skrupelloses Machtstreben und grotesker US-Alltagswahnsinn bestimmen seit jeher die Welt von GTA.
items.feedText: In der langen Wartezeit auf den neuesten Teil hat die Wirklichkeit die Satire der Spiele in beiderlei Hinsicht längst eingeholt. GTA 6 reagiert darauf, indem es seiner zynischen Weltsicht eine Liebesgeschichte entgegensetzt.
items.body:
# Liebe in Zeiten der Rackets

## Liebe in Zeiten der Rackets

Skrupelloses Machtstreben und grotesker US-Alltagswahnsinn bestimmen seit jeher die Welt von GTA. In der langen Wartezeit auf den neuesten Teil hat die Wirklichkeit die Satire der Spiele in beiderlei Hinsicht längst eingeholt. GTA 6 reagiert darauf, indem es seiner zynischen Weltsicht eine Liebesgeschichte entgegensetzt.

„We got x before GTA 6“ – diese Formel hatte sich in den vergangenen Jahren als eines der populärsten Memes des Internets etabliert. Was auch immer sich an Unwahrscheinlichem in der Welt ereignete, es wurde zum nächsten Meilenstein des schier endlosen Wartens auf den neuesten Teil der erfolgreichen Videospielereihe. Wir hatten eine globale Pandemie vor Grand Theft Auto VI , zwei Trump-Präsidentschaften, Kriege in Europa und im Nahen Osten. Irgendwann schien es dann nur noch eine Frage der Zeit, bis auch der Dritte Weltkrieg oder die KI-Apokalypse auf dieser Liste landen würden: Würde die reale Welt untergehen, noch bevor wir endlich in die virtuelle flüchten durften? Wenn nicht, dann musste GTA 6 aber bitte schön mehr sein als ein Videospiel; es musste uns erlösen, zumindest vorübergehend, von den Zumutungen unserer polykrisengebeutelten Gegenwart.

Seit dem 19. November, 13 Jahre nach dem Erscheinen des Vorgängers, haben wir GTA 6; die Welt steht noch, und: Gemessen an den Verkaufsrekorden (erfolgreichster Verkaufsstart eines Unterhaltungsprodukts) und den euphorischen Kritiken (99 von 100 Punkten bei den Fachkritikern) wird das Spiel dem Hype tatsächlich gerecht. Die Memes und Schlagzeilen, die überlasteten Download-Server und auffällig vielen Krankmeldungen zum Release: Für ein langes Wochenende hat GTA 6 eine Erfahrung popkultureller Gleichzeitigkeit hergestellt, wie es sie in Zeiten algorithmisch fragmentierter Medienöffentlichkeiten kaum noch gibt. Und das Spiel selbst? Keine Revolution des Mediums, sehr wohl aber seine vorläufige Vollendung. Die Entwickler von Rockstar Games trumpfen mit einer Spielwelt von beispielloser Detailfülle und atmosphärischer Dichte auf, mit technischer Brillanz und einer Überfülle spielerischer Möglichkeiten. Allein die Open World – die künftig auch im Online-Modus spielbar sein dürfte – ist groß genug, um sich darin für die Dauer der nächsten ein, zwei Weltkrisen zu verlieren.

## Die Rackets sind los

Seit dem Debüt der Reihe 1997 folgt die Welt der GTA-Spiele einer Logik, die der Philosoph Max Horkheimer Anfang der 1940er-Jahre im US-Exil auf den Begriff des „Rackets“ brachte. Ursprünglich eine Slangbezeichnung für organisierte Kriminalität, insbesondere für Schutzgelderpressung, wurde der Begriff von Denkern der Frankfurter Schule auf die Herrschaftsverhältnisse der Gesellschaft im Allgemeinen übertragen. Horkheimer wollte damit den marxistischen Klassenbegriff erweitern: Der Kampf um Macht und Einfluss verläuft nicht ausschließlich entlang von Klassengrenzen, sondern auch zwischen bandenartig organisierten Interessengruppen, die Schutz und Privilegien gewähren gegen Loyalität und Gehorsam.

Bei GTA funktioniert alles nach diesem Racket-Prinzip: die zahlreichen Verbrecherbanden natürlich, aber auch Unternehmen, Polizei und Politik. Typisch für die Reihe ist außerdem, dass der Spieler selbst in die Rolle eines Racketeers schlüpft: Man beginnt meist als Kleinganove, knackt Autos oder treibt Schulden ein, erledigt die Drecksarbeit für immer mächtigere Gangsterbosse und arbeitet sich hoch in der kriminellen Hierarchie.

Das zweite Markenzeichen der Reihe ist ihre beißende Satire auf die amerikanische Gesellschaft: Die fiktiven Radiosender und grotesk überzeichneten Figuren nehmen Waffenwahn und Starkult, Pornografisierung und religiösen Fanatismus aufs Korn. Während der kriminelle Aufstieg in den frühen Spielen noch eher lustvoll zelebriert wurde, rechneten die späteren mit dem amerikanischen Traum ab.

Damit stand die Spielereihe zuletzt vor einem seit Trumps erstem Wahlsieg 2016 vielfach diagnostizierten Dilemma der politischen Satire: Die Wirklichkeit hat die Satire längst eingeholt. Bei GTA gilt das gleich in zweifacher Hinsicht: Nicht nur wirken die vulgären, moralisch enthemmten Charaktere angesichts der realen amerikanischen Politakteure und ihrer Entourage aus alternden Rockstars und exzentrischen Tech-Milliardären kaum noch überzeichnet. Auch die Racket-Logik hat sich längst in Washington breitgemacht, weshalb Horkheimers nie vollendeter Theorieansatz ausgerechnet seit Trumps Präsidentschaft wieder verstärkt Beachtung findet. Das Weiße Haus wird dieser Tage wie ein privates Firmenimperium geführt, in dem familiäre und geschäftliche Interessen, persönliche Loyalitäten und politischer Einfluss auf geradezu mafiöse Weise ineinandergreifen.

So boten die 13 Jahre seit dem letzten Teil unzählige Szenen jener GTA-haften Mischung aus Absurdität und Brutalität: den QAnon-Schamanen , der mit Büffelhörnern das Kapitol stürmte, Elon Musk, der auf der Bühne eine Kettensäge schwang, oder ICE-Beamte, die wie marodierende Banden durch die Straßen von Minneapolis zogen. Donald Trump selbst wirkt ohnehin wie aus einem GTA-Spiel entsprungen. Tatsächlich tauchte in gleich mehreren frühen Teilen mit dem skrupellosen Medien- und Immobilienmogul „Donald Love“ eine Trump-Karikatur auf.

## Liebe statt Satire

GTA 6 versucht nun nicht, die neue amerikanische Wirklichkeit durch immer schrillere Überzeichnungen zu überbieten. Ein Glück, denn es gibt heute kaum etwas Langweiligeres als Trump-Parodien. An satirischen Seitenhieben mangelt es freilich auch diesmal nicht – sie gelten nun auch der Influencer-Kultur und dem Kulturkampf –, doch sind sie ein Stück weit an die Peripherie gerückt.

Den erzählerischen Kern bildet diesmal eine überraschend einfühlsame Liebesgeschichte um Jason und Lucia, ein Ganovenpaar nach dem Vorbild von Bonnie und Clyde, das im fiktiven US-Bundesstaat Leonida nach einem missglückten Coup immer tiefer in eine weitgespannte Verschwörung gerät. Die beiden sind selbstverständlich keine Unschuldslämmer. Sie rauben, betrügen und töten, wie es sich für GTA-Protagonisten gehört, sind dabei jedoch immer wieder den Machenschaften mächtigerer Gangster ausgeliefert. Ihr eigentliches Ziel ist indes nicht der Aufstieg in der Unterwelt, sondern der Ausstieg daraus – ein Stück Normalität, familiäres Glück.

Das führt zu Missionen, wie man sie aus der Reihe bislang nicht kennt und die nicht bei allen Spielern auf Begeisterung stoßen. Während Lucia noch im Gefängnis sitzt, kann Jason das Haus auf Vordermann bringen, Blumen und Lebensmittel für ihre Rückkehr besorgen. Später gilt es, die Bewährungsauflagen einzuhalten, um das Sorgerecht für Lucias kleinen Sohn nicht zu gefährden, oder beim Versuch, ein gemeinsames Bankkonto zu eröffnen, nicht an der miserablen Bonität der beiden zu scheitern.

items.feedText:

Plus: 🎁 14 more stories you might like, 🧰 6 tools, and 📚 3 papers. Unlike OpenAI's earlier October 2 result, which set an upper bound of 2.25 over complex numbers, the new paper claims…
items.body:
### 🧮 OpenAI claims it solved a 1960s math problem

[↗ Primärquelle: unite.ai](https://www.unite.ai/openai-preprint-reports-9-4-bound-for-matrix-multiplication/)

- OpenAI researchers have published a preprint claiming to pin down the exact exponent for square matrix multiplication at 2.25, settling a question about how fast the operation can grow that has puzzled mathematicians since the 1960s.
- Unlike OpenAI's earlier October 2 result, which set an upper bound of 2.25 over complex numbers, the new paper claims matching upper and lower bounds over every field, counting the minimum arithmetic operations rather than measuring speed on real hardware.
- The November 24 paper comes with a Lean formalization, a machine-checkable proof framework, and a second paper on Euclidean geometry supplying the lower-bound method, though the claims still await review by the wider mathematical community.

### 🧠 Nvidia's Jensen Huang says he's in daily therapy

[↗ Primärquelle: thenextweb.com](https://thenextweb.com/news/jensen-huang-apology-nvidia-staff-therapy-shares-fall)

- Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told employees he is now spending more than an hour each day in therapy, speaking during an hour-long company-wide meeting on Tuesday, a day after returning to lead the chipmaker.
- Huang apologised for breaking Nvidia's code of conduct, which triggered his departure on November 12 after reports of several extramarital relationships, and said he had asked his wife and children for forgiveness.
- He insisted his reinstatement, announced on Monday, was entirely the board's decision, rejecting President Trump's public claim of personally lobbying for his return and denying it stemmed from his 'tech bro' standing.

### 🎵 Tidal to delete 29 million AI-generated songs

[↗ Primärquelle: thenextweb.com](https://thenextweb.com/news/tidal-delete-29-million-ai-generated-songs)

- TIDAL plans to wipe every fully AI-generated track from its catalogue starting December 9, pulling roughly 29 million songs, with the clean-up expected to finish by the start of 2027.
- Robert Andersen, who runs TIDAL at parent company Block, said the service will also block 80,000 to 85,000 AI-made tracks each day, acting after 43% of music sent to it over the past 90 days was detected as AI.
- TIDAL already labelled and cut royalties for AI tracks in July but found that wasn't enough, noting 96% of such songs get no plays; detection tools can mistag music, so users may ask support to fix a label.

### 🚨 Microsoft declared 'Code Red' after historic 24-hour outage

[↗ Primärquelle: siliconangle.com](https://siliconangle.com/2026/11/24/microsoft-declares-internal-code-red-after-nearly-24-hour-microsoft-365-outage/)

- Microsoft has declared an internal "Code Red," its top alert level, to rebuild how it handles major failures after a nearly 24-hour outage on Nov. 12 and 13 knocked out Exchange Online and other Microsoft 365 services.
- The outage hit Outlook, Teams and the Copilot assistant, disrupting governments, trading firms and airlines, and Microsoft blamed a July defect in its networking gateway servers that left more than 80% of them unresponsive at the worst moment.
- Microsoft now wants to resolve worldwide incidents within an hour using AI agents to diagnose problems, part of five workstreams including load shedding and geographic traffic partitioning, which experts warn could spread bad fixes just as fast.

### 🕵️ CIA data system hacked possibly by China

[↗ Primärquelle: gizmodo.com](https://gizmodo.com/u-s-spying-agencies-reportedly-hacked-2000845088)

- Hackers broke into an open-source intelligence system used by the CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, exposing some unclassified information, though officials said no classified data was affected.
- The breached system gathers and analyzes publicly available data from the internet, commercial satellites and private data brokers, which analysts combine with classified spying to draw insights the ODNI has invested in recently.
- Huntress's Ben Bernstein warned the breach still matters because an adversary seeing what analysts search for could reveal US intelligence priorities and blind spots, and such networks stay hard to secure since they must face the public internet.

### 🇪🇺 EU plans €50B fund for AI and quantum

[↗ Primärquelle: thenextweb.com](https://thenextweb.com/news/eu-50bn-sovereign-tech-equity-fund-ai-quantum)

- The European Commission has proposed a €50 billion Sovereign Tech Equity Fund that would buy direct stakes in European AI and quantum computing firms, aiming to cut the bloc's reliance on US and Chinese technology.
- Confirmed today, the fund would make bigger, riskier, and longer-term bets than existing EU schemes, with its legal basis sitting inside the Quantum Act presented the same day in Strasbourg.
- Tech chief Henna Virkkunen said the fund would back all technologies the EU deems critical, as Europe draws only about 5% of global venture capital and worries its best startups move abroad for funding.

# Konkurrenz für Fender & Co.? Japanische Traditionsmarke ab sofort in Deutschland verfügbar

## Bacchus Guitars jetzt bei Hyperactive, E-Gitarren und Bässe

## Japanische Gitarrenbaukunst kommt nach Deutschland

Bacchus Guitars

Bacchus Guitars ist ein japanischer Hersteller für E-Gitarren und E-Bässe. Die sorgfältig zusammengestellten Instrumente sind jetzt über Hyperactive Audiotechnik in Deutschland erhältlich.

## Bacchus Guitars: Jetzt bei Hyperactive erhältlich

Bacchus Guitars steht für die Kombination von japanischer Handwerkskunst und moderner Fertigung. Die Marke bietet Instrumente in verschiedenen Preisklassen vom Einsteiger-Bass bis zur handgefertigten Premium-Gitarre an. Hinter Bacchus steht der Traditionshersteller Deviser mit Sitz in Matsumoto in der Präfektur Nagano. Dessen Geschichte geht bis ins Jahr 1977 zurück, als der legendäre japanische Gitarrenbauer Yasuo Momose zusammen mit einem kleinen Team die Akustikgitarren-Marke Headway ins Leben rief.

Heute stellt Deviser unter verschiedenen Labels hochwertige Instrumente her, unter anderem im hauseigenen Custom Shop namens „Aska Workshop“, wo die Bacchus Handmade Series gefertigt wird.

Bacchus hat moderne Gitarren, darunter unter anderem S-Type- und T-Type-Modelle sowie J-Bässe und P-Bässe, im Portfolio. Der deutsche Vertrieb Hyperactive Audiotechnik hat die japanische Marke jetzt ins Programm aufgenommen. Neben Händlern können dort auch Privatkunden Instrumente kaufen.

## Preis und Verfügbarkeit

Japanische Instrumente genießen seit jeher einen guten Ruf! Die Instrumente von Bacchus sind also allemal einen Blick wert! Die Preise reichen von etwas über 300 Euro für Einsteigermodelle bis hin zu knappen 4.000 Euro für Modelle aus der Premiumlinie.

items.body:
# Diskussion um Kürzungen im EU-Haushalt: Keine Agrarsubventionen, kein Hunger

## Diskussion um Kürzungen im EU-Haushalt : Keine Agrarsubventionen, kein Hunger

Kommentar von

Die EU würde auch ohne Milliardenzahlungen für Landwirte genügend Lebensmittel produzieren. Das Geld sollte lieber für die Umwelt eingesetzt werden.

25.11.2026

17:51 Uhr

teilen

Diesen Artikel teilen

Maisernte in Österreich: Auch ohne Agrarsubventionen wäre die Selbstversorgung der EU laut einer Modellrechnung gesichert Foto: Daniel Scharinger/imago

B auernverbände verbreiten angesichts der Verhandlungen über das künftige EU-Budget Angst: Sie suggerieren, dass die Europäische Union sich ohne die bislang 54 Milliarden Euro Agrarsubventionen pro Jahr nicht mehr selbst mit genügend Lebensmitteln versorgen könnte. Doch das ist falsch.

Selbst wenn die EU sämtliche Landwirtschaftssubventionen streichen würde, produzierte sie immer noch etwas mehr Getreide, als sie selbst verbraucht. Der Selbstversorgungsgrad läge bei 104 Prozent. Das hat vor Kurzem eine vom Naturschutzbund in Auftrag gegebene Berechnung auf Grundlage des international etablierten Agrarmodells Capri gezeigt. Demnach wäre auch die Selbstversorgung etwa mit Obst und Gemüse sowie mit Fleisch kaum verändert. Der Weizenanbau würde sogar leicht zulegen.

Zwar müssten ohne staatliche Zuschüsse gerade einige oft kleinere Höfe aufgeben, die kaum Gewinn machen. Aber deren Land würde in der Regel nicht brachfallen, sondern von rentableren Betrieben übernommen werden. Dass es so kommen würde, legt die historische Entwicklung nahe: Obwohl die Zahl der Betriebe stark gesunken ist, bleibt die landwirtschaftlich genutzte Fläche in Deutschland ziemlich stabil .

taz debatte

Die taz ist eine unabhängige , linke und meinungsstarke Tageszeitung. In unseren Kommentaren, Essays und Debattentexten streiten wir seit der Gründung der taz im Jahr 1979 . Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.

Auch andere Studien zeigen: Niemand in der EU würde ohne Agrarsubventionen hungern. Die Importmengen würden sich ebenfalls kaum verändern. Die sozialen Auswirkungen der möglichen Hofschließungen wären gering, weil schon heute beispielsweise in Deutschland lediglich rund 1 Prozent der Beschäftigten in der Landwirtschaft arbeiten, von denen wiederum nur ein Teil betroffen wäre. Aufgeben müssten vor allem Nebenerwerbsbetriebe.

Subventionen für Landwirte lassen sich dadurch rechtfertigen, dass die Bauern zum Beispiel auf Bio umstellen oder ihre Tiere besser halten als vorgeschrieben. Leider hat die EU-Kommission in ihrem geplanten Budget genau für solche Maßnahmen – anders als für die ineffizienten Einkommenszuschüsse – keine Mindestwerte vorgesehen. Das sollte sie nachholen.

Jost Maurin Redakteur für Wirtschaft und Umwelt

items.body:
# Trump Is Desperate For a Ukraine Deal, but the Window Is Closing

## Trump Is Desperate For a Ukraine Deal, but the Window Is Closing

## He wants a profitable, Kremlin-friendly peace before the Democrats seize Congress.

### Trump’s Second Term

Ongoing reports and analysis

The clock is ticking. Sources in the White House say U.S. President Donald Trump wants a Ukraine peace deal by early January—before the Democrats, riding high after their stunning midterm election win this month, come sweeping in to take control of Congress. “The Americans are pushing hard and there’s some concern that it would need a great deal of Ukrainian concessions to get anywhere near a deal,” one European official told the Financial Times . “The Americans are in a hurry, Putin is in no hurry,” another said.

But wait—what’s the rush? Why exactly does Trump have to get a deal before the new Congress convenes? Surely he can find plenty of allies in the House and Senate who would be happy to support a just and equitable peace in Ukraine. After all, his goals are purely humanitarian; as he keeps telling us, he just wants to stop the killing.

The clock is ticking. Sources in the White House say U.S. President Donald Trump wants a Ukraine peace deal by early January—before the Democrats, riding high after their stunning midterm election win this month, come sweeping in to take control of Congress. “The Americans are pushing hard and there’s some concern that it would need a great deal of Ukrainian concessions to get anywhere near a deal,” one European official told the Financial Times . “The Americans are in a hurry, Putin is in no hurry,” another said.

But wait—what’s the rush? Why exactly does Trump have to get a deal before the new Congress convenes? Surely he can find plenty of allies in the House and Senate who would be happy to support a just and equitable peace in Ukraine. After all, his goals are purely humanitarian; as he keeps telling us, he just wants to stop the killing.

If saving lives were really his priority, there are plenty of things that Trump could have done by now to achieve that end. He could have increased humanitarian and financial aid to the Ukrainian government. Along with other weapons to bolster Kyiv’s defenses, he could have sent Patriot missiles to protect Ukrainian civilians from ballistic missile attacks, which Russia has been steadily ramping up in recent months. And, even more importantly, he could have pressured Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the war, rather than gutting sanctions passed by Congress and allowing Moscow to sell diesel fuel on global markets (which hasn’t helped U.S. consumers but has given Russia more funding for its war).

“The United States government is actually trying to get a very good deal for Russia,” as military historian Phillips O’Brien recently told a Ukrainian newspaper. “That’s its starting point.” He dismisses Trump’s professed humanitarian concern, arguing that Trump’s ideological affinity for Putin-style authoritarianism and persistent contempt for Kyiv are driving him to accommodate Russia’s interests while treating the Ukrainians as an afterthought.

The urgency with which Trump is pursuing this agenda also has a tangible financial component. He thinks that Russia is a potential gold mine, and he wants to wet his beak. The Kremlin understands this perfectly well, and the Russians have been working hard to service his expectations. Indeed, the list of potential business deals Moscow is offering Team Trump seems to be growing by the day. Putin has tasked Kirill Dmitriev, the head of Russia’s sovereign wealth fund, to pitch tempting proposals to Trump’s negotiating team, led by son-in-law Jared Kushner and real estate tycoon Steve Witkoff. The deals on offer include oil and gas investments and sales of aluminum and critical minerals; many of them would require the lifting of current Western sanctions before funding can flow, a huge incentive for Putin. Dmitriev has claimed that the total value of the projects under discussion amounts to $14 trillion—wildly fanciful but just what Trump wants to hear.

Trump and his cronies stand to benefit personally from these deals. A Texas financier named Gentry Beach, who has close ties to the Trump family, has already signed an agreement with Russian natural gas company Novatek. Dmitriev has suggested that Elon Musk’s Boring Co. could take part in a project for a tunnel underneath the Bering Strait ; it’s a nonsensical notion but demonstrates just how deftly the Kremlin knows how to cater to the Trump World mindset. Trump, of course, wants a cut of his own. In October, the New York Times reported that one of the multibillion-dollar oil deals under discussion with Russia would benefit Middle Eastern investors with links to Kushner and Witkoff. And these are only the projects that we know about.

Hence the need for speed. Trump is clearly hoping that a peace deal will continue to yield dividends to himself and his friends long after he leaves office. Said differently, the White House is holding a fire sale of U.S. foreign policy to the highest and most likely bidder, which in Trump’s eyes is Putin. In that sense, Trump’s Ukraine policy is merely an extension of his broader program of replacing the U.S. national interest with his own—what the Atlantic ’s Anne Applebaum has aptly called an “ empire of grift .”

A post on Trump’s Truth Social account on Nov. 19. Donald Trump/Truth Social

But first, he has to get a deal signed, and that is looking less likely by the day. The president’s much-ballyhooed trilateral summit in Shenzhen, which was supposed to make Trump look like a global titan, ended without any sort of palpable progress on the Ukrainian front. The terse final communique didn’t mention either Iran or Ukraine (although it did offer up a vague swipe at the International Criminal Court). Neither Chinese President Xi Jinping nor his vassal Putin seems to have regarded the war in Ukraine as worth mentioning.

That has left Trump, the man who repeatedly claimed that he’d stop the war within 24 hours of taking office, sounding increasingly desperate . On his way back from the summit in China, he assured European leaders that the Kremlin was keen on peace: “Putin wants to end the war. He wants the deal done. He is getting tired of this.” Shortly thereafter, Putin demonstrated his peace-loving credentials by raining missiles down on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s hometown, killing a 7-year-old boy and a 20-year-old paramedic and wounding 52.

items.title: Trump Officials Overstate Role in Drug-Death Decline
items.subtitle: Trump administration officials, and the president himself, have taken credit for a decline in fatal overdoses, citing a “sealed” or “secure” border…
items.feedText: But overdose deaths were already falling when Trump took office, and experts told us there’s little evidence his enforcement policies have been major drivers of that trend. items.body:
Trump administration officials, and the president himself, have taken credit for a decline in fatal overdoses, citing a “sealed” or “secure” border and actions against cartels, including airstrikes on alleged drug boats. But overdose deaths were already falling when Trump took office, and experts told us there’s little evidence his enforcement policies have been major drivers of that trend.

In some statements, the White House has also misleadingly referred to a 40% drop in overdose deaths “from the Biden-era peak” — without mentioning that more than half of the decline happened while Joe Biden was still president.

The release of the latest drug-death figures from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention this month, which showed fatal overdoses continuing to decline, prompted celebratory statements from the White House.

President Donald Trump’s immigration policies are “crushing the overdose crisis,” the White House said in a Nov. 16 [news release](https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/11/president-trumps-immigration-policies-are-saving-american-lives/), adding that “overdose deaths have now declined for 18 straight months under President Trump. After Democrats refused to secure the border and allowed cartels to flood American communities with poison, that pipeline is now being choked off.”

“It’s because of President Trump’s common-sense policies, like securing our borders, dismantling and eliminating narco-terrorist organizations, and employing primary and early prevention efforts within our communities that thousands of American lives are being saved each year,” Sara Carter, director of the White House’s Office of National Drug Control Policy, [said](https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/11/u-s-drug-overdose-deaths-decrease-for-18th-consecutive-month-under-trump-administration/) in a separate news release the same day.

Those statements echo how Trump himself has talked about the fentanyl crisis in recent months. In rallies and other appearances before and after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, he’s repeatedly talked about [reducing](https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-speech-political-rally-choctaw-oklahoma-october-1-2026/#144) the [flow](https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-speech-first-responder-rose-garden-lunch-october-15-2026/#38) of [drugs](https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-speech-rnc-midterm-convention-dallas-september-9-2026/#62) over the [southern border](https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-speech-political-rally-myrtle-beach-south-carolina-august-21-2026/#124) and [striking](https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-speech-new-military-shipyard-baltimore-october-6-2026/#60) [alleged](https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-speech-midterm-political-rally-san-antonio-texas-october-7-2026/#125) [drug](https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-speech-midterm-political-rally-sioux-city-iowa-october-22-2026/#152) [boats](https://youtu.be/FHE3DAJXsMM?t=1655) off the [coast](https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-remarks-bilat-xi-jinping-china-apec-shenzhen-november-19-2026/#10) of Latin America. At an Oct. 21 rally in South Carolina, for example, he [claimed](https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-speech-midterm-political-rally-pendleton-south-carolina-october-21-2026/#130) drugs coming across the border were “down 67 percent,” while military strikes on drug boats had nearly eliminated trafficking by sea.

“Each one of those boats will kill 5- to 10,000 people,” he said. “So you can’t feel that bad when you see those rockets go right through the middle of it.”

(We’ve written [before](https://www.factcheck.org/2026/06/trump-makes-unsupported-claims-about-drug-flows/) that his claims about how much he’s reduced the quantity of drugs flowing into the country are not supported by the available data, which measure only what authorities seize and not the total amount of drugs entering the U.S.)

Vice President JD Vance similarly linked declining overdose deaths to the administration’s border policies at a campaign rally in Maine in August.

“We helped keep drugs out of Maine communities,” he [said](https://youtu.be/nsf9hI56g8s?t=1827), citing the state’s declining overdose fatalities. “We sealed the border, and that’s what happened, my friends. And that’s why we did it.”

While fatal overdoses have indeed [declined](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nvss/vsrr/drug-overdose-data.htm) during Trump’s time in office, it’s a continuation of a trend that began in 2023. Experts are still debating the reasons for that decline. Better access to treatment, wider availability of overdose-reversal drugs, China’s moves to restrict fentanyl precursor chemicals during the Biden era and a depleted population of at-risk individuals are among the proposed explanations.

Drug-policy experts told us there’s little evidence that Trump’s border policies, boat strikes or other enforcement actions have had a major impact on U.S. overdose-death rates.

“The fall in overdose deaths started in 2023, and the greatest decline so far was in 2024,” [Katharine Harris](https://www.bakerinstitute.org/expert/katharine-neill-harris), a fellow in drug policy at Rice University’s Baker Institute for Public Policy, told us by email. “They have continued to decline while Trump has been in office, but the trend was already well underway.”

[Jonathan Caulkins](https://www.heinz.cmu.edu/faculty-research/profiles/caulkins-jonathanp), a professor and drug-policy expert at Carnegie Mellon University, said it’s not unusual for an administration to overstate its effectiveness on this issue.

“Essentially every presidential administration, at least since the creation of the Office of National Drug Control Policy [in 1988], has spun news on the drug front to claim credit and say we’re wonderful,” he said.

## Drug Death Drop Started Under Biden

Overdose deaths skyrocketed in the U.S. over the past several decades, as successive waves of the opioid crisis — first prescription painkillers, then heroin and later fentanyl — took hold.

The crisis became especially deadly once fentanyl, a highly potent synthetic opioid, began to supplant heroin in the U.S. in the 2010s. According to CDC data, drug deaths [rose](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nvss/vsrr/drug-overdose-data.htm) from around 53,000 in 2015 to more than 112,000 in the 12 months ending in August 2023. Most of those deaths were linked to opioids.

items.body:
Conversations about NASA were the norm around the dinner table during Ashley Knight’s childhood. Her parents worked at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, and discussions about happenings at the agency continued even when they came home from the office.

“I remember a poignant dialogue we had after the space shuttle Challenger disaster,” Knight recalled. “However, we talked just as much about the engaging work my parents were doing inside Goddard’s gates.”

Her father Lyle Knight was a mechanical engineer, while her mother Julia Knight worked the bulk of her career in human resources. They brought their daughter on center for Take Your Child to Work Day and other events, and over time she became hooked.

“I saw the chambers where spacecraft and instruments were being tested, as well as other facilities used to help further space exploration. Above all, I witnessed the passion and collaborative spirit everyone had at Goddard,” Knight said. “As a child, I found it incredibly fascinating.”

Ashley Knight (right) on a visit to NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md., while her parents were employees.

Photo courtesy of Ashley Knight

It all came full circle in late August when, after growing up around NASA and later working several contractor roles for the agency, Knight and a number of her colleagues in the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer were sworn in as federal employees as part of a workforce directive to strengthen the agency’s technical core competencies by bringing mission-critical positions into the civil service.

She began her Goddard career more than two decades ago following graduation from the University of Maryland in nearby College Park. As the job search began after commencement, one organization inevitably stood out, along with one particular mission.

When she came across a contractor job opening at Goddard in support of the Hubble Space Telescope team, Knight jumped at the opportunity.

“Hubble was doing amazing things, and I always admired how they fixed the faulty mirror,” she said, referring to how astronauts and team members corrected an early spherical aberration during the observatory’s first servicing mission. “It was exciting to become involved with such a flagship mission, especially coming right out of college.”

As a project support analyst, Knight assisted engineers with test plans, data gathering, and hardware procurement for Hubble’s fifth and final shuttle servicing mission.

Knight stands in front of space shuttle Atlantis, which was used for the Hubble Space Telescope’s fifth and final shuttle servicing mission, while she was a project support analyst for the Hubble team.

Photo courtesy of Ashley Knight

Following the mission’s completion in 2009 and subsequent end of the Hubble shuttle servicing era, she took on a similar role with the Robotic Refueling Mission in what was then the Satellite Servicing Capabilities Office at Goddard – now known as NASA’s In-Space Servicing, Assembly, and Manufacturing Capabilities Office.

Knight left Goddard momentarily afterward to perform contracting work in support of the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory in Washington. After a phone call, she found her way back as a contractor program analyst in the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer, helping manage labor budgets within programs by avoiding funding lapses and ensuring employees received their paychecks on time.

Following the August ceremony, Knight now carries the title of budget analyst in the Program Analysis Office within the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer, performing many of the same critical duties as a civil servant.

“While many functions are similar, transitioning into the civil service makes it easier for my colleagues and I to help keep NASA’s missions going from the financial aspect,” said Knight. “We have more autonomy to perform certain government-related tasks by being on the government side.”

The civil service also provides additional training and growth opportunities for such positions.

“Ashley is a great team player. This conversion is a fantastic milestone because it unlocks new avenues for her learning and development, and allows us to integrate her into new roles,” said Linnette Morales, Knight’s supervisor in the Program Analysis Office. “I am thrilled she can now fully access the opportunities on the civil servant side, immensely benefiting both her continued career growth and our organization.”

The workforce directive, entitled “Restoring NASA’s Core Competencies” and announced by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman in February, is part of a broader effort to expand the agency’s critical institutional knowledge, increase resources essential for mission success, and maintain U.S. leadership in space exploration.

“The directive has given our office an opportunity to rebalance positions across the organization and remove limitations that were applied to those who were previously not government employees,” said Lisa Kelleher, Goddard’s chief financial officer. “We are now better able to insource many of our experienced contractor staff, allowing us to build up our in-house core competencies in areas such as budget analysis and accounting, and in turn increase our support for mission success.”

For Knight, she sees an increasing importance for her organization and hopes to make impactful contributions, especially as work taking place at Goddard helps NASA return a crewed mission to the lunar surface, build a Moon Base, and eventually send humans to Mars.

“We’re the go-between between NASA Headquarters and Goddard programs, and it’s our job to make it a seamless transition for projects to use money they’ve been given to help get these projects off the ground,” she said. “It’s both vital and exciting with the lunar and Mars endeavors, and I’m proud to play whatever role I can.”

Decades after first following her parents around center, and now following in their footsteps as a NASA civil servant, Knight is as captivated by Goddard and its people as she was during her early visits.

“Through the years, I’ve noticed everyone remains driven by teamwork and achieving the mission,” she said. “Everybody wants to succeed together by working toward the same goal, and I’m grateful I can continue to be part of it all.”

# Kosmisches Pech für einen Stern – was passiert, wenn er ein Schwarzes Loch verschluckt?

## MIT-Studie: Können atomgroße Schwarze Löcher ganze Sterne von innen zerstören?

Der Großteil aller Materie im Kosmos bleibt für Teleskope dunkel und gibt der Physik seit Jahrzehnten Rätsel auf. Nun zeigen Berechnungen aus den USA, wie sich versteckte Überreste aus der Frühzeit des Alls doch noch aufspüren lassen.

Kosmisches Pech: Stern schluckt Schwarzes Loch... (Bild: Shutterstock/muratart)

Forscher:innen um den Physiker Ore Gottlieb vom Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge haben dieses Szenario durchgerechnet. Atomgroße Schwarze Löcher könnten demnach Sterne von innen zerstören, wie in einer im Fachjournal „The Astrophysical Journal“ veröffentlichten Studie zu lesen ist.

Gemeint sind sogenannte primordiale Schwarze Löcher, die theoretisch im ersten Sekundenbruchteil nach dem Urknall aus dichter Materie entstanden sein könnten. Anders als frühe große Schwarze Löcher im jungen Kosmos wären solche hypothetischen Objekte höchstens so groß wie ein einzelnes Atom, aber so schwer wie ein Asteroid.

Noch leichtere Exemplare hätten sich über Jahrmilliarden durch quantenmechanische Teilchenabstrahlung, die sogenannte Hawking-Strahlung, längst vollständig aufgelöst. Zwischen 100 Milliarden und 100 Billiarden Tonnen Masse bleibt dagegen eine Beobachtungslücke, in der solche Objekte die Dunkle Materie bilden könnten.

## Schwerkraft von Planeten lenkt kleine Schwarze Löcher in fremde Sterne

Trifft ein solches Mini-Schwarzes-Loch im Alleingang auf einen Stern, bremst das dichte Sterngas den Eindringling wegen seiner geringen Masse kaum ab. Das Objekt durchquert den Stern einmalig mit hoher Geschwindigkeit und fliegt anschließend weiter durch den freien Weltraum .

A discovery inside a pr…
items.body:
Did a real news station from Branson, Missouri report that a plane missing for 13 years had been discovered in an unexplored cave in the Ozark Mountains? No, that's not true: "Branson Area Breaking News" is not a real news station, but a Facebook page published with a Satire/Parody disclaimer in the bio. The SynthID Detector hosted by Google determined that the image of the plane in the cave was made or edited with OpenAI.

The claim appeared in [a post](https://x.com/SmolfSmolf7/status/2125376066508505163) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261125151937/https://x.com/SmolfSmolf7/status/2125376066508505163) ) by the account @SmolfSmolf7 on X on Nov. 24, 2026. The caption began:

> Plane That Vanished 13 Years Ago Discovered Deep Beneath Ozark Mountains, but 212 People Remain Missing

> A discovery inside a previously unexplored cave near Branson has reopened one of Missouri's most baffling aviation mysteries after explorers located a commercial passenger jet that disappeared without a trace 13 years ago.

This is how the image in the post appeared at the time of publication:

*(Image source: post by @SmolfSmolf7 on X.)*

The caption continued:

> The aircraft, which vanished in 2013 with 212 passengers and crew members aboard, was discovered sitting almost completely intact inside an enormous underground chamber. Despite years of searching, no wreckage or evidence of the missing flight had ever been recovered.
> Explorers initially spotted the aircraft's tail protruding from the darkness before realizing an entire passenger jet was resting on the rocky cave floor.
> Investigators entering the aircraft reportedly discovered luggage still packed inside overhead compartments, personal belongings scattered throughout the cabin, and passenger seats largely undisturbed. However, there was no sign of the 212 people who had been aboard.
> Even more puzzling, the cave's known entrances are far too small to accommodate an aircraft of that size. Investigators have yet to determine how the jet could have reached the underground chamber without sustaining catastrophic damage.
> The discovery has raised new questions about what happened during the flight's final moments and where its passengers may have gone.
> Authorities are now examining the surrounding cave system for additional evidence, including several unexplored tunnels extending deeper beneath the Ozark Mountains.
> For families who have spent 13 years waiting for answers, the discovery has brought renewed hope, but the greatest mystery remains unsolved.
> The airplane has finally been found. The 212 people aboard have not.

A text caption on the image, in the style of a news chyron, reads:

> BRANSON AREA BREAKING NEWS
> MISSING JET WITH 212 PEOPLE FOUND INSIDE OZARK CAVE

The image appears to be AI-generated. Lead Stories uploaded the image to the SynthID Detector hosted by Google (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261125154251/https://synthid.com/image-detection) ). The tool found a SynthID watermark, invisible to the human eye, which came from an OpenAI tool (pictured below). The detection results read:

> SynthID was detected
> This media was made or edited with OpenAI
> Please note that this media may have been edited further since then.

*(Image source: SynthID.)*

The story originated from the Satire/Parody Facebook page [Branson Area Breaking News](https://www.facebook.com/profile.php?id=100069951171618) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261125152204/https://www.facebook.com/people/Branson-Area-Breaking-News/100069951171618/) ). The Intro reads:

> We are a world renowned satirical news organization & have received many awards for our breaking news stories! ***All content on our page is original***

The story about the plane found in a cave was [posted](https://www.facebook.com/100069951171618/posts/plane-that-vanished-13-years-ago-discovered-deep-beneath-ozark-mountains-but-212/1459956503012708/) on Nov. 23, 2026 (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261125152426/https://www.facebook.com/100069951171618/posts/plane-that-vanished-13-years-ago-discovered-deep-beneath-ozark-mountains-but-212/1459956503012708/) ).

items.subtitle: A review of the US president's financial disclosures shows Donald Trump's investment portfolios have regularly traded shares in the tech giant.
items.feedText: Image source, Reuters By Thomas Copeland and Alison Benjamin , BBC Verify Published 1 hour ago Donald Trump's investment portfolios have bought or sold shares in chipmaker Nvidia at least 44 times this year, a review of the US president's financial disclosures shows. Trump's most recent public declarations of his investment trading show that between January and September the portfolios purchased between $5.2m and $17m (£4m and £13m) in Nvidia stock - and sold between $4.4m and $12m. items.body:
# Trump’s accounts traded Nvidia shares 44 times this year, records show

Image source, Reuters By Thomas Copeland and Alison Benjamin , BBC Verify Published 1 hour ago Donald Trump's investment portfolios have bought or sold shares in chipmaker Nvidia at least 44 times this year, a review of the US president's financial disclosures shows.

Trump's most recent public declarations of his investment trading show that between January and September the portfolios purchased between $5.2m and $17m (£4m and £13m) in Nvidia stock - and sold between $4.4m and $12m. His portfolios held between $12.5m and $58m of Nvidia shares at the end of 2025.

Financial disclosures to the Office of Government Ethics report a low and high range of transaction values, so a more precise analysis of how much Nvidia stock was traded is not possible.

The period of recent turmoil at Nvidia and volatility in its share price is not covered by the disclosures. In the last two weeks, co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang resigned and then Trump played a significant part in his reinstatement.

The White House has said that Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third parties and neither he nor his family "has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold".

Huang resigned on 12 November after reports of extramarital affairs, including with one woman who has alleged ties to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia's share price dived following news of his resignation.

But on Monday Nvidia's board announced the 63-year-old was being reinstated as CEO.

Trump told US media he had "made the deal" to "convince" the tech giant's board to bring Huang back. The board said it had "received input from senior levels of the United States government" that he posed "no national security risk".

Nvidia's share price surged 31% on Monday following Huang's return. About $1tn (£763bn) was added to Nvidia's market value, but the company's shares are still trading below their value before reports of Huang's alleged affairs began to circulate.

However, concerns remain among both Republican and Democratic politicians about Huang's actions and Nvidia's compliance with US controls over the export of advanced computer chips to China, as well as Trump's involvement in getting him reappointed as CEO.

Image source, Getty Images Nvidia's chip technology and investments have been critical to the growth of the artificial intelligence (AI) industry , leading to it becoming one of the world's most valuable companies.

The firm now represents more than 6% of the S&P 500 share index, according to State Street financial services. This makes it the second most valuable company on the index after Apple, whose shares Trump's accounts also frequently trade.

Nvidia also ranks highly in many global indices, meaning that investment accounts held around the world, including pensions, are likely to include its shares.

Our analysis of Trump's Nvidia trades does not include other investment products held by him which may include its shares.

Trump made at least $2.2bn (£1.7bn) from a variety of investments and commercial activities, according to the financial disclosure report for the first year of Trump's second term.

Barbara Perry, a presidential historian at the University of Virginia's Miller Center, told the BBC there is "no precedent for this," adding: "It's beyond anything we've ever seen in the presidency."

Additional reporting Becky Dale
