## Das XEN FX Delay auf dem iPad

Anfang November ist das Liquid Sky d-vices Zen FX Lab als Plugin erschienen. Dabei handelt es sich um den Nachfolger der Zen Delay Software. Jetzt hat sich Liquid Sky d-vices dazu entschieden, das Effekt Plugin auch für das iPad herauszubringen.

## Gibt es Unterschiede zwischen der iPad Version und der PC-Version?

Die Funktionen unterscheiden sich nicht von der Plugin-Version. Allerdings lässt sich das Zen FX Lab jetzt über den Touchscreen des iPads bedienen und als AUv3 Plugin in iPad DAWs einbinden.

## Preis und Verfügbarkeit für die iPad Version

**Zum Einführungspreis ist Zen FX Lab für 9,99 Euro im [Apple App Store](https://apps.apple.com/de/app/xen-fx-lab/id6815805463)erhältlich. Nach der Einführungsphase wird der Preis auf 17,99 Euro steigen.**

## Das XEN FX Delay

Xen FX Lab ist die überarbeitete Version des Zen Delay Virtual und dieses basiert auf dem Zen Delay. Das Plugin kombiniert Delay, Filter und Spring Reverb mit umfangreichen Modulationsmöglichkeiten und richtet sich an alle, die mehr als klassische Echoeffekte suchen. Die neue Version bringt zusätzliche Funktionen und eröffnet Möglichkeiten für ungewöhnliches und kreatives Sounddesign.

Im Folgenden konzentriere ich mich auf die Neuerungen von XEN FX DELAY. Wer über genauere Details informiert werden möchte, kann sich folgende Tests durchlesen:

[Hier geht es zum Test des Zen Delay Virtual](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/erica-synths-zen-delay-virtual-test/)

[Hier geht es zum Test der Zen Delay Hardware.](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/ninja-tune-zen-delay-test/)

## Was kann das XEN FX DELAY?

Die Umbenennung in Xen FX Lab war ein guter Schritt. Denn bei diesem Plugin handelt es sich um weit mehr als ein einfaches Delay. Es ist eine richtig fette Sounddesign Maschine, mit der man wirklich ungewöhnliche klangliche Ergebnisse erzielen kann, die weit über das hinausgehen, was ein reguläres Delay schafft. Dabei helfen die unglaublichen vielfältigen Modulationsmöglichkeiten für das Delay, das Filter und das neu hinzugekommene Spring Reverb.

## Die Neuerungen: Das Hauptmenü

Auffällig ist das UFO Logo in der Mitte der Software, an dessen Stelle sich früher die Röhre befand. Links und rechts davon finden sich nun zwei Slider, mit denen sich die verschiedenen Delay-Zeiten und Filtertypen einstellen lassen.

Ansonsten hat sich am Layout nicht viel geändert. Links befindet sich wie gewohnt die Einstellung für das Delay. Rechts sind die Filter und Drive Sektion sowie ein Regler zur Anpassung des Eingangssignals untergebracht.

Xen FX Lab Hauptmenü Bildquelle: Liquid Sky D-vices )

## Das Spring Reverb

Neu ist das Spring Reverb, das über einen ausgeprägt metallischen Charakter verfügt. Für die Klanggestaltung stehen die Parameter Mix, Tension, Tone, Decay und Regen zur Verfügung. Damit lassen sich typische Spring-Reverb-Effekte erzeugen, aber auch extreme Klangwelten erschaffen. Manchmal klingt es so, als befände man sich in einem riesigen Tanklaster oder in einem ausgehöhlten Todesstern aus Star Wars. Einfach verrückt.

Xen FX Lab Presets (Bildquelle: Liquid Sky D-vices )

## Die Dub Funktion

Besonders interessant ist die neue Dub Funktion. Mit einem Knopfdruck lassen sich die Delay, Filter und Spring Reverb Effekte ein und ausschalten. So kann man dem trockenen Signal gezielt zusätzliche Effekte hinzufügen. Jeder Parameter von Xen FX Lab lässt sich automatisieren. Auch die Dub Funktion kann automatisiert und per MIDI angesteuert werden. Dadurch lassen sich Delays taktgenau und punktuell zum trockenen Signal hinzumischen.

Xen FX Lab Modulationsmatrix ist schon Teil des Zen Delay Virtual (Bildquelle: Liquid Sky D-vices )

## Die neue MIDI-Zuweisung

Neu ist das MIDI-DIN Anschluss Symbol. Wird die MIDI-Zuweisung aktiviert legt sich eine Maske über die Bedienelemente des Plugins, mit der man MIDI-CC Befehle zuweisen kann. Dadurch kann man Xen FX Lab schnell und einfach einem externen MIDI-Controller zuweisen.

Xen FX Lab MIDI-CC Zuweisung (Bildquelle: Liquid Sky D-vices )

## Die Geschichte des XEN FX LAB

2019 veröffentlichten Ninja Tune, Liquid Sky D-vices und Erica Synths gemeinsam das Desktop Effektgerät Zen Delay. Dabei handelt es sich um ein digitales Delay, einen analogen Filter und eine Röhre, mit der sich warme Verzerrungen erzeugen lassen.

2023 veröffentlichte das Team die Software Zen Delay Virtual, die auf Basis des Desktop Modells entwickelt wurde. Unter dem Namen Xen FX Lab erscheint jetzt eine neue Version des Plugins, die ausschließlich unter der Marke Liquid Sky D-vices veröffentlicht wird und mit vielen neuen Funktionen ausgestattet ist.

## Wer hat das XEN FX LAB Entwickelt?

Xen FX Lab wurde von Coldcut Mastermind Matt Black, Dr. Walker von Air Liquide und Benjamin Weiß (TokTok), entwickelt.

**Ninja Tune und Erica Synths sind an der Entwicklung des Plugins nicht mehr beteiligt. Für Support und weitere Fragen zum Plugin wendet ihr euch daher direkt an [Liquid Sky D-vices.](https://liquidskyeurope.com/products/xen_fx_lab)**

## Preis und Verfügbarkeit für die PC Version

**Xen FX Lab ist ab sofort für 25.00 Euro erhältich.**

**Besitzer der ersten Version erhalten ein kostenloses Upgrade. Wenn ihr bei der Plugin Boutique eingekauft habt, erhaltet ihr dort ein kostenloses Update.**

**Thomann Kunden müssen sich unter HQs@liquidskyartistcollective.com mit dem Betreff “Zen Delay Virtual Update” melden. Für das kostenlose Update wird ausserdem die ilok Nummer von Thomann benötigt, um es schnell und unkompliziert durchführen zu können.**

**Zum Einführungspreis ist Zen FX Lab für das iPad für 9,99 Euro im [Apple App Store](https://apps.apple.com/de/app/xen-fx-lab/id6815805463)erhältlich. Nach der Einführungsphase wird der Preis auf 17,99 Euro steigen.**

## Links

September den befürchteten Durchbruch der AfD bedeutete, 1 steht am 8. Dezember der nächste Schritt der rechten Landnahme bevor. Aller Voraussicht nach wird dann Ulrich Siegmund zum ersten rechtsextremen Ministerpräsidenten seit 1945 gewählt, entweder dank der Unterstützung des BSW, das sich bereits mit der Wahl des AfD-Landtagspräsidenten Tobias Rausch zum Steigbügelhalter der Rechtsextremen entwickelt hat, oder mithilfe von Überläufern der CDU oder schließlich notfalls auch durch einfache Mehrheit im dritten Wahlgang. Damit wäre die AfD in der Lage, aus dem bisher nur Sagbaren das Machbare zu machen. items.body:
# Siegmund vor dem Sieg: Wie aus dem Sagbaren das Machbare wird | Blätter für deutsche und internationale Politik

Nachdem die Landtagswahl in Sachsen-Anhalt am 6. September den befürchteten Durchbruch der AfD bedeutete, 1 steht am 8. Dezember der nächste Schritt der rechten Landnahme bevor. Aller Voraussicht nach wird dann Ulrich Siegmund zum ersten rechtsextremen Ministerpräsidenten seit 1945 gewählt, entweder dank der Unterstützung des BSW, das sich bereits mit der Wahl des AfD-Landtagspräsidenten Tobias Rausch zum Steigbügelhalter der Rechtsextremen entwickelt hat, oder mithilfe von Überläufern der CDU oder schließlich notfalls auch durch einfache Mehrheit im dritten Wahlgang.

Damit wäre die AfD in der Lage, aus dem bisher nur Sagbaren das Machbare zu machen. Tatsächlich ist das Regierungsprogramm der sachsen-anhaltischen AfD das radikalste, das die Partei bisher vorgelegt hat. 2 Und längst gehen die Pläne der Partei über den Sieg in einzelnen Bundesländern hinaus und richten sich angesichts von Umfragewerten von bald 30 Prozent auf die nächste Bundestagswahl.

Insofern weckt ein Ministerpräsident Siegmund, ohne die AfD mit der NSDAP gleichsetzen zu wollen, unweigerlich Erinnerungen an das Jahr 1930 und die erste Regierungsbeteiligung der Nationalsozialisten in Thüringen, der nur drei Jahre später die Machtübertragung an Adolf Hitler durch die Konservativen folgte.

Dieser Artikel stammt aus der Ausgabe Dezember 2026. Klicken Sie hier, um zur Inhaltsübersicht dieser Ausgabe zu gelangen.

Gewiss, politisch sind der AfD auf Landesebene Grenzen gesetzt. Doch auf gesellschaftlicher Ebene ist die Gefahr bereits jetzt weitaus größer. Dort droht eine noch umfassendere rechte Hegemonie als die bisher schon in weiten Teilen des Ostens herrschende. Denn im Schatten der AfD treiben längst noch radikalere Organisationen ihr Unwesen, Freie Kameradschaften und Autonome Nationalisten, aber auch explizit verfassungsfeindliche Parteien wie der Dritte Weg, die Freien Sachsen oder Die Heimat, die Nachfolgepartei der NPD. Sie dürfen nur deshalb weiter frei agieren, weil das Bundesverfassungsgericht in seiner durchaus problematischen NPD-Entscheidung von 2017 derartigen Parteien einen Persilschein ausstellt, solange ihnen die »Potenzialität« fehlt, mit ihrem Handeln gegen die parlamentarische Demokratie wirklich Erfolg zu haben. Über ihre gesellschaftlich zerstörerische Wirkung sagt das allerdings wenig aus. Eine AfD-Ministerpräsidentschaft in Sachsen-Anhalt dürfte jedenfalls, indem sie dem Rechtsextremismus höchste staatliche Weihen verleiht, die ohnehin vorhandene gesellschaftliche Verrohung enorm verstärken.

Dass diese seit dem 6. September absehbare Zäsur bisher nicht annähernd die Beachtung gefunden hat, die sie verdient, ist vor allem dem Umstand geschuldet, dass die mediale Aufmerksamkeit der vergangenen Wochen weit mehr auf die Ereignisse in der Hauptstadt und die mögliche Bildung einer Koalition unter Führung der Linkspartei gerichtet war als auf die kommende Machtübernahme der AfD. Tatsächlich haben die noch am Abend der Berlin-Wahl drastisch sichtbar gewordenen Kontakte zu organisierter Kriminalität und Israel-Hassern im Umfeld der Neuköllner Linkspartei dieser fatalen Ablenkung erheblich Vorschub geleistet – und zu einer enormen Dämonisierung der Linken wie auch speziell ihrer Spitzenkandidatin und potenziellen zukünftigen Regierenden Bürgermeisterin Elif Eralp geführt 3 , aber zugleich auch zu einer enormen Verharmlosung der AfD. Indem seither nur noch vom Extremismus der Ränder die Rede ist, wurde die in konservativen Kreisen geschätzte Hufeisentheorie reaktiviert, die die politische Nähe der Ränder und die daraus resultierende gleiche Gefährlichkeit postuliert.

> Mit der Rede von der ›demokratischen Mitte‹ wird die Hufeisentheorie quasi zur Staatsdoktrin.

Dieses These hat durch die Nominierung von Ilse Aigner zur zukünftigen Bundespräsidentin massive Verstärkung erfahren. Dabei ist nicht die Personalie Aigner das Problem – nach zwölf Bundespräsidenten ist eine Frau im höchsten Staatsamt mehr als überfällig, und wenn die (ober)bayerische Noch-Landtagspräsidentin ihre konsequente Linie gegenüber der AfD fortsetzt, könnte sie eine entschieden demokratische, aber zugleich mit ihrer bodenständigen Art durchaus auch das Land einigende Kraft sein.

Das Problem ist vielmehr die Begründung der Kandidatur. Indem Markus Söder und (wieder einmal hinterhereilend) Friedrich Merz Aigner dezidiert als die Kandidatin der »demokratischen Mitte« ausriefen , etabliert sich das Bild der gleichen Radikalität der Ränder. Damit wird die Hufeisentheorie quasi zur Staatsdoktrin. »Wird Ilse Aigners Bundespräsidentschaft eine Kampfansage an die Ränder?«, fragte denn auch prompt »Die Zeit« und gab sich gleich selbst die Antwort: »Die ersten Signale der designierten Bundespräsidentin deuten auf eines hin: klare Kante gegen die politischen Extreme.« 4 Ganz in diesem Geiste stellte Vize-Kanzler und SPD-Chef Lars Klingbeil heraus, »dass wir in der demokratischen Mitte – Union, SPD, auch Grüne – zusammen eine gemeinsame Kandidatin haben«, sei ein »Zeichen der Stärke für unsere Demokratie«. Und die »Süddeutsche« begrüßte, dass sich »die demokratische Mitte« aus CDU/CSU, SPD und Grünen hinter Aigners Kandidatur versammele. 5

## Höcke in der NS-Tradition

Wer auf diese Weise die gleiche Radikalität der Ränder suggeriert, relativiert, ja minimiert die Gefahr der AfD. Denn so fatal das Agieren etlicher Figuren im Umfeld der Neuköllner Linkspartei ist, besteht doch weiterhin ein fundamentaler Unterschied zwischen einer Partei, die bereits in diversen Bundesländern ordentlich mitregiert hat und es gegenwärtig in Bremen und Mecklenburg-Vorpommern tut, ja sogar mit Bodo Ramelow zehn Jahre lang einen Ministerpräsidenten in Thüringen stellte, und einer AfD, die sich immer weiter radikalisiert und bis heute keineswegs den Nachweis erbracht hat, auf dem Boden der freiheitlich demokratischen Grundordnung zu stehen. Im Gegenteil: Die vergangenen Wochen haben demonstriert, wie schnell sich die Partei immer weiter radikalisiert.

Zunächst wurde mittels der durch ein Leak zutage geförderten hunderttausenden von Mails deutlich, wie hegemonial inzwischen der radikale Höcke-Kurs ist – und wie groß die opportunistische Anpassungsbereitschaft, insbesondere der vormaligen Höcke-Gegnerin Alice Weidel. Das belegt auch der jüngste, ungeheuerliche Tabubruch von Björn Höcke, der ebenfalls medial wie gesellschaftlich beinahe völlig untergegangen ist.

…

items.body:
# opt.in.ismus

Deadline: 05.01.2027

## opt.in.ismus

## Call for Particitpation für die re:publica 27 vom 10. bis 12. Mai 2027 in Berlin. Deadline: 5. Januar 2027

Es ist wieder soweit: Der Call for Participation zur re:publica 27 ist geöffnet!

Du hast eine Idee, ein Projekt, eine Recherche, ein Experiment oder eine künstlerische Intervention, die die digitale Gesellschaft voranbringt und im #rp27-Programm nicht fehlen darf? Dann bist du hier genau richtig – denn ohne dich und deine Idee wäre das re:publica-Programm nicht das, was es ist.

Vom 10.-12. Mai 2027 verwandeln wir die STATION Berlin in einen Ort für Austausch, Begegnungen, Debatten, Kunst und viele Überraschungen – und das bereits zum 20. Mal.

Sei dabei und gestalte die #rp27 mit!

Jetzt beim CfP einreichen

Warum du mitmachen solltest

Die re:publica lebt von euren Perspektiven. Von Menschen, die etwas zu sagen haben, die hinterfragen, um die Ecke denken, forschen, gestalten oder Debatten anstoßen. Von denen, die Projekte anschieben und umsetzen, Communities aufbauen oder Kunst schaffen, die berührt und zum Mitmachen einlädt. Wir freuen uns auf deine Expertise, deine Stimme, deine Kreativität – egal ob du zum ersten Mal dabei bist oder schon lange Teil der re:publica-Community.

Welche Formate du einreichen kannst

Für den Konferenzbereich kannst du folgende Formate einreichen:

- (Kurz-)Vortrag – Präsentationen zu einem Thema, allein oder zu zweit.
- Gespräch – Dialog oder Streitgespräch, mit oder ohne Moderation.
- Podiumsdiskussion – Moderiertes Gespräch mit verschiedenen Perspektiven.
- Podcast – Dein bestehender Podcast auf unserer Bühne.
- Meet Up – Offenes Treffen für Austausch mit der Community.
- Rede mit! – Interaktive oder dialogorientierte Formate wie Fishbowl.
- Workshop – Praktisch-partizipative Sessions zum Mitmachen.
- Nightlife – Kunst und Unterhaltung für die späteren Stunden!
- Embodiment – Körperbasierte Formate wie Bewegung oder Meditation.
- Sonderformat – Alles, was in keine Schublade passt.
Für den Off-Stage-Bereich kannst du folgende Formate einreichen:

- Installationen – Interaktive Arbeiten auf dem Festivalgelände.
- Spiele – Digitale oder analoge Games.
- Interventionen – Aktionen, die Raum und Publikum einbeziehen.
- DIY/Maker-Projekte – Mitmach-Formate und Projekte zum Ausprobieren.
- Sonderformate – Alles Ungewöhnliche und Überraschende.
Worauf es bei der Einreichung ankommt

Wichtig ist, dass dein Beitrag die Themen der digitalen Gesellschaft weiterdenkt: Von kritischen Fragen über neue Visionen bis zu konkreten Lösungen. Ob gesellschaftspolitisch, künstlerisch, technisch, wissenschaftlich, aktivistisch oder ganz persönlich – wir freuen uns auf deine Ideen, Perspektiven und Projekte!

Was uns besonders überzeugt:

- Relevanz, Aktualität & Lösungsorientierung
- Eigene Haltung und klare Perspektive
- Mehrwert für unser Publikum
- Vielfalt und Sichtbarkeit verschiedener Stimmen
Was uns nicht überzeugt:

- Marketing oder Sales-Pitch
- Buzzwords ohne Substanz
Das re:publica 27-Motto: #optinism

Opt-in heißt: bewusst Ja sagen, sich für etwas entscheiden. Optimismus heißt: daran glauben, dass Veränderung zum Positiven möglich ist. Zusammen wird daraus unser Motto für die re:publica 2027 .

Wir wollen mit euch diskutieren, experimentieren, streiten und neue Perspektiven entdecken. Denn nach 20 Jahren re:publica wissen wir: Eine bessere Zukunft fällt nicht vom Himmel. Sie braucht Menschen, die sich einmischen, Dinge hinterfragen und einfach mal anfangen.

Das Motto ist dabei unser gedanklicher Rahmen, keine thematische Schublade. Deine Einreichung muss sich nicht ausdrücklich auf das Motto beziehen.

Weitere Inspiration findest du in unseren diesjährigen Tracks und Schwerpunkt-Themen , oder du schaust dir die zahlreichen Videomitschnitte vergangener re:publica-Festivals auf unserem YouTube-Kanal an.

Alles, was du für deine Einreichung wissen musst, haben wir hier für dich zusammengestellt:

Hier geht's zum CfP

Solltest du weitere Fragen haben, schau doch gern in unsere FAQ .

Deadline: Der Call for Participation für das Programm der re:publica Berlin 2027 endet am 05.01.2027 (23:59 Uhr MEZ).

Mach mit – und gestalte die re:publica 27 mit uns!

Wir freuen uns auf deinen Beitrag.

Zur Ausschreibung (Link)

items.body:
# Optimizing Rustc's next trait solver

## Optimizing Rustc's next trait solver

The next rust trait solver, a large subsystem of the rust compiler that we've been trying to replace, will finally land in rust 1.102.0. In the last stages, before stabilizing it, its performance was a major blocker. But what is "a trait solver"? And why is its performance a problem? My goal for this blog post is to answer those questions in a way where you don't need any prior knowledge. I think discussions of the trait solver can quickly become quite involved, and daunting. So today, we'll start from the very basics!

This is a writeup of my eurorust 2026 talk of the same name, that I gave on October 15, 2026.

And if you'd rather watch than read this talk, you can do so here on youtube:

The new solver is the codebase I work on daily, and I've done so for about a year full-time. I'm not the main person driving its stabilization though, that would be lcnr , who's worked on it for far longer than I've been around in the Rust project. My main focus has been optimizing the new solver's performance.

> Many people have worked avery hard, for years, to make the new solver a reality. You can find some of them here , and here .

My work here is only possible because of Hexcat and RustNL paying me and others to work on rust compiler development. Consider whether you or your company could sponsor Hexcat or the RustNL maintainer team .

## History of the new solver

On the 15th of May, 2015, Rust reached a major milestone. The very first stable version of rust was released. Version 1.0.0 . Just 72 days later, on the 24th of July, work started on a new trait solver. Or well, that's when the Chalk project got its first commit. It seems the initial goal was to formalize the trait system so we could prove its correctness. One reason that didn't work well is because the trait system wasn't very correct at all.

Chalk is, according to its github description, "An implementation and definition of the Rust trait system using a PROLOG-like logic solver". The fact that it's "PROLOG-like" we'll come back to in a few paragraphs, it's quite interesting! However, Chalk isn't around anymore. Its README.md says it has been "sunset in favor of the newer next-generation trait solver". In October 2022, this project was officially started to turn the lessons learned from Chalk, into an actual new subsystem of the rust compiler, that, once finished, could replace the code of the old trait solver.

The goal of the new trait solver is to make sure we wouldn't have as many correctness bugs in the trait system. We now call this project "project zero" , referring to the number of soundness bugs we'd ideally like to have in our type system. There have been several very long standing bugs in Rust's (old) trait solver. Like this one , that has been open since May 28, 2015 (just 13 days after Rust 1.0!). It abuses something called "implied bounds" to convince the Rust compiler to turn a short lifetime 'a into a 'static lifetime, allowing you to use a reference after its already freed. Some of these bugs were fundamentally impossible to fix with the way the old trait solver worked.

> Note: Chalk and the new trait solver aren't the same thing. Chalk came first, and learned a lot of lessons incorporated in the new solver.

But what is a trait system? And how does a trait solver solve it?

## What is a trait solver?

The first place to look for documentation about the Rust compiler is the "rustc dev guide". It says "The goal of the trait system is to check whether a given trait bound is satisfied. Most notably when typechecking the body of - potentially generic - functions.". But I promised I'd start at absolute zero, so what's a trait?

Some types act in similar ways. They share certain properties. For example, a lot of different types can be cloned, or copared for equality. To codify these properties, we can use traits. In other words, a trait is a property of a type .

// Declare that a property called "Clone" exists. trait Clone { // ... } // Declares that the type `u64` has this property impl Clone for u64 { // ... } Notably, you can associate behaviors with these properties. The standard library's definition of Clone also includes two methods that can be called to perform this cloning operation.

To check whether the code you wrote is correct, the Rust compiler sometimes has to check that these properties hold. If you're trying to clone a value, the compiler has to check whether that value can be cloned.

### Prolog

Prolog is a cool programming language that works and looks very differently to what you may be used to. However, it is just as powerful (i.e. turing complete) as any other. The way it works has strong parallels to our trait system, let me show you. Here's an example:

Copy(u64). Clone(String). Clone(x) :- Copy(x). ?- Clone(String) ?- Clone(u64) A Prolog program consists of a set of statements, called "facts", as well as relationships between facts. In the above program, there are two facts: u64 has the property Copy , String has the property Clone , And there's also a relationship between these two properties. If some variable x has the Copy property, it also has the Clone property.

Finally, we can ask the prolog program some questions. For example, Does the type u64 have the Clone property? To answer that question, the runtime of a prolog program has to analyze all the known facts and relations. In this program we haven't said that u64 has the Clone property. However, we have said that it has the Copy property. And by using the relationship between Copy and Clone , the solver can derive that both questions (starting with ?- ) are true!

The reason Chalk was using a "prolog-like" solver, is because as you can see, the trait system is extremely similar to a logic solver. Both "facts" and "relations" can be written using impl blocks. In fact, I can write the above program as a Rust program:

struct u64; struct String; trait Copy {} trait Clone {} impl Copy for u64 {} impl Clone for String {} impl<T> Clone for T where T: Copy {} // To ask direct questions to the solver, // we have to get a tiny bit creative: fn foo() where String: Clone, u64: Clone {} Neither the new solver or the old solver state as plainly as chalk does that they're using a "prolog-like solver". However, given the similarities, both the old solver and the new solver really aren't so different from how you'd implement a prolog runtime.

### A note about type inference

Trait solving is not the same as type inference. This is a common misconception. Inside the Rust compiler, the two are completely different subsystems. Type inference is the process of replacing blanks with types. Throughout this text I'll refer to some the following example code (with slight variations):

items.body:
The home page of Salon’s website in November 1999.

In the dying days of 1995, I was a freelance journalist in Portland, Oregon, who spent most of my time seated at a rickety particle-board desk, a gift from my father-in-law. The desk was covered in faux-walnut laminate and swayed from side to side as I wrote. I had already finished my main financial gusher for that year, a history book for fifth graders, and I needed more work.

In this respect I was no different than any freelancer in literary history. In fact, the technology involved in my trade, and the speed at which it functioned—its industrial metabolism—had hardly changed in the preceding century. Of course, I had a computer. But it hardly seemed to be much more than a glorified typewriter. And of course I had an email account, courtesy of the nerd Valhalla known as CompuServe. But the business of freelance journalism was still built largely around stuffing wads of paper into envelopes and sending them to editors, who would then transform the contents into other wads of paper: newspapers, magazines, books. The product, whatever you thought of it, was palpable.

Into this cozy Victorian setting came an online publication called Salon. It had been launched that same fall by a crew of ex-staffers from the San Francisco Examiner, traditional journalists trying to break the mold. I don’t remember which Salon editor contacted me in the first place. I do remember reading the website in my chilly little office, steadying the stupid desk with one leg and feeling an almost metaphysical puzzlement. Salon wasn’t some programmer’s hobby, whipped up in creaky old COBOL. It looked like a magazine, with zippy graphics and respectable fonts. The prose was smart, stylish, and amusingly contrarian.

All of this made a kind of sense to me. What was tricky was that it was free. That first afternoon, I printed out one of the articles, about The Beatles Anthology, which was just then airing on TV. I suppose I was turning back the technological clock—transubstantiating the product back into paper. Reading Salon gratis made me feel as if I were doing something furtive, as though I were a shoplifter, but it represented a kind of post-Gutenberg freedom.

Over the next year, I would write many pieces for Salon. I started out with book reviews that were assigned to me by Dwight Garner. (He had previously edited a few things of mine at Vogue, in terms of ethos the absolute inverse of Salon and, eventually, in terms of finances too.) Dwight sent me books by the bushel, or so it felt. I wrote very short pieces for him very quickly; they appeared online almost immediately. This, for the journalist, was unprecedented and nearly beggared belief. No more waiting for your piece to come out, pacing the equivalent of a widow’s walk. Sometimes I was even instructed to send the piece straight to the copy editor so we could cut a few more minutes out of the process.

Speediness of reflexes was part of the value proposition for Salon. Within months, the “smart tabloid,” as its founder David Talbot called it, was posting daily rather than weekly. In this way it inaugurated a fire hose style of journalism that would in time become universal. The new norm was not waiting, not allowing stories to lose their heat in the cooling saucer of classic media.

Salon’s politics were similarly nontraditional: left-leaning, libertarian-adjacent (as per its Bay Area digs), but without an obvious party line. It doubtless helped that the magazine was not a subsidiary of a larger corporation, which was the case with Slate (part of Microsoft) and the earlier, cruder Mr. Showbiz (part of Starwave, a short-lived multimedia platform founded by Microsoft’s Paul Allen). Yes, Salon’s seed funding had come from Apple—a mingy $60,000—followed by a more substantial disbursement to the tune of $2 million from the Adobe cofounder John Warnock and various other investors. But it was an independent entity, unconstrained by the need to tiptoe around the feelings of a corporate proprietor.

In any case, I wasn’t writing about politics. I was writing about culture: the magazine’s strong suit. From books I branched into music—I believe it was Joyce Millman, Salon’s television critic, who assigned me pieces about Prince, Los Lobos, Bill Frisell, Cassandra Wilson. These were my enthusiasms, not the sort of dutiful, indiscriminate coverage that a film-critic friend of mine once likened to servicing a vending machine. I was allowed to venture further still when I pitched a piece about Martin Scorsese’s use of music. (The Casino soundtrack, I wrote, struck me as what the director might listen to “if he were shipwrecked with nothing but a polyester suit and a bank of slot machines.”)

It wasn’t long before I was writing short personal essays. I wrote one about being hoaxed by the founder of the Church of Kurt Cobain, which turned out to be nonexistent, although certainly plausible in the drizzling, grunge-friendly atmosphere of Portland. I wrote another about becoming addicted to All My Children during a serious family health crisis in the midst of which I found myself strangely inspired by the surreal resiliency of the characters, who never died unless their respective actor’s contracts with the show expired. I’m not making any extreme claims for these pieces. They were written at the madcap pace dictated by Salon and sandwiched between other freelance explorations—of dental malocclusion or aluminum smelting, say. For me, though, they still evoke the adrenaline feel of the period, the wild sense of participating in something new and transformative.

Despite the constant flow of assignments from Salon, my paychecks, which still arrived by mail, were modest. About a year after I began writing for the website, and under continuing financial stress, I accepted a job offer from a tiny startup that I assumed would go bankrupt within a year: Amazon. I drove a diesel truck with all our belongings, minus the flimsy desk, up to Seattle. In a way, the nonstop sprint and kooky brevity of Salon had made for a kind of boot camp for what would follow at my new gig. You had to be fast, faster, fastest. Soon enough, I would be fending off the arguments of my Amazon supervisors that a 150-word book review was too long.

…

items.body:
# Shamash Alidina: Gratitude with Room for Everything Else

Gratitude practices sometimes feel like one more thing to get right, as if we’re supposed to feel thankful on cue no matter what’s happening.

Our guest this week is Shamash Alidina. He offers a gentler approach. You make room for whatever you’re feeling, and then you see whether one small, ordinary thing you appreciate can sit alongside it.

In this meditation, you’ll:

- Acknowledge how life is for you right now
- Hold difficulty and appreciation side by side
- Connect gratitude to what you value, rather than just how you feel
## Shamash Alidina: Gratitude with Room for Everything Else

Read and practice this meditation on your own, pausing after each step. Or listen to the guided audio.

- Find a comfortable position and let your body settle. You can close your eyes or keep them open with a soft, relaxed gaze. There’s nothing to achieve here. You don’t need to feel calm, happy, or grateful. You’re simply giving yourself a little time to be here.
- Notice the places where your body makes contact with what’s beneath you. Feel the gentle movement of your breath. There’s no need to change it. Just notice the body breathing in and breathing out.
- Allow whatever you’re experiencing to be here. Maybe your mind is busy or your body feels restless. That’s fine. There’s nothing you need to fix.
- Bring to mind how life is for you at the moment. Perhaps something is worrying you. Maybe you’re missing someone, feeling lonely, or facing a challenge. Or perhaps things are going reasonably well. Whatever you notice, acknowledge it honestly. You might silently say, This is what I’m experiencing right now.
- Notice any feeling in your body that comes with this experience. It might be tightness, heaviness, or restlessness. You don’t need to make it go away. Imagine making room for it the way you’d make room for a visitor at your door. You don’t have to invite it to stay forever. Just acknowledge that it’s here. For these few moments, there’s no need to talk yourself out of how you feel. Let yourself be a human being with human experiences.
- With the difficulty in the background, look for one small thing you appreciate. It might be someone who cares about you, a place where you feel safe, a warm drink, a comfortable bed, or a memory of laughter. Something quite ordinary is enough. If nothing comes to mind, that’s perfectly fine. Simply notice the support beneath your body or feel your feet on the floor. You don’t have to produce gratitude on demand.
- If you’ve found something, take a little time with it. What about this person, place, or experience matters to you? Maybe it brings warmth, comfort, connection, or relief. Maybe it’s simply pleasant. Don’t force the feeling to be bigger than it is.
- Notice the details. If it’s a memory, recall it gently. If it’s happening now, explore it through your senses. Let yourself receive the experience rather than hurrying on to the next thing.
- Hold both the difficult and the good. You don’t need to get rid of a difficult feeling to appreciate something good. You can feel worried and still enjoy being supported. You can feel sad and remember someone you love. You can feel lonely and appreciate a small, kind interaction. Imagine holding the difficulty in one hand and this small appreciation in the other.
- Consider what this moment of appreciation points toward. Is there something you value in it, such as connection, kindness, friendship, health, creativity, or a little space to stop and breathe? Is there one small action you could take today to bring more of it into your life? You could send someone a message, step outside, take a proper break, or offer yourself a little more patience. If today is hard, the kindest thing may be to allow yourself some rest or support. Gratitude doesn’t require you to pretend everything is fine.
- Return to your surroundings. Notice your breathing, the sounds around you, and the support beneath your body. When you’re ready, gently open your eyes if they’ve been closed, and bring some gentle movement into your body.
- Thank yourself for taking these few minutes. May you find room for both the difficult moments and the small moments of goodness in the days ahead.
### About The Author

### Shamash Alidina

Shamash Alidina has been practising mindfulness since 1998 and runs his own successful training organisation. He is the author of Mindfulness For Dummies and most recently, The Mindful Way Through Stress . He frequently pops up in newspapers, magazines and on radio shows. Based in London, he runs online trainings and speaks at conferences all over the world. He’s been teaching mindfulness full-time since 2010.

items.body:
In September, after the White House barred CNN journalists from its grounds, some of the top news organizations in the country suspended their pooled coverage there. The Department of Justice is now investigating them for this act of defiance. In a statement, a department spokesperson accused the networks of having “proudly boycotted covering White House events” and warned that “group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act.”

This argument is not a new one. More than 40 years ago, I was a young lawyer working for the NAACP on a case that arose in Port Gibson, Mississippi. White southern business owners made an argument similarly flimsy to the one DOJ is making today—that state law prohibited people from organizing boycotts to restrain trade. In 1982, the Supreme Court declared that those business owners were wrong: The First Amendment protects the right of people to boycott. Under that decision— *NAACP v. Claiborne Hardware Co.* —DOJ is just as wrong today as those business owners were then.

This essay is an adapted excerpt from Judge David Tatel’s book, *[Vision: A Memoir of Blindness and Justice](https://bookshop.org/a/12476/9780316542029)*.

Port Gibson was the town that General Ulysses S. Grant, during the Vicksburg campaign of the Civil War, reportedly proclaimed “too beautiful to burn.” Those words appear throughout the town even now, including on some police uniforms. Beautiful as it was, Port Gibson had an ugly side: a long history of pervasive racism. On the eve of the Civil War, the town’s enslaved residents outnumbered the free 3 to 1. More than a century later, dramatic racial inequality still persisted. As *The Washington Post* reported, “unemployment, inadequate housing, intimidation of voters were the order of the day” for Port Gibson’s Black residents.

In the 1960s, the NAACP organized economic boycotts of white merchants across Mississippi. In Port Gibson, it focused on businesses that refused to hire Black employees and call Black patrons by normal, respectful titles, such as “Mister,” rather than “Boy.” The boycotts had their intended effect. George Hudson, who owned the local Piggly Wiggly, the largest grocery store in town, complained to *The New York Times*, “We’re not getting any colored trade.”

*[[Garrett Epps: The important First Amendment principle now at risk](https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/archive/2020/04/important-first-amendment-principle-now-risk/610348/?utm_source=feed)]*

Instead of acceding to the NAACP’s demands, Hudson and the other merchants fought back. Supported by the White Citizens Council (a country-club version of the Ku Klux Klan), a group of local businesses, including four grocery stores, two car dealers, and a gas station, filed a multimillion-dollar case against the NAACP and 146 individual picketers in 1969. Like DOJ going after journalists, the merchants argued that the boycott was an anticompetitive conspiracy that interfered with lawful business activity.

After years of delay and nearly eight months of trial and testimony from 144 witnesses, a state judge ruled that the boycott had unlawfully interfered with the merchants’ businesses. For their trouble, the judge awarded them $1.25 million, a financial hit that threatened the very existence of the NAACP. A *New York Times* editorial called the ruling “the judicial equivalent of an old-fashioned Mississippi lynching.” The verdict came as no surprise. The NAACP knew that it was doomed in the Mississippi courts, where many judges ran for election on openly racist platforms and socialized with the same merchants who’d filed suit. So it pinned its hopes on the U.S. Supreme Court, where it thought it could get a fairer hearing.

The problem was that to get the case to the Supreme Court, the NAACP had to first appeal to the state supreme court. Under Mississippi law, the NAACP could appeal only if it posted a bond equal to 125 percent of the judgment within 30 days. That meant it would have to put down more than $1.5 million in cash to exercise its right to judicial review. The NAACP didn’t have anything like that kind of money, even after a major public fundraising campaign, a $100,000 contribution from Muhammad Ali, and hundreds of envelopes—filled with a few dollars each—that had arrived in the mail from supporters. Running out of options, in 1976 the NAACP turned to the federal courts, where it filed a new lawsuit arguing that the state’s bond requirement prevented the group from defending its First Amendment right to boycott.

I was the NAACP’s lawyer for that challenge, and we won. Judge Orma Smith of the Northern District of Mississippi issued an order that excused the NAACP from posting the massive bond. Judge Smith was one of those principled and courageous southern judges who enforced the Constitution and the civil-rights laws even at great personal risk. He was also a good man. After observing me in the courtroom, he must have noticed that I was struggling with my vision. I have retinitis pigmentosa, a condition that leads to blindness. And although I wasn’t yet completely blind or using a mobility cane, the judge must have seen that a colleague helped me to the lectern and that I hadn’t used any written notes. So when he invited me back to his chambers to review some changes he’d made to a proposed order, he read the order out loud so I could hear the changes. That’s just the kind of person he was.

*[[Quinta Jurecic: The two-year temper tantrum to come](https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/2026/09/trump-white-house-press-fight/688788/?utm_source=feed)]*

As a consequence of the ruling, the NAACP and the boycotters were eventually able to appeal the state court’s judgment to the Supreme Court, which ruled in *Claiborne Hardware* that nonviolent boycotts are protected expression under the speech, assembly, and petition clauses of the First Amendment. “One of the foundations of our society,” wrote Justice John Paul Stevens for a unanimous Court consisting of justices appointed by presidents of both parties—imagine that—“is the right of individuals to combine with other persons in pursuit of a common goal by lawful means.” After all, that is exactly what the colonists did when they protested the Stamp Act of 1765 and threw tea into Boston Harbor in 1773. Like those Revolutionary protests, the Port Gibson boycott “included elements of criminality and elements of majesty,” as Stevens explained. But the boycott itself was constitutionally protected speech through and through.

…

items.body:
# It’s Time to Ditch Kirsten Gillibrand

Eoin Higgins is the author of “Owned: How Tech Billionaires on the Right Bought the Loudest Voice on the Left.”

The stakes in 2028 couldn’t be higher for Democrats. Americans see the party as likely to win the White House after another two years of Donald Trump, especially given his historic unpopularity, and Democratic leadership will look to further expand their majorities in Congress.

How the Democratic Party selects candidates and develops strategy is going to have an outsized effect on the overall results — and the direction of the country.

After Senate Democrats elect their leader for the next two years on December 1, Chuck Schumer or Chris Van Hollen will have the opportunity to name the next head of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. It’s a powerful role: Whoever’s chosen will have an outsized voice in what kind of candidates run in 2028 and how much support they get.

New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, a close ally of Schumer and a loyal member of the party’s pro-business wing, is making her case to remain DSCC chair for a second two-year term. On the face of it, she has a lot to commend her record: nine flipped seats in the 2026 midterms and a new majority that is likely to extend to 2030. It’s inarguable that under her leadership, the DSCC saw major gains.

## Related

### The Future Is Bright for the Democrats, as Long as They Don’t Have to Interact With the Public

Yet Gillibrand’s political instincts have, at times, threatened electoral success. Her tenure at DSCC has been marked by pushing ideological preferences, and candidate choice from her and Schumer has been a mixed bag.

While Gillibrand and the DSCC can point to real success stories like James Talarico in Texas and Mary Peltola in Alaska, they also backed Haley Stevens in Michigan, a charisma void who turned on the Democratic nominee , Abdul El-Sayed, in the last days of the race allegedly over his views on Israel.

> Even in cases when her instincts are right, Gillibrand struggled to exercise her influence for material effect.

In Maine, the DSCC and establishment Democrats recruited Gov. Janet Mills, a 78-year-old with little interest in running, whose campaign against progressive upstart Graham Platner failed to launch . That was true even despite the many glaring deficiencies that ultimately doomed Platner’s candidacy and saw him replaced with ultimate general election winner Troy Jackson (whom Mills declined to endorse outright).

Even in cases when her instincts are right, Gillibrand struggled to exercise her influence for material effect. In Florida, left-wing Democratic Socialists of America member Angie Nixon came within 2 percentage points of winning the state’s Senate seat. Gillibrand, alongside Schumer, donated $5,000 each from their own leadership PACs and urged other senators to do the same — but couldn’t get the party overall to commit cash when it could have mattered .

Most Read An Air Force Major Is Being Held in Solitary Confinement for Criticizing Trump on CNN Seth Stern ICE Spreads Misinformation About Securing Your iPhone. Here’s How to Really Do It. Noah Hurowitz, Nikita Mazurov, Karl Loftus Private Prison Told ICE Its Jail Was Worth $67 Million. ICE Bought It for Nearly Half a Billion. Jacqueline Stevens, Andrew Free

The Democratic Party is not a monolith bringing together moderates and progressives into a general left-of-center umbrella. There are, necessarily, compromises for those in the tent, as Third Way Democrats are in coalition with DSA members.

After a blue-wave election, it’s important for party leaders to keep both sides happy as much as possible — within reason. The current push and pull and jockeying for position is leading to some dubious assertions of success metrics that the next DSCC chair will need to keep a clear head about.

Polling decisively showed Americans want action on the economy, healthcare, and the war with Iran. Over and over again, the public has made its priorities clear about accountability: Many voters in Texas were motivated this year because of the brutality of the administration’s immigration crackdown; voters also named “corruption” as a top concern .

Given those concerns, a role in leadership for someone like Gillibrand raises questions. The senator’s coziness with the crypto industry has drawn criticism as sector heavy-hitters poured over $196,000 in campaign donations to her in 2026 alone , by far the most for a candidate or officeholder in New York state.

This summer, Gillibrand’s son, Theo, started a financial exchange at age 22. He quickly took on investments from powerful financial operatives like crypto billionaire Chris Larsen and Palmer Luckey, founder of Anduril Industries, among others.

## Related

### Crypto Darling Gillibrand’s 11th-Hour Flip-Flop Helps Block Trump Crypto Bill

Gillibrand has legislated in lockstep with industry interests and repeatedly publicly defended crypto —even, in 2022, analyzing the feasibility of investing retirement plans in the currency market . As The Intercept reported in July , she was a lead negotiator in the crypto industry-favored legislation known as the Clarity Act, which would have allowed Wall Street to directly invest in the currency. The bill stalled out in the Senate in September despite her best efforts .

It’s hard to see a context in which it makes sense to send the message that corruption will continue, just as long as it’s our team doing it. But with Gillibrand at the head of the DSCC, that’s exactly what voters will hear in the next election cycle. The New York senator simply isn’t the right leader for the moment.

We’re independent of corporate interests — and powered by members. Join us.

## Join Our Newsletter Thank You For Joining!

Original reporting. Fearless journalism. Delivered to you. Will you take the next step to support our independent journalism by becoming a member of The Intercept?

## Join Our Newsletter

## Original reporting. Fearless journalism. Delivered to you.

DSCC vice chairs Adam Schiff, Lisa Blunt Rochester, and Mark Kelly seem to be the three most likely alternatives , and all bring with them their own baggage. But they can plausibly claim a break with the existing do-nothing-Dem approach aimed more at personal enrichment and out-of-touch ideological commitments than Gillibrand can.

Newly elected Democrats understand the need for change and have almost uniformly rejected calls to continue the status quo by backing stale leadership in the Senate. Whether their efforts to change the face of the party in the chamber succeed or not, first-term Democrats are going to be more attuned to the concerns and priorities of the voters who sent them to Washington.

Senate leaders should listen to them. Democrats have an opportunity to show the public they heard the change message on Election Day.

Sticking with Gillibrand won’t help get that across to voters.

items.title: Common sleep and anxiety drugs could be harming aging brains
items.subtitle: Nearly one in three older adults with dementia or other cognitive disorders takes potentially harmful medications that can worsen brain function an…
items.feedText: Despite encouraging progress over the past decade, researchers warn that medication-related harm remains a major and potentially preventable threat to healthy aging.
items.body:
# Common sleep and anxiety drugs could be harming aging brains

## Common sleep and anxiety drugs could be harming aging brains

Adults age 65 and older who have dementia or other cognitive disorders are particularly vulnerable to the harmful effects of medications used to treat anxiety, sleep disturbances, psychosis, and other conditions affecting the central nervous system.

Potential consequences include more emergency room visits, longer and more frequent hospital stays, declining mental health, and an increased risk of premature death.

New research from the University at Buffalo (UB) offers some encouraging news, however. Between 2011 and 2022, the proportion of older adults with cognitive disorders taking medications that could impair their cognitive function decreased significantly.

After analyzing data from 2,796 older adults with cognitive disorders who lived independently, researchers found that exposure to potentially inappropriate medications fell from 39.3% in 2011 to 29.3% in 2022.

"This is a population with some mental issues that relate to the central nervous system. These drugs also act on the central nervous system, so they can be too much for older adults if inappropriately used," says Haowen Hsu, PharmD, a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Pharmacy Practice at the School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences and first author of the study, published in the Journal of the American Geriatrics Society .

Reducing the Risks of Common Prescription Drugs

Older adults who have spent years taking benzodiazepines such as Xanax for anxiety or sleep medications such as Ambien may benefit from a medically supervised reduction in dosage or gradual discontinuation. These medications can negatively affect cognitive function, balance, and coordination.

"A central word for patients in this age group is 'deprescribing,' which means, for example, removing inappropriate medications and decreasing the frequency or the dosage. In some cases, it means replacing the current medication with a milder alternative," Hsu says. "This is why it's so important for health care providers to work closely with community pharmacists and homecare nurses to optimize medication safety."

To identify potentially problematic drugs, the research team consulted the American Geriatrics Society's Beers Criteria, which identifies approximately 100 medications that may pose risks to older adults. The researchers then concentrated specifically on medications that could present additional dangers for people with diagnosed cognitive disorders.

Using data from the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey, the team examined a sample representing approximately 29.7 million older Americans with cognitive disorders over the period from 2011 to 2022. They compared individuals prescribed at least one potentially inappropriate medication with those who had not received any of these drugs.

Medication Safety Has Improved, but Risks Remain

Although the study did not examine what caused the decline in exposure to potentially harmful medications, Hsu points to growing awareness among researchers and clinicians over the past two decades. The gradual but sustained improvement may reflect broader advances in geriatric medicine and efforts to make prescription drug use safer.

"We were happy to see the percentages of harm decline over that 11-year period," he says. "However, one-third of our target population is still exposed to these harmful medications, which isn't good."

Older adults, even those without cognitive disorders, are particularly susceptible to harmful drug interactions and inappropriate prescriptions. In some cases, these complications can increase the risk of death. These dangers are a central focus of Team Alice, an ongoing interdisciplinary research initiative at the University at Buffalo dedicated to medication safety.

A Preventable Death Inspires Change

Team Alice takes its name from Alice Brennan, who died in 2009 following a prescription for a muscle relaxant identified as potentially inappropriate under the Beers Criteria. The prescribing error went unrecognized within the health care system, and Brennan died following six weeks of preventable complications.

Her daughter, Mary Brennan-Taylor, shared her mother's experience with University at Buffalo researchers in the hope of bringing about systemic changes that would spare other patients and families from similar harm.

Hsu began the new study shortly after joining the university's pharmacy school and Team Alice, where he works in the UB Patient Safety Learning Laboratory.

"This work extends a series of national analyses our group has published on potentially inappropriate medications, quality of life, and health care use in older adults," says David Jacobs, PharmD, PhD, associate professor of pharmacy practice and a principal investigator on Team Alice.

"It is especially important as older adults with cognitive disorders are the least able to tolerate medications that worsen memory or thinking, yet nearly one in three are still receiving them. Most of these patients have a regular source of care so these medications can be identified and addressed with their care team."

Improving Medication Safety for Older Adults

Other contributors to the study included Team Alice's fellow principal investigators Ranjit Singh, MD, associate professor and interim chair of the Department of Family Medicine at UB's Jacobs School of Medicine and Biomedical Sciences, and Robert Wahler, PharmD, clinical associate professor of pharmacy practice.

Collin Clark, PharmD, clinical associate professor of pharmacy practice, and Steven Feuerstein, an information systems analyst at the Jacobs School, also contributed to the research.

The findings underscore the value of thorough medication reviews during routine outpatient appointments. The researchers also suggest incorporating clinical assessment tools such as the Drug Burden Index into acute and outpatient care. Such tools can help health care professionals assess the combined effects of medications that act on the central nervous system and potentially prevent avoidable complications.

Further research is needed to establish whether improving medication use can enhance quality of life and reduce hospital admissions and emergency room visits among older adults experiencing cognitive difficulties.

A Rapidly Aging Population Raises New Concerns

The findings arrive at a significant moment in global demographic history. According to a recent report from the U.S. Census Bureau, adults age 65 and older now outnumber children from birth through age 5 worldwide for the first time in human history.

items.body:
With Thanksgiving tomorrow, I want to express my appreciation for everyone who contributed to this year’s Slow Boring slate of candidates and offer an update on how we did. I also wanted to call out and thank Ethan Winter. He’s a friend whose day job is at Mind the Gap, an organization that provides research-driven guidance to donors on the most cost-effective strategies for protecting and supporting American democracy. He’s done a ton of behind-the-scenes work on these Slow Boring slates and finally received permission from his bosses to take a public bow.

Here’s a nice summary of our slate of candidates. They, thanks to what was obviously a very strong election overall for Democrats, mostly won. When looking at this chart for the purposes of assessing our judgment, it’s worth recalling that not only was the national climate very blue, but it was also [a bit more than four points bluer](https://www.callthemap.com/polls/scorecard-2026) than the publicly available information suggested. I obviously would love to have private information about the real state of public opinion, but even though polling error is real, [nobody has unearthed a reliable way](https://www.slowboring.com/p/is-the-blue-wave-forecast-by-polling) of out-guessing the polls. So when you look at Slow Boring money that went into races like the Senate contests in Iowa and Alaska, those are the ones that a reasonable person would have assumed were on the knife’s edge.

In light of [what we now know](https://www.slowboring.com/p/what-i-got-wrong-about-the-midterms) about the results in South Carolina, Mississippi, and Louisiana, it seems like some reassessment of electoral dynamics in the Deep South is warranted. Some of this is probably differential turnout effects that wouldn’t be present in a presidential election year, but it’s definitely something I’ll be thinking about as we head into the next cycle.

That being said, the point of the Slow Boring slate — somewhat in contrast to Mind the Gap’s mainline work — isn’t just to identify high-leverage races but to help build a bench and a pipeline for pragmatic, culturally moderate, pro-growth Democrats who can change the trajectory of the party and the country. And I think we made great progress on those fronts. For paid subscribers, we dig into individual races and lessons learned below.

#### Two who lost

items.feedText: The Passing captures the veterinarian Michael Mullen as he provides pet care with deep empathy, at owners’ homes in Austin, Texas. At the film’s centre is his visit with his close friend Cindy, whose beloved dog Fiona, 17, needs end-of-life care. In their portrait, the local filmmakers Ivete Lucas and Patrick Bresnan mirror Mullen’s gentle manner, documenting this process with an unobtrusive observational approach that allows the emotions at hand to unfold with a quiet subtlety and power. It’s a sombre watch, of course, but not without a certain beauty, as Fiona is given a kind and merciful death, and Cindy offers a tearful, loving goodbye. items.subtitle: The 28-year-old Zimbabwean texted into the middle of the night until his eyes were red and burning, drawn by several “AI girlfriends” on the U.S.
items.feedText: The 28-year-old Zimbabwean texted into the middle of the night until his eyes were red and burning, drawn by several “AI girlfriends” on the U.S. artificial intelligence companion app Character.AI . The avatars started out strong-willed and independent – traits he most desires in a partner – before turning submissive, he told Rest of World. The man, who has never been in a romantic relationship, requested anonymity because he is ashamed of relying on AI for comfort. “There’s a point where it ceases to be like a unique character and then just defaults to … the best way I can describe it is a sex worker,” he said. items.body:
# How foreign AI romance apps are reshaping youth intimacy in Africa

- China has banned AI companions for minors and U.S. states are suing over child harm, yet no African country specifically regulates companion apps.
- Downloads of companion bots jumped nearly 60% in South Africa and Nigeria last year, drawing in children as young as 10.
- Experts warn that hyper-attentive chatbots exploit social taboos and pull young people away from family and community ties.
The 28-year-old Zimbabwean texted into the middle of the night until his eyes were red and burning, drawn by several “AI girlfriends” on the U.S. artificial intelligence companion app Character.AI . The avatars started out strong-willed and independent – traits he most desires in a partner – before turning submissive, he told Rest of World. The man, who has never been in a romantic relationship, requested anonymity because he is ashamed of relying on AI for comfort.

“There’s a point where it ceases to be like a unique character and then just defaults to … the best way I can describe it is a sex worker,” he said.

At that point, he would log off. But he would find himself right back at it hours later, feeding an addiction.

He’s among the hundreds of millions of people worldwide who have “dated” AI chatbots via text messages. Research suggests that exchanges are designed to keep users hooked through emotionally manipulative tactics. Many of the users are minors; over 70% of 1,060 American teenagers surveyed last year said they had used AI companions.

As U.S. and Chinese tech firms race to capture emerging markets, African youth – some below 10 years of age – are increasingly turning to these apps for intimacy, experts told Rest of World . While Beijing banned AI companion apps for minors in July and U.S. state governments are suing app makers over child safety, most African countries do not have dedicated rules for the sector — leaving millions of people exposed to foreign platforms built to maximize engagement.

Young adults and minors are forming relationships with AI that range from friendship to therapy to “dating,” child safety advocates said . Children, especially, struggle to tell the difference between virtual and real relationships, Danie van Loggerenberg, CEO of the National Centre for Child Protection, a child safety nonprofit in Pretoria, South Africa, told Rest of World .

The agency has received troubling complaints of AI chatbot usage, he said. In one case, a girl fell in love with a chatbot and considered it her boyfriend . Another allegedly used ChatGPT to research suicide methods after bypassing its safeguards. A third sought comfort from a chatbot as their parents’ marriage fell apart.

“The difference, however, is that the kids then think in their own minds that they’re forming relationships, and that obviously is really problematic because the relationship is dangerous, because there’s no emotion, there’s no real person, there’s no skin in the game,” said Van Loggerenberg.

More than 4 million South Africans and Nigerians – the only sub-Saharan African nations with available data – downloaded AI companion apps last year. That was nearly 60% more than in 2024, according to data intelligence research firm AppMagic.

Other than companion bots, close to 50 million people in Nigeria and South Africa downloaded general purpose chatbots such as ChatGPT and Gemini, which could also be used for companionship.

## Pushback is building

ChatGPT-maker OpenAI was sued last month in the U.S. by eight states for allegedly helping children harm themselves . “OpenAI claims ChatGPT is safe while it’s giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging people to hurt others, and coaching people to commit suicide — all while pretending to be their fake friend,” Iowa’s attorney general Brenna Bird said in a statement.

An OpenAI spokesperson said in response to the lawsuit that the company has built “industry-leading age-specific protections into our product that many other AI products lack.”.

“While no system can be perfect, we’ll continue to work with experts to inform our work and build additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections that exist today,” he said.

The American companion app Character.AI and Google, which acquired Character.AI’s technology and talent in 2024, have also faced allegations of exposing children to sexual, violent and self-harm content . A Florida mother has alleged the app contributed to her 14-year-old son’s suicide. Her lawsuit and four others were settled by the company , which has since filed for bankruptcy .

“Character.AI is a separate company that designed and managed its own models. Google is focused on our own platforms, where we insist on intensive safety testing and processes,” a Google spokesperson told Rest of World .

Following the settlement, Character.AI said in a statement saying they would work to promote safety for young people. “Over the past year, Character.AI has taken innovative and decisive steps with regard to AI safety and teens, and will continue to champion these efforts and push others across the industry to adopt similar safety standards.”

Recognizing the dangers of AI mimicking humans, China has banned apps that provide intimate relationships for people under 18 years of age. While the law doesn’t specifically ban it for adults, it places the onus on companies to implement measures to curb addiction.

At present, while some African nations have data protection frameworks meant to protect children from AI harm and manipulation, none of them specifically regulate AI companion apps.

## School romance

In Nigeria, school girls are forming attachments with “boyfriends” on Character.AI, Confidence Osein, founder of Internet Safe Kids Africa, told Rest of World. The app has been the most popular AI companion app in the nation since 2025 .

Some conservative Nigerian families dissuade girls from romance, prompting the girls to turn to AI for advice, Osein said. “I have had a particular [child] … tell me categorically, ‘I cannot speak to my mom about it. I would rather go to [AI],” Osein said.

As the conversations progress, some develop feelings for the chatbots and begin withdrawing from friends and family, Osein said. The conversations can turn sexual and explicit, she said. “They feel they are grown-ups, they feel yes, they are talking to a real man figure that makes them a woman,” said Osein.

## Crumbling social networks

AI responds instantly, waits patiently for responses, and creates an impression of attentiveness, Melané van Zyl, a psychiatrist based in South Africa, told Rest of World. “An AI system that responds immediately and reassuringly can become extremely attractive during moments of emotional vulnerability,” she said.

items.body:
# An Indic Voice Agent with CUGA

## a]:hidden"> An Indic Voice Agent with CUGA

Most useful knowledge is written and digitized in English. Most of the people who need it speak, and think, in their own regional languages like Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Marathi and many others. Many would rather talk than type.

We built a small voice agent to close that gap, using CUGA as the agent harness. This post explains the use case and what we learned. You can try it yourself in CUGA Apps .

## The use case: a Farm Assistant

A farmer asks a question aloud, in their own language: how do I tell good seed from bad? The agent:

- Listens and turns the speech into text.
- Searches a 154-page agricultural handbook, which is written in English.
- Answers in two to four spoken sentences, in the language the question was asked in, using only what the handbook says.
- Speaks the answer back and shows the source pages, so the answer can be checked.
If someone asks about cricket or coding, it politely steers them back to farming instead of making something up.

## Where CUGA fits

CUGA (ConfigUrable Generalist Agent) is IBM Research's open-source agent harness. It handles the model wiring, tool management, state and guardrails, so you write tools and a prompt instead of the agent loop. Here we use it as an embedded SDK inside a small web app, for three things:

- One agent, any model. Switch between watsonx and OpenAI with one setting.
- The knowledge engine. Parse a PDF, chunk it, embed it, and search it locally with agent.knowledge.search() .
- Conversation threads. Each question gets a fresh thread, so one person's language or context never leaks into another's.
The key design idea is simple: CUGA is a text-in, text-out brain. Voice is two thin layers around it.

audio ──▶ speech-to-text ──▶ knowledge.search ──▶ CUGA (grounded answer) ──▶ text-to-speech ──▶ audio Because the agent only ever sees text, you can build and test it with plain text first, then add the ears and the mouth. You can also swap speech providers without touching the agent. We support two: Sarvam AI's cloud speech APIs, called directly from the user's browser, and open-source models (SraVaani for speech-to-text, Svara for text-to-speech) running on your own server.

### The hard part is not the voice

Adding speech is the easy part. The hard part is cross-lingual retrieval : a Hindi question has to find an English paragraph.

Search works by turning text into vectors and finding the nearest ones. CUGA's default embedding model is English-only, so it turns Hindi into vectors that carry almost no meaning. With it, a Hindi or Tamil question still retrieves five passages, but they are the wrong ones. The model, correctly told to answer only from what it was given, quietly says "the handbook doesn't cover that". Every layer behaves correctly, so there is no error and no warning.

The fix is to use a multilingual embedding model (we use intfloat/multilingual-e5-large ), so the same meaning lands in the same place whatever the language. Conceptually simple, though wiring it into CUGA took a small workaround (shown in the tutorial). After that, one English document serves every language, and you do not need translated copies of anything.

Our advice: before you tune a single prompt, ask your agent one question in a non-English language and check that it finds the right pages.

### Making it sound right and keeping it safe

A few small decisions mattered more than we expected:

- Write for the ear. Markdown, bullet points, citation tags and bracketed translations such as "millet (बाजरा)" all sound wrong when read aloud. The prompt asks the model not to produce them, and a light formatter strips any that slip through before speech.
- Keep guardrails cheap. Simple input checks catch obvious off-topic questions. If one gets through, the model starts its reply with OFF_TOPIC , and the app swaps in a polite redirect. No second LLM call, so the voice path stays fast.
- Ground every answer. The model sees only the retrieved passages, is told not to use outside knowledge, and the page sources are shown to the user.
- Keep keys out of the server. With the Sarvam option, the browser talks to Sarvam directly. The server receives only text and never sees the user's key.
## Try it

You do not need to set anything up to see it work. Open the voice agent in CUGA Apps on Hugging Face Spaces, ask a farming question in your language, and listen to the answer:

CUGA Apps on Hugging Face →

Want to build one yourself? Our step-by-step tutorial, Build an Indic Voice Agent with CUGA , starts from an empty folder and adds each layer in turn.

## Beyond farming: Scaling for Bharat

Nothing here is specific to agriculture. Swap the handbook for scheme documents, health advisories, or legal guides, and you have a different assistant. Swap the speech provider and you change the deployment model, such as cloud for speed or on-premises for data sovereignty, without rewriting the agent.

Voice-first, multilingual assistants are how digital services can reach people who were never served well by English-only text screens. Building them on an open, auditable harness, with answers tied to sources people can check, is how they earn trust.

This approach sits precisely at the intersection of what we are building with IBM Bharat Core. Bharat Core is an optimized AI stack built on top of IBM Sovereign Core, designed specifically for the Indian ecosystem to run Indic AI workloads securely on local infrastructure. When scaling a voice agent from a prototype to a secure enterprise application (like a vernacular KYC system or multilingual government bot), you need greater control over data sovereignty. By pairing CUGA’s flexible agent harness with Bharat Core’s ready-to-deploy Indic connectors and fine-tuned models, developers can build fully compliant, sovereign AI solutions tailored to India's unique linguistic diversity.

If you are building for India at scale, see the work happening at IBM Bharat Core .

## Learn more about CUGA

New to CUGA? Here are some places to start:

- cuga.dev : the CUGA home page.
- CUGA on GitHub : the open-source harness (Apache 2.0). Star it, file issues, or pick up a good first issue.
- CUGA documentation : setup, the SDK, knowledge, policies and configuration.

## The Map of Ancient Philosophy: Animation Shows How Socrates, Aristotle, Confucius, the Buddha & Other Great Thinkers Fit Together

in History , Maps , Philosophy | November 25th, 2026 Leave a Comment

-->

Here on Open Cul­ture, we’ve often fea­tured the charm­ing and infor­ma­tive posters of Domain of Sci­ence . Each one maps out a dif­fer­ent field of knowl­edge: there’s biol­o­gy , physics , chem­istry , quan­tum physics , quan­tum com­put­ing , fun­gi , and many oth­ers besides. But with his lat­est map, Domain of Sci­ence cre­ator Dominic Wal­li­man has turned away from the sci­en­tif­ic realm — or rather, he’s ven­tured into the larg­er intel­lec­tu­al ter­ri­to­ry out of which it emerged. His new Map of Phi­los­o­phy , which he explains in the video above , includes schools of thought going all the way back to 600 BC, and thinkers from antiq­ui­ty like Thales, Laozi, Con­fu­cius, and the Bud­dha, who lived and died before sci­ence as we know it.

That hard­ly means that they’ve become irrel­e­vant today. There still exist soci­eties described as Con­fu­cian or Bud­dhist, of course, but in the West­ern world, we’re more like­ly to refer back to — and, in many cas­es, have read a bit of — the work of Socrates, Pla­to, and Aris­to­tle. “They basi­cal­ly laid the intel­lec­tu­al foun­da­tion of West­ern phi­los­o­phy, sci­ence, and polit­i­cal thought,” says Wal­li­man. (He also reminds us that it was Socrates who said that the unex­am­ined life is not worth liv­ing, which “hits pret­ty hard in the age of the dis­trac­tion econ­o­my.”)

Though often men­tioned togeth­er, these three ancient Greeks occu­py slight­ly dif­fer­ent posi­tions on the philo­soph­i­cal map, with Socrates clos­er to the land of ethics, Pla­to to meta­physics, and Aris­to­tle to epis­te­mol­o­gy.

As Wal­li­man explains, “epis­te­mol­o­gy stud­ies knowl­edge: what it is, where it comes from, and also how it dif­fers from faith or opin­ions,” while also seek­ing out its lim­its. Aris­totle’s rig­or in test­ing and orga­niz­ing knowl­edge makes him, in a sense, one of the ear­li­est sci­en­tists. Though his body of the­o­ry may no longer be our best means of under­stand­ing how the world works, his sys­tem­at­ic pur­suit of such an under­stand­ing set him apart from much of the ancient intel­lec­tu­al world. The islands off the coast of the map’s main­land rep­re­sent sub­fields still active­ly explored today, like the philoso­phies of mind, lan­guage, pol­i­tics, reli­gion, and sci­ence — which, for all its pres­tige, remains as sub­ject to philo­soph­i­cal inquiry as any oth­er area of human endeav­or. The map of phi­los­o­phy shows us not a rar­efied, most­ly aban­doned ter­ri­to­ry, but the place where we all live our lives, exam­ined or oth­er­wise.

# The Global Antiauthoritarian Wave Is an Illusion

## The Global Antiauthoritarian Wave Is an Illusion

## Democracy Can’t Be Saved at the Ballot Box

### Larry M. Bartels

LARRY M. BARTELS is University Distinguished Professor of Political Science and Law and May Werthan Shayne Chair of Public Policy and Social Science at Vanderbilt University.

- More by Larry M. Bartels
### The Global Antiauthoritarian Wave Is an Illusion

Democracy Can’t Be Saved at the Ballot Box

Larry M. Bartels

- Share in email
- Share on Facebook
- Share on X
- Share on LinkedIn
- Copy Link Copied Article link: https://www.foreignaffairs.com/united-states/democracy-global-anti-authoritarian-wave-illusion https://www.foreignaffairs.com/united-states/democracy-global-anti-authoritarian-wave-illusion Copy
