In 2022, many observers celebrated the results of the United States’ midterm elections as a victory for democracy. The Republican Party underperformed at the ballot box, and some of the candidates most outspoken in support of former President Donald Trump’s historic effort to overturn the 2020 election outcome were among the casualties. President Joe Biden concluded that the American people “have proven once again that democracy is who we are.” New York Times reporters Nick Corasaniti, Reid Epstein, and Jonathan Weisman concurred, writing that the midterm outcome demonstrated “the resilience of the country’s democracy” as the electorate rejected “openly extremist Republican candidates.”

But that rosy interpretation was more the result of wishful thinking than careful analysis. Most of the Republicans who lost were simply bad, inexperienced candidates. In fact, Republican members of Congress who had flouted the democratic process by voting to decertify electoral votes on January 6, 2021, suffered no discernible penalty at the polls, while the minority who had stood up for the rule of law faced stiff backlash from their party’s establishment and from primary voters. And, of course, two years later, Trump stormed back into the White House.

In this year’s midterms, Trump’s party took another, even bigger beating. And again, there has been a rush to celebrate the result as a triumph for democratic values. NPR reported that “one of the big, clear winners of the midterms is American democracy itself.” Amanda Taub, an international affairs columnist at The New York Times , upped the ante, writing that “An anti-authoritarian wave appears to be crashing over elections around the world.” Just as in 2022, however, there is reason to fear that this optimistic account seriously misconstrues what happened at the polls on November 3 and what the result means for the future. History shows that voters in the United States, as in other democracies, are much more focused on the competence of their political leaders and their own well-being than on adherence to democratic procedures. To imagine that they have suddenly become guardians of democratic norms is to misunderstand the electorate’s role in the democratic process—and to underestimate the chronic susceptibility of the American political system to democratic backsliding.

### BELIEFS VS. BUTTER

It is natural to “feel pride,” as the New York Times editorial board put it, in the notion that ordinary citizens “stood up” for democratic principles at the ballot box. Democracy is the United States’ civil religion, and the voice of the people is the closest thing Americans have to the voice of God. But as the British jurist and historian Henry Sumner Maine observed in 1885, the oracle of democracy is often “not as intelligible as might be desired.” Electoral behavior is complex, and interpretations of election outcomes constructed in the hours and days after a vote often turn out to be far off the mark. Voters in democracies are less ideological than analysts generally assume. They are also less committed to abstract democratic norms than high-minded observers might hope. In a 2020 study, the Yale political scientists Matthew Graham and Milan Svolik used survey experiments to test the impact of democratic norm violations on Americans’ support for hypothetical candidates. They concluded that “only a small fraction of Americans prioritize democratic principles in their electoral choices when doing so goes against their partisan identification or favorite policies.” In 2022, real voters demonstrated the same point with their willingness to support Republican members of Congress who had participated in Trump’s bogus “stop the steal” effort.

This year, the exit polls run by a consortium of American news organizations provided superficial support for the notion that the midterm “blue wave” was an explicit rejection of Trump’s continuing assault on democratic norms. These surveys asked voters which of six issues was the most important facing the country. A third of respondents chose “the state of democracy,” and an overwhelming proportion of those who did, 79 percent, voted for Democratic congressional candidates. Taken at face value, these data suggest that more than a quarter of the electorate voted Democratic because they opposed Trump’s efforts to subvert American democracy.

Alas, people’s explanations for their own behavior are often misleading. Responses to list choices of this sort are particularly sensitive to the specific options presented and their favorable or unfavorable connotations. Given the choice, most people would probably prefer to attribute their votes to principled support for democracy than to pique at the price of gas. But when a separate YouGov poll conducted just after the vote asked an open-ended version of the same question, only five percent of voters spontaneously cited government corruption or the undermining of democracy as the most important factor motivating their choice.

A closer look at the exit poll data offers additional grounds for skepticism regarding the importance of democratic principles for the 2026 midterm outcome. The largest swing away from the Republican Party, more than 30 points, was among young voters—who are generally much less supportive of democracy than other age cohorts. (A 2025 Kettering Foundation survey, for instance, found that although 89 percent of Silent Generation respondents agreed with the proposition that “democracy is the best form of government,” only 54 percent of Gen Z respondents did.) To suppose that young people are now the vanguard of a sudden urge to defend democracy is implausible.

# Intellectual telescopes

## Intellectual telescopes

In a pre­vious post , I tried out an analogy for AI-assisted work: the pantograph, a once-ubiquitous tool for trans­forming human draw­ings vastly larger or minutely smaller, allowing human-sized hands to per­form nimbly at dif­ferent scales.

Here’s another analogy from the com­ments sec­tion on Scott Aaronson’s blog :

> In any case, I recently saw this num­ber­phile video on the Rie­mann hypoth­esis with Jon Keating. At some point, Brady asks him some­thing like “Is it pos­sible that the proof of the Rie­mann hypoth­esis is some­thing that no human can understand, that our hardware, our brains, just can’t process?” And Keating replies “Yes, that is pos­sible. Humans have faced this before. If I want to see the stars, I would quite like to see them with my own eyes. But there are cer­tain things in the uni­verse that the Hubble space tele­scope can see that my eyes can’t see. And I am pre­pared to accept that the Hubble space tele­scope does a better job than my eyes. And I just look at the pic­tures it pro­duces, in wonderment”.

I like this a lot. Although, it’s impor­tant to say the formal math lan­guage Lean is as much “the space tele­scope” here as the AI lan­guage models; they wouldn’t be able to pro­duce any­thing leg­ible or ver­i­fi­able without it.

Finally, it strikes me that this kind of work is very impor­tant —  it’s the equiv­a­lent of actu­ally ren­dering space tele­scope “images” (which are just streams of numbers) into pic­tures, very prob­ably false-colored, that humans can con­sider and appreciate.

P.S. Of course, you could also use another analogy , emphasis mine … 

> As long as there are prob­lems to solve, and as long as we bring some­thing to their resolution, I think we should ride the AI dragon . We should enhance ourselves, move up in abstraction, and let the dragon deal with what it does better than us. [ … ]

> I doubt that riding the dragon can be a pro­gram for the steady-state ASI sce­nario (if there is one), but it can be a pro­gram for now. The dragon is get­ting bigger every three months. It may ride itself at some point, but so far few can ride it properly. Those who do not ride it now may never be able to ride it in the future, at least not to find new things.

 … which, from the title of this blog, you already know I love 🤓

items.body:
# Wie Wespen einander am Gesicht erkennen

Unser menschliches Gehirn ist darauf spezialisiert, Gesichter zu erkennen. Das geht so weit, dass wir sogar dazu neigen, Gesichter in unbelebte Objekte wie Steckdosen, Autos oder Wolken hineinzuinterpretieren. Frühere Studien haben bereits gezeigt, dass spezielle Nervenzellen in unserem Gehirn, die sogenannten Gesichtszellen , detaillierte Merkmale von Gesichtern kodieren und uns damit ermöglichen, uns das Aussehen tausender Menschen zu merken .

## Kleines Hirn, komplexes Sozialleben

Doch auch soziale Insekten sind teils erstaunlich gut darin, ihre Artgenossen am Gesicht zu erkennen. „Ähnlich wie Primaten haben weibliche nordamerikanische Papierwespen (Polistes fuscates) die Fähigkeit zur individuellen Gesichtserkennung entwickelt, die sie nutzen, um Kooperationen und Konflikte innerhalb ihrer Gemeinschaften zu regeln“, berichtet ein Team um Christopher Jernigan von der Cornell University in New York.

Unter anderem merken sich die Wespen, wer welche Position in der sozialen Hierarchie einnimmt. Das gilt sogar, wenn sie als unbeteiligte Zuschauerinnen Kämpfe zwischen Nestgenossinnen beobachten. „Bei einer erneuten Begegnung behandeln sie die Siegerin dieses Kampfes anders als die Verliererin“, sagt Jernigan. „Trotz ihrer kleinen Gehirne und ihres relativ einfachen Sehvermögens führen sie ein wirklich komplexes soziales Leben, das sich um diese spezielle Fähigkeit dreht, einander zu erkennen.“

## Spezialisierte Nervenzellen

Gemeinsam mit seinen Kollegen hat Jernigan nun erforscht, wie die Gesichtserkennung im Wespenhirn funktioniert. Dazu fingen sie wildlebende Wespen ein, machten sie durch Kälte weitgehend bewegungsunfähig, fixierten sie dann mit Wachs und platzierten Elektroden in ihrem Gehirn. Anschließend präsentierten die Forschenden den Tieren verschiedene Bilder als Stimuli, darunter Gesichter und seitliche Körperaufnahmen von Artgenossen, geometrische Formen sowie Aufnahmen von anderen Insekten, Blumen und Autos.

„Wir haben dabei eine lokalisierte Population von Neuronen gefunden, die analog zu den menschlichen Gesichtszellen sind und die wir als ‚Wespenzellen‘ bezeichnen“, berichtet das Forschungsteam. „Diese Neuronen feuern selektiv bei Bildern von Wespen, die deren Kopf von vorne zeigen.“ Weitere Versuche mit bearbeiteten Wespengesichtern in schwarz-weiß oder Farbe enthüllten, dass manche Nervenzellen im Wespenhirn auf Formmerkmale und Kontraste spezialisiert sind, während andere auf unterschiedliche Farbverteilungen reagieren.

## Parallelen zur menschlichen Gesichtserkennung

Obwohl das Gehirn der Wespen wesentlich weniger komplex aufgebaut ist als unseres, haben die sozialen Insekten offenbar evolutionär unabhängig einen ähnlichen Mechanismus zur Gesichtserkennung entwickelt. Die Forschenden betonen jedoch, dass die Wespenzellen unseren Gesichtszellen zwar ähneln, aber nicht mit ihnen gleichzusetzen sind. „Sie stellen eine einzigartige Lösung für ein ähnliches Problem dar“, erklären Jernigan und seine Kollegen.

Dennoch hoffen die Forschenden, dass die Einblicke ins Wespenhirn auch neue Erkenntnisse über die menschliche Gesichtserkennung ermöglichen. Gerade durch den einfacheren Aufbau könnten sich Grundprinzipien der visuellen Verarbeitung, die womöglich auch für den Menschen gelten, bei den Wespen besser identifizieren lassen. „Wenn wir die Verbindungen zwischen den Schaltkreisen sowie die Rolle von Erfahrungen bei der Entstehung der Identitätserkennung besser verstehen, kann uns das dabei helfen, unser eigenes Gehirn besser zu verstehen“, sagt Jernigan.

Quelle: Christopher Jernigan (Cornell University, Ithaca, New York, USA) et al., Cell, doi: 10.1016/j.cell.2026.10.052

Personally I absolutely hate this feature as it has bitten me so many times and I cannot once remember it helping me. items.body:
# Abolish Lock Poisoning

- Armin Ronacher 's Thoughts and Writings blog archive projects talks about Abolish Lock Poisoning written on November 25, 2026 Rust has a curious feature that I don’t think the language would land today, if it was not there for a long time: mutex poisoning. When some Rust code panics while holding a std::sync::Mutex , the mutex is poisoned . That means that any further call to lock() returns a PoisonError . The motivation for this feature is that an object might have some internal invariants that need to be upheld and panicking in the wrong moment might invalidate reasonable at and leave an object behind in a broken state. Personally I absolutely hate this feature as it has bitten me so many times and I cannot once remember it helping me. The libs team is discussing making the non-poisoning locks the default in the next edition but entirely expectedly it has caused quite a few people to jump to the defence of the feature. In this post I want to make my personal case why poisoned locks should either be entirely removed or be made the exception. Primarily this is because I have yet to come across code in the wild that handles a poisoned lock correctly. On the other hand I have come across enough code that mishandles it and as a result behaves worse than a parking_lot lock would which does not support poisoning. Josh Triplett put it quite strongly in a hackernews comment: “In the entire history of the standard library, we have never once seen a single report of anyone attempting to recover from poison.” When a panic happens with a lock held, there are two reasonable reactions: shut the process down, or carry on and ignore the flag. With panic = "abort" you get the former and poisoning never comes up. From all the evidence I have seen, with unwinding, the idiomatic lock().unwrap() picks the worst option of all. That’s because it neither stops the process nor lets it continue as it will turn every further lock into a panic with sometimes disastrous effects. But that is not the only issue with the system today. So here I want to share some of the issues and with some references to real world code of how people got bitten. The Error Holds the Lock One subtle aspect to the poisoning is that the PoisonError needs to hold the guard. That’s because in order to ignore the poison flag, you need to fetch the guard from the error object. Holding on to the error means holding on to the lock! That can cause common code that does error wrapping / error conversions into a deadlock hazard. The innocent looking m.lock()? in a function returning Box<dyn Error> or similar keeps the mutex locked for as long as the error lives ( #159930 ). This can also happen with if let. For instance in cc-switch you can see that they had a test hung because a if let Ok(..) = lock() { .. } else { .. } fallback locked the same mutex again while the unnamed PoisonError from the condition still owned the guard. PC-AI had the same bug in a match arm. Another case can be found in ox-embed-server . Panic To Outage Deviously poisoning does not fail fast and done wrong, it fails forever. The original panic happens once, on one thread, often somewhere unrelated from future failures. Every later lock().unwrap() on that lock now however panics as well, and because so much Rust code survives panics (thread pools, request handlers, tokio tasks, FFI boundaries), the process stays up and becomes useless: In RLS a failed cargo build panicked with ENV_LOCK held which made any subsequent runs impossible .
- Mozilla’s application-services saw PoisonError rise to rank 5 in crash stats and moved to parking_lot after they concluded they did not benefit of poisoning handling.
- A Neon safekeeper on staging failed every timeline lookup after a panic with a global lock held, and the original panic could not even be found in the logs.
While not live services, test suites show the same general issue. One failing test poisons a shared static and every test after it fails with PoisonError . This problem showed up for cargo , deno , polars and rustc itself.

## Attempt At Recovery

If you recover with into_inner() , the flag stays set and every later access takes the recovery path again. And remember that for the first nine years of Rust after the poisoning feature landed, you could not even clear it as clear_poison arrived only in 1.77. Not clearing the flag means that potentially expensive side effects will happen from that point onwards:

goose-in-a-pond rebuilt its decoder state on every transcription after a single panic, librefang logged the same warning on every access, and a pool threw its model away on every return.

## Nobody Relies on It, Not Even std

So who is handling poisonings? I’m really not sure, definitely not the standard library. Every place where the standard library’s own code ignores it. Standard I/O has done so since March 2015 , two months before 1.0, because “any poison must have been the result of user code which the lock isn’t protecting”. A common issue with a lot of poisoning errors that never had anything to do with the mutex that was held.

Same with the panic output capture , the backtrace lock and the WASI environment lock . They all do the same and unsurprisingly there is an open PR to move std’s internal mutexes to nonpoison .

And I would argue the ecosystem has largely come to the same conclusion. Tokio’s own locks don’t poison. Internally it wraps the std one in an adapter that removes poison . When it landed Carl Lerche remarked “ I rather pretend lock poisoning isn’t a thing .” In one case Eliza Weisman needed into_inner to unlink a waiter during drop, or “we’ll leave the list with a potentially dangling pointer”. I want to point to this in particular because this is a case where poisoning stood in the way of memory safety which is commonly argued as a reason you want poisoning.

Wasmtime, crossbeam-channel, tracing-subscriber always ignores lock poisoning. rust-analyzer switched to parking_lot after cancellation poisoned its solver like RLS did before. The parking_lot maintainer described it as an anti-feature that hurts usability and reliability to which I strongly concur.

## Why Only Mutex?

Another aspect here is why this is done on Mutex but not on RefCell . Surely if the case for poisoning is that some code temporarily breaks an invariant, panics, and someone else observes the broken state, then this should apply to more cases.

Take the usual example that argues in favor of poisoning and replace Mutex with RefCell , and you have exactly the same problem . Threads are not needed at all and this is not hypothetical either as tokio catches every task panic. Paired with a LocalSet the panic comes back as a JoinError , the next borrow() succeeds and reads a null pointer exactly like the mutex example from the issue.

…

items.body:
# Irreducible Governance Structure for Autonomous Agent Systems: Fair Allocation, Strategy-Proofness, and Multi-Scale Composition

## Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

- [Submitted on 19 Nov 2026] Title: Irreducible Governance Structure for Autonomous Agent Systems: Fair Allocation, Strategy-Proofness, and Multi-Scale Composition Authors: Marcelo Fernandez View a PDF of the paper titled Irreducible Governance Structure for Autonomous Agent Systems: Fair Allocation, Strategy-Proofness, and Multi-Scale Composition, by Marcelo Fernandez View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Autonomous agent governance is commonly framed as a problem of enforcing correct execution. However, in multi-agent systems, an equally fundamental question precedes execution: which agents are allowed to act. In this paper, we show that allocation is not an auxiliary concern but a structural component of governance. When multiple agents compete for execution under constrained resources, any allocation mechanism introduces unavoidable trade-offs between fairness, efficiency, and resistance to strategic manipulation. We formalize this through a set of impossibility results, including Sybil amplification and the incompatibility of desirable allocation properties. We then show that these allocation constraints cannot be resolved within a single layer of control. Instead, they propagate across the system, interacting with execution atomicity, state enforcement, and behavioral drift. This leads to a multi-scale governance structure composed of four orthogonal dimensions: temporal (atomicity), state (enforcement), behavioral (drift monitoring), and population (allocation). Our main result is an irreducibility theorem: under finite observability, no governance architecture can collapse these dimensions without loss of correctness or stability. Allocation, in particular, acts as a first-class constraint that prevents simplification of the governance stack. We validate these results through a series of analytical constructions and empirical ablations, showing that removing or approximating any layer leads to systematic failure modes. This work reframes agent governance as a structural problem: not only how actions are executed, but how access to execution is determined, and why these decisions impose irreducible architectural requirements. Comments: 19 pages. AI News for 11/23/2026-11/24/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, [544 Twitters](https://twitter.com/i/lists/1585430245762441216) and no further Discords. [AINews' website](https://news.smol.ai/) lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, [AINews is now a section of Latent Space](https://latent.space/p/2026/). You can opt in/out of email frequencies!

## AI Twitter Recap

**Frontier Models as Research Engines: VP ≠ VNP, Protein Design and 948 Kernel Bugs**

- VP ≠ VNP, posted by two labs: An Anthropic GitHub repo reportedly contains a proof by an internal Claude research model that VP ≠ VNP. This is the algebraic analogue of P vs NP, posed by Valiant in 1979, and implies that polynomials such as the permanent lack small circuits over every field ([@kimmonismus](https://x.com/kimmonismus/status/2125131886271795290), [repo pointer](https://x.com/BlancheMinerva/status/2125085344555053363)). OpenAI's counter-release: OpenAI then posted its own proof and says it was "obtained on November 6, 2026." Neither lab named a model or published an announcement ([@AndrewCurran_](https://x.com/AndrewCurran_/status/2125289527531245998)).
- Scope: The result does not imply P ≠ NP, which still requires general Boolean circuit lower bounds ([@ZhihuFrontier](https://x.com/ZhihuFrontier/status/2125170512011944026)).
- Speculation: Curran argues that both labs are sitting on unreleased results and repeats unconfirmed rumors of cryptography breakthroughs. Treat this as opinion.
- Riemann proof clarifications: Levent Alpöge says the "250,000+ pages" claim was a joke. He released only the Lean code because he could not produce a readable writeup, and called it "full of garbage obviously, but compiles" ([@kimmonismus](https://x.com/kimmonismus/status/2125148979880964496), [@simonw](https://x.com/simonw/status/2125001984029921636)). Lineage claim: A Zhihu analysis traces Alpöge's key method to a short OpenAI proof excluding Landau–Siegel zeros. This is an attributed inference ([@ZhihuFrontier](https://x.com/ZhihuFrontier/status/2125200727140438125)).
- GPT-6 protein design, wet-lab validated: OpenAI released a preprint showing GPT-6 models designing new protein shapes and sequences through reasoning and code, without specialized bio models ([@OpenAI](https://x.com/OpenAI/status/2125334383490105601)). Results: 14 of 107 resequenced proteins showed binding. 128 of 182 redesigned small antibodies and 179 of 272 antibody fragments retained binding ([details](https://x.com/OpenAI/status/2125334392814051724)).
- Cost caveat: On a prior DNA task, GPT-6.1 Sol was about 2,000x more expensive per task than a specialized model ([@_lewtun](https://x.com/_lewtun/status/2125358915881984347)).
- GPT-6 Cyber and the Linux kernel: In one run, GPT-6 Cyber helped validate 948 Linux kernel bugs that could grant local root and generated patches for maintainer review ([@OpenAI](https://x.com/OpenAI/status/2125007927098699827)).
- Discovery beyond verifiable domains: A historian says GPT-6.2 Astra identified the vicomte de Chabot as the artist of an anonymous 1808 Yale sketchbook in 22 minutes. It also surfaced an obscure microfilmed diary whose handwriting and itinerary matched the sketches ([@HistoryGPT](https://x.com/HistoryGPT/status/2125213218045858149)). Exoplanet candidates: Amateurs using Codex and Astra searched Kepler and TESS data. One 13.8-day signal was independently confirmed by a SETI astronomer, and 49 TESS candidates were flagged ([@OpenAI](https://x.com/OpenAI/status/2125305606685053416)).
- Robotics saturation: GPT-6.2 Astra on Codex scored 97% on RoboDojo-RC Tier 1 across 120 real-robot trials, and RoboDojo is being retired ([@robocurve](https://x.com/robocurve/status/2125028977194786857)). New environments: Einsia released RoboUniverse-10K, a set of 10,807 verifiable Isaac Sim tasks built from real manipulation videos. The top frontier score on held-out tasks is 85.8%, while 7 of 11 models score ≤10% ([@EinsiaAI](https://x.com/EinsiaAI/status/2125235490567897265)).

**Gemini 4 Neon Rollout and Frontier Model Moves**

## Retributive Justice

Retributive justice is best understood as the form of justice committed to the following three principles:

- that those who culpably commit certain kinds of wrongful acts, paradigmatically serious crimes, morally deserve to suffer proportionate punishment;
- that it is morally right or intrinsically good—without reference to any further goods that might arise—for some (legitimate) punisher to impose the punishment they deserve; and
- that punishment must not be imposed in the absence of desert or exceed what would be proportional to the wrongful action.
While retributivism was for a long period of time disregarded as “a barbaric remnant of superstitious thought that more rational forms of society would sweep away” (Bennett 2014: 4446), recent work on retributivism has gained much support in the philosophy of punishment, making retributivist views among the dominant candidates for a positive justification of punishment. Still, critics continue to voice the charges of barbarism (Tadros 2011) and moral repugnancy (Scanlon 2008), and many features of retributivism—especially the notions of desert, proportionality, the normative status of suffering, and the ultimate justification for retribution—remain contested. Though theories of retributive justice have ancient and medieval roots, this entry focuses on contemporary conceptions of retributive justice.

- 1. Introducing Retributive Theory 1.1 On Punishment

## 1. Introducing Retributive Theory

### 1.1 On Punishment

Retributivism offers a justification of punishment. While the definition of punishment is itself a matter of controversy, punishment generally refers to the deliberate or intentional imposition of burdens or suffering on wrongdoers for an act or omission that the punisher believes to be (a culpable) wrong. (The entry on legal punishment discusses this concept in depth.) This definition includes both punishment as it is imposed by the state in the public sphere for the commission of crimes and punitive responses to wrongdoing in other spheres, including the private and the institutional. Still, the challenge of justifying state punishment is the most pressing, as the forms of punishment imposed by the state generally involve sanctions that are different in kind from and more onerous than those imposed outside the political sphere, paradigmatically involving the deprivation of basic human rights (to life, liberty, and property, among others).

Punishment is often analyzed in terms of two constituent parts: censure (or condemnation) and sanction (or hard treatment, that is, treatment that involves a hardship imposed on the person being punished, or at the very least the withdrawal of a benefit to which they would otherwise be entitled).

### 1.2 Basic Strengths and Weaknesses

### 1.2.1 Intuitive Appeal

Many share the intuition that those who commit wrongful acts, especially serious crimes, should be punished even if punishing them would produce no other good (see Darley & Robinson 2002). Consider, for example, being the sentencing judge for an offender who has been convicted of rape. How should you sentence him? You may have the intuition that he should not be “let off easy”. If so, you might think that this reflects the importance of incapacitating him, deterring him and others from future criminal acts, or publicly condemning the crime. But now suppose that he has since suffered an illness that has left him physically incapacitated so that he cannot rape or commit other violent crimes again. Moreover, he has enough money to support himself without resorting to criminal activities. You therefore have no need to take steps to prevent him from committing future crimes. Still, others might be emboldened if you don’t punish him. So suppose further that you could “sentence” him to spend his days on a tropical island of his choosing, where he can relax and enjoy himself, as long as he regularly reports to an island prison to be videoed in prison garb, footage of which is made publicly available, ensuring thereby that others harbor the false belief that he is suffering for his crime. If you believe that this could be done with no prospect of detection, should you choose such a sentence? Many share the intuition that this would be unjust. They believe that the wrongdoing should not go unpunished, even if punishment would achieve no other downstream good (see, e.g., Moore 1997: 98–101).

Not only is retributivism in this way intuitively appealing, the primary alternative, consequentialist theories of punishment that focus on deterrence, incapacitation and rehabilitation, seem to confront a deep problem: They have difficulty accommodating a core retributivist commitment, namely that these goals cannot justify imposing punishment on those who have done no wrong. They also have trouble explaining the discomfort most have with imposing disproportionately large punishments on those who have committed only minor wrongs.

Both of these sources of retributivism’s appeal have clear limits. The positive intuition can be challenged with the claim that it is merely the reflection of a morally dubious psychological propensity to feel an excess of what Nietzsche, in the Genealogy of Morals (1887), called ressentiment :

> a witches’ brew [of] resentment, fear, anger, cowardice, hostility, aggression, cruelty, sadism, envy, jealousy, guilt, self-loathing, hypocrisy and self-deception. (Moore 1997: 120)

And the argument that retributivism better justifies punishment than consequentialist alternatives presupposes that punishment is justifiable (for criticism of this premise, see Golash 2005; Boonin 2008), and that there are no alternatives that are better than both (for three alternatives, see Quinn 1985; Tadros 2011; Lacey & Pickard 2015a).

# Frontiers | A hardware-aware open-source framework for design space exploration of mixed-signal spiking neural networks

## ORIGINAL RESEARCH article

Front. Neurosci. , 25 November 2026

Sec. Neuromorphic Engineering

Volume 20 - 2026 | https://doi.org/10.3389/fnins.2026.1982497

## A hardware-aware open-source framework for design space exploration of mixed-signal spiking neural networks

- S N Sayma Nowshin Chowdhury 1 †
- V N Vineeta Nair 1 †
- T F Taseen Forhad 1 †
- A N Aishwarya Natarajan 2
- C H Corey Hart 3
- S S Sahil Shah 1 *
- 1. Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of Maryland, College Park, MD, United States
- 2. Hewlett Packard Labs, Milpitas, CA, United States
- 3. Lockheed Martin, Philadelphia, PA, United States
- See more
Article metrics

## Abstract

Introduction:

Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing at the edge requires simulation tools that can capture the non-ideal behavior of mixed-signal spiking neural network (SNN) hardware while supporting system-level design exploration.

Methods:

This work presents an open-source hardware-aware simulation framework for mixed-signal SNNs that enables comparative analysis across neuron, synapse and architecture choices. The framework supports multiple neuron models, including Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF), Hodgkin-Huxley (HH) and Axon-Hillock (AH), together with non-volatile analog synapses based on floating-gate transistors and ReRAM devices. By incorporating device-level non-linearities directly into PyTorch-based training and inference, the tool enables optimization of physical synaptic parameters rather than idealized abstract weights.

Results:

The framework is evaluated on standard neuromorphic benchmarks, including N-MNIST, DVS Gesture and Spiking Heidelberg Digits (SHD). For each model dataset configuration, it reports classification accuracy together with hardware-oriented metrics such as silicon area, power consumption and quantization sensitivity. In addition, mismatch analysis has been implemented to capture the impact of real silicon fabrication-based effects, such as device-to-device and transistor-level variability, on network behavior.

Discussion:

These capabilities enable cross-layer design space exploration and help identify neuron-synapse configurations that best satisfy application-specific constraints on accuracy, energy efficiency, area and hardware fidelity.

## 1 Introduction

Edge devices support a wide range of applications, including remote monitoring and sensing, continuous vital-sign and physiological-signal monitoring and autonomous ground and aerial robots operating in unknown environments ( Baek et al., 2025 ). The data generated by these sensors are increasingly processed using machine learning algorithms. However, edge devices are severely constrained by size, weight, area and power (SWAP), motivating the exploration of new circuit and system architectures that can efficiently process sensor data at the edge.

Neuromorphic architectures, particularly spiking neural networks (SNNs), offer a promising approach for energy-efficient edge intelligence by drawing inspiration from the event-driven operation of the brain. Unlike conventional rate-encoded neural networks, SNNs operate through discrete spike events that closely mirror the temporal dynamics of biological neurons, offering inherent advantages in energy efficiency and temporal information processing ( Maass, 1997 ; Schuman et al., 2017 ). This event-driven computation model becomes particularly compelling when implemented on neuromorphic hardware platforms, where the spatially co-located memory and compute elements enable significantly higher energy efficiency compared to traditional von Neumann architectures ( Davies et al., 2018 ; Akopyan et al., 2015 ; Painkras et al., 2013 ; Park et al., 2014 ). The biological plausibility of SNNs extends beyond their spike-based communication to encompass local learning mechanisms such as spike-timing dependent plasticity (STDP) ( Caporale and Dan, 2008 ), which demonstrate substantially lower memory requirements and power consumption compared to conventional error backpropagation algorithms.

The implementation of SNNs on mixed-signal neuromorphic hardware presents both significant opportunities and substantial challenges. Mixed-signal circuits have demonstrated superior energy efficiency compared with digital implementations ( Mead, 1990 ; Indiveri and Liu, 2015 ; Qiao et al., 2015 ; Chatterjee et al., 2019 ; Rubino et al., 2023 ); however, they are inherently affected by non-linearities and process variations that can degrade network performance ( Nair et al., 2025 ).

These hardware non-idealities introduce a fundamental gap between the theoretical performance of SNN algorithms developed in software and their practical deployment on analog neuromorphic circuits. This gap is illustrated quantitatively in Figure 1c using the SHD benchmark dataset. SHD contains complex spectro-temporal patterns, making it particularly sensitive to hardware non-idealities ( Cramer et al., 2020 ). When weights trained in snnTorch ( Eshraghian et al., 2023 ) are directly mapped onto the mixed-signal neuromorphic SNN without hardware-aware compensation, the classification accuracy decreases by 63.49% (700-200-100-20 fully connected network). In contrast, training the same network directly with the hardware models in the loop (hardware-aware training) yields 62.30 ± 3.35%, which recovers the accuracy to a level comparable to the software baseline. Hence, conventional training can converge to solutions that are more sensitive to parameter perturbations, whereas hardware-aware training encourages flatter minima that are inherently more robust to weight variations and non-idealities, consistent with the observed benefits of wide flat minima in neural network optimization ( Figure 1b ; Baldassi et al., 2020 ). As a consequence, the conventional approach of compiling software-trained parameters directly onto mixed-signal hardware often requires extensive calibration and fine-tuning of on-chip biases and voltages, increasing engineering effort and limiting the accessibility and scalability of neuromorphic computing solutions. This disconnect between algorithm development and hardware realization represents a critical bottleneck in the design of deployable neuromorphic systems.

Figure 1

Impact of hardware non-idealities on neuromorphic learning and inference: (a) Software training assumes ideal linear weight behavior. (b) Standard software training leads to narrow minima that are sensitive to hardware mismatches and non-linearities. Consequently, (c) direct deployment of SnnTorch-trained weights onto the floating-gate and Axon Hillock hardware model results in accuracy degradation in the SHD task due to (d) shifts in the decision boundary and a corresponding increase in misclassification rate.

items.body: When observers interact with an object, each observer generates a different sequence of images. However, which image statistics underlie their perceptual judgments, and whether this self-generated visual input explains what they perceive, remain unclear. We analyzed the first-person recordings of a virtual-reality experiment in which 19 observers judged whether an object was metal or glass while exploring the object with the hand, with the head, with both, and without moving. The object was rendered in two shapes at five levels of physical metallicity and in four illumination environments; every observer saw every stimulus but did so through a different video. Simple image statistics pertaining to the object, to its relation with its surround and to the changes in these properties as the observer explored predicted observers' responses effectively. Critically, when observers disagreed with regard to the same stimulus, their own videos predicted which observer said metal more accurately than chance, and this observer-specific information emerged mainly in the few seconds that preceded the response. The predictive cues identified in this context included the coverage of the optic flow, contrast, highlight coverage, luminance, and the object's luminance and color relative to its surround; furthermore, their importance varied across observers. Thus, active exploration generates different visual evidence for different observers, and their material judgments follow the evidence that they generate.

items.body:
# From formal verification to bug-finding in CHERIoT

The Cerise project 1 was started almost 10 years ago at Aarhus University. Its goal is to develop formal methods to verify properties of capability machines, in particular involving non-monotonicity, and to prove end-to-end results in the presence of unknown code. Cerise has been extended to model different aspects of capability machines, and has involved work by and collaborations with several other universities, including Dominique Devriese’s research group at KU Leuven, and the universities of Cambridge and Edinburgh.

Cerise started as pen-and-paper proofs about idealised machines and focused initially on reasoning about control-flow integrity of encapsulation for stack-based calling conventions, but over time our research group has scaled up the approach along three dimensions. First, we made our proofs foundational: Cerise now builds on the Iris separation logic framework inside the Rocq theorem prover, which has been critical to ensure correctness despite the growing intricacy of our proofs. Second, we have investigated how to reason about a wider range of properties, e.g., involving MMIO and attestation. Third, we made Cerise work with an instruction set closer to the CHERIoT Sail model, and verified programs using those instructions.

When I started my PhD, CHERIoT had just been announced. I seized the opportunity to apply the verification techniques of Cerise to the CHERIoT switcher, for example to check that it isolates compartments and enforces no-capture. To that end, we started a sub-project of Cerise, which we call Griotte 2 .

As part of our verification effort in this Griotte project, we uncovered two bugs in the CHERIoT switcher: (1) the ability for a malicious (or buggy) scheduler to resuscitate an exited thread in a deprecated state, thereby getting access to a capability that it should not be able to have access to anymore, and (2) the ability for a malicious caller to leverage the stack high watermark register to trigger a fault in the switcher, thereby getting access to the callee’s stack frame and thus private data.

## Reasoning about unknown code

The CHERI/CHERIoT threat model includes interactions with unknown compartments containing arbitrary code, which can be buggy or malicious, and which can share objects in memory. Reasoning about arbitrary code is hard, because it requires characterising all the possible behaviours of that code. The challenge is that when trying to characterise what an unknown compartment can affect, we have to account not only for what it is passed directly (if an unknown compartment is physically passed a write capability to a region of memory, then it is behaviourally passed the ability to overwrite that region of memory), but also what it is passed indirectly—and this involves not only recursive access (if an unknown compartment is physically passed a read capability to a region of memory, then it is behaviourally passed the ability to acquire whatever ability is given by the capabilities in that region of memory), but also access through non-monotonic domain transitions (if an unknown compartment is physically passed a sealed entry point capability to a “counter” compartment’s incr function, then it is behaviourally passed the ability to affect the counter—but only by incrementing it). A unique feature of Cerise is the ability to reason also about the latter part of the challenge.

What makes it difficult to design such a characterisation is that it should at the same time be precise enough, and simple enough to verify the programs that we care about. At a very high level, Griotte defines a language to succinctly describe what is affected—and to state that something is not affected. The kind of properties that we want to describe are not only memory safety properties (if I share a buffer to the caller, then I have the guarantee that it cannot access the global data that I never shared), but also no-capture properties (if I share a buffer to the caller with its global permission stripped, then I have the guarantee that it cannot preserve a copy across calls), and many others (including secrecy, etc.).

## Separation logic and logical relations

Technically, we developed a reasoning system in two parts. First, we defined (and proved sound) a separation logic that allows us to verify known code line by line, showing that it satisfies expected pre- and post-conditions, and that it preserves the expected invariants. We used this both on the code of the switcher, and on the code of specific compartments of interest, for example a key-value store 3 . We designed this separation logic so it is reusable, and we expect that other such compartments of interest could be verified with it.

Second, we defined a logical relation in separation logic, which is effectively an over-approximation of the effect of unknown code that can be used by the separation logic to reason about a jump to unknown code (through the switcher) in one single step. As such, it works like a universal contract 4 for CHERIoT. Crucially, the frame rule of separation logic tells us that if we can establish that the resources (both in an informal sense, and in the technical sense of separation logic) of the caller are disjoint from those of the logical relation, then they will be preserved by the call.

For example, if calling unknown code with a capability to a shared buffer, while keeping some private data, the logical relation requires that the unknown code is only passed capabilities that are safe to share in a technical sense.

We then define a universal contract, stating that if an adversary has only access to safe to share capabilities, it can then execute safely and only produce other safe to share capabilities.

## Verification in the presence of compartments and a trusted switcher

We started by developing a simplified model of CHERIoT and a mini version of the CHERIoT-RTOS. In particular, we modelled the compartmentalisation mechanisms and the cross-compartment call path of the switcher. Our simplified model mirrors the main features of the CHERIoT hardware (including the new deep locality and deep immutability permissions). While our mini switcher doesn’t follow CHERIoT’s switcher instruction-by-instruction, it implements the same steps.

In this model, we proved on a range of small examples that the CHERIoT hardware-software co-design implements the expected memory-safety properties, and that the switcher’s overall design enforces both compartmentalisation and stack safety.

items.body:
# New leaks reveal the iPhone 18e will have a redesigned camera plateau - Engadget

- Big Tech
- Apple
## New leaks reveal the iPhone 18e will have a redesigned camera plateau

We've also got further confirmation the iPhone Air 2 will have a second camera.

Diego Thomazini/Getty Images Add Engadget on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover Apple seems to have adopted a new strategy for the iPhone launch, splitting it into two phases. After launching the premium iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo in September, Apple is preparing new versions of the lower-priced models — and it looks like they'll look a lot more like the more expensive iPhones. CAD images of the new iPhone 18e seen by Engadget show a redesigned camera bump on the back of the phone, similar to the one on the Pro models. The images come from a source familiar with Apple's supply chain who who had previously shared accurate tips on the colors of the iPhone 17 and iPhone 18 Pro before they were announced.

The current iPhone 17e doesn't have a camera bump — instead, the lens has a small protrusion and sits flush against the back of the phone, with the microphone and LED flash also embedded in cutouts directly in the rear glass. But according to CAD images seen by Engadget, Apple appears to be considering changing that with the iPhone 18e. The renders show an almost square camera bump measuring about 28 mm by 35 mm that houses the single rear camera, the LED flash and the rear microphone. It's somewhat similar to the camera module on the M5 iPad Pro (which you can see in the image below).

Interestingly, it seems that the iPhone 18e will be the only model to feature this new camera plateau. The same files include the CADs for the base iPhone 18 and the iPhone Air 2, both of which are expected to launch alongside the 18e next spring. The base iPhone 18 will keep the exact same design, but now with a thicker camera module — increasing from 3.45mm (0.14 inches) to 3.8mm (0.15 inches). Apple has been using the same 48-megapixel Sony IMX904 sensor for its base models since the iPhone 15, so a thicker camera module could mean new sensors or upgraded cameras.

As for the iPhone Air 2, the CADs seen by Engadget corroborate previous rumors that Apple's ultra-thin phone will feature a second rear camera — not a surprise given that its single lens was one of the main complaints about it . Although the Air 2 will remain 5.6mm thick, the camera module will increase in thickness from 3.45mm (0.14 inches) to 3.8mm (0.15 inches), with the two lenses aligned horizontally. Bloomberg' s Mark Gurman, the leaker Digital Chat Station and analyst Jeff Pu have all said Apple is adding an ultra-wide lens to the second-generation Air, and the CAD images back those reports up.

Also, the iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 are expected to keep the same Dynamic Island as current models rather than the smaller cutout on the iPhone 18 Pro . Of course, these changes may end up being scrapped and never see the light of day, since Apple still has some time before they hit the stores next year.

items.body:
I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months.

Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply.

Coding agents in November 2025

Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5. With hindsight, this was a consequential model.

In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said:

Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach.

This held up.

Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025.

Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant.

The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right. It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself.

Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks.

The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work.

Fable class models in June/July

We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release, due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them.

In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5 - a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work.

After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn't get it back until July 1st.

For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models. My definition of these:

In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive, after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug.

A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm.

Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook.

I'd currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as "cheap Fable"). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well.

These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model.

3D modeling and game development in September/October

Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they'll produce credible models of almost anything you ask for.

I first noticed this with Claude Fable 5, but it really kicked into gear with Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and most recently the Gemini 4 family. Here's Gemini 4 Neon's attempt at "Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data", for example.

3D spatial awareness is crucial if you want to use vision LLMs for robotics. I don't know if 3D modeling capabilities are a side-effect of the labs focusing on that or vice-versa.

Back in August I experimented with having Fable 5 build me a raccoon heist game. It had 3D graphics, looked like a game, and played really poorly. GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra did a much better job but the game itself was still pretty dull after the first 90 seconds of play.

I was somewhat relieved that designing a game that was fun appeared to remain a uniquely human pursuit. I even used that in a talk in September to reassure people that us humans still had a role to play!

Then, I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 "This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun." And it worked. My Command & Conquer-style RTS went from boring to deeply entertaining overnight, after Opus spent 12 hours playtesting new features and rebalancing the gameplay.

Opus 5.5 was the first model I'd used that appeared to understand fun. I've since worked on several little game projects where prompts like "Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful" produced results that kept me engaged for significant amounts of time.

Opus 5.5 came out on September 22nd, 2026. I've been to two different conferences since then where people showed me game projects they'd been working on that really did feel like proper, worthwhile games.

The indie games scene has descended into a full-blown culture war over AI-assisted programming. A lot of people are calling GTA VI the last pre-generative AI blockbuster.

It feels like another inflection point to me.

Is Fable 5.2 an inflection point too?

I'm still trying to decide if Fable 5.2 represents a new inflection point, or just another incremental improvement.

I'm getting so much done with that model right now!

It seems to have taste that almost exactly matches my own. I have been burning through all sorts of gnarly problems that I've been thinking about (or procrastinating on) for several years now. The release notes for Datasette 1.0a42, 1.0a43, and 1.0a44 - plus LLM 0.37, 0.37.1, 0.37.2, 0.37.3, and 0.38 - all in the last three weeks, represent a flood of fixes, features and improvements.

If this does represent an inflection point, the key feature seems to be that if you can imagine and then clearly describe a piece of software, Fable can build it. That's a wild thing to say, but it matches my experience over the past few weeks.

Software development has transformed beyond recognition in the last year. I don't think I'll ever go back to typing most of my code by hand.

…

items.body:
Steven Nelson, writing for The New York Post:

> President Trump claimed Monday that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang could
> have become a leader in China’s artificial intelligence industry
> if he hadn’t been reinstated to the US firm — telling CNBC in a
> phone interview that the 63-year-old has “got a little blood
> there” despite being born in Taiwan.
> “If we didn’t do this, I could see China coming in and saying to
> Jensen, ‘Hey, how would you like to come to China?’ — He’s got
> a little [Chinese] blood in him. He’s got a little blood there — ‘How would you like to come to China and head up Huawei?’”
> Trump told CNBC in a phone interview, during which he called
> Huang, 63, a “national treasure” despite his affair with an
> alleged Chinese spy.
> “If Jensen was angry enough, if he was treated badly, maybe he
> could do that.”

This was during Trump’s [50-minute phoner on CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/23/trump-nvidia-jensen-huang.html). [As I noted](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2026/11/23/nvidia-board-reinstates-jensen-huang) yesterday, on his Truth Social blog, [Trump wrote](https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117666141823845971):

> On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a
> Great Patriot and National Treasure.

Think about how perverse Trump’s worldview is that he simultaneously declares that Jensen Huang is a “Great Patriot and National Treasure” *and* that Huang would be justified in moving to China to help the United States’ geopolitical archrival in the AI arms race “if he was treated badly”.

[★](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2026/11/24/patriotism-trump-style)

items.title: Silence and Love
items.subtitle: Music is the hand of silence cupped to hold the feeling of being alive, lifted to the lips and tasted.
items.feedText:
What differentiates music from noise is the touch of silence — the deliberate interstices between the tones, the still points in the rush of sound. As in music, so in life: “Listen to the silence inside the illusion of the world,” Jack Kerouac wrote to his first wife turned lifelong friend in reckoning with the meaning of life, “and you will remember the lesson you forgot.”

items.body:
Music is the hand of silence cupped to hold the feeling of being alive, lifted to the lips and tasted.

What differentiates music from noise is the touch of silence — the deliberate interstices between the tones, the still points in the rush of sound.

As in music, so in life: “Listen to the silence inside the illusion of the world,” Jack Kerouac wrote to his first wife turned lifelong friend in [reckoning with the meaning of life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/03/12/jack-kerouac-golden-eternity/), “and you will remember the lesson you forgot.”

Silence is the listening presence through which you hear the music of your own life, presence purified to become peace — a peace greater than joy and unburdened by understanding, a peace the other word for which may be love.

There is no piece of music that has scored more of my waking days and my writing hours than “Spiegel im Spiegel” by the Estonian composer Arvo Pärt, whose virtuosity with sound springs from his relationship to silence — something he articulates with poetic concision in a series of reflections recently shared by his son:

> Silence is always more perfect than music. You must simply learn to hear it. Silence is utterly full.
> […]
> When we speak of silence, we must keep in mind that it has two wings: Silence can be both outside of us and within us.
> The silence of our soul, over which even external noise has no power, is actually more crucial. But is also much more difficult to achieve.

A generation before him, Kahlil Gibran had captured this difficulty with piercing pointedness. “You talk when you cease to be at peace with your thoughts,” he charged in his [timeless meditation on silence, solitude, and the courage to know yourself](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/11/21/kahlil-gibran-prophet-talking/). Pärt puts it more gently:

> One does not have to speak.
> But one must love.
> One does not have to compose, one does not have to write a book.
> But one must love…
> If you do not speak, thinking, and even prayer, is clearer, and there is more space left over for love.

I have always felt that the quality of silence two people can share is one of the great measures of love — something the young poet Babette Deutsch captured beautifully a century ago:

> SILENCE
> by Babette Deutsch
> Silence with you is like the faint delicious
> Smile of a child asleep, in dreams unguessed:
> Only the hinted wonder of its dreaming,
> The soft, slow-breathing miracle of rest.
> Silence with you is like a kind departure
> From iron clangor and the engulfing crowd
> Into a wide and greenly barren meadow,
> Under the bloom of some blue-bosomed cloud;
> Or like one held upon the sands at evening,
> When the drawn tide rolls out, and the mixed light
> Of sea and sky enshrouds the far, wind-bellowed
> Sails that move darkly on the edge of night.

### donating = loving

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing *The Marginalian* (which [bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/10/22/brain-pickings-becoming-the-marginalian/) for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a [donation](https://www.themarginalian.org/donate/). Your support makes all the difference.

### newsletter

*The Marginalian* has a free weekly newsletter. It comes out on Sundays and offers the week’s most inspiring reading. Here’s [what to expect](https://mailchi.mp/brainpickings/janna-levin-rebecca-elson-anne-lamott-james-gleick). Like? [Sign up.](https://www.themarginalian.org/newsletter/)

items.body:
The trajectory from researcher to top executive at a leading R&D organization doesn’t happen overnight. It took Anthony Vetro nearly 30 years to climb the corporate ladder at Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, in Cambridge, Mass. He joined MERL in 1996, right out of college, and he has worked there ever since.

Vetro probably is best known for his research in multimedia signal processing, focusing on video compression.

Anthony Vetro

Employer

Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, in Cambridge, Mass.

Title

President and CEO

Member grade

Fellow

Alma mater

Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school)

He became an IEEE Fellow in 2011 for his contributions to video coding, three-dimensional television, and multimedia adaptation.

Mitsubishi Electric has moved away from making televisions. It now focuses on developing systems including ones used for defense, electronics, the energy industry, and space exploration.

His ascension up the executive ranks began in 2018, when he was named a vice president and director of MERL. In 2023 he was appointed its president and CEO.

He also works closely with the company’s new U.S.-based innovation facility in Cambridge. And he recently took on a dual role as deputy head of Mitsubishi Electric’s global R&D activities, including in Asia and Europe.

Vetro credits IEEE with helping him develop his management skills after he served in several IEEE Signal Processing Society leadership positions. He also learned from his key roles in establishing international standards for digital image formats and video compression, he says.

“Between my IEEE activities, standards work, and some of the business shifts in Mitsubishi Electric, I eventually graduated to more management leadership roles,” he says.

A multimedia pioneer

Vetro is the son of immigrants. His father came to the United States from Italy and his mother from Sweden when they were both in their early 20s. They settled in New York City, on Staten Island.

Although neither parent went to college, his father stressed the importance of education to his son at an early age.

“My father started in the mailroom and worked his way up to eventually managing communication accounts and infrastructure for large financial companies,” he says. “My mother worked in banks, first as a teller and later doing bank reconciliation after pursuing some professional certifications.

“Through their jobs, they saw people with college degrees getting better positions and promotions, so education was something really ingrained in me.”

Vetro says he developed a passion for mathematics and engineering in middle school. He was accepted into the Staten Island Technical High School, a specialized pre-engineering institution. There he solidified his interest in pursuing a career in the field.

“A lot of students didn’t know what they wanted to major in at college, but I knew fairly early,” he says.

He was accepted into the accelerated bachelor’s and master’s engineering degree programs at the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school). He began his bachelor’s degree program in 1992 and the master’s program in 1994.

“As part of the master’s degree program, I needed to do a thesis,” he says. “I wasn’t sure exactly what it would be on. Soon after taking my first course on image processing, I was certain that was an area I wanted to work in.”

It was an interesting time, he says, because broadcast television was going through a major transformation, shifting from analog to digital during the early 1990s. It was long before streaming services, he notes.

“I feel that industry-level engagement in IEEE is very vital to the organization in maintaining high relevance in the community and fulfilling its mission of fostering technological innovation and excellence for the benefit of humanity.”

“The idea of being able to come up with compact ways to represent this very rich information was really appealing to me,” he says. “I’m also a visual learner. I liked seeing images, and there was some nice math behind them, too.”

After he earned both degrees in 1996, Mitsubishi Electric hired him for its technical staff. He conducted research on multimedia signal processing, focusing on video compression.

“The opportunity to work on projects around digital TV broadcasting and image processing attracted me,” he says.

He conducted research in video conferencing, Internet and mobile streaming, and video coding technology, widely used for broadcasting, DVDs, and Blu-ray discs. He developed several technologies including digital TV receivers and displays, surveillance and camera-monitoring systems, automotive equipment, and satellite imaging systems.

Another advantage of joining the company, he says, was that it allowed him to pursue a doctorate in electrical engineering, also from Polytechnic, while working.

“That really sealed the deal,” he says. He received the degree in 2001.

The road to management

After six years as a technical staff member, he was promoted in 2007 to manage the group working on digital video coding, processing, and streaming. Seven years later, Vetro became its deputy director, a top-level management position that he held until 2018.

“After working for about 10 years exclusively on video compression processing technology, there were some shifts in our company’s business. Its overall strategy began to change,” he says, “so I became interested in broadening my experience beyond video.”

He was asked to lead the lab’s speech and audio team. It was more development-oriented, he says, and focused on vehicle infotainment and speech interfaces before Alexa and Siri existed. He pivoted the team’s focus more toward research and established strategic paths tailored to emerging opportunities within the organization. Recognizing emerging trends in sensing and information security, he formed groups that worked on them.

Mitsubishi Electric’s first U.S. innovation hub

To help spur innovation between Mitsubishi Electric and its U.S. customers, the company in June opened Serendie Street Boston, its first digital transformation hub in the United States. It’s colocated with MERL.

The new office is modeled after the first Serendie Street collaboration space, which Mitsubishi Electric launched in 2024 in Yokohama, Japan.

The word serendie is a combination of serendipity and digital engineering, according to the company’s website. Serendie is the digital platform designed to foster collaborations between data, people, and technology, it says. The space where people interact to extract ideas from the data is called “the street.”

The platform brings together researchers, startups, customers, and partners to identify new products, test them, run pilot programs, and scale them up.

Vetro says he’s excited about the endeavor.

items.body:
Was passiert eigentlich, wenn wir eine App auf dem Smartphone öffnen? Oft deutlich mehr, als auf dem Display zu sehen ist. Neben Verbindungen, die eine Anwendung für ihre eigentliche Aufgabe benötigt, können Kontakte zu Analyse-, Werbe- und Trackingdiensten entstehen. Android zeigt zwar an, wie viele Daten einzelne Apps übertragen, nicht aber, mit welchen Servern sie dabei kommunizieren. Wer nachvollziehen möchte, welche Netzwerkverbindungen eine Anwendung aufbaut, benötigt [zusätzliche Werkzeuge](https://www.kuketz-blog.de/empfehlungsecke/#app-verkehr).

Genau hier setzt [RethinkDNS](https://rethinkdns.com/) an. Die quelloffene Android-App vereint Netzwerkmonitor, Firewall und DNS-Filter. Sie funktioniert ohne Root-Rechte und kann sowohl einzelne Netzwerkverbindungen sichtbar machen als auch Internetzugriffe kontrollieren. Mit Blocklisten lassen sich zudem viele bekannte Werbe- und Tracking-Domains sperren.

Dieser erste Teil ist bewusst als Einstieg gedacht: Wir installieren RethinkDNS, nehmen es in Betrieb, schauen uns zwei Wege der DNS-Filterung an und untersuchen beispielhaft den Datenverkehr des DB Navigators. Eine möglichst restriktive Firewall ist noch nicht das Ziel. Zunächst soll nachvollziehbar werden, was RethinkDNS tut und welche Entscheidungen die Nutzer selbst treffen können.

## 1. Wie funktioniert RethinkDNS?

Um RethinkDNS sinnvoll einzusetzen, sollte man zunächst verstehen, welche Aufgaben die einzelnen Funktionen übernehmen und wo ihre Grenzen liegen:

- Netzwerkmonitor: Er zeigt, welche Anwendungen mit welchen IP-Adressen kommunizieren und welche DNS-Anfragen auftauchen. Das schafft Transparenz, ist aber noch kein Beleg dafür, welche konkreten Inhalte übermittelt werden.
- Firewall: Sie erlaubt es, den Internetzugriff einzelner Apps gezielt einzuschränken. Das ist beispielsweise sinnvoll für Anwendungen, die keinen Internetzugang benötigen oder nur unter bestimmten Bedingungen kommunizieren sollen, etwa ausschließlich über einen WireGuard-Tunnel. Auch einzelne Domains oder IP-Adressen lassen sich gezielt erlauben oder blockieren.
- DNS-Filterung: Anfragen an bekannte Werbe-, Tracking- oder Schadsoftware-Domains können anhand von Listen blockiert werden. Häufig kommt eine Verbindung dadurch gar nicht erst zustande.

Ein kurzes Beispiel: Eine App fragt nach tracker.example und bekommt von der DNS-Filterung keine reguläre IP-Adresse. Sie kann diesen Namen dann auf dem üblichen Weg nicht mehr zum Verbindungsaufbau verwenden. Das funktioniert aber nicht bei jeder Form des Trackings. Verwendet eine App eine direkte IP-Adresse, einen eigenen verschlüsselten DNS-Kanal oder dieselbe Domain für notwendige Inhalte und Tracking, stößt die DNS-Filterung an Grenzen.

### Warum verlangt die App eine VPN-Verbindung?

RethinkDNS verwendet die [VPN-Schnittstelle von Android](https://developer.android.com/develop/connectivity/vpn), um den Netzwerkverkehr lokal entgegenzunehmen und nach Regeln zu behandeln. Die Bezeichnung »VPN« bedeutet hier nicht, dass der gesamte Internetverkehr zu einem externen VPN-Anbieter geschickt wird oder die eigene IP-Adresse verborgen wäre.

Allerdings gibt es eine praktische Konsequenz: Pro Android-Nutzerprofil kann normalerweise nur eine VPN-Verbindung gleichzeitig aktiv sein. Wer bereits eine andere VPN-App verwendet, muss deren Zusammenspiel mit RethinkDNS prüfen. Die integrierten [WireGuard-Möglichkeiten](https://www.wireguard.com/) behandeln wir in einem späteren Teil.

## 2. Installation und Bezugsquellen

RethinkDNS ist über verschiedene Quellen erhältlich, darunter [F-Droid](https://f-droid.org/packages/com.celzero.bravedns/), [GitHub](https://github.com/celzero/rethink-app), die [Projektwebsite](https://rethinkdns.com/download) und den [Google Play Store](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.celzero.bravedns). Die Wahl der Bezugsquelle ist nicht ganz unerheblich, denn die angebotenen Varianten unterscheiden sich unter anderem bei den eingebundenen Google-Komponenten. Für diese Anleitung verwende ich Version 0.5.8 aus F-Droid.

Die Varianten von F-Droid und IzzyOnDroid kommen ohne Google-Bibliotheken aus. Seit Version 0.5.7 wurde Firebase Crashlytics auch aus den GitHub- und Website-Versionen entfernt. Die Play-Store-Version enthält dagegen weiterhin Crashlytics zur Fehlerberichterstattung. Diese ist laut Entwickler standardmäßig deaktiviert und muss unter »Konfigurieren -> Einstellungen -> Stabilitätsprogramm« ausdrücklich aktiviert werden. Ohne diese Zustimmung werden keine Absturzberichte über Crashlytics übermittelt. Wer solche Google-Komponenten grundsätzlich vermeiden möchte, greift zur F-Droid-Version.

Hinzu kommt ein funktionaler Unterschied: Die [geräteinternen Blocklisten stehen nach Entwicklerangaben](https://github.com/celzero/rethink-app/issues/3028) nicht in der Play-Store-Variante zur Verfügung. Wer diese Option nutzen möchte, sollte daher eine entsprechende andere Variante installieren.

Die F-Droid-Ausgabe von RethinkDNS. Auf dieser Variante basieren die folgenden Schritte.

Nach der Installation erscheinen vier kurze Einführungsseiten zu VPN, Firewall und DNS-Filterung. Man kann sie lesen oder überspringen. Sie sollen einen Überblick vermitteln, sind aber keine zusätzliche Konfiguration. Danach zeigt RethinkDNS zunächst » NICHT GESCHÜTZT « an. Das ist normal: Die App ist zwar installiert, verarbeitet aber noch keinen Netzwerkverkehr.

## 3. RethinkDNS zum ersten Mal starten

Mit einem Tipp auf »START« beginnt die Einrichtung. RethinkDNS erklärt zunächst, weshalb es eine lokale VPN-Verbindung benötigt. Anschließend erscheint die Android-Systemmeldung »Verbindungsanfrage«. Hier bestätigen wir mit »OK«. Android weist ausdrücklich darauf hin, dass die App den durch die VPN-Schnittstelle geleiteten Netzwerkverkehr überwachen kann. Genau diese Position benötigt RethinkDNS für seine Aufgaben. Sie setzt zugleich voraus, dass man der Anwendung vertraut.

Android fragt vor dem ersten Start nach der Erlaubnis, eine VPN-Verbindung einzurichten.

Nach erfolgreichem Start zeigt RethinkDNS den Status » GESCHÜTZT « an. Das bedeutet zunächst, dass die Anwendung aktiv ist und den Netzwerkverkehr verarbeitet. Auf der Startseite erscheinen außerdem Informationen zum verwendeten DNS-Dienst sowie zu erlaubten und blockierten Verbindungen.

RethinkDNS läuft. Oben wird der verwendete DNS-Dienst angezeigt, darunter folgen Firewall- und Aktivitätsinformationen.

### 3.1 Was passiert nach dem ersten Start?

Im Ausgangszustand dürfen die installierten Apps grundsätzlich weiterhin auf das Internet zugreifen. RethinkDNS überwacht ihre Netzwerkverbindungen, sperrt aber nicht automatisch einzelne Anwendungen. Wer den Internetzugang bestimmter Apps unterbinden möchte, muss dafür eigene Firewall-Regeln einrichten.

items.body:
photo cred: my dad

## 1.

A few years ago, some researchers put ants and humans in a head-to-head battle of wits. The task was to maneuver an awkwardly sized object through a series of obstacles, like this:

Humans and ants competed both as individuals and in groups. The humans were forbidden from communicating with one another (I guess to make the playing field more level with the ants?), and they were made to wear sunglasses and masks to prevent any nonverbal signals. The ants were allowed to do whatever they wanted, on account of them being ants. Researchers “incubated” the objects in cat food and rubbed them with tuna to make them “seem like attractive food items to the ants” (I assume humans were spared this step).

I have read the paper multiple times and I still don’t really understand why they did any of this, but [the videos they made are really cool](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2414274121):

I bring this up because watching those videos, I think to myself: that’s exactly what writing is. It’s maneuvering an awkwardly sized idea into someone’s head. It’s getting the thing wedged in the wrong spot and then backing up to reorient it. It’s wondering why something that looks so easy can be so hard. And occasionally, the whole thing reeks of tuna.

## 2.

Trying to write drives most people nuts, but nobody ever told me that there’s a good nuts and a bad nuts.

Bad nuts is when you’re sitting there thinking the same thing over and over again, or thinking nothing at all, just drumming your fingers on the desk and checking your email every 17 seconds, like “hmm...words...words...what *is* a word...”. This is both painful and pointless.

Good nuts is when you’re trying a million things a minute and almost all of them are failing. Like:

> Does it go like this?
> No.
> Does it go like this?
> No.
> Does it go like THIS?
> No.
> Does it go like t*h*i*s?
> No.
> Does it go like T~H~I~S?
> YES

This is also painful, but it ultimately results in something that you want to show other people. In this way, it is very similar to getting your unibrow waxed.

[↗ experimental-history.com](https://www.experimental-history.com/p/everything-i-know-about-writing)
