items.body:
The soulful deep greens and browns of British Columbia’s forests weave together with ferns and moss, catching the light through the tops of ancient firs and cedars. The trees sway, and the earth rises and falls among the rocks.

But in this case, the view isn’t from the trail. It is a painting by Canadian artist Emily Carr on display in the [Vancouver Art Gallery](https://www.vanartgallery.bc.ca/art-of-wellbeing/), and some of those who are experiencing it are doing so because it was prescribed by their health care provider. How they ended up there is the result of a bit of creative thinking that honors the role of art in healing.

In 2025, the gallery partnered with BC Parks Foundation to extend [PaRx](https://www.parkprescriptions.ca/), Canada’s national nature prescription program, to include the gallery. PaRx is a successful initiative that has included an estimated 2 million prescriptions issued by more than 20,000 health care providers. Typically, these prescriptions are for time outdoors, with added benefits, like free transportation, to reduce barriers to access.

Using art as an entry point into nature as a formal intervention is novel—the first collaboration of its kind between a nature prescription program and an arts institution in the world, according to Sirish Rao, the gallery’s co-CEO and executive director. While art-based prescriptions are gaining in popularity, this program goes a step further, integrating engagement with nature in a gentle, accessible way. Other institutions around the world are looking to the Vancouver Art Gallery program as a model initiative that can be replicated in other communities to support people’s well-being.

*Credit: Vancouver Art Gallery*

## An artful approach to treatment

The process starts when a health care provider like a doctor, nurse, or therapist determines that a patient might benefit from a prescription to spend time in nature, including around the nature-inspired visual art at the gallery. The benefits can be many: combating isolation, engaging mentally and physically during a gallery visit, and experiencing awe and beauty.

The prescription to Vancouver Art Gallery includes free admission for the prescription holder and a guest, as well as a printed guide that offers prompts and questions to consider—for example, to notice the varied shades of green Carr used, or imagine a walk along a trail she painted—along with research about the benefits of experiencing nature. Participants are guided through “slow looking” as the act of learning through observation, imagination exercises, and physical movement—yes, swaying in an art gallery is encouraged.

After the visit, guests are invited to continue the immersion at a local nature space, with free carshare minutes to get there if needed. The art prescription guide suggests nearby parks where participants can walk or hike, extending slow looking from a curated indoor experience to the outdoors if they choose. And they can return to the gallery as often as they like by retaining their original prescription. On site, they can join free workshops, and a coloring book offers a contemplative experience at home.

This is an example of social prescribing, a worldwide movement that serves as a complement to clinical care and typical medication prescriptions by prescribing from a wide range of activities that support physical and mental health. Beyond art galleries and nature walks, this can include music classes, exercise sessions, or gardening programs. The prescription is personal and can be tailored to patients’ needs and interests.

Carla Fry is a West Vancouver psychologist and educator with more than 20 years of clinical experience. She says the art gallery prescription has been a gift for participants, especially those who face physical, mental, social, or even financial or transportation barriers to accessing nature. Many are surprised that they don’t have to pay anything for the experience.

“For them to understand that so many people have come together to create this opportunity, I think that in and of itself is special,” Fry says. “They say, ‘Wow, my community cares.’ The possibility that this exists, it’s available, it’s free—there’s something about that... that’s noteworthy.”

Fry is one of the professionals who gives these kinds of prescriptions to her clients. It’s another tool available to promote well-being.

“Of course, I’m never telling them to go. We talk about this as a prescription, but I always present it as ‘here’s an opportunity to meet some of your goals, and here’s what the opportunity looks like,’” she says.

As yet, no one has declined her prescription.

“They’re surprised that something so seemingly simplistic as slowing down and really looking, really living in front of the art or in nature is actually an intervention,” Fry says. “People in our culture are set up to think that growth has got to be painful, growth has got to be difficult, growth has got to be expensive, growth is going to take a long time. When I bring forward an intervention of going to a location, and your job as a client of mine is to appreciate, the first reaction is surprise. It opens up an entire conversation—‘I can just appreciate my life and not always be grinding to make it better.’ It’s a special process for me to witness.”

## Awe and nature in community

The goal is to do more than increase the number of people who have exposure to art, though that might be a side effect. The formal prescription to nature through art is designed to reduce stress, anxiety, and social isolation. The ability to bring a guest, as well as the opportunity to experience art with other patrons, is key.

“There are other people there; these aren’t private viewings. But of course, sometimes people don’t feel connected to others in a room. Sometimes they do; sometimes it’s enough to feel that they’re part of a community. But others really benefit from being able to have a shared experience where they can reflect in real time and reflect afterwards,” Fry says.

Paula Toledo is the mental health advisor and lead well-being consultant at Vancouver Art Gallery, leading the [Richardson Family Art of Wellbeing Lab](https://www.vanartgallery.bc.ca/art-of-wellbeing/). The lab aims to connect the community to art as a means to improve mental and physical well-being, drawing on a collaboration of researchers, scientists, physicians, and Indigenous Elders and healers.

Toledo came to this work through the personal experience of losing her husband and her mother within months, while also caring for her newborn child. That grief and her recovery changed the course of her life and her career in wellness.

“When we encounter something so vast that it transcends our current understanding of the world, it can be very mysterious,” Toledo says:

…

items.body:
My mother tongue is Thai, but for a long time I couldn’t swear in Thai. That was because the international school I went to banned us from speaking Thai on campus. *No native languages, all the better to improve our English*. It was quite a colonial relationship. I remember the colonial roots of my English every time an American complements my fluency, now that I live in the US.

Because of the school ban my Thai was polite, sweet, but not cool. I had no slang. I could not swear. This changed in the last two years of high school. I did the International Baccalaureate, which then required fifty hours of service from each student in order to graduate with the IB diploma. That seemed like a lot of hours to me! I remember my reluctance to leave the beautiful school campus with its duck ponds and Thai sala and venture into the great unknown of the Klong Toei slums.

I was matched to work in an orphanage of kids with HIV. I squeal for babies and toddlers, and was thrilled. Thailand was early to destigmatize HIV/AIDS. I ended up spending years in this orphanage, holding babies with many wonderful volunteers. What bliss, truly. I learned the carrot dance that the toddlers were obsessed with then; I can still sing it. Then, to my chagrin, I was moved out of the baby and toddler center to be with the adolescents. I think there was some glamour to having an international school student among the older kids. I sensed status in their jostling to speak with me. When the teenagers heard me speak, they fell over themselves laughing. How did I sound like such a child! They taught me to swear. We spoke in slang. In my time in Klong Toei, my Thai finally entered adolescence.

I learned a lot in those fifty hours of volunteer service, which I ended up exceeding. First, service feels wonderful. Maybe in the very beginning it was uncomfortable because of self-consciousness—and who could be more self-conscious than a teenager. But even adolescent me was able to relax the *certainty that everyone was judging her* and enjoy the camaraderie. I brought candy, and we’d walk around in a big pack of teenagers through the slum.

I learned that when the rains come, the slum is first to flood and last to drain; I learned it loses power all the time; I learned that people can be proud of where they’re from even when home is a shack made from corrugated tin. I learned that phad thai is best made on a street-side wok; I learned that Muay Thai keeps kids, especially boys, out of trouble. I learned that no one begs nor steals if they can help it; I learned that people are generally kind and keen for friendship. It was a life-changing year, as it was meant to be.

Reflecting back on that period, I am struck by how effective it was to have a service requirement. We studied economics in IB and learned about purchasing power parity, which is the relative cost of a Big Mac in Cambodia, say, versus the US. But walking those streets, paying for food, looking away as buddies fished coins out of pockets, the cut-open plastic water bottles used to beg, and drains—that was a different education in the cost of living. Knowledge moved from head to heart.

Service can be a force-function to generosity. Some of us are born with access to our tender and generous nature; some of us have quite a crust around the heart. For whatever reasons (the causes and conditions of [karma](https://tricycle.org/buddhism-dharma/#samsara-karma-rebirth)) many of us have learned to armor the heart.

All of us are affected by culture, which is a collective karma. Thailand has a collective culture of generosity. It is startling and real. Don’t worry—there’s a shadow side to Thai culture too. I wrote a whole novel to process it.

The culture of the United States is not what I would call an open and generous one. There seems to be fear around opening the heart. It sounds like: *If I’m generous, someone will take advantage of me.*

It’s probably a well-earned fear. But we cannot begin to walk the path of a [bodhisattva](https://tricycle.org/glossary/bodhisattva/) without *dana*, generosity.

We cannot begin to walk the path of a bodhisattva without *dana*, generosity.

In the temple where I teach, students have asked what you should do if you can’t just produce generosity. What then?

It’s a brave question to voice in a room. This is the answer: Force-function generosity with service. Find a way to log fifty hours of service, and the generosity will be there in your heart by the end of that time.

We remain stuck in spiritual adolescence if we have not had a significant period of service and generosity in our lives. Spiritual adolescence is a preoccupation with comfort and status. It can last our whole life if we let it.

If you are ready to progress to adulthood, I recommend engaging in service. Letting go of individual protectiveness, and feeling the wide river of the heart’s flow is actually a relief. It is freeing in and of itself (though it is not Enlightenment). Push the edges of your comfortable existence and commit significant hours to service. It will widen the aperture of your heart and bring flow again. In Thai the word “kindness” literally means “water of the heart.” My mother tongue is wise. Kindness does flow. It arises naturally, without effort. Giving comes naturally, without effort. When there is flow. If there isn’t flow, we have to poke a hole in the armor of the heart. You poke a hole through service.

If you’ve traveled to developing countries from the US, you might have noticed the baseline generosity of most people. One reason for this is because people from a poor place have had to take responsibility for collective well-being. When you are from a poor country, you *know* that no one is coming to bail you out. Here in the US we might have a fantasy of FEMA or the President or the National Guard coming to people’s aid.

They do, sometimes. And, turning away because the National Guard has been deployed is a way of making the suffering of people connected to us Not Our Problem. That is the easy egoic slide away from responsibility. In Thailand, when it floods, people pick up a bucket.

Eventually, if you continue on this path, all action is service. You find that you’ve planted yourself in the place of service. It is your purpose. It feels good. It’s the only place you want to reside.

Things can even look similar, on the outside, whether you’re doing service or not.

An example of this is Yo-Yo Ma. Born a prodigy, no matter what, Ma probably would have spent his life playing music. But we don’t hear Ma playing just Bach for the rest of his life. (Sublime Bach!)

items.subtitle: These four Kontakt instruments from Soundsphat deliver thousands of highly editable, release-ready presets.

items.body:
These four Kontakt instruments from [Soundsphat](https://www.soundsphat.com/cassiopeia-soundsphat-production-suite-1)deliver thousands of highly editable, release-ready presets. Let’s see what sample-based sound design has to offer your productions.

Software synthesizers completely revolutionized the way music was made, and the sound of almost every genre of music has changed as a result. But arguably at least as influential to the music we hear today were sample-based instruments, such as those made for NI’s Kontakt.

From meticulously recreated playable orchestras to special effects and sound design tools, everybody with a computer can produce more complex, modulatable tones in seconds than the entire BBC Radiophonic Workshop could manage in decades.

But with so many analogue-modelled soft synths on the market today, it feels like we rarely use sampled instruments for our core sounds. Which is where the Cassiopeia bundle of Kontakt instruments comes in.

Guided by Grammy-nominated Christian Beat Hirt, Soundsphat aims to deliver a definitive selection of production-ready presets, complete with performance and modulation options, and all of the envelope, filter, and effects controls you could desire.

## Production Suite 1 Overview

There are four instruments in the package: Cassiopeia, Landlord Stabs, Zerotone 6, and The Riga Piano. Each has its own sonic concept but all share a similar interface and layer-based approach to sound design, so we'll devote most of this review to the headline instrument, Cassiopeia, then explain how the others each riff on this concept.

Cassiopeia is based around four sound layers. The first two play host to the core sound layers like multisampled analogue synth layers, custom wavetables, acoustic-instrument-sourced waveforms, and more. The second two are sound-design-focused layers, including everything from bird calls and bells to subs and metal clangs. You can even add your own layers.

In terms of content, the headline figures are pretty impressive: a 422 GB library size (compressed to around 350 GB on your drive) with 58,000 samples, 120 custom wavetables, and 3,922 multisampled patches.

The sound design is top-notch throughout and the biggest selling point of this package by far. You could absolutely make complete, great-sounding tracks with nothing more than the sounds on offer here. Every kind of patch is covered, from basses and leads to pads and effects. And they’re incredibly polished, rich, slathered in effects, and ready to use.

For all that variety, though, this collection does very much have a distinct vibe. And it’s aimed squarely at the dancefloor and energetic playlists, so if you don’t like those kinds of sounds, this probably won’t be your bag.

## Cassiopeia In Use

Once you’ve found your sounds there is a powerful range of editing options.

The main interface is fairly uncomplicated with an X-Y modulation matrix for simultaneous real-time modulation of multiple effects and some headline parameters such as pitch bend range, filter cutoff and resonance, tone, volume, and velocity sensitivity. Plus buttons to add/mute each of the four sound layers that make up a Cassiopeia patch.

Cassiopeia’s main page and X-Y modulation control

There are then six editing pages. EDIT offers up various controls. For example, polyphony, portamento, and a chord maker feature. Then you can apply up to nine effects: Reverb/convolution, Room, Comp, Delay, EQ, Tape, Chorus, Flanger, and Phaser, with detailed controls for each.

The EDIT page, with its nine effects

Next comes ADSR, offering up assignable envelope control for volume, cutoff, and pitch of each individual layer. This is very welcome, but unfortunately brings us to the first of only two gripes about this synth. The way you assign the envelopes to the layers is really unintuitive, and hard to understand even after reading the manual. You use the same on/off button to assign a voice to an envelope group as you do to call up that voice’s individual envelope settings. It’s definitely worth revisiting in an update.

Envelopes for volume, cutoff and pitch on the ADSR page

Speaking of which, the LFO page has the same sound-shaping benefits and confusing assignment system as ADSR.

The LFO page

Luckily the ARP window is not confusing at all, offering a powerful and intuitive step-sequence-style programmer and all of the swing and timing controls you’d hope for. There’s even a randomize function.

It’s no surprise, then, that some of the most satisfying patches in the whole instrument are found in the ARP preset category – there’s just something fundamentally usable about them, enhanced by the top-tier sound design of each patch. Just keep an eye on the timing as you’ll find most arp-based patches need between −5 and −20 ms of track delay to slot into a project.

The ARP page’s step-style programmer

The MIX window comes next, with level and pan controls for each of the four layers, plus individual per-layer controls for things like pitch (semitones and cents), high- and low-pass filters, and Body and Silk (for boosting or easing low-mid and high-mid frequencies, respectively).

The layer-based architecture of Cassiopeia patches means you’ll probably spend a lot of time in this window, and it’s powerful and well laid out. It’s a shame, then, that there’s some real jank to the level fader controls – it can be really hard to get hold of them with the mouse pointer, particularly if you’ve previously pulled one all the way down.

Per-layer controls on the MIX page

Finally, there’s SOUND MENU, which allows you to swap different sound layers in or out. The options for each layer are neatly labelled and categorized, so if you’re the experimental type you’ll find hundreds of options allowing for many thousands of permutations.

Swapping layers in the SOUND MENU

## What About The Rest Of The Bundle?

Landlord Stabs uses the same basic design to deliver a selection of over 500 chord and stab-based presets. Named after the legendary [Landlord stab](https://www.attackmagazine.com/technique/synth-secrets/make-rave-stabs-like-the-landlord-stab/), this instrument goes further, with organs, orchestral-style, and other hits. If you’re after rave leads, look no further, but there’s much more to it than that.

Landlord Stabs

Zerotone 6 next, and this one is as close as the bundle gets to a conventional synthesizer, but still very much based on layered elements and inventive modulations. It gets its core sounds from two analogue synths – the Sequential Circuits Prophet-10 and Studio Electronics SE-1, judging from the images – allowing real-time blending, bending, and cross-modulation of the various waveforms in a custom granular engine. It sounds great, offers a bunch of usable presets, and has oodles of scope for user sound design.

…

items.title: Was zehn Jahre Wissenschaftskommunikation.de verändert haben
items.subtitle: Wissenschaftskommunikation ist politischer geworden und muss sich in einer zunehmend polarisierten Welt behaupten.
items.feedText: Annette Leßmöllmann und Markus Weißkopf sprechen zum zehnjährigen Jubiläum von Wissenschaftskommunikation.de über Erfolge, Herausforderungen und notwendigen Wandel. Am 24. November 2016 ging Wissenschaftskommunikation.de online. In unserem Schwerpunkt zum zehnjährigen Jubiläum blicken wir auf prägende Entwicklungen zurück und fragen, wo die Wissenschaftskommunikation heute steht. Mit welcher Idee und welchem persönlichen Anspruch seid Ihr 2016 an der Gründung von Wissenschaftskommunikation.de beteiligt gewesen?…
items.body:
Wissenschaftskommunikation ist politischer geworden und muss sich in einer zunehmend polarisierten Welt behaupten. Annette Leßmöllmann und Markus Weißkopf sprechen zum zehnjährigen Jubiläum von Wissenschaftskommunikation.de über Erfolge, Herausforderungen und notwendigen Wandel.

Am 24. November 2016 ging Wissenschaftskommunikation.de online. In unserem [Schwerpunkt zum zehnjährigen Jubiläum](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/wo-steht-die-wisskomm/)blicken wir auf prägende Entwicklungen zurück *und fragen, wo die Wissenschaftskommunikation heute steht.*

**Mit welcher Idee und welchem persönlichen Anspruch seid Ihr 2016 an der Gründung von Wissenschaftskommunikation.de beteiligt gewesen?**

**Markus Weißkopf** ist Redakteur des Research.Table bei Table.Media. Er war Geschäftsführer von Wissenschaft im Dialog und hat dort unter anderem die Plattform Wissenschaftskommunikation.de aufgebaut. Foto: WiD

Markus Weißkopf: Kurz zuvor hatten Wissenschaft im Dialog und der Bundesverband Hochschulkommunikation gemeinsam die [Leitlinien zur guten Wissenschaftskommunikation](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/leitlinien-zur-guten-wissenschaftskommunikation-85129/) veröffentlicht. In dem Zuge hatte die Community viel über gemeinsame Werte, aber auch über die Professionalisierung der Wissenschaftskommunikation diskutiert. Wissenschaftskommunikation.de sollte unter anderem eine Plattform für diese Themen bieten.

Annette Leßmöllmann: Die Plattform sollte zeigen: Wissenschaftskommunikation bedeutet mehr als nur Pressemitteilungen und Hochglanzmagazine. Mir war es ein Anliegen, Forschung und Praxis zusammenzubringen und somit die [Vermittlung der Wissenschaftskommunikationsforschung](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/kategorie/forschung/) voranzutreiben. Zum einen, um praxisrelevante Ergebnisse bekannt zu machen, zum anderen, um die theoretische Weiterentwicklung, die Interdisziplinarität und die Selbstreflexion des Forschungsfeldes zu zeigen. Gleichzeitig sollten Praxisfragen für die Forschung nachvollziehbar werden, um neue Forschung anzustoßen.

**Annette Leßmöllmann** (@annetteless.bsky.social) ist promovierte Linguistin und hat am Karlsruher Institut für Technologie (KIT)* den Lehrstuhl für Wissenschaftskommunikation mit dem Schwerpunkt Linguistik inne. Sie lehrt in den Bachelor- und Master-Studiengängen „Wissenschaft – Medien – Kommunikation“ (@WMKstudium).

**Welche Fragen oder Konfliktlinien aus der Gründungszeit beschäftigen die Community bis heute?**

Weißkopf: „Als Anlaufstelle Nr. 1 hat sich das Online-Lexikon Wikipedia im Internet längst etabliert. Die Wissenschaft sollte das Potenzial von Wikipedia für die Vermittlung fundierten Wissens ernsthaft prüfen.“ Das hat eine Pressesprecherin [im Rahmen des ersten Schwerpunkts „Zukunft der Wissenschaftskommunikation“](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/blick-nach-vorn-wie-sieht-die-wissenschaftskommunikation-der-zukunft-aus-5-13517/) geschrieben. Natürlich ist das Prüfen wissenschaftsimmanent. Aber im Bereich der Kommunikation können wir es uns nicht erlauben, jahrelang zu prüfen. Die Wissenschaft hat nun ein Engagement bei oder für [Wikipedia](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/format/wikipedia/) so lange geprüft, bis es zu spät war. Nur einzelne Einrichtungen wie die Universität Innsbruck bilden hier Ausnahmen. Da würde ich mir manchmal mehr Mut zum Experimentieren wünschen!

Leßmöllmann: Was sich bereits vor zehn Jahren angekündigt hat: Wissenschaftskommunikation muss sich für Wissenschaftsfreiheit einsetzen und ist – teilweise notgedrungen – wesentlich politischer geworden. Dass sie in Interessenslagen und Machtstrukturen eingebettet ist und dass es als machtvoller kommunikativer Akt angesehen wird, wenn jemand „bestimmt“, was wahr oder falsch ist – das war damals eher ein Gedankenexperiment, ist heute aber deutlich als Konflikt zu spüren.

Es wird für die Wissenschaftskommunikation viel schwieriger, wenn es den Entscheider*innen reicht, dass sich etwas wahr anfühlt, auch wenn es nicht wahr ist. Dass etwa politische und gesellschaftliche Entscheidungen gegen den vorherrschenden wissenschaftlichen Konsens getroffen werden, ist angesichts der Klimakrise deutlich bedrohlicher und krisenhafter spürbar als noch vor zehn Jahren.

### „Wissenschaftskommunikation muss sich für Wissenschaftsfreiheit einsetzen und ist – teilweise notgedrungen – wesentlich politischer geworden.“

Annette Leßmöllmann

**Direkt mit dem ersten Schwerpunkt des Portals haben wir damals auf die** **[Zukunft der Wissenschaftskommunikation](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/zukunft-der-wissenschaftskommunikation/)** **geblickt. Welche damaligen Hoffnungen und Befürchtungen haben sich aus Eurer Sicht bewahrheitet und welche nicht?**

Leßmöllmann: Es hat sich die Hoffnung bewahrheitet, dass heute stärker darauf geachtet wird, Kommunikationsaktivitäten wissenschaftlich fundiert zu evaluieren. Zudem hat es funktioniert, dass sich die Community intensiver vernetzt und dass Forschung und Praxis enger zusammenarbeiten.

Es gab auch den Wunsch, dass Wissenschaftskommunikation stärker Teil der Gesellschaft und des täglichen Austauschs über die relevanten Themen der Zeit wird. In einem Aspekt hat sich der Wunsch bewahrheitet, allerdings anders als gedacht: Durch [generative Künstliche Intelligenz](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/themen/kuenstliche-intelligenz/) sind Wissen und Wissenschaft jetzt noch einfacher und dialogischer zu erreichen.

Gleichzeitig wurde die DIN-Norm der Kommunikation aufgeweicht: Es ist nicht mehr sicher, ob das Kommunizierte auch stimmt. Dies trägt zu einer Wissenskrise bei. Etwas dystopisch und pointiert formuliert: Gesagt und geglaubt wird, was gut klingt und auf die Interessen der eigenen Peer Group einzahlt. Das zeigt, dass wir in einer völlig anderen Welt als vor zehn Jahren leben. Die Rolle des Wissens, die demokratische Verankerung und die Wissenschaftsfreiheit stehen zur Debatte.

Das Gründungs-Team (ohne Markus Weißkopf) bei der Präsentation der Plattform im Dezember 2016. Thorsten Witt, Esther Kähler, Beatrice Lugger, Annette Leßmöllmann, Christian Humm und Ulrike Brandt-Bohne. Foto: Gesine Born/WiD.

**Was muss gute Wissenschaftskommunikation heute leisten, was bei der Gründung des Portals noch eine deutlich geringere Rolle gespielt hat?**

Weißkopf: Natürlich markierten der Brexit und die Wahl Trumps im Jahr 2016 nochmal eine Beschleunigung des Populismus, doch einige Entwicklungen waren schon abzusehen. Dennoch muss man sagen, dass die Macht der Tech-Konzerne, die autokratischen Tendenzen auch im „alten Westen“ und der Aufstieg der Rechten aus der Perspektive von 2016 ein Worst Case-Szenario darstellen. Dazu kommen der Ukraine-Krieg und die Konflikte im Nahen Osten.

items.body:
This is a linkpost for pacing-ai.com. I encourage folks to read it via the site (which has interactive graphs and expandables), but we’ve copied the text here as well.

We offer a concrete proposal for pacing the frontier.

1. Transparency: Verified Compute Allocation Disclosures (VCAD)

2. Reallocation: Shift compute away from capabilities R&D

The first component is Verified Compute Allocation Disclosures (VCAD): AI companies regularly disclose their compute usage, and an independent auditor verifies the disclosures. The second component is to reallocate compute away from capabilities R&D and toward other use cases, such as serving customers and safety research (non-capabilities R&D).

We roughly estimate that pacing via compute reallocation starting January 2027, with a 15% cap, would delay the intelligence explosion by a year. This is most likely insufficient to prevent AI takeover (or mitigate other problems created by RSI), and so this year should be used to implement a more durable policy regime such as Plan A or Plan S.

Nearly every approach to pacing, including ones built on safety and security requirements, strongly benefits from VCAD:

Any pacing proposal that actually slows down AI development must do so either by reducing one of the inputs to AI development (such as training compute, experiment compute, or automated or human labor), or by implementing a safeguard that results in using inputs less efficiently (e.g., avoiding neuralese).

Something like VCAD is evidently needed for compute restrictions. For other input restrictions and safeguards, VCAD is highly desirable to prevent attacks of the form “don’t follow this restriction/safeguard on some compute, and hide or misreport that compute.”

With VCAD, competitors and the public can trust a company that says it is pacing. As evidence of risk grows, this could enable a “race to the top”. If regulation later mandates pacing, a VCAD process that companies have already built and stress-tested makes that regulation faster to write and more workable.

Given the urgency of the situation, we elected to publish this relatively quickly. We are not very confident in any given detail of our proposal. Nevertheless, we think it represents a step forward in concreteness for pacing proposals and hope that we and others can quickly turn this into something workable.

VCAD Implementation Proposal

We propose that AI companies take the following steps to estimate and disclose their compute usage:

How AI companies could estimate compute usage

The basic proposal is:

Step 1: Logging. Implement logging infrastructure that logs all workloads running inside the AI company, along with relevant metadata.

Each company should create a database that accounts for all the compute (measured in GPU-hours) that the company uses (more detail on the scope here). Each entry in the table should have the GPU-hours used by the workload, and depending on which of the following categories of workload it fits into, it should have the following metadata attached to the log:

Step 2: Classification.

Classify the logged jobs according to whether they contributed to capabilities R&D (detailed proposal here).

Weight the jobs by how many quality-adjusted GPU-hours they used (detailed proposal here).

Step 2 involves three substages: 2.1) Aggregate GPU-hours. 2.2) Classify workloads into capabilities vs. non-capabilities. 2.3) Estimate idle compute.

2.1) Aggregate GPU-hours. Getting an overall estimate of compute use requires aggregating across heterogeneous GPUs into a single unified GPU-hr metric (e.g., “H100-equivalents”). We discuss this in more detail in an appendix.

2.2) Classify workloads into capabilities vs. non-capabilities, using a mixture of AI classification and manual human classification. By “capabilities” compute, we mean compute that has any positive capabilities effects — including work that has capabilities and safety externalities. This centrally includes:

Experiments to improve algorithms and data

Data generation or filtering

Training more capable AIs

Internal inference in service of the above

Unfortunately, it’s hard to give a crisp definition of this, and there are many edge cases. The exact definition isn’t that important so long as it isn’t possible to use internal non-capabilities compute in a way that has large capabilities externalities. We discuss this in more detail in a supplement here.

2.3) Estimate idle compute. By idle compute, we mean compute that is not turned on or is not in use. This includes:

Hot spares

Downtime

New racks that haven’t started use

When Step 2 is complete, the company will have an internal estimate of compute allocation such as the following:

The categories are defined as follows:

Serving customers: compute used to serve customers, including via API, web interfaces (e.g., Claude.ai), and desktop (e.g., Claude Code). We also call this category “External Inference”.
The “trained on” box is the subset of external inference that feeds back into capabilities, either by being directly trained on, paraphrased and then trained on, or similar.

Safeguard classifiers: monitors checking for misuse

Internal Inference: inference compute used for internal AI company use. This includes evaluations, internal coding agents, and RL rollouts.
We subdivide internal inference into capabilities and safety, where safety compute refers to the internal inference that doesn’t have significant capabilities externalities.

Non-Capabilities R&D: R&D compute that has minimal capabilities externalities.

Capabilities R&D: all other R&D compute.

See Supplement C for more detail on the definitions.

Step 3: Disclosure. Publicly report a breakdown of how much compute was spent in each category, and whether it counted as capabilities (red) or non-capabilities.

The AI company publishes a disclosure of the compute allocation. We could imagine, for example, a disclosure every two weeks covering compute allocation over that period. This report should include:

An overall estimate of compute allocation

An overview of the methodology used to make and audit that estimate

An analysis of possible mistakes, discrepancies the auditor was not able to resolve, and an estimate of the error rate

Chip-conversion ratios

Descriptions of N (e.g., 30) non-capabilities projects, randomly sampled in proportion to compute

We recommend that AI companies publish this disclosure through a channel that punishes misreporting. As a starting point, it should be part of the company’s SB 53 frontier AI framework. As soon as possible, it should move to a channel with real liability, such as being included in financial disclosures or directly required by regulation with sufficient teeth to deter violation.

Even with improved reporting channels, there would still be risk of:

Deception from AI executives

items.body:
Art by Thomas Cole via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cole_Thomas_The_Course_of_Empire_Destruction_1836.jpg)

Sometime in the mid-2010s, just as liberalism was getting replaced by “progressivism”, the conservatism that I had grown up with was getting replaced by something we then called the “alt-right”. Whereas the old conservatism was based on Christian faith, libertarian economics, and flag-waving patriotism, the alt-right saw America as a white racial nation-state, rejected the idea of free markets, and was basically irreligious and isolationist.

Over the course of two Trump presidencies and one Biden interregnum, the alt-right matured and grew into what I now call [the New Right](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/understanding-americas-new-right). In doing so, it basically took over from conservatism as the guiding ideology of the GOP base — though not (yet) of the GOP as a whole. Whereas the alt-right was a naked white-power movement, the New Right sees things in broader “civilizational” terms. It has embraced the idea of Christianity, not as a faith or a lifestyle, but as a tribal affiliation defining ingroup and outgroup. Its foreign policy matured into something concrete — a desire to [wield American policy on behalf of “Western Civilization”](https://www.foreignaffairs.com/united-states/new-rights-grand-strategy-after-trump).

At the grassroots level, the New Right also added some new components. It merged with the [Covid antivax movement](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/the-alternate-reality-of-rfk-and) to become skeptical of modern medicine, public health, and life science in general. It partially merged with [the incel movement](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/dating-advice-for-men), telling young men that their sexual frustration was the fault of progressivism. It [veered even more strongly into antisemitism](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/jewish-americans-are-feeling-unsettled), probably feeling liberated to do so by rising antisemitism on the left in the wake of the Gaza war. And it added a strong component of [anti-Indian hatred](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/the-anti-american-right), seeing Indians as a uniquely vulnerable target among recent immigrant groups.

Anyway, it’s too early to say that this movement has *failed*. Yes, the Democrats won one midterm election, but Trump is still the President, and he has shown zero inclination to reverse course on any of his most New Right-aligned policies. He has made Stephen Miller, the ultimate anti-immigration crusader, his chief of staff, and [posted a picture](https://www.nbcnews.com/world/europe/trump-friend-greeting-putin-causes-alarm-europe-ukraine-rcna610373) of himself hugging Vladimir Putin with the caption “My Friend”. Meanwhile, the New Right still has a fairly robust online presence.

But it’s impossible to deny that the winds have shifted. The midterms made it clear that even if the New Right sticks around for the long term, it won’t have a monopoly on power. That will make it essentially impossible for it to follow through on its long-term agenda. Basically, the notion that wokeness and internal disputes would cause the Democrats to permanently collapse as a party has been falsified.

Already, some prominent figures are backing away from the New Right. Elon Musk, who once stood on a stage and declared himself “Dark MAGA”, now says he’s not even MAGA at all, and is instead a political moderate:

And the CEO of Palantir is calling himself a Democrat:

Meanwhile, Bo French, the Texas candidate who lost an election after complaining about Indian fans at a UT football game, has been [kicked out of his country club](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/18/bo-french-texas-country-club-membership-01173063).

The New Right’s online activists and commentators are in a state of deep despair:

Others are tweeting ever more histrionic demands for a civil war that absolutely no one seems interested in actually fighting:

What enthusiasm still *does* exist on the New Right tends to be concentrated on the movement’s most extreme fringe, which focuses on getting attention by bashing Trump and MAGA and saying ridiculous, extremist stuff. For example, *[Politico](https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/11/18/the-far-right-leaves-trump-behind-01172242)* [reports](https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/11/18/the-far-right-leaves-trump-behind-01172242) on the “Christ is King” conference, run by a guy named Joel Webbon:

> [F]or Webbon, the problem was also that MAGA hadn’t gone far enough. He wanted even harsher deportation policies. He wanted a total repudiation of Israel. He wanted to curtail women’s right to vote, to criminalize abortion and homosexuality, and to expel Jews and non-Christians from public office…The event attracted a notorious set of online agitators, including conspiracist Alex Jones and Nick Fuentes, the 28-year-old white nationalist and antisemite, who made a rare public appearance as a guest speaker…
> There are, in Webbon’s telling, few “guys” capable of leading this faction…He did put forward a few “guys” who might fit the bill, naming electoral losers like [James] Fishback, one of the weekend’s main draws, who recently lost [a gubernatorial primary] to a MAGA-backed candidate by 37 points in Florida…Webbon also went on to name Bo French, the far-right candidate for Texas Railroad Commissioner who ultimately lost by some 670,000 votes to a Democrat after making anti-immigration a centerpiece of his campaign.

(There are also various [loonies from overseas](https://vimeo.com/1248089901?fl=pl&fe=vl).)

These are all signs of a movement that’s on the way down. It may return someday — communism sort of did, after all — but its hopes of transforming America over the next few decades are fading. It’s not over yet, but it’s looking more and more that way.

A big part of the reason for that failure, of course, is that Americans simply do not buy what the New Right wants to sell them. Regular Americans [generally like (legal) immigration](https://news.gallup.com/poll/712289/americans-support-immigration-down-strong.aspx), and they [don’t see racial and religious heritage](https://yougov.com/en-us/articles/52636-what-makes-someone-american-heritage-constitution-declaration) as an important determinant of who is a real American. It’s very hard to sell people a product they don’t want.

But there are also various strategic errors that the New Right made. To be clear, I’m *glad* these mistakes were made; I have zero desire to see a movement like the New Right hold power in my country. I just think it’s interesting and instructive to think about what the mistakes were.

…

The Cassi team kindly wrote [a post responding to my agenda](https://substack.com/home/post/p-226170904) - most notably, they are pretty confident in their conditional forecasts and say they’re already providing them to institutional paid customers.

If you’re another AI forecasting startup I forgot to mention, feel free to get in touch with me at scott@slatestarcodex.com. Again, I’m not trying to play favorites (although companies that give me free demo access are naturally more likely to have results from their products mentioned in posts).

items.body: Background: Mental health conditions are a leading cause of disability and economic burden worldwide. Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) may widen access, but economic evidence from community mental health settings, including low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), has not been synthesized by perspective, time horizon, and comparator type. Objective: This study aimed to assess the cost-effectiveness of DMHIs delivered in community mental health settings. Methods: This systematic review followed the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020 guidelines and was registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO CRD420251141326). PubMed, Scopus, the Directory of Open Access Journals, and the Cochrane Library were searched for economic evaluations published from January 2010 to June 2025 involving adolescents (aged 10 years and older) through older adults with mental disorders. Two reviewers independently screened studies, and the quality was appraised using the Consensus on Health Economic Criteria (CHEC) list. Costs were standardized to 2025 US $, and findings were synthesized narratively. Results: Of 2478 records identified, 20 economic evaluations were included: 16 randomized controlled trials, 3 decision-analytic models, and 1 uncontrolled single-arm study, conducted in high-income countries and LMICs (Kenya, Lebanon, China, and Southeast Europe). Depression (n=11, 55%) and anxiety (n=7, 35%) were the most frequent targets. Of 20 studies, 10 (50%) used a health care payer perspective only, 1 (5%) study used a societal perspective only, and 9 (45%) used both perspectives; time horizons ranged from 2 weeks to 10 years. Thirteen (65%) studies were cost-effective at the willingness-to-pay thresholds applied, and 4 (20%) were not; 3 (15%) did not state a threshold. Among the 16 studies reporting quality-adjusted life years, 4 (25%) were dominant (less costly and more effective), 11 (69%) were more costly and more effective, and 1 (6%) was less costly and less effective. The BlueIce smartphone app for self-harm and the NIDUS-Family (New Interventions for Independence in Dementia Studies) dementia intervention were dominant, whereas a societal perspective made some interventions cost-saving, such as Step-by-Step in Lebanon. Interventions that were not cost-effective included those evaluated in Germany, the United States, and Southeast Europe, and 1 psychosis trial with a high incremental cost-effectiveness ratio. Methodological quality was high in 15 (75%) studies, moderate in 4 (20%), and low in 1 (5%). Conclusions: DMHIs in community settings can offer good value for money, particularly guided internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy for depression and anxiety, and may be cost-saving from a societal perspective. The evidence is limited by short time horizons (often 12 months or less), waitlist and usual care comparators, and heterogeneous outcome measures. Future evaluations should use longer follow-ups, active comparators, and a common utility measure, ideally the EQ-5D questionnaire. Trial Registration: PROSPERO CRD420251141326; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251141326

items.body:
John Sanford, at UCR Magazine, has produced a terrific [popular summary](https://news.ucr.edu/ucr-magazine/fall-2026/does-ai-dream-of-electric-sheep) of my work on AI consciousness and AI rights -- the best I have read so far. If you're looking for an approachable synthesis of my main ideas on this topic, this is it.

**Does AI Dream of Electric Sheep?**

Philosopher Eric Schwitzgebel can’t say for certain if AI will achieve consciousness, but that uncertainty poses a major ethical dilemma

The eeriest scenes in the film “Blade Runner,” the sci-fi classic about artificial life gone rogue, involve a test to distinguish humans from nonhumans.

Examiners confront the test subjects with morally and emotionally provocative scenarios to determine whether they are replicants, bioengineered androids that resemble humans. If they are, then certain physiological reactions, such as their pupillary and blush responses, will betray a lack of empathy that humans naturally have. At least, that’s the premise.

The movie, which came out in 1982, is based on Philip K. Dick’s iconic 1968 novel “Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?” On a weeknight in September, I watched it again for the first time in decades. The next day, I went to see Eric Schwitzgebel, distinguished professor of philosophy at UC Riverside, in his office on campus.

I wanted to learn more about his work on the challenges of assessing consciousness in artificial intelligence.

Rapid advances in computer science over the past few years have made the prospect of nonanimal sentience a distinct possibility. Many of the world’s most respected thinkers believe it is imminent. Some believe it has already arrived.

In a recent survey of about 580 AI researchers, 25% said they expect AI consciousness by 2034, and 70% by 2100. Schwitzgebel cites these findings in two forthcoming books, which he wrote in quick succession in part to prepare us for what he believes is an unprecedented question of enormous moral weight, hurtling toward us like a freight train.

Schwitzgebel, 58, is friendly and composed, with a broad face, white hair, and an impish, gap-toothed smile. When I met him, he was sitting at his desk in front of a window, wearing a T-shirt, shorts, and beat-up running shoes, his office crammed with books and papers.

items.body:
Last week, the AI company Anthropic went public in what became the largest IPO in American history. Given my sustained criticism of Anthropic’s beliefs and actions, many people have asked me for my opinion on this event.

The good news for the curious among you is that I captured my thoughts in an op-ed for *The New York Times*, which they published Thursday, the same day that Anthropic went public. It was titled “[Don’t Play Anthropic’s Game](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/19/opinion/anthropic-ipo-ai-regulation.html),” and it opens as follows:

“By the close of the stock market today, Anthropic will have become a central pillar of the American economy. This is deeply concerning to me, because it’s unclear how many of the retail and institutional investors handing over their money to Anthropic realize that they are, in some sense, funding a doomsday cult that also happens to build enterprise software.”

My use of “doomsday cult” isn’t facetious; it underscores a critical reality. As many have reported ([including myself](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/05/opinion/ai-silicon-valley.html)), the leaders of Anthropic have long believed that AI is destined to transform the human species, either delivering a utopia or killing us all. They see themselves, with their highly rational minds, trained on long hours during the 2000s debating these issues on blogs like *Less Wrong* and *Overcoming Bias*, as the select few who must rise up to guide humanity through this next evolution.

This may sound like hyperbole, but it’s not. [It’s exactly what they believe](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jt508VjX2H8).

Some ask, “Why is this a problem? If any company is going to advance AI, shouldn’t it be one that cares about bad outcomes?”

As I elaborate in my op-ed, the situation is not so simple. Anthropic’s belief that transformational AI is imminent has made it reckless. Anthropic now releases models faster than they can build safeguards because they believe the fate of the human race depends on getting to superintelligent AI first. (Case in point: earlier this year, they announced they were relaxing rules that required them to slow down development if models became hard to control. Their reason? If they applied such rules “unilaterally,” other – presumably less righteous – parties might get ahead of them in the race.)

Indeed, Anthropic stated a key rationale for their IPO is to raise the money needed to accelerate investments in so-called “recursive self-improvement,” where AI systems upgrade themselves. This is, of course, a terrible idea, as it creates models that are even less safe and harder to understand. Anthropic acknowledged these risks in its S-1 filing, but sees no alternative if they’re to continue as humanity’s shepherd through this revolution.

It’s unclear to what degree they even care about profits or building a durable business. As I summarize in my op-ed:

“It’s a business plan that starts with a lot of red ink and then abruptly ends with superintelligence arriving and rendering money superfluous.”

To be clear: generative AI is an incredibly important technological revolution. It brings with it great promises and real risks. But the right way to navigate these innovations can’t possibly be to let a small number of people in Silicon Valley, who have been worshipping AI as a millenarian agent since well before LLMs entered the scene, gather as much money as possible to fund their self-proclaimed role as prophets who will lead the rest of us to their idiosyncratic vision of a better future.

#### In Other News

For more on the question of whether Amodei and company are right in their beliefs that we’re on a trajectory toward superintelligence, check out [my recent technical article](https://spectrum.ieee.org/ai-superintelligence-debate) for the *IEEE Spectrum*, which lays out an engineering case against the feasibility of AI superintelligence. (You should also consider signing up for the Spectrum’s always insightful [AI Alert newsletter](https://spectrum.ieee.org/ai-alert-signup).)

items.body:
Berlin, 23. November 2026 – Heute berät der Innenausschuss des Deutschen Bundestags über den Entwurf für das KI-Migrationsverwaltungsgesetz (KIMVG). Mit dem Gesetz soll Migrationsbehörden erlaubt werden, KI-Systeme mit Daten aus Visums- und Asylverfahren entwickeln und einsetzen zu dürfen. Bereits vergangene Woche hat AlgorithmWatch mit 36 weiteren Organisationen einen gemeinsamen Appell unterzeichnet und darin konkrete Nachbesserungen in den Bereichen Datenschutz, Evaluation und Transparenz gefordert. Darüber hinaus kritisiert AlgorithmWatch, dass der jetzige Gesetzentwurf zu vielen Behörden erlaubt, beim Einsatz von KI Grundrechte einzuschränken.

Nora Oppermann, Junior Policy Managerin bei AlgorithmWatch, kommentiert:

„Das KIMVG soll einem kaum begrenzten Behördenkreis ermöglichen, mit hochsensiblen Daten eigene KI-Systeme zu entwickeln. Dazu zählen 225 Auslandsvertretungen, 585 kommunale Ausländerbehörden und sämtliche Dienststellen der Polizei. Zwischen touristischen Visa aus Nordamerika und Asylgesuchen von geflüchteten Menschen aus Kriegs- und Krisengebieten wird dabei kein Unterschied gemacht.

Hinzu kommt, dass das KIMVG einen automatisierten Abgleich von Angaben aus den Anträgen mit öffentlich zugänglichen Daten aus dem Internet erlauben soll, beispielsweise von Social-Media-Plattformen. Dabei handelt es sich um ein Verfahren, das wir sonst nur von Nachrichtendiensten und aus der Strafverfolgung kennen und dessen Nutzen aufgrund seiner Anfälligkeit für Fehler und gefälschte Daten stark umstritten ist. Antragstellende werden so nicht nur für intransparente KI-Experimente ausgenutzt, sondern zudem unzuverlässigen automatisierten Entscheidungen ausgesetzt.

Ohne Vorgaben für eine Begrenzung des Einsatzes, die Qualität der Daten, eine unabhängige Kontrolle der Systeme und strikte Transparenz droht der Einsatz von KI im Migrationsbereich zu einem undurchsichtigen und diskriminierenden Fiasko zu werden.“

## Ergänzende Informationen:

items.body:
In my usual summaries of cultural drift, I describe key parameters that have been going bad in the last few centuries re the evolution of cultures. Here I mention 3:

> A few centuries ago… the world had 100Ks of peasant cultures, most facing frequent wars, pandemics, and famines, in an economy that took a millennia to double. But then we merged peasants into a hundred or so national cultures, and then those into just a few world cultures, all of which got so rich, healthy and peaceful that they almost never die. Also, the world economy now doubles every twenty years, fifty times faster than before. So now we are likely in trouble. Every cultural feature has a min scale at which it can vary; below that scale, people have to do it the same. We are doing fine re features that can vary at small scales, but in trouble re features that set game-theoretic equilibria, and so can only vary at large scales. ( [↗ overcomingbias.com](https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/five-slogans-re-cultural-drift) )

The other param I usually mention is the fluctuation rate. While centuries ago peasant cultures were quite conservative, trying not to change, we moderns give our highest status to cultural activists who successfully cause big changes to culture. Alas such changes do not usually much promote adaption.

However there are other relevant parameters. The recent cut in global variety is due to many features of culture moving up to larger scales, some to near global scales. But, as many cultural features remain set at smaller scales, like corporate cultures set at firm scales, fewer cultural features are being set at these largest scales. And thus the scope of cultures at our largest scales is declining. *Cultural scope* is another key parameter.

In addition, while the structure of most practices of ancient peasants were set by their culture, and hard to change, in the modern world we allow and even expect great change and variation in most tech and business practices. This limits the scope of modern cultures even more. And cultural drift in a culture of smaller scope is drift in a lower-dimensional space, and so probably less severe.

This suggests another at least partial fix to cultural drift: further cut cultural scope, i.e., how many aspects of our behavior are set by culture, and so hard to vary locally.

One way to cut the scope of culture would be to rely less on prestige in key social institutions like medicine, law, academia, etc. I’ve made many proposals along these lines, which could greatly improve such areas of life. Alas, our world is far more tolerant of innovations in physical arrangements, relative to social arrangements.

This has been a key fact of my life. I started out in physics and computer science, where I noticed that the world eagerly sought even minor innovations. Which were hard to find, as so many sought them. Then when I got into social science I noticed that it seemed far easier to innovate there. I figured I must be especially good at this, but didn’t realize that it is easy for many to find social innovations, as the world mostly just doesn’t adopt the social innovations that people find.

While it doesn’t at all seem crazy that we might be able to further reduce the scope of our largest-scale cultures, we just don’t understand very well what determines such scope, or what has enable many big prior cuts in such scope. But work to figure this out might pay big dividends.

items.title: KOMMENTAR: Abitur 2027 – warum „Sprache in politisch-gesellschaftlichen Verwendungszusammenhängen“ in jede Oberstufe gehört
items.subtitle: Kaum ein Abiturthema zeigt so deutlich wie dieses, dass es ihn gibt: einen modernen Deutschunterricht, der die Aufgabe ernst nimmt, jungen Menschen…
items.feedText: Ein Kommentar. Es gibt Abiturthemen, bei denen man als Lehrkraft erst einmal Überzeugungsarbeit leisten muss. Bei denen man vor einem Kurs steht und begründen muss, warum es sich lohnt, sich mit etwas zu beschäftigen, das auf den ersten Blick weit weg ist vom eigenen Leben. Ich habe solche Stunden oft genug gehalten. Und ich habe auf diesem Blog auch schon dafür gestritten, dass man sie halten sollte. „Sprache in politisch-gesellschaftlichen Verwendungszusammenhängen“ gehört nicht dazu. Der sperrige Titel täusch…
items.body:
Kaum ein Abiturthema zeigt so deutlich wie dieses, dass es ihn gibt: einen modernen Deutschunterricht, der die Aufgabe ernst nimmt, jungen Menschen Orientierung in einer digitalen Gesellschaft zu ermöglichen. Ein Kommentar.

Es gibt Abiturthemen, bei denen man als Lehrkraft erst einmal Überzeugungsarbeit leisten muss. Bei denen man vor einem Kurs steht und begründen muss, warum es sich lohnt, sich mit etwas zu beschäftigen, das auf den ersten Blick weit weg ist vom eigenen Leben. Ich habe solche Stunden oft genug gehalten. Und ich habe auf diesem Blog auch schon [dafür gestritten, dass man sie halten sollte.](https://bobblume.de/2019/10/06/diskussion-sollte-goethes-faust-teil-des-lehrplans-sein/)

„Sprache in politisch-gesellschaftlichen Verwendungszusammenhängen“ gehört nicht dazu. Der sperrige Titel täuscht. Denn worum es hier geht, tragen die Schülerinnen und Schüler jeden Tag in der Hosentasche mit sich herum.

## Wo das Thema im Abitur 2027 eine Rolle spielt

In Nordrhein-Westfalen, Berlin und Brandenburg, Hessen, Niedersachsen und Schleswig-Holstein ist das Themenfeld im Abitur 2027 ausdrücklich als Schwerpunkt ausgewiesen, mit leicht unterschiedlichen Akzenten. Mal geht es um politisch-gesellschaftliche Kommunikation zwischen Verständigung und Strategie, mal um den Sprachgebrauch in unterschiedlichen Medien, mal um Rhetorik und Medienwandel. In den übrigen Ländern, etwa in Baden-Württemberg und Bayern, sind genau die Aufgabenformate gefragt, an denen sich das Thema hervorragend üben lässt: die Analyse pragmatischer Texte, die Erörterung und das materialgestützte Schreiben.

Mit anderen Worten: Es ist eines der zentralen Felder des Deutschabiturs.

## Worum es eigentlich geht

Wie wird Sprache eingesetzt, um zu überzeugen, zu mobilisieren, auszugrenzen? Wo legt jemand seine Gründe offen, und wo will er bloß wirken? Diese Fragen konnte man früher an Bundestagsreden und Leitartikeln stellen. Das fällt nicht weg, aber es kommt auch etwas hinzu: Die politisch-gesellschaftliche Kommunikation, die Jugendliche tatsächlich erreicht, hat nochmals völlig andere Formen und Kanäle: ein KI-generiertes Video, das Empörung erzeugt und am Ende einen Shop verlinkt. Ein [Finanzpodcast, der von „Systemmedien“](https://www.t-online.de/leben/kolumne-bob-blume/id_100330412/finanz-influencer-und-podcasts-werden-jugendliche-zum-rechtsruck-verleitet-.html) spricht und damit mehr transportiert als eine Meinung. Eine Kommentarspalte, in der niemand den Text gelesen hat, über den alle streiten. Ein Feed, in dem auf das Kriegsvideo der Tanzclip folgt.

Das ist politische Sprache. Nur eben nicht mehr im Plenarsaal, sondern zwischen zwei Wischbewegungen. Und wer diese Sprache nicht durchschaut, wird von ihr beeinflusst oder [im schlimmsten Fall manipuliert.](https://substack.com/@netzlehrer/p-211289258)

## Kein Entweder-oder

Nun könnte man einwenden, das sei die übliche Anbiederung an die Lebenswelt. Ein bisschen TikTok, damit es sich zeitgemäß anfühlt. Den Einwand muss man ernst nehmen, ich habe ihn selbst oft genug erhoben. An anderer Stelle habe ich beschrieben, dass Deutschunterricht auf [drei Ebenen zur Teilhabe an Kultur](https://bobblume.de/2021/05/31/diskussion-was-soll-und-kann-deutschunterricht/) befähigt: durch basale Grundfertigkeiten, durch die Auseinandersetzung mit Alltagskultur und durch die Hochkultur. Die mittlere Ebene ist diejenige, die sich am schnellsten verändert. Gerade deshalb darf man sie nicht dem Zufall überlassen.

Und es geht nicht um ein Entweder-oder. Wer Kleist liest, lernt etwas über Macht und Sprache vor Gericht. Wer ein Empörungsvideo analysiert, lernt etwas über Macht und Sprache im Feed. Beides schärft denselben Blick. In der Diskussion um den Faust habe ich geschrieben, dass man Kompetenzen an unterschiedlichen Inhalten lernen kann, aber nur an bestimmten Inhalten unterschiedliche Kompetenzen. Die Sprache der digitalen Öffentlichkeit ist ein solcher Inhalt. An ihr lernt man zu analysieren, zu urteilen und selbst zu schreiben. Und nebenbei etwas, das in keinem Erwartungshorizont steht: den Schritt zurück.

## Fazit

Man kann lange darüber streiten, wie viel Gegenwart der Deutschunterricht verträgt. Bei diesem Thema muss man es nicht. Wenn Schule der Ort sein soll, an dem junge Menschen lernen, sich in der Welt zu orientieren, dann muss sie sich mit der Sprache beschäftigen, in der diese Welt heute verhandelt wird. Nicht obwohl sie den Schülerinnen und Schülern so nah ist, sondern weil sie es ist. Relevanz ist hier kein Zugeständnis an die Jugend. Sie ist der Grund, warum das Thema in die Schule gehört.

## Unterrichtseinheit

**Abitur 2027: Sprache in Politik und Gesellschaft – analysieren, erörtern und materialgestützt schreiben mit echten Kolumnen**

Wie funktioniert politisch-gesellschaftliche Kommunikation im Netz? Dieses Abiturpaket bereitet Grund- und Leistungskurse auf den Schwerpunkt „Sprache in politisch-gesellschaftlichen Verwendungszusammenhängen“ vor. Es arbeitet mit echten Kolumnen, die auf WEB.DE und t-online erschienen sind: über Empörungsvideos, radikale Influencer, „Decline Porn“, Kommentarkultur, KI und soziale Medien. Dazu kommt ein wissenschaftlicher Essay als theoretischer Rahmen. Alle Texte sind rechtssicher einsetzbar.

[Zum Material- und Unterrichtspaket](https://eduki.com/de/material/2478468/abiturpaket-2027-sprache-in-politik-und-gesellschaft-1)

## In eigener Sache

Vielleicht ist es euch aufgefallen: Auf diesem Blog war es in letzter Zeit ruhiger. Das liegt nicht daran, dass mir die Themen ausgegangen wären, sondern daran, dass ich vor allem auf Substack schreibe. Dort erscheint jeden Samstag mein Newsletter „Stimme für Bildungswandel“, mit Kommentaren zu Bildungsthemen, Gesprächen und regelmäßig auch mit Material für den Unterricht. Wenn ihr mögt, schaut dort gern vorbei. Die Anmeldung ist kostenlos.

items.body:
Roden Readers —

Fall! Finally! Jacket weather! Sweaters! Snow on Fuji! Oh, my!

What has been going on this past month? A whole lotta hermiting. I’ve been on a decidedly teenager-like (or Mishima-like, if you prefer; the man almost never rose before noon) schedule, which my body clock seems to love, working late into the night and passing out around two or three and then waking up around ten or eleven, pounding a big ol’ smoothie, and then working like mad from noon to six, breaking for a nice dinner with friends, and then diving back under until my futon calls. This is an ideal schedule for me. Because I am insane. I basically never shifted back from Europe time to Japan time in October. Also, a smoothie + slow, delicious dinner turns out to be a great eating schedule? I feel light and energetic. Am I an adult? I’m not sure. I do push-ups and walk 10,000 steps a day. Such is the glamorous life of being self-employed at forty-six years old while the world speedruns its own unique flavor of insanity in the background. Is the singularity here yet?

items.body:
Hi everyone!

I’ve recently released open-source firmware for the original (mk1) AKAI APC Mini.

It comes with improved fader handling, a simple web updater (using WebMIDI, so it won’t work in Safari out of the box).

And today I’ve added serialosc support and a built-in Lua VM.

You can update yours simply by visiting Open APC Mini — Firmware Uploader.

The source code is here: GitHub — Open APC Mini.

During the first update you will need to power-cycle your APC after the first bootloader handshake. Look for this message in the log: Application accepted unlock (ACK 0x15). Waiting for USB re-enumeration into bootloader... Also if you have Ableton running it is better to quit it before updating.

It would be so great if someone could try it with a Norns, because I am too broke to own one right now Would love to hear how it goes!

items.title: On the day the Riemann hypothesis fell to AI, I took my son for a walk
items.subtitle: He’d been a tad sick, feverish the night before, with frenetic dreams about huge spiders.
items.feedText: He’d been a tad sick, feverish the night before, with frenetic dreams about huge spiders. But he was already bouncing back with color in his cheeks. The perfect afternoon weather helped. Strange fall we’ve been having, isn’t it? The days just seem warmer and warmer. I wish I had brought a camera or my phone, just for a picture to share. items.body:
He’d been a tad sick, feverish the night before, with frenetic dreams about huge spiders. But he was already bouncing back with color in his cheeks. The perfect afternoon weather helped. Strange fall we’ve been having, isn’t it? The days just seem warmer and warmer.

I wish I had brought a camera or my phone, just for a picture to share. After a day of drawing and reading in his room he was in full 5-year-old form, with his outsized personality, and wearing an oversized Frog and Toad shirt, and of course his hair was stuck up from his fever dreams (that curly blond hair everyone comments on). And so it would have been nice to have a photo or a video of us walking in and out of the patches of the golden hour, and in and out of the currents of warm air, and of his cackling, of all his many delightful cackles. He’d found a thick staff that looked like something Gandalf would have used and was shaking it at things.

We passed a perfectly still pond where the water looked black and in the black water was perfectly reflected the trees and sky and us ourselves. He dipped the staff in to touch “the me on the other side.”

Off the path from the trees and the black water pond there was a clearing, and since it lay in the sunlight, and since I am drawn to patches of sunlight, we walked out into it. Beside us ran the neighborhood stream that feeds into the black water pond and its reflection, which was still there and still perfect without us.

In the sunlight of the clearing we could hear the stream’s trickle and we squinted around.

At this age he and I can talk about anything. We find nothing mundane, we comment on it all, all we do is talk. It’s wonderful.

“Oh, I just remembered,” I said. “The neighbors said the coyotes live around here. In a den right off the stream.”

“Well, I have my staff.”

“And luckily, there’re only 4,” I said. I’d seen them together as a pack several times.

“Well, they’re outnumbered!” he said, delightedly. “I’m 5!”

He took up his wizard’s staff and shook it. I laughed. I thought it was clever, a clever joke. He’s oh so clever.

That night he asked if we’d be doing math, as we often have for the better part of a year now. Just 20 minutes a day, and we’re almost through arithmetic.

“No, maybe tomorrow,” I said. I’d rather just let him play in his room.

But it won’t be tomorrow, either.

“L’étang à Montgeron” by Claude Monet

This week we look at BAAJA, rayon for missiles, US gas consumption, Cyberarmageddon, and more. Roughly 2/3rds of the reading list is paywalled, so for full access become a paid subscriber.

No essay this week, but I’m working on a long follow up to my [technological search essay](https://www.construction-physics.com/p/technology-as-a-search-problem) that should be out next week.

## Housing and Cities

A neat dataset showing the relationship between excess deaths and temperature in cities around the world. You can really see the sensitivity to high temperatures in places without AC. [[Our World in Data](https://ourworldindata.org/part-one-how-many-people-die-from-extreme-temperatures-and-how-could-this-change-in-the-future)]

The Senate passes the permitting reform bill BAAJA. [[NYT](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/19/climate/senate-passes-baaja-permitting-bill-energy.html)] And Kalshi now gives BAAJA a 75% chance of becoming law. [[Kalshi](https://kalshi.com/markets/kxpermitbill/american-affordability-and-jobs-act/kxpermitbill-26sep)] And New Mexican Senator Martin Heinrich is in the Economist arguing for BAAJA. “ The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act—which the Senate voted to advance on November 9th and which I co-sponsor with another Democrat and two Republicans—does not remove environmental considerations, the ability to litigate projects or the ability for local communities to comment. Those are necessary. But it does make these reviews a standardised part of a predictable process.” [[The Economist](https://www.economist.com/by-invitation/2026/11/15/a-plan-to-end-americas-most-expensive-bottleneck?giftId=ZDFhYjYzMTYtM2UxZi00Njg0LTk4NzEtMWM4NzNlZDk3OTdl)]

New type of nimbyism just dropped: people opposed to delivery drones flying over their backyard. [[WSJ](https://www.wsj.com/lifestyle/amazon-delivery-drones-4807e976?st=wrqyyy)]

How Dubrovnik, the Croatian city where King’s Landing scenes were shot in Game of Thrones, is coping with huge masses of tourists and (checks notes) Montenegrin drug cartels. [[The Times](https://www.thetimes.com/world/europe/article/how-to-save-a-city-from-mass-tourism-when-the-mob-wants-you-dead-0g7d626m2)]

## Manufacturing

From the annals of manufacturing bottlenecks: producing more Patriot missiles requires, among other things, a specialized rayon fabric called Raycarb, processed by a single US company who sources it from a tiny number of companies (apparently just two), who are unable or unwilling to ramp up capacity as fast as the US would like. “ Only one rayon product of this kind is approved for use in the most advanced Patriot missiles, and it comes from the Kansas factory of a single supplier, Park Aerospace. With Patriot stockpiles shrinking, the Pentagon official pushed Park for more rayon to help ramp up missile production. It soon became clear that the company’s hands were tied. The problem lay not in Kansas but thousands of miles across the Atlantic near the vineyards of Bordeaux in France. That’s where Park’s supplier, ArianeGroup—a maker of space rockets and ballistic missiles—produces the carbonized rayon fabric, which it then ships to Park for further processing. ArianeGroup had been clear that supply was limited. ” [[WSJ](https://www.wsj.com/world/europe/patriot-missile-rayon-problem-3f39dc98)]

Manufacturing automation startup Hadrian is buying Kutztown Foundry and Machine, a company that makes castings for, among other things, nuclear submarines. [[Manufacturing Dive](https://www.manufacturingdive.com/news/hadrian-acquiring-kutztown-foundry-machine-f6-upgrade-expand-pennsylvania/874947/)]

The US Marine Minerals Administration, formerly the BOEM, held an auction for seabed mining rights on 31 million acres of seabed near American Samoa. [[Maritime Executive](https://maritime-executive.com/article/trump-administration-auctions-deep-sea-mining-areas-at-20-cents-per-acre)]

China produces a lot of air conditioners. [[X](https://x.com/simongerman600/status/2120487160621015178?s=20&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email)]

Apparently Tesla will sell you a Cybercab, under a somewhat strict set of conditions. “ Tesla is now inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use at $29,990, but the car won’t move unless you also pay $299 a month for an “Autonomy Subscription.” And it only works inside Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas in Texas and Florida, the same geofences that have turned out to be significantly smaller than what Tesla advertises.” [[Electrek](https://electrek.co/2026/11/13/tesla-cybercab-personal-use-orders-299-subscription-geofence/)] And a factory to produce Tesla’s Optimus is under construction at Giga Texas. [[YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SBnEKGe3i14&t=210s)]

A bunch of planned naval vessels have been cut by the US Senate appropriations committee. [[X](https://x.com/LegasovAnalytic/status/2122539419152568761)]

The GAO says the F-35 program has about 26 million spare parts, collectively worth about $31 billion, spread around 700 sites around the world. [[Tom’s Hardware](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/pentagon-struggles-to-account-for-usd31-billion-in-missing-f-35-aircraft-parts-weeks-after-shipment-was-swiped-by-china-tracking-of-estimated-26-million-parts-is-outdated-inaccurate-and-incomplete-says-watchdog)]
