items.body:
Pundits who dismissed the Shenzhen summit as a mere photo-op lacking substance missed the point. The significance of the conclave was precisely its enframing symbolism, showcasing a new world in which the rules-based order has been supplanted by spheres of influence accommodating each other.

The city of Shenzhen itself is a prism through which we can observe today’s power relations and the evolution of events over recent decades bringing us to this point.

**Unplugged Computers in China’s Future Tech Hub**

I first visited Shenzhen in 1986, arriving there by tram from Hong Kong and walking across the mainland border. There was barely any bustle, no crowds or traffic and a couple of tall buildings at the most. At our modest hotel, a squatting gardener was clipping the grass with a pair of scissors. The place still exuded the languorous vibe of the fishing village of 30,000 it had been not long before it was designated a “special economic zone” by Deng Xiaoping to attract foreign capital and technology.

On an inspection tour of sprouting industrial parks with then-former California governor Jerry Brown, our hosts proudly showed us what they called a tech hub. What then passed for “data centers” were cavernous, virtually empty warehouses with scores of desktop computers on worktables gathering dust — none were even plugged in.

What seemed embarrassing at the time turned out to be beyond impressive 40 years later. Shenzhen today is a literally glittering technopolis of 20 million people regarded as China’s “Silicon Valley” where Huawei, Tencent, DJI and BYD are all located. It is the center of gravity of China’s AI battle with the United States.

The invitation to visit had come some years earlier from Xi Zhongxun, then Party chief of Guangdong province (where Shenzhen is located) and the father of China’s current leader, Xi Jinping. The elder Xi had come to California in 1980 looking for investment in the special economic zone as a key platform of Deng’s policy of “reform and opening up” to the world. On that visit, he met Gov. Jerry Brown and toured the state, including stops at tech sites in the then-fledgling Silicon Valley (Apple and Intel were about it in those days) and Disneyland, where he gamely shook hands with Mickey Mouse.

Courtesy of the National Committee on U.S.-China Relations

Years later in 2012, when Brown was governor again for a second time, Xi Jinping, then-vice-president of China on his way to the top, visited California. The irony was not lost on either leader when the governor inquired whether China was interested in helping finance California’s bullet train, already in the works for nearly 20 years.

A Chinese delegation later met with the governor at the Peninsula Hotel in Beverly Hills to discuss possibilities, but the idea never panned out. Those who had once come cup in hand to the Golden State now offered financing terms too tough to abide. By 2026, China had built a 30,000-mile network of bullet trains spanning its vast country. California and the U.S. still have yet to build one.

On that 1986 trip to China, Brown and I also met at Zhongnanhai, the secluded leader’s compound in Beijing, with the ideology chief and youngest member of the ruling Communist Party Politburo at the time, Hu Qili. In a wide-ranging conversation that touched on topics from the “spiritual pollution” of Western influence to Tibetan Buddhism, Hu noted that the Chinese military had reduced its forces by one million soldiers. Many military installations, he said, were converting to commercial applications in light industry and heavy-truck production. Several military aircraft plants were now making refrigerators and motorcycles.

To this, Brown quipped, “If the army is making refrigerators, you must think the polar bear [what the Chinese called Russia] is hibernating.” Laughing, Hu simply replied that since Russia “couldn’t even consolidate control of Cambodia, it is only inviting great trouble to try anything with China.”

Opening then to America while hostile to an ebbing Soviet empire, Hu insisted that “China’s armed forces are sufficient to resist hegemonist efforts from the bear if they come.”

> “The one key power left out of the 1945 Yalta talks that shaped the international order in the dying days of World War II is now setting the agenda for what comes next.”

## The Tiananmen Turn

It was in that atmosphere that Gorbachev visited Beijing in May 1989 and met with Premier Zhao Ziyang as tensions with the authorities were mounting on Tiananmen Square. In the wake of the student massacre that June, the liberal-leaning Zhao was purged for revealing “state secrets” to Gorbachev by telling him that Deng, who would order the repression, remained the power behind the throne even though he had formally retired. Hu was also purged.

This was a “ludicrous accusation,” Gorbachev told me later. The real issue, as he saw it, was his advice that the student occupation should be defused politically through negotiation, not force. “I was confident a political solution could be found. I was wrong, unfortunately,” the last Soviet leader lamented.

Deng had drawn the line on Party control that Gorbachev was erasing in Moscow. Deng’s open palm on the economy clenched into an iron fist on political reform. Ever since, Gorbachev’s “new thinking” has been vilified in Beijing as a recipe for the collapse of the Party-state, and something to be avoided at all costs.

## A World Safe For Spheres Of Influence

When Vladimir Putin emerged in the tumultuous years after the Soviet collapse, China’s sympathy with a more amenable Russia returned. As the post-Cold War years wore on, the “hegemonist threat” for China shifted to America, even as it prospered from the relationship.

In the end, China’s leaders came to strategically favor a trusted autocrat ruthlessly obsessed with dominating his own neighborhood over a meddling America endlessly endeavoring, in their minds, to subvert China’s governing system and keep the nation down. Party ideologues, Xi above all, are convinced that the American political class, implicitly if not explicitly, concurs with Bill Clinton’s remark when he was president that China was on “the wrong side of history.” Like many others in those days, Clinton wrongly presumed trade winds would blow open the society.

With a militarily mighty but economically feeble and dependent Russia at its side, China’s leaders have grown more confident in their capacity to contain America in a world made safe for spheres of influence.

The few words spoken for public consumption at the Shenzhen summit about zones of “civilizational values” and the primacy of state sovereignty over international law were code for the long-standing views of Xi and Putin, which the American president has now openly embraced.

## Tech Trips The Thucydides Trap

items.body:
Die Nachbarn waren bereits genervt. Während nebenan im japanischen Pavillon, im Zeichen kollektiver Fürsorge, Ei Arakawas lebensechte Babypuppen behutsam herumgereicht wurden und die Schweizer auf der anderen Seite in einer feinfühligen Gruppenausstellung neue Formen des Zusammenlebens verhandelten, fiel der russische Pavillon zuerst dadurch auf, dass aus ihm heraus unüberhörbar lauter Techno über das Gelände schallte.

Es ist der zweite Preview-Tag Anfang Mai auf der – nun endenden – Biennale in Venedig und trotz Jury-Rücktritt, Minister-Boykotten, EU-Gelder-Entzug und einer Pussy-Riot Performance ist der *Padiglione russo* demonstrativ für die Fachbesucherinnen geöffnet.

Anstatt also ob der fortwährenden Kriegsgreuel wie in den Vorjahren die Segel zu streichen, wählte die russische Führung für die 61. Ausgabe der internationalen Kunstschau eine offensive Taktik. Dabei kamen Kulturtechniken zum Einsatz, die bereits in der Sowjetunion praktiziert wurden.

**Prazdniki**

Wer sich von den 140BPM nicht abschrecken ließ und seine Reiztoleranz testen wollte, der wurde im Innern des Zarenbaus nicht enttäuscht. Hier konkurrierten auf drei Etagen verschiedene Formate, Ästhetiken und Medien um die Aufmerksamkeit der Besucher. Ohne erkennbare inhaltliche Bezüge reihten sich überbordende Blumengestecke an Männer in Tiermasken, Nadelhölzer in Keramiktöpfen an mobile Bildschirme und Pappmaché-Köpfe im Manga-Stil an Ensembles eklektischer Sitzmöbel.

Der Kern der sensorischen Überrumpelungstaktik war aber sicher die improvisierte Bar mit freiem Alkoholausschank. Moscow Mule gratis per tutti. Frei nach dem Titel der Ausstellung: »Der Baum wurzelt im Himmel«, hielten hier Dissoziation und Eskapismus in ihrem Lauf weder Ochs noch Esel auf.

Grob übersetzt beschreibt *Prazdniki* einen Feiertag, je nach Kontext mit der Konnotation von Beschäftigungslosigkeit und Müßiggang. Diese Form von »sozialer Anästhesie« hat ihren Ursprung in den Ablenkungsstrategien der Sport- und Maiparaden der 1930er-Jahre unter Stalin. Während auf dem Land Millionen Menschen durch den Holodomor verhungerten und der Große Terror seinen Höhepunkt fand, organisierte der Diktator auf dem Roten Platz gigantische, farbenfrohe *Prazdniki* mit blühenden Blumen, jungen Athletinnen und Athleten und erbaulicher Musik.

Der Unterschied zu Sowjetzeiten besteht darin, dass hier eine Enklave im dämonisierten Westen bespielt wird. Einem Potemkinschen Dorf gleich wird eine Normalität inszeniert, hinter deren Fassade es gewaltig bröckelt. Denn während in den Gärten Venedigs versucht wird, das geneigte Publikum zu vernebeln, sendet die heimische Kriegsmaschinerie im Stundentakt Kamikaze-Drohnen gen vermeintliches Brudervolk.

**Dvoemyslie**

Dieses „Doppeldenk“ mag vor den Augen der Welt zum Scheitern verurteilt sein. Doch in Russland selbst, glaubt man den Umfragen, scheint es in Teilen zu verfangen. *Dvoemyslie*, dieser vom Soziologen Juri Lewada geprägte Begriff, beschreibt den Zustand einer tief gespaltenen Psyche. Er befähigt den Menschen, zwei zueinander im Widerspruch stehende Wahrheiten zu akzeptieren. So kann die private Einsicht in die Kriegsschuld des Regimes in Einklang mit der Partizipation an staatlicher Kunstproduktion stehen.

Als in meiner Gegenwart ukrainische Künstler – in betont freundlichem Tonfall – russische Kollegen ansprachen, um eine Konversation zu stimulieren, wurde betreten abgewinkt. Die Konfrontation mit der ukrainischen Realität war ihnen sichtlich unangenehm.

Dies ist eine weitverbreitete Anpassungsstrategie in autoritären Systemen: die Fragen nach eigener Schuld und indirekter Mittäterschaft ignorieren, um das berufliche Überleben im Apparat zu ermöglichen. Sie blendet die eigene Rolle am Systemerhalt aus und ermöglicht es Künstlerinnen und Künstlern, ohne schlechtes Gewissen ihrer Arbeit in staatlichen Institutionen nachzugehen. Anstatt ins Exil zu flüchten, wählt man die innere Emigration oder macht sich mit dem System gemein. Man denke nur an Arno Breker oder Veit Harlan, die in Zeiten des Nationalsozialismus ihren Karrierehöhepunkt fanden.

Wie viel Anstrengung diese Kompartmentalisierung erfordert, wird klar, wenn man sich vor Augen führt, wie eng die Verbindungen in den Kreml sind. Kuratorin Anastassija Kornejewa ist nicht nur die Tochter eines Geheimdienstgenerals beim staatlichen Rüstungskonzern Rostec, sondern betreibt zusammen mit der Tochter von Außenminister Sergej Lawrow eine Galerie in Moskau. Und nachdem einer der einflussreichsten Kulturfunktionäre des Landes, der Eremitage-Direktor Michail Piotrowski, russische Kulturschaffende als »Militaristen« und jede russische Ausstellung im Ausland als eine »Spezialoperation« bezeichnet hatte, ist es nicht abwegig, diesen Pavillon als Teil der hybriden Kriegsführung zu begreifen.

In der UDSSR wusste die Mehrheit der Bürger, dass die Staatspropaganda vom Aufbau des Kommunismus eine hohle Phrase war. Dennoch beteiligten sich Millionen an staatlichen Paraden und unterschrieben Treuebekundungen. Man lebte in einer Doppelmoral: Privat hörten viele verbotene Musik oder lasen *Samisdat*, öffentlich zitierte man die Parteidoktrin.

Die beteiligten russischen Akteure in Venedig wissen natürlich um den Angriffskrieg in der Ukraine, die Zerstörung ukrainischer Kulturstätten und die Zensur im eigenen Land. Und haben sich dennoch entschieden, an einer staatlichen Inszenierung mitzuwirken. Dass selbstkritische Beiträge fehlen und stattdessen Unterhaltungsware präsentiert wird, ist die logische Konsequenz.

**Ruski Mir** **und der Versuch Post-Kolonialer Einbettung** Als die basslastige elektronische Musik mit einem Mal verstummte, übernahm ein Tuwa-Kehlkopfsänger im Keller des Hauses und bereicherte das inkongruente Ambiente mit ethnischen Klängen.

Gäbe es neben dem Goldenen und Silbernen Löwen noch einen Preis für Zynismus, hätte Russland ihn ohne Zweifel verdient. Das Land, dessen imperiale Ambitionen mit dem Blut der Ukrainer:innen bezahlt werden, versucht durch die vermeintliche Solidarität mit den Ländern des globalen Südens eine Art antikoloniale Allianz zu schmieden. Ungeachtet der Tatsache, das Russland seit Jahrhunderten durch Landnahme, ethnische Säuberungen, kulturelle Assimilation und Ressourcen-Hegemonie eine imperiale Politik verfolgt, versucht es sich in Täter-Opfer-Umkehr auf die Seite der Entrechteten zu schlagen. So hat es im Jahr zuvor Bolivien eingeladen, den Pavillon zu bespielen. Wer sich wunderte, weshalb, durfte in Erfahrung bringen, dass kurz zuvor der russische Staatskonzern Rosatom Millionenverträge mit Bolivien zur Erschließung der riesigen bolivianischen Lithiumvorkommen unterzeichnet hatte.

Dieses Jahr sollte es laut Ausstellungstext um nichts Geringeres als das Metaphysische gehen. Was sich aber tatsächlich hinter den Dingen verbirgt, ist die Ausflucht vor der moralischen Verantwortung der Gegenwart, gepaart mit der Schutzbehauptung von Russophobie und Cancel-Culture.

…

# Depth pro 2 monocular

We present Depth Pro 2, an approach to estimating dense metric depth for images and video at full resolution. By analyzing prior methods for monocular depth estimation, we find that they commonly trade off temporal consistency and boundary sharpness: multi-frame methods favor consistency, single-frame methods favor sharpness. To overcome this trade-off, we train a single, scalable network that processes both images and video and predicts depth maps at native resolution. Depth Pro 2 produces depth maps that are metrically accurate, sharp, and temporally consistent all at once, outperforming…

Play

### Featured clips

The Two Questions That Opened Amazon Board Meetings

20:45

Meeting Jeff Bezos for First Time

26:21

The Quality All Founders Need to Succeed

29:21

The Gamification Checklist Behind Great Products

45:00

Tips for Brainstorming 100 Ideas an Hour

Bing Gordon is the former Chief Creative Officer of Electronic Arts, Amazon board member, and a partner at Kleiner Perkins.

He served on Amazon’s board for more than a decade, a seat he earned after giving Jeff Bezos five ideas. The first was Amazon Prime. Bing describes the week two directors told him they wanted to resign, and the fix he proposed: Bezos opens each meeting with what’s on his mind, and six-page memos replace slide decks.

He explains Bezos’s first rule for the board, “first, do no harm,” and the “institutional no” Bezos wanted the board to help Amazon avoid. He lays out the three behaviors Bezos looks for in people who are right a lot, why Bezos dropped one-on-ones, and how every Amazon candidate faces a seven-person interview loop built on the leadership principles.

Bing then turns to what games taught him. He explains why moving a game from an 80 to a 90 doubles sales, why Steven Spielberg recut films until nobody left their seat, and how expansion packs for The Sims shaped his pitch for Prime.

He shares the David Ogilvy lessons that never made the books, including that 90% of people who recall an ad remember the headline and only 25% remember the body copy.

**Available Now: [YouTube](https://youtu.be/EsNvJrkgAr4?si=9bYvgZBHNosigLKe) | [Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/episode/2D0zv8io3fTmXKK92a4cHk?si=3359859315f34cd2)**|**[Apple Podcasts](https://podcasts.apple.com/ca/podcast/learning-from-bezos-jobs-and-spielberg-bing-gordon/id990149481?i=1000803770770) | [X](https://x.com/shaneparrish/status/2125200843481711087?a=P9Pgv1GUv1mvTxjPAGk&s=20) | [Transcript](https://fs.blog/knowledge-project-podcast-transcripts/bing-gordon/)**

## Tiny Lessons

Some of my favorite ideas and lessons from this episode.

**Founders, Leadership, & Boards**

- “The board members who say, ‘You should do this, you should do this,’ are dangerous, especially if they’re confident and handsome.”
- “When your board says, ‘Let’s bring in experienced people for adult supervision,’ you have to get those people off your board because adult supervision usually means somebody who’s over the hill, has a great resume and is not willing to roll up their sleeves.”
- “The board’s number one job should be help the founder be a learning machine and see the future.”
- “Behind closed doors, we have a debate. As a manager and team, when we walk out the door, we never second guess each other in public.”
- “Don’t argue with tone of voice, but argue with data, put the problem out in the middle of the room, and then let’s come up with a point of view.”
- Push the ability to say yes as far down in the organization as possible, or layers of bureaucracy will create an institutional no that kills your speed.

**Decision-Making, Learning, and Culture**

- “People who are right a lot are constantly willing to change their mind.”
- “Most humans have trouble updating their decision process with new data.”
- “It’s very likely that the founders who tap out at about 500 people have voted not to keep learning.”
- “The values you espouse have no correlation to company success. What’s correlated is the values you espouse get built into the company daily fabric, and that’s what’s important.”
- “Always know more than anybody in the room about your client’s business.”
- Skeptical optimists win because they can hold a big, life-changing idea in one hand while clearly seeing how it might fail in the other.

**Creativity, Quality, and Product**

- “The good to great usually happens after everybody’s worn out.”
- “The people that you hear about at the top of their game almost all push crazily when other people think they’re done.”
- “The beginning of great creativity is generating a lot of ideas.”
- “Trust your instincts and test your ideas.”
- “Engineers tend to value their work based on how hard it was to do, not how valuable it is to the customer. So you need to give them gaps around customer experience, not around engineering challenge.”
- “Most economists think that the perfect price is a single point and it turns out the perfect price is always a range and you can influence that through emotion.”
- If you have to tell customers you are high quality, they assume you are cheap.

**Investing, Motivation, and Life**

- “Pay attention to your stupid ideas. If people tell you it’s stupid, what they’re really saying, it’s one end of the bell curve or the other, and now your job is to figure out which.”
- “The stuff that everybody likes is usually not a great investment. Could be an okay investment, not a great investment.”
- Stop spending your energy trying to fix your losers and put it into riding your winners.
- If you want people to stay engaged in a game where they don’t always win, create a second currency that rewards their participation. (Think Casinos).

items.body:
As of iOS, iPadOS, visionOS, and macOS 27, there is now a WebKit API to enable [Global Privacy Control (GPC)](https://www.w3.org/TR/gpc/), an emerging web standard. As a developer using WebKit APIs like WKWebView, or WebPage for SwiftUI, you can add your own user setting to control it.

The [specification](https://www.w3.org/TR/gpc/) as of November 10, 2026, says:

> “Global Privacy Control is designed to allow users to express a preference to opt out of sharing and cross-context targeted advertising”

According to the California Office of the Attorney General’s [webpage](https://www.oag.ca.gov/privacy/ccpa) for the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) as of November 10, 2026:

> “This landmark law secures new privacy rights for California consumers, including: (…) The right to opt-out of the sale or sharing of their personal information including via the [GPC](https://www.oag.ca.gov/privacy/ccpa/gpc)”

## API

There is a new WKWebpagePreferences property, globalPrivacyControlEnabled. Setting it to YES on the preferences object handed back from the navigation-policy delegate opts that navigation into GPC. This applies to the whole document tree produced by the navigation. Once enabled, both navigator.globalPrivacyControl and the Sec-GPC: 1 request header are active for the main frame, its subframes, and their subresources.

The Swift WebPage API exposes the same capability through a WebPage.NavigationPreferences property, isGlobalPrivacyControlEnabled.

### Apple Developer Documentation Links

- [WKWebpagePreferences / globalPrivacyControlEnabled](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/webkit/wkwebpagepreferences/globalprivacycontrolenabled)
- [WebPage.NavigationPreferences / isGlobalPrivacyControlEnabled](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/webkit/webpage/navigationpreferences/isglobalprivacycontrolenabled)

## Example Usage

### Swift (WKWebView)

func webView(
_ webView: WKWebView,
decidePolicyFor navigationAction: WKNavigationAction,
preferences: WKWebpagePreferences
) async - > (WKNavigationActionPolicy, WKWebpagePreferences) {
preferences.globalPrivacyControlEnabled = userPrefersGlobalPrivacyControl
return (.allow, preferences)
}

### Swift (WebPage)

func decidePolicy(
for action: WebPage.NavigationAction,
preferences: inout WebPage.NavigationPreferences
) async - > ### Objective-C

- (void)webView:(WKWebView *)webView
decidePolicyForNavigationAction:(WKNavigationAction *)navigationAction
preferences:(WKWebpagePreferences *)preferences
decisionHandler:(void (^)(WKNavigationActionPolicy, WKWebpagePreferences *))

items.body:
This article explains how LLMs encode and process token position information by covering classic and contemporary methods like RoPE. It’s essentially a comprehensive journey where we will work through the mechanisms with visual examples, a little math, and a small PyTorch implementation. And, of course, we will then also look at how modern architectures adapt or omit explicit positional encodings.

Below, you can find a preview of which positional embedding choices are used in 2026 open-weight models. We will discuss these choices later after covering the underlying mechanisms.

Figure 1: A preview of the gallery’s 2026 architectures, grouped by positional encoding. Architecture figures taken from my [LLM gallery](https://sebastianraschka.com/llm-architecture-gallery/).

But why spending so much time writing/reading about this rather minor building block? LLMs keep evolving, and as I was preparing a new article on the latest LLM architecture trends this year, I realized that I never covered the positional information methods used in LLMs in any article so far. So, instead of letting the other article get out of hand, I thought it might make sense to publish this as a standalone building block for the upcoming LLM architecture and trends analysis.

Also, over the years, many readers have asked me for a tutorial on relative positional embeddings (aka RoPE) to follow up on the learned absolute embeddings used in GPT. It’s been on my TODO list for a long time, so I finally revisited my old draft and put this walkthrough together, which will cover

- different positional methods in LLMs;
- (finally) how RoPE works;
- what methods are used by recent open LLMs.

Note that this article assumes some familiarity with basic LLM architectures and works well as a follow-up to [Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch)](https://sebastianraschka.com/books/#build-a-large-language-model-from-scratch). If the concepts and computation of the attention internals, particularly query, key, and value vectors, are a little fuzzy, I recommend checking my [self-attention walkthrough](https://magazine.sebastianraschka.com/p/understanding-and-coding-self-attention) as a refresher:

The article is also very technical and likely too detailed for some. However, I really wanted to have this foundation out there for future articles to reference. And no worries, the next one will return to a more comfortable style.

**PS: I started experimenting with Substack’s new “perks” system. As a thank-you to supporters, I’ve added [image exports and metadata](https://magazine.sebastianraschka.com/perks) from the architecture gallery for you to use in your own analyses.**

PPS: If you are already familiar with how position embeddings work, feel free to fast-forward to Section 6, *Positional choices in modern architectures*.

Note that this article may be best read in a web browser than an email client. I recommend checking out the [web view here](https://magazine.sebastianraschka.com/p/understanding-positional-embeddings), which also has a navigation bar on the left side.

## 1. Where position information enters an LLM

Let’s start with the overall architecture. A tokenizer encodes the input text into token IDs. Next, the input token embedding layer of an LLM maps each of these IDs to a vector of numbers. We usually refer to these entries in that vector as “features” (similar to classic ML). The transformer blocks inside the LLM then modify these vectors using attention and feedforward layers. Lastly, the model’s output layer produces logit scores (converted into probabilities) for the next token.

The following shows this path in GPT-2 (a relatively classic LLM) and MiniMax-M3 (a more recent LLM released this year; a placeholder for most other recent LLMs). As we can see, the architectures are not too different from each other, but before we get to the positional information parts, let’s focus on the orange blocks for now (the token embedding layers) and the transformer blocks above them; the other architecture differences aren’t needed for this explanation.

Figure 2: Token embedding layers in GPT-2 and MiniMax-M3, highlighted in orange. (Side note: M3’s first three out of 60 feedforward layers are dense not MoEs.)

A token embedding layer, shown in the figure above, maps each token ID to a vector. Position information is then added afterward. Concretely, and as we will discuss in more detail later, GPT-2 adds a position vector to each token embedding before the modified embedding enters the first transformer block. On the other hand, MiniMax-M3 adds the positional information in each transformer block using a method called RoPE inside attention.

We will talk about these methods in more detail later, but first, let’s start with the big picture information explaining why explicit positional information is added or needed.

### 1.1 Why add positional information?

Consider the following two input sentences as a simple example:

- “The red fox jumps over the gray fox.”
- “The gray fox jumps over the red fox.”

Changing the word order changes which fox does the jumping, as illustrated in the following figure.

Figure 3: Changing the word order changes which fox jumps.

For the examples in this article, we will treat each word as one token for simplicity. (As you know, real tokenizers can split words into smaller subword tokens.) The first sentence then has eight token positions, from 0 through 7.

Figure 4: Token IDs and positions in the toy sentence.

# Assume the following small vocabulary.
# Real vocabularies typically have 50k to 200k entries
vocab = {
"The": 0,
"red": 1,
"fox": 2,
"jumps": 3,
"gray": 4,
"over": 5,
"the": 6,
}

(If you are interested in how vocabularies are built, check out my [tokenizer materials on GitHub](https://github.com/rasbt/LLMs-from-scratch/tree/main/ch02/05_bpe-from-scratch).)

Note that “fox”, which appears twice in the input sentence, gets the same token ID 2 in both cases. And since they both have the same token ID, irrespective of the position in the input sentence, they would get the same embedding vector from the embedding layer. (For those who are interested in more details on how this selection from the embedding table looks like, check [Appendix A](https://sebastianraschka.com/supplementary/positional-embeddings/#appendix-a-token-embedding-lookups).)

Now, let’s consider a regular self-attention mechanism with no positional encoding (and no causal mask), where every input token can attend to every other token in the input. In this scenario, swapping any two words, like “red” and “gray”, would still result in the same embeddings and attention scores between each token pair.

…

items.body:
*Housekeeping:*

- There will be a reader meetup in SF on December 10: [RSVP here.](https://luma.com/mk1c03jk)
- I’ll be in Stockholm on November 26 and made [a Luma event if someone wants to meet up](https://luma.com/8ga6l729). You can also dm me on Substack.

If you read writing advice, you’ll often stumble upon all of these rather abstract rules, such as “show, don’t tell,” “open the essay with a concrete story to engage people,” and so on. I don’t find advice like that useful at all. These sorts of maxims remind me of the small notes I might jot down to myself to remember the directions to a friend’s house—“left, right, past the oak tree, right.” Well, that might describe the right way, but it is a very rough map of the terrain, and if it turns out that the person who wrote the notes forgot to mention something—or perhaps was going somewhere other than you—their advice will lead you completely astray.

To develop a good toolbox, I find it much more fruitful to take the texts that I feel do whatever I want to learn best and read them slowly, repeatedly, with a pencil in hand. It’s like taking a slow, attentive walk around the neighborhood, getting a deep *feeling* for the landscape, for what it means to write at the highest levels. I will usually form a few theories about why the text is so powerful and I might spot a few techniques I can put into my toolbox, but these theories and techniques will be much more idiosyncratic and tentative than the ones I get from consuming writing advice: I will create tools that are meaningful to *my* projects, and my taste, and I will hold the tools with a light hand, knowing full well that they are just a rough guess, derived from a limited reading.

Last weekend, I did such a close reading of the piece that David Foster Wallace wrote about John McCain’s failed campaign for the Republican presidential nomination in 2000—the one that was originally published as “The Weasel, Twelve Monkeys and the Shrub,” a sprawling ~15,700-word essay in the April 13 issue of *Rolling Stone,* and later republished in a three-times-as-long “director’s cut” ebook called, first, *Up, Simba*, and later, *McCain’s Promise*. It is a New Journalism-derived sort of essay-reportage hybrid, where DFW travels around with the McCain campaign’s press bus, fails to interview any of the main players, and instead hangs around with the cameramen and sound technicians, but does little of the standard journalistic scene-setting and interview-quoting, in favor of a kind of writing that is a crossover between diary and essay.

I have read the book-length version of *McCain’s Promise* four times, I think, and the short version, once or twice. The immediate excuse for the last two + one rereads was that I wanted to understand how DFW integrates interviews and scene-setting into his essayistic reflections (and for the answer to that see this footnote1), but what I ended up focusing most on during the actual reading was the question: how on earth does he manage to make the reading so engaging and have such strong narrative momentum when most of it is just very long and detailed descriptions of the interior of a bus and the different kinds of phones people use on the bus and so on?

#### How DFW creates narrative momentum

items.body:
The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is a major setback for the US development of an open model ecosystem. Nvidia still has the financial interests in supporting open models, which are to avoid concentration in power among a few customers who would develop their own chips and reduce Nvidia’s profits, but supporting the open ecosystem is a tricky puzzle more than an engineering problem to grind out a solution on.

Nvidia’s business operations are famously extremely dependent on Jensen as an operator, so it is a consensus opinion that there are challenges ahead (or even more high-profile departures through chip-smuggling investigations or plain-old sharks circling more poachable talent). Nvidia’s number one goal is to stabilize the ship, deliver to customers in the next 24 months, and prevent implosion. Open models have been one of Jensen’s more ambitious, founder-style bets. He has been flooding the zone with funding in a way that will very likely dry up.

Interconnects AI is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

In this period, the open model economy is in its nascency. These are crucial years for establishing use-cases, revenue flow, and motives to continue training the next generation models. I discussed the sensitivity of these early years in my recent talk at Fireworks Forge ([slides](https://natolambert.com/slides/2026/fireworks/talk.html), [recording](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zsO5RktNB7k)). The core of the argument is one upside for open models, a reason to be optimistic, and one downside.

The positive case is that the open model economy has correctly latched onto “ownership of intelligence” and enterprise post-training as a crucial lane. What is to be determined is exactly how big the downstream market is.

The downside is that the true *long-term* benefit of open models, as truly commoditized intelligence, is very far from realization with compute in such short supply. In the near term, where [inference startups are also struggling to get enough chips](https://www.theinformation.com/articles/ai-inference-startups-quietly-buying-chips) (because Anthropic and OpenAI are buying so much capacity), there’s little margin competition on open-weight models. If open-source models are also served at giant inference margins, as we learned with DeepSeek’s [DeepInfer](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepinfer) release, they’re far from a commodity. In this paradigm, the closed labs with better economies of scale and integration from model to datacenter and chips will win. I expanded on this challenge in [my recent piece on the open model economy](https://www.interconnects.ai/p/how-well-can-we-measure-open-model).

Together, a lot still needs to go right for open models to be a meaningful economic engine. Jensen’s support, and protection, gave the ecosystem time to figure this out.

Jensen was more than a cheerleader. He would stop a lot of shit from going wrong once early winds were stirring. He was willing to use his power on open models.

There’s a major swell in Democratic government funding towards [candidates that want to regulate the AI industry, fostering “safety”](https://www.axios.com/2026/10/14/ai-safety-regulation-election-spending-50-million). Many of these people feel a need to do something and have general opinions that open models are unsafe, while not being educated on the complexities of their benefits. My biggest near-term worry is sloppy regulation at the state level, followed by national regulation. We’ve been [one, strong Chinese open-weight model away from a crisis](https://www.interconnects.ai/p/6-months-to-live-for-open-models) since this summer. It still holds – especially as we enter a new, turbulent equilibrium of cybersecurity. We have not seen a major hack driven by a popular Chinese open-weight model, but it is a matter of when, not if. We need someone to encourage caution and an ecosystem perspective when the “open-weight hawks” come hunting.

Knocking over the open-source AI domino today is easy — if done, unwinding the downstream concentration of power, reduction in safety research, and stifling of long-term innovation is far harder. On public data, it looks like balancing long-term innovation versus short term risks, but this is due to how horribly hard it is to measure the open model economy (e.g. the most valuable aspects of it run on private infrastructure). It’s a recurring challenge facing the ecosystem and my work.

As a brief aside, the extent to which the media ecosystem is revolving around timing today, rather than exact availability of information, is incredible. All of these Jensen affairs were known, but getting them out at the right time, right after the midterm political swing, took down the king.

The same goes for the Jacob Coxon brouhaha this summer. All of that safety culture around top labs was well known, but the right timing around datacenters and the Overton window made it a national issue. This could very well happen at some point for open model safety, as it tends to be harm, risk, or safety-related narratives that drive the modern media algorithms. I cannot imagine my work on open-science driving such a media cycle, because it will never happen.

[Share](https://www.interconnects.ai/p/open-source-ai-without-jensen?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&action=share)

The only lasting solution to this is to incubate a truly frontier open model player in the US. For example, I agree completely with Dylan Patel, CEO of SemiAnalysis, on a core problem in the US open model ecosystem. From a recent ChinaTalk + SemiAnalysis [emergency podcast](https://youtu.be/2jqSNHWdHEY?t=1737):

> Jordan Schneider: I do want your guys’ take on just how bad this is, that Jensen’s now off the table for the future of American innovation. And we should talk about open models. I mean, he was the big champion, right? Dylan, you were talking earlier — I still don’t understand quite why someone didn’t just spend a few billion dollars and make something better than Kimi or DeepSeek and open source it.
> Dylan Patel: Not that easy. It’s not money, it’s talent, man. All of the most talented people primarily work at Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepMind, and Meta TBD, right? And then those who don’t are split across a hundred different startups. I mean, yes, Thinking Machines has a cracked team, but is Thinking Machines as good as Moonshot? No. Moonshot skill-wise is probably just as good as the US labs. They just have a big deficit in compute and deployment. So I think if we don’t have a scale advantage, then you don’t win. Yes, these smaller labs have spent a lot of money on models. But DeepMind, Grok, Meta have regularly fallen behind the frontier of Chinese labs, and they’re spending more. So it’s not just, oh, spend a few billion dollars and you can make a model that’s better.

…

items.title: Revealed: The secret files on UK arms exports to Israel
items.subtitle: After a months-long investigation, Channel 4 News’s FactCheck team has obtained a dossier of exclusive new files on UK arms export licences to Israel.

items.body:
After a months-long investigation, Channel 4 News’s FactCheck team has obtained a dossier of exclusive new files on UK arms export licences to Israel.

The files give us major new insights into UK companies’ arms sales to the Israeli government during its war on Gaza, which has killed at least 75,000 Palestinians.

Our revelations raise questions about the former Conservative government’s policy on arms sales, as well as the current Labour government’s stated policy on the ongoing export of military aircraft parts.

We’re going to take you through the files step by step.

## The basics – what is an export licence?

When a UK company wants to sell arms abroad, it needs to apply to the UK government for an arms export licence – this document is like a permission slip.

Public data on these licences is limited. It doesn’t tell us whether the licences have actually been used to export weapons, or who in a given country would be using them.

But through repeated Freedom of Information requests to the Department for Business and Trade, FactCheck has now obtained several line-by-line snapshots of active arms export licences for Israel. The snapshots are from July 2024, July 2025 and July 2026.

Our new data captures which licences were active, not just for the country of Israel, but specifically for use by the Israeli government – which we understand means the Israeli military. And it also includes “usage notes”, which tell us whether a given licence has been used to export goods during a specific period of time.

## The Conservative government

On 7 October 2023, attacks on Israel by Hamas – which is proscribed as a terror group by the UK – left 1,200 people killed and 251 taken hostage. Israel then began its biggest ever bombardment of Gaza.

It was then that the International Court of Justice ruled there was a plausible risk of genocide in Gaza. Soon after, in April 2024, hundreds of UK lawyers, including former Supreme Court justices, issued a legal opinion saying that the UK must urgently suspend arms sales to Israel.

The then-Conservative UK government did not suspend arms sales.

Our first snapshot of new data reveals that, as the Conservatives were leaving office in July 2024, there were still 67 military export licenses left active where the Israeli government was an end user.

Those licences permitted the sale of a wide range of items – including parts for:

- combat aircraft
- military helicopters
- combat vehicles
- equipment for the launch and control of munitions
- military communications equipment
- military navigation equipment
- other military aircraft
- training ammunition, and more.

The total value of the active licences was around £164m. That represents an upper limit on what could have been exported under single issue licences. But the data also includes other types of open licence, which allow an unlimited value of exports.

We can reveal for the first time that, by July 2024, at least 25 of those 67 active licences had actually been used to send military parts to the Israeli government, since October 2023.

The licences that were used by UK companies to export goods during the war included licences for parts for:

- targeting equipment
- military aero engines
- combat aircraft
- military aircraft
- trainer aircraft
- parts for surface-to-air missiles.
- Targeting equipment refers to equipment which allows you to find, and aim weapons at, a target on the ground.

One of the used licences was a high value £25m licence for parts and software for “military aero engines”, which could include engines for military aircraft or drones. The data does not reveal the exact value that was actually exported. Another was an £88m licence for parts of “combat aircraft”.

The combined value of the used licences was around £150m. Again, this represents an upper limit on what would have been exported, and the actual value of the items sent was likely lower.

Two of the licences had been exhausted, meaning their full value was exported. These included one worth around £66,000 for trainer aircraft parts, and another worth around £109,000 for combat aircraft parts. It’s not clear whether the full value was exported during the war on Gaza.

We spoke to Professor Janina Dill, Dame Louise Richardson Chair in Global Security at the Blavatnik School of Government, University of Oxford. She told FactCheck that the UK “should have used [its] leverage” as a major arms exporter to Israel and “while there is a great deal of contestation around the question whether Israel is commiting genocide in Gaza”, it was “hardly contestable in 2024” that it was “committing grave breaches and war crimes”.

The Conservative Party did not respond to our repeated requests for comment about this story.

Israel has repeatedly denied the accusations that it has committed genocide or breaches of international law in Gaza.

## The Labour government

In July 2024, Keir Starmer’s Labour government entered power.

And by September 2024, the new administration said it wanted to suspend around 30 arms export licences for Israel, citing concerns over breaches of international law.

It said it was suspending exports that could be used by the Israeli military in Gaza. And it explicitly mentioned targeting equipment, and parts for military aircraft, including helicopters, fighter jets and drones.

But there were two big carve outs in the policy.

Firstly, Labour said it would continue to allow the sale of military training items, because they wouldn’t be used directly in conflict.

And secondly, the Labour government said it wouldn’t try to stop all exports of parts for the F-35 — a type of fighter jet used by Israel and NATO allies — because the exports went to a global pool that benefited multiple countries.

The Labour government refused to give us the full list of licences it suspended – even under Freedom of Information laws. It cited commercial sensitivity and confidentiality. It said if we figured out the names of the companies holding the suspended licences, we might, “potentially incorrectly”, link those firms to potential war crimes.

But by looking at the snapshots which the government did release, and comparing the active licences before and after Labour’s suspensions, we can corroborate some of what Labour announced about its suspensions.

For example, targeting equipment did disappear from later lists of active export licences, after Labour’s suspensions. As did other licences covering parts for military helicopters and combat vehicles. So that data fits with what Labour said it would do.

But many export permissions remained active under the Labour government.

Some of the licences that remained active for the Israeli government under Labour included parts for:

…

items.body:
Cover Image by [Gustavo Fring](https://www.pexels.com/@2206740/) from Pexels

*By Althea Need Kaminske*

Perhaps one of the more obvious pieces of advice that I give medical students about learning is to remember that our brains are in our bodies. Yes, I know that these are very smart, high achieving students who know quite a bit about anatomy and biology. But I also know that in an educational system and society that focuses so much on productivity, it can be easy to compartmentalize our lives. To become so focused on maximizing spaced retrieval practice (yay!) that we forget to prioritize sleep, nutrition, and exercise (boo!). In high-stress and fast-paced environments it can be difficult to remember that we are, ultimately, animals. Creatures that need sleep, a healthy diet, and daily walks.

A recent meta-meta-analysis by Singh et al. (2025) examined the effectiveness of exercise for improving cognition (1). The analysis included 133 meta-analysis, which themselves comprised a total of 2,724 randomized control trials. I’ll break down the results, but the overall finding was pretty notable: **exercise, even light intensity, benefits general cognition, memory, and executive function across all populations.**

The meta-meta-analysis classified outcomes into three categories: general cognition, memory, and executive function. General cognition was measured by scales like the Mini-Mental State Examination, Montreal Cognitive Assessment, and the Alzheimer’s Disease Assessment Scale - Cognitive Subscale which are used in medical settings to assess overall cognitive functioning. Memory was measured by instruments like the Wechsler Memory Scale and Verbal Learning Test which measure short-term memory and episodic memory. Executive function was measured by tools like the Digit-Span Test, Digit Span-Backwards, Digit-Span Forwards, and Trail Making Test Part A and B which measure visual and verbal working memory and attention.

## General Cognition and Exercise

There was a significant effect of exercise for improving general cognition. This effect was found across all age groups. The effect varied as a function of exercise type, with a moderate-to-large effect for exergames, and a small-to-moderate effect for aerobic, dance, mind-body, mixed mode, resistance exercise, and other. The effect of exercise on general cognition did not vary as a function of exercise intensity, however interventions that lasted for 1-3 months had the greatest effect on general cognition compared to interventions lasting 4-6 months or greater than 6 months. Finally, the beneficial effects of exercise on general cognition did not vary as a function of session frequency, session duration, or weekly duration.

## Memory and Exercise

There was a significant effect of exercise on memory. This effect was stronger in children/adolescents than in older adults (though benefits were still present in older adults). The effect also varied as a function of exercise type, with large effects for exergames, small-to-medium effects for aerobic, dance, mind-body, mixed mode, and resistance exercise. The effect of exercise on memory did not vary as a function of exercise intensity or intervention length. Further, the beneficial effect of exercise on memory did not vary as a function of session frequency or duration (there was an insufficient number of studies to draw conclusions about weekly duration).

## Executive Function and Memory

There was a significant effect of exercise on executive function. This effect was stronger in children/adolescents than in older adults (though benefits were still present in older adults). The effect also varied as a function of exercise type with exercises categorized as “other” as having a greater effect compared to aerobic, dance, exergames, mind-body, mixed mode and resistance exercise. The effect of exercise on executive function did not vary as a function of exercise intensity or intervention length. Further the beneficial effects of exercise on executive function did not vary as a function of session frequency, session duration, or weekly duration.

## Why does exercise benefit cognition?

The authors propose two potential ways that exercise improves cognition. First, there are several physiological mechanisms that might lead to cognitive improvement. The release of neurotrophic factors, increased vascularisation of the brain, greater dendritic spine density, enhanced synaptic plasticity, and reduced systemic inflammation (1). Your brain is in your body! Exercise improves overall brain health.

Second, the authors highlight the fact that exergames appear to be a particularly potent form of exercise. They suggest that this particular mode of exercise not only confers some of the physical benefits listed above, but may be particularly potent because of the challenging cognitive aspect of the exercise. Exergames require you to recall movements, recognize cues, and memorize steps.

## Exercise and ADHD

While there were benefits of exercise for all populations, the authors note that the benefit appears to be greater for those with ADHD. They highlight a few potential reasons for this. First, many of the studies examining exercise and ADHD involved children and adolescents, which is a population that was more responsive to exercise in general. Second, given that the hallmark of ADHD is struggles with executive function, they suggest that ADHDers simply had more room for improvement. Finally, they point out that one of the proposed mechanisms for working memory deficits in ADHD are altered neural activity in areas of the brain associated with working memory. Exercise may improve neural activity in these areas through enhanced blood flow and neuroplasticity. While further research is needed to test these theories, and to extend them to adult populations, this provides some initial evidence for a relatively low-cost tool for helping with the management of ADHD.

## Takeaways

Overall, I think the results of this meta-meta-analysis are really encouraging. Exercise - any exercise - can benefit cognition. Whether it’s a 20 minute walk after dinner, lifting weights, or breaking out the Nintendo Wii, adding movement into your routine can improve your cognition, memory, and focus.

My dog, Oden, who reminds me to go for walks every day.

…

Canadian singer [Bebe Buckskin](https://bebebuckskinmusic.com/), an Indigenous artist from [northern Alberta’s boreal muskeg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Alberta), performed a powerful cover of [Black Sabbath](https://laughingsquid.com/?s=Black+Sabbath)‘s classic [“War Pigs”](https://laughingsquid.com/amharic-war-pigs-sax-guitar/) in both English and Cree while sitting on a glorious throne. Buckskin had also painted her hands red to match the song’s sadly prescient theme.

The cover is from Buckskin’s new album *[Matriarchal Anarch](https://music.apple.com/us/album/matriarchal-anarchy/6831466893)y*, which also includes her Cree take on Led Zeppelin’s [“Immigrant Song”](https://laughingsquid.com/immigrant-song-cree-languange/).

Buckskin [shared on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DZ2rDj8JDhw/) why she sings classic rock in Cree.

> My favorite way to celebrate my Indigeneity is language revitalization through music!

items.title: The Australian Shuffle
items.subtitle: Shuffle a deck of cards and divide it into four packets.
items.feedText: Pick up any packet, look at the top card, and remember it. Spell out the phrase AUSTRALIAN SHUFFLE, transferring one card from the top to the bottom of the packet for each letter. Now apply the phrase Down Under — put the top card down on the table, and the next card under the packet. Continue doing this until you’re holding a single card. It’s the card you memorized. (By Josh Jay, based on a principle discovered by Alex Elmsley.)
items.body:
Shuffle a deck of cards and divide it into four packets. Pick up any packet, look at the top card, and remember it.

Spell out the phrase AUSTRALIAN SHUFFLE, transferring one card from the top to the bottom of the packet for each letter.

Now apply the phrase Down Under — put the top card *down* on the table, and the next card *under* the packet. Continue doing this until you’re holding a single card.

It’s the card you memorized.

([By Josh Jay, based on a principle discovered by Alex Elmsley.](https://doubledeal.wordpress.com/2010/10/23/wanna-see-a-trick-2/))

items.body:
You've heard that Disneyland has a huge colony of feral cats who roam the park at night, hunting mice and other rodents who come in to get a meal from the trash people leave behind. The company doesn't talk about them because, after all, their mascot is a mouse. And specifically because Disney doesn't talk about those cats (much), internet legends have grown up around them.

The cats moved in on their own because they found shelter where they wouldn't be bothered by people. Yes, they are managed by the park's administration now, but that was a gradual shift over time, and doesn't happen in the way you've been told. Cats don't follow instructions, especially feral cats. The Imagination Files dug into the stories about these cats and busts some myths about their history and status, including the most famous cat. The one thing he doesn't tell us is who gets to clean all those litter boxes.

items.body:
The surprising benefit of a common enemy

Sallust’s Theorem is that fear of an external enemy promotes internal social unity.

Perhaps more pertinent is the other side of Sallust’s Theorem: the absence or removal of an external enemy leads to internal moral decay and conflict.

Sallust, or more fully Gaius Sallustius Crispus, was a Roman historian and politician around the time of Julius Caesar. Remarkably, several of his works have remained intact to be read over 2000 years later.

Sallust describes unity in the face of common enemies and decline in their absence at several points in the history of Rome’s Republic. His strongest example is the fear of Carthage.

Here’s Sallust in his work The War with Jugurtha, chapter 41 (Latin terms included):

“…before the destruction of Carthage the people and senate of Rome together governed the republic peacefully and with moderation. There was no strife among the citizens either for glory or for power; fear of the enemy (metus hostilis) preserved the good morals of the state.

But when the minds of the people were relieved of that dread (formido), wantonness and arrogance naturally arose, vices which are fostered by prosperity. Thus the peace for which they had longed in time of adversity, after they had gained it proved to be more cruel and bitter than adversity itself.

For the nobles began to abuse their position (dignitas) and the people their liberty (libertas), and every man for himself robbed, pillaged and plundered. Thus the community was split into two parties, and between those the state (res publica) was torn to pieces.” (quoted from Neal Wood, see below)

Sallust sees Rome’s rise and decline as a psychological progression from liberty through glory and ambition to avarice (greed).

You may remember Carthage from the Colosseum scene in the film Gladiator, where Maximus is forced to represent the Carthaginians in Rome’s great victory at the “Battle of Carthage.” It doesn’t go to plan.

Tim Marshall introduced me to Sallust’s Theorem in his fascinating and relevant book Prisoners of Geography. He summarises Sallust’s idea in terms of alliances: “alliances are only strong with the fear of a common enemy.”

In some ways, Sallust’s Theorem is about the danger of getting what we want. We may resent a demanding boss, a fierce local rival, a struggle to build ourselves up from nothing, or a powerful business competitor, yet find that they gave us purpose and brought out the best in us as a group. We can miss them when they’re gone.

—

I believe the term Sallust’s Theorem was introduced by Neal Wood in Wood, N. (1995). Sallust’s Theorem: A Comment on “Fear” in Western Political Thought. History of Political Thought, 16(2), 174–189.

items.title: Women in Tehran are changing society by dressing as they choose, in numbers too large to stop
items.subtitle:
Parisa Khoshnami at Aeon:

Photo by Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/via Getty Images

What is happening in Tehran now is the quiet discarding of rules t…

Women up and down the city are removing their scarves and manteaus – the loose, knee-length coats they were required to wear over their clothes in public – and adopting the latest trends: capri trousers, cropped and close-fitting clothes, bare arms, midi skirts, bare legs. items.body:
Parisa Khoshnami at *Aeon*:

Photo by Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/via Getty Images

What is happening in Tehran now is the quiet discarding of rules that have governed daily life for decades. A few inches of [visible hair](https://aeon.co/videos/in-an-act-of-resistance-elahe-forgoes-a-hijab-at-a-family-party) used to be the whole argument, but it is no longer the point. Women up and down the city are removing their scarves and manteaus – the loose, knee-length coats they were required to wear over their clothes in public – and adopting the latest trends: capri trousers, cropped and close-fitting clothes, bare arms, midi skirts, bare legs. Enjoying this new freedom, they parade along Iranshahr (rather aptly, the street takes its name from the old Persian word for the land of the Iranians), where shops that used to sell manteaus and headscarves have switched to blouses and T-shirts.

A young woman whom I’ll call Mina puts the shift in blunter terms. ‘It isn’t optional anymore,’ she said. ‘You cannot leave the house in ordinary clothes. You have to be put together.’ She does not wear a headscarf anymore, and nor does anyone she goes out with. On the streets where people go to be seen, she tells me, hardly anyone does. In Tehran, those who can afford it wear the latest designer clothing. But in small Iranian towns, local workshops turn out such good copies of the latest Parisian and New York trends that anyone can now dress head to toe in ‘Chanel’, whatever their class.

More [↗ aeon.co](https://aeon.co/essays/its-not-political-the-young-fashionistas-of-tehran).

items.title: DNGDNGDNG ~ Vestigio
items.subtitle: There is something strangely archival about Vestigio, the latest album by Peruvian duo DNGDNGDNG (formerly Dengue Dengue Dengue).

items.body:
There is something strangely archival about *Vestigio*, the latest album by Peruvian duo **DNGDNGDNG** (formerly Dengue Dengue Dengue). Its rhythms and sonic patterns have an uncanny familiarity, as though they belonged to an established musical tradition, yet their origins are difficult to locate precisely. They seem to come from a geographical territory that has yet to be mapped, let alone explored. The artwork by [Joseph Melhuish](https://www.instagram.com/josephmelhuish/) reinforces this impression, depicting mysterious objects that might be archaeological remains of an unknown civilisation, past or future.

The recognisably Peruvian elements of their earlier releases have become harder to identify. As the duo explained in our interview, they are no longer interested in reproducing traditional rhythms but in extracting certain characteristics and rebuilding them in unfamiliar contexts. This is what gives *Vestigio* its peculiar character: the music feels familiar without quite belonging anywhere. Rhythmic structures drawn from different traditions are dismantled and recombined with influences from deconstructed club and drum and bass. On “Inercia”, fractured beats and abrupt shifts in rhythm create a sense of constant movement, an approach revisited on “Purpúrea”. Clipping, distortion and resonance are integral to the percussion itself, rather than effects added afterwards. The result is an ebullient album whose rhythmic vocabulary seems to have been invented from fragments of several different musical cultures.

There is also a darker side to *Vestigio*, most explicitly expressed in the closing track, “Noche Obscura”. Its title references the *dark night of the soul*, a period of spiritual crisis and eventual awakening. The voices declaring “Están matándonos” (They are killing us) and “¡Nunca más!” (Never again) give the piece an unmistakable political significance. As the duo explained, the track reflects their opposition to state violence and oppression, informed by Peru’s political reality but extending to conflicts and human rights abuses elsewhere.

The title *Vestigio* refers to something that survives a transformation. Here, traces of Peruvian musical traditions remain embedded in the rhythms, but their origins have become almost impossible to identify. What makes the album so intriguing is precisely this tension between recognition and disorientation: the sense of hearing something familiar while being unable to say exactly where it comes from.

Photo by Alejandro Loayza Grisi: Masks by Tween Muizen

To learn more, we reached out to Felipe and Rafael.

**Vestigio is described as your most radical sonic departure to date, with familiar elements of your music broken apart and reconstructed. How did this transformation come about, and what traces of your earlier work, from [Zenit & Nadir](https://denguedenguedengue.bandcamp.com/album/zenit-nadir) to [Fiebre](https://denguedenguedengue.bandcamp.com/album/fiebre) and [Agita2](https://denguedenguedengue.bandcamp.com/album/agita2), do you recognise in the new album?**

I think *Agita2* was something of a precursor to *Vestigio*. It was already pointing toward the sonic direction we wanted to explore on the album. Maybe not every track, but several of them contain some of that essence.

There’s also something of the darkness of *Fiebre*, certain percussive elements, and some connections to *Zenit & Nadir*. I think the album contains a little bit of each of our previous records.

The idea was to take specific elements from our music, break them apart, and reconstruct them in a different context. Not necessarily to bring back a sound exactly as it was, but to transform it and take it somewhere else.

At the same time, we wanted to push the energy and intensity of those elements much further. I think that combination of deconstruction, reconstruction, and the search for greater intensity is one of the main ideas behind *Vestigio*.

**In earlier interviews, you spoke enthusiastically about Afro-Peruvian polyrhythms and the possibilities of combining live percussion with electronics. On Vestigio, rhythm seems to emerge from the interaction of distortion, clipping and resonance, often becoming jagged and unstable. How has your approach to rhythm and sound design evolved, and what role do traditional Peruvian musical forms still play in your compositions?**

On this album, we tried to work more with compositions built from scratch. We still use samples and recordings, but we don’t necessarily build the tracks around them anymore.

Now we’re more interested in capturing the essence or feeling of certain rhythms and musical elements, then transforming them and placing them in a different context.

Traditional Peruvian rhythms are still part of our musical language, but we no longer feel the need to reference them directly or reproduce them in a recognizable way.

That gives us more freedom to create music that doesn’t necessarily belong to a specific genre.

For example, there are elements of Pandilla music and other rhythmic traditions, but we’re not trying to recreate those sounds. We’re interested in taking certain characteristics, breaking them apart, and using them to build something different.

In that sense, the idea of breaking things down and reconstructing them also describes our current approach to rhythm and sound design.

**Your back catalogue reveals an appetite for unlikely musical encounters, from reworking [Chabuca Granda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chabuca_Granda) and [Zambo Cavero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arturo_%22Zambo%22_Cavero) to combining shoegaze with dembow on [BambaPack](https://denguedenguedengue.bandcamp.com/album/bambapack-vol-1). More recently, you’ve collaborated with Prisma on Abisal, while Vestigio features [Los Hijos de Lamas](https://www.instagram.com/loshijosdelamas/), [Siete Catorce](https://www.instagram.com/sietecatorce/?hl=en) and [Only Now](https://www.instagram.com/kusharora/). What attracts you to these collaborations, and how do they challenge or expand your musical vocabulary?**

We’ve always been interested in collaborating with artists whose music we admire. They’re usually projects we’ve been following for a long time and that make us curious, especially when we hear something that surprises us and makes us wonder how they came up with that sound.

I think an important part of collaborating is precisely that curiosity about how other people develop their ideas and what can happen when we combine them with our own.

Experimentation and fusion have always been fundamental to Dengue Dengue Dengue, so working with other artists is a natural extension of that philosophy. It allows us to bring in new perspectives and reach places we might not have reached on our own.

items.title: Distinct trajectories and predictability of individual grouping patterns in dolphins link social ageing to longevity
items.subtitle: Meehan, Barbara Class, Shinichi Nakagawa, Meredith MacQueeney, Vivienne Foroughirad, Janet Mann, Celine H.
items.feedText: Recent work has unearthed strong relationships between ageing and average sociability. Clear patterns of decreases in average sociability are observed across taxa; many of these are sex-specific. items.body: Recent work has unearthed strong relationships between ageing and average sociability. Clear patterns of decreases in average sociability are observed across taxa; many of these are sex-specific. Individuals, however, generally deviate from population averages, and discounting individual variance in behaviour could disguise mechanisms of adaptation, selection, and developmental stability. Using 40 years of behavioural data from Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins, we provide new insights into social ageing. We achieve this by simultaneously measuring both mean (repeatability) and variance (predictability) in group size—a trait reflecting social interaction preference—across the population and throughout individual lifespans. Double hierarchical location-scale modelling reveals a multidimensional response; at both the population and individual level, the mean trait response (plasticity) and variance (malleability) of group size change with age. At a population level and for most individuals, average group size increases then declines in later life. This decline is more pronounced in males, though males are consistently in larger and more predictable groups than females at all life stages. Population predictability of group size increases throughout life, consistent with our prediction that social preferences strengthen with age. Individuals which are highly sociable are also highly predictable, and increased sociability and predictability both appear correlated with longevity. The positive correlation between increasing predictability and longevity leads us to hypothesise that individuals develop social competence by refining their social experiences. This process likely involves increasing social selectivity and optimising social choices to achieve a net fitness benefit. These findings provide novel insights into social ageing and illustrate how studying variance in social traits can capture processes of social competence, selectivity, and adaptation of social phenotypes occurring within an individual’s social environment.

items.subtitle: After I sold my company, I had to learn about long-term investing.

items.body:
After I sold my company, I had to learn about long-term investing.
The best books all emphasized the importance of owning a diverse portfolio of uncorrelated assets that rise and fall independently.
If one crashes, the rest don’t.

Don’t put everything into stocks or real estate or commodities or any one market.
Don’t put it all into America or Europe or Asia or any one place.
Don’t over-invest in what’s popular or familiar.
Invest equally into the entire world economy.

I apply this metaphor to worldviews.

You start with the perspective of your parents and culture.

But you are over-invested in one or two worldviews.

You have to deliberately diversify - to intentionally invest in other perspectives.

When your government or media says some country is the enemy, it’s a good sign that place has an uncorrelated perspective.
The governments have conflicting interests, but the people there are not bad people.

When another culture feels completely foreign, weird, and wrong, it means you are under-invested in that worldview.

Even in your own country, right versus left or whatever.

When the “other side” seems crazy, you need to balance your portfolio.

Invest some understanding until you hold some of those perspectives.

If people can predict your opinion on something, based on your opinion on something else, then your worldview is too correlated.

To be an independent thinker, own a diverse portfolio of uncorrelated perspectives.

items.body: Across animal taxa, females commonly mate with more than one male, even in monogamous mating systems. These extra-pair copulations and resulting young may increase the fitness of the female via a variety of mechanisms. The ‘good genes’ hypothesis suggests that socially monogamous females mate outside their pair bond to increase the fitness of their offspring via indirect genetic benefits, because extra-pair males do not provide parental care. We tested this hypothesis by quantifying extra-pair paternity in nonmigratory, food-caching mountain chickadees (Poecile gambeli). Chickadees rely on spatial cognition to recover scattered food caches, and variation in spatial cognition is associated with increased survival, longer lifespan, and is heritable. However, less is known about the role of sexual selection on spatial cognitive abilities. In the current study, we found that (1) males with better spatial cognitive abilities sired more extra-pair young and produced heavier offspring in their own nests compared to their poorer-performing counterparts, and (2) extra-pair males had significantly better spatial cognition than the social males they cuckolded. These results suggest that sexual selection shapes the evolution of spatial cognition in food-caching chickadees and are consistent with the good genes hypothesis, which posits that females gain indirect genetic benefits via extra-pair young.

items.body:
**Editor’s Note:** This story originally appeared in [On Balance](https://www.artnews.com/t/on-balance/), the ARTnews *newsletter about the art market and beyond. [Sign up here](https://cloud.email.artnews.com/artnews-signup/)* *to receive it every Wednesday.*

It’s Thanksgiving week and, for those of us who live and breathe the art market, that means only the briefest of breaks between the all-important November auction season and the year’s grand finale at Art Basel Miami Beach. But before we turn to Miami, a quick post-mortem on the marquee sales just passed.

Perhaps more than in any other industry, the health of the art market is in the eye of the beholder. Do you measure it by overall totals? By sell-through rate? By the number of bidders, or the number of guaranteed lots? By the ratio of hammer prices to estimates? Each figure tells a slightly different story, leaving plenty for our resident market whisperers to debate. But before we turn this week’s column over to the advisers, let’s set out some basic figures.

According to data from ARTDAI, the November evening sales at Christie’s, Sotheby’s, and Phillips generated $2.03 billion, a modest 7.5 percent increase over 2025, but the highest total since 2022. Sotheby’s led the pack with $1.16 billion, clearing $1 billion and taking more than half of the three houses’ combined total for the second straight year. (Its share rose to 57 percent from 53 percent. Christie’s share dropped to 38 percent from 43 percent, while Phillips’s ticked up to 5 percent from 4 percent, pushed by the [$44.6 million Modigliani sculpture.](https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/phillips-evening-sale-modigliani-sculpture-2026-november-1234806710/))

And yes, the $384 million gap between Sotheby’s and Christie’s is roughly what the Blaquier-Arrieta collection brought in on its own: [$412 million](https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/sothebys-modern-art-sale-blaquier-arrieta-van-gogh-1234806802/) on just 12 lots. Winning those big consignments really does matter.

But for all those gaudy totals, there was a definite sense watching the week’s sales that bidding was uneven, thin, and at times absent entirely. Blame fickle collectors, sure, but it seems the auction houses pushed their estimates to the limit. Per ARTDAI, hammer prices across the various-owner sales in November 2025 came in 17 percent above the low estimates and at roughly 80 percent of the high estimates. This season, hammer prices for the same sales (i.e. excluding the Blaquier-Arrieta single-owner sale) were flat against the low estimates and just 69 percent of the highs. As Sotheby’s CEO Charles Stewart [said](https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/sothebys-modern-art-sale-blaquier-arrieta-van-gogh-1234806802/) after the Blaquier-Arrieta sale last week, “Our estimates weren’t shy.”

But does an aggressive auction house make for a weak market? Or is this the same market we’ve seen for the last few cycles—one that is choosy, blue-chip and provenance-driven, and competitive for the right objects—just approached differently by the specialists? That’s what we asked the advisers, along with their takes on everything from the spread of guarantees to that $190 million van Gogh.

*Answers have been edited for clarity and concision.*

items.body:
** The latest on Trump’s approval rating**

**Updated November 24, 2026**

After rebounding slightly to 38 percent, Donald Trump’s approval rating is back on the downswing. **Today, 37 percent of Americans approve of the job he’s doing, while 60 percent disapprove**.

Show more Show less

Just 18.9 percent of Americans *strongly* approve of Trump, dangerously close to the 18.3 percent who *weakly* approve. If the president continues to get less popular, those figures could flip in the not too distant future. **-EMD** **, 11/17/26**

**See also: [Iran War support dashboard](https://www.natesilver.net/p/iran-war-polls-popularity-approval).**

This is the landing page for Silver Bulletin presidential approval ratings. We’ll regularly update the charts below as new polls about Donald Trump’s approval rating come in.1 This page is designed to be [viewed on the web](https://tinyurl.com/3fzxm9wc) rather than in our email client or in the Substack app.

[Click here for more information on how the average works](https://www.natesilver.net/p/silver-bulletin-polling-average-methodology). The Silver Bulletin average weights more reliable polls heavily — you can **[find our latest pollster ratings here](https://www.natesilver.net/p/pollster-ratings-silver-bulletin)**.

### The topline: So, just how popular is Trump?

Our default average reflects a combination of all polls, whether conducted among adults, registered voters or likely voters. If a pollster releases multiple versions of the same survey, we use the all-adult version of the poll before the registered voter version.2 This is because all Americans have a say in how popular the president is — whether or not they vote.

### The polls: What do the surveys say?

Each poll gets an “influence” score based on its pollster rating, its sample size, its recency, and how often a pollster is publishing numbers.3 Sometimes, surveys with mediocre pollster ratings have more weight in the model just because they were conducted very recently or polled more people.

Inevitably, there’s a lot of disagreement from survey to survey, not just because of [statistical variation](https://www.natesilver.net/p/dont-let-randomness-make-a-fool-of) but because pollsters have [long had trouble pegging down Trump’s popularity](https://www.natesilver.net/p/polling-is-becoming-more-of-an-art). By clicking on the “adjusted results” tab, you can see how [the “house effects” adjustment](https://www.natesilver.net/p/silver-bulletin-polling-average-methodology) that corrects for these predictable differences works in our model. You can also **[click here to download every Trump approval poll in our database](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/e/2PACX-1vS-FKWVTTFtJT6u56e0bqdfoMcXvDO1DUChsJ3jQAMB2lZk2SMqVfmg7dGjclTYkYWz-Pm5lfcLPjp4/pub?output=csv)** — including some additional details not shown in the chart below.

### The issues: What do Americans think of Trump’s policies?

Pollsters don’t just ask about Trump’s overall job approval, they also ask about how well he’s dealing with different issues. We’re tracking how the public feels about Trump’s handling of four topics: the economy, immigration, trade and tariffs, and the cost of living.

[↗ natesilver.net](https://www.natesilver.net/p/trump-approval-ratings-nate-silver-bulletin)
