items.title: De-fanging dangerous triggers in GitHub Actions across an organization
items.subtitle: Lobsters Security & Privacy • Lobsters Security
items.feedText: The maintainers behind these projects weren't careless. These triggers look harmless in a workflow file, and the unsafe version is one line away from the safe one. Insecure triggers can run workflows with access to your secrets, and a stranger can start them. When someone opens a pull request from a fork, the pull_request trigger runs their code with a read-only token and no secrets. pull_request_target looks almost the same in a workflow file and behaves very differently. It runs with a read/write token and access to your repository and organization secrets.
items.body:
# Python Software Foundation News: De-fanging dangerous triggers in GitHub Actions across an organization

- Python Software Foundation News: De-fanging dangerous triggers in GitHub Actions across an organization Wednesday, November 18, 2026 De-fanging dangerous triggers in GitHub Actions across an organization Authors: Mike Fiedler, Seth Larson On December 2, 2026, GitHub will start blocking the pull_request_target trigger by default in public repositories. If that sentence means nothing to you, this post is for you. If it fills you with dread, it is also for you. The short version: a handful of GitHub Actions triggers let a stranger on the internet start a workflow that may have access to your secrets. On a GitHub Team or Enterprise plan, you can turn them off for every repository in your organization with one policy. On a Free plan, you can do it one repository at a time. Set the policy up, check what it would block, then enforce it. Mike Fiedler, PyPI Safety and Security Engineer, and Seth Larson, Security Developer in Residence, have removed dangerous triggers and applied these policies to the Python Software Foundation (PSF) stewarded GitHub organizations ( psf , python , pypi ). They also wrote up technical documentation on how to roll these policies out to your own projects and organizations. The full details and technical documentation are available on the Alpha-Omega blog . Have dangerous triggers caused real incidents? Yes, repeatedly. A few that have affected projects hosted on PyPI directly: Ultralytics, December 2024 . The project's GitHub Actions workflows were compromised and the build cache was poisoned, which put malicious releases on PyPI. Seth wrote PyPI's analysis. William Woodruff's write-up traces the entry point to a pull_request_target workflow.
- LiteLLM and Telnyx, March 2026 . Malicious releases of both packages were published after an API token was exposed through an exploited Trivy dependency. StepSecurity traced the Trivy compromise back to a pull_request_target workflow exploited three weeks earlier. We worked with both maintainer teams on token rotation, release removals, and moving to Trusted Publishers, which both projects have since adopted.
- elementary-data, April 2026 . A workflow triggered by comments puts the comment text straight into a shell script. One crafted comment on a pull request ran with a token that could be written to the repository. The attacker used it to commit a malicious file and push a release tag, and the project's own release pipeline published the result to PyPI.
The maintainers behind these projects weren't careless. These triggers look harmless in a workflow file, and the unsafe version is one line away from the safe one.

## Why are these triggers dangerous?

Insecure triggers can run workflows with access to your secrets, and a stranger can start them.

When someone opens a pull request from a fork, the pull_request trigger runs their code with a read-only token and no secrets. That's the safe one.

pull_request_target looks almost the same in a workflow file and behaves very differently. It runs with a read/write token and access to your repository and organization secrets. GitHub built it for chores like labeling pull requests from forks, where the workflow never touches the contributor's code. The trouble starts when a workflow checks out the pull request and runs it anyway:

on : pull_request_target jobs : test : runs-on : ubuntu-latest steps : - uses : actions/checkout@v6 with : # a stranger's code ref : ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }} # running with your secrets - run : make test

Anyone with a GitHub account can open that pull request. Their code now runs with your credentials. This is called a "pwn request", and GitHub's docs describe it as the root cause of multiple supply-chain compromises.

The issue_comment trigger carries the same risk. This trigger fires when anyone comments on an issue or pull request, and the workflow runs with the repository's token and secrets. Sometimes the victim is a "comment /test to run CI" bot that checks out the pull request and runs their code. Sometimes the workflow pastes the comment text into a templated shell command, and the comment turns out to inject different instructions into the workflow shell.

### How did Alpha-Omega support this work?

That support is what gives us the time for the work behind this post:

- Seth wrote PyPI's analysis of the Ultralytics attack
- Mike and Seth worked with the LiteLLM and Telnyx maintainers during their incident, and wrote up the guidance for everyone else
- Mike set up the event policy for the pypi GitHub organization
- Seth is working to migrate the few remaining repositories using insecure triggers in the python GitHub organization before enabling the event policy
- Mike and Seth wrote this guide so other organizations can do the same!
### About the Python Software Foundation

The PSF is a non-profit whose mission is to promote, protect, and advance the Python programming language, and to support and facilitate the growth of a diverse and international community of Python programmers. The PSF supports the Python community using corporate sponsorships, grants, and donations. Are you interested in sponsoring or donating to the PSF so it can continue supporting Python and its community? Check out our sponsorship program , donate directly here , or contact our team!

items.body:
My thanks to Semantical for sponsoring DF last week to promote Ivy, the to-do list that ends. Typical to-do lists run forever. Ivy runs for one day. The concept is delightfully simple, but very effective. Each morning you make of list of things to do today, adding new items or pulling from a list of “ideas”. At the end of the day, whatever was left undone from your list goes back into the pool of ideas. Tomorrow starts empty.

The concept and the app’s name are inspired by the “[Ivy Lee Method](https://duckduckgo.com/?q=ivy+lee+method)”, a simple 100-year-old productivity system based on the idea of making a *short* prioritized list each day. You can add as many ideas as you want, and you can access your list of ideas at any time by just pulling down on the screen. Ivy never forgets anything, but the *current* list of tasks in front of you is never overwhelming. Start your day and your list of tasks for today is available as a Live Activity. Other features include focus sessions, Screen Time shields, and a daily journal.

[Ivy is currently on iPhone](https://apps.apple.com/app/apple-store/id6747921058?pt=1363339&ct=Daring-Fireball-Post&mt=8) (optimized for Duo, naturally), with a native Mac app in the works. It is truly native — SwiftUI, UIKit, and Meta — and integrates with both Reminders and Calendar. It’s just a beautiful app — one of those apps that’s worth trying just to feel it.

[★](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2026/11/22/ivy)

items.subtitle: Lobsters Computing Community • Lobsters Community
items.feedText: TL;DR: GitHub Actions accepts several invalid YAML productions, making it difficult (read: impossible) to parse some real-world action and workflow definitions with a properly conforming YAML parser. This is related to zizmor#1116 , which has been bugging me for a year and a half. Last April, a user reported that zizmor was rejecting a workflow containing a step that looks like this: - name : Create NPM Remote Repository JSON uses : jsdaniell/create-json@v1.2.3 with : name : " npm-remote-template.json " json : ' { "key": "npm-remote", "rclass": "remote", "packageType": "npm", "url": "https://registry.npmjs.org" } ' Apart from the use of a multi-line flow-style string for the json: key, nothing particularly stands out about this step. Except: it isn't valid YAML! YAML says this about flow-style nodes that are nested inside of a block-style parent collection (read: map or array):
items.body:
# TIL: GitHub Actions accepts invalid YAML

- All TILs Homepage Blog 2026-11-22 github
- github-actions
TL;DR: GitHub Actions accepts several invalid YAML productions, making it difficult (read: impossible) to parse some real-world action and workflow definitions with a properly conforming YAML parser.

This is related to zizmor#1116 , which has been bugging me for a year and a half.

Last April, a user reported that zizmor was rejecting a workflow containing a step that looks like this:

- name : Create NPM Remote Repository JSON uses : jsdaniell/create-json@v1.2.3 with : name : " npm-remote-template.json " json : ' { "key": "npm-remote", "rclass": "remote", "packageType": "npm", "url": "https://registry.npmjs.org" } ' Apart from the use of a multi-line flow-style string for the json: key, nothing particularly stands out about this step.

Except: it isn't valid YAML! YAML says this about flow-style nodes that are nested inside of a block-style parent collection (read: map or array):

> Flow nodes must be indented by at least one more space than the parent block collection. Note that flow nodes may begin on a following line. Source : YAML 1.2.2 § 8.2.3

That means the correct syntax is instead:

- name : Create NPM Remote Repository JSON uses : jsdaniell/create-json@v1.2.3 with : name : " npm-remote-template.json " json : ' { "key": "npm-remote", "rclass": "remote", "packageType": "npm", "url": "https://registry.npmjs.org" } ' The difference is barely visible:

- }' + }' YAML is a big and complicated spec, so it didn't even occur to me that this was invalid. Instead, I opened tree-sitter-yaml#36 to "fix" it. I've now opened tree-sitter-yaml#51 to revert that misbegotten fix.

On GitHub's side, I'm not sure if they have a clean path towards spec conformance here. Much of the code behind Actions is proprietary, but it seems likely that the underlying parser on their end is YamlDotNet .

Actions appears to use YamlDotNet 5.3.0 , which was released in 2018 . However, even upgrading to the newest version (18.1.0 as of writing) wouldn't fix this particular bug, since it's still present on that version (note the !isSingleQuoted guard).

My best guess is that a 2020 patch ( YamlDotNet#467 ) only fixed the double-quoted form because YAML's official test suite only tests rule 8.2.3 with a double-quoted string, despite it applying to both forms.

items.title: ★ A Week With the New Privacy Controls in MacOS 27.3 Beta 2
items.subtitle: On Monday, when the second betas of the v27.3 OSes came out, I posted about Apple adding the new privacy controls they had promised a month prior,…

items.body:
On Monday, when the second betas of the v27.3 OSes came out, [I posted about Apple adding the new privacy controls](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2026/11/16/macos-27-full-disk-access) they had [promised a month prior](https://daringfireball.net/2026/10/apple_full_disk_access), in the wake of Meta’s Muse app [surprising some users](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2026/09/22/aten-muse) with what information it had access to (e.g., incoming iMessages) after being granted Full Disk Access — which authorization some users just clicked right through. I also posted a link to Apple’s [corresponding new support documents](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2026/11/16/apple-support-full-disk-access). My initial take on Monday:

> I’m installing it now, but from what I’ve seen so far, these
> changes not only alleviate my concerns that Apple might
> over-tighten the screws, I actually think they add clarity and
> give users more, not less, control over their Macs.

After a week, I’m willing to call it: this overhaul of these settings and permissions is a win. I really like the way that, for apps asking for Full Disk Access, users can now grant access to a list of folders instead. That’s what I mean about these new settings giving users *more* control.

Are these new dialog boxes “scarier”? Yes, and the point is, they should be. You should be slightly jolted into attention when an app prompts for any of these permissions. The question is whether they are unnecessarily scary. I would say no, not at all. The descriptions are fair and accurate. Is it unnecessarily scary to show you thumbnails of your personal photos before permitting Full Disk Access that would grant an application unfettered access to your personal photos? No! It’s a bit of a jolt to see them, but that’s just reducing the abstraction. The words “full disk access” feel different than actually *seeing* a snapshot of what full disk access entails.

Might this discourage some Mac users from granting Full Disk Access to AI agent apps? Yes. And it should! Users who actually understand the stakes will not be dissuaded by these new permissions — when granting them is what they know they want to do. Additionally, I think these new dialog boxes represent very good UI design. [They look like a new modern take on MacOS “system chrome” design](https://www.macrumors.com/2026/11/16/macos-27-3-full-desk-access/) — not skinny iPhone-sized alerts.

My only gripe about the new stuff is the prominent menu bar indicator that now appears when one app is controlling another. You can’t turn it off (except via an undocumented hidden defaults setting), and it’s distracting on most Macs, and *extra* distracting on the new MacBook Pros with PROLED displays because on those Macs, it appears in the Dynamic Island! [Chance Miller, on Threads](https://www.threads.com/@chancehmiller/post/Df0aHZQoIVJ) (with screenshots):

> Most of the changes in macOS 27.3 are reasonable, but this Live
> Activity thing for system access has got to go. It’s way too
> aggressive.
> It takes over the Dynamic Island on the new MacBook Pro!

As I write this article on a new MacBook Pro review unit, I have 8 of these indicators in my Dynamic Island: [Scroll Reverser](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2024/06/18/scroll-reverser), [Keyboard Maestro Engine](https://www.keyboardmaestro.com/main/), [HazeOver](https://daringfireball.net/2026/03/hazeover), [SteerMouse Manager](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2024/05/06/hackett-logitech-mouse-driver), [Moom](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2024/10/09/moom-4-app-store), [Chest](https://chest.boringbar.app/) (a promising new utility for managing menu bar icons), [System Events](https://developer.apple.com/library/archive/documentation/LanguagesUtilities/Conceptual/MacAutomationScriptingGuide/HowMacScriptingWorks.html), and a new text snippet expansion utility I’m beta testing.

Every one of these apps is running all of the time for me. This indicator being on, all the time, for every one of them isn’t helping me notice unusual activity. If anything, if Apple doesn’t rethink this idea, it’s going to make me *miss* the indication if an app is taking advantage of access permissions in an unwanted or unexpected way.

Zac Hall, Miller’s colleague at 9to5Mac, published an article on Tuesday [showing the command-line defaults incantation to disable this](https://9to5mac.com/2026/11/17/how-to-hide-the-new-macos-27-3-menu-bar-indicator/). That’s better than not being able to disable it at all, but I expect Apple to revisit this based on feedback. It seems like a well-intentioned feature that was designed by people who didn’t realize how many always-on utilities “control other apps”.

items.subtitle: Here's the NVD page for the CVE with some additional useful context.
items.feedText: Paulos Yibelo · pwn.ai · 21 November 2026 Our previous research into ImageMagick's format handling and security policies showed how files with trusted extensions such as .jpg and .png could be handed to an unexpected interpreter. In this article, we show how we reached Ghostscript through most of the applications we tested, exploited a memory corruption bug in its font loader, and bypassed its -dSAFER sandbox to achieve remote command execution across widely used software. On 25 September, we posted a short announcement naming some of the applications and services our research had reached. The list came from following file-processing dependencies across products that otherwise had little in common. That gave us two connected questions to investigate: which interpreters could we reach through ordinary application features, and could those interpreters safely process the files we sent?
items.body:
# How We Hacked the Pipes — Upload2Shell

## How We Hacked the Pipes — Upload2Shell

Paulos Yibelo · pwn.ai · 21 November 2026

Our previous research into ImageMagick's format handling and security policies showed how files with trusted extensions such as .jpg and .png could be handed to an unexpected interpreter. In this article, we show how we reached Ghostscript through most of the applications we tested, exploited a memory corruption bug in its font loader, and bypassed its -dSAFER sandbox to achieve remote command execution across widely used software.

On 25 September, we posted a short announcement naming some of the applications and services our research had reached. The list came from following file-processing dependencies across products that otherwise had little in common.

That gave us two connected questions to investigate: which interpreters could we reach through ordinary application features, and could those interpreters safely process the files we sent? We continued into Ghostscript's internals and found several independent bugs of varying impact. We reported them to Artifex and worked with affected platforms to harden their file processing. Some of those bugs are still being fixed.

This article follows one of the more interesting findings. Upload2Shell , now CVE-2026-125396 , is a use-after-free in Ghostscript's Type 1 font loader. It gave us a write-what-where primitive: the ability to choose both the data written and its destination in native memory. A crafted document could use that control to alter the state enforcing -dSAFER and run commands as the rendering process.

Almost every application we tested with file uploads could be tricked into passing a file with a trusted extension to Ghostscript. A feature as routine as cropping an image or generating a preview could expose the interpreter. With the primitive working, we followed those conversion paths back out to their remote entry points.

## How an image upload reaches Ghostscript

Consider a PHP application generating a preview. Its code calls Imagick, the PHP binding to ImageMagick. ImageMagick selects a format handler, which may delegate the rendering to Ghostscript or another interpreter. The upload endpoint does not have to start gs itself; it only has to pass the file to a library that will.

Our WordPress-shaped preview proof reached that delegate through Imagick::readImage($input . '[0]') . The filename ended in .pdf , but the bytes were PostScript; ImageMagick handed them to Ghostscript under -dSAFER . The exploit also needed a Type 1 font file. In this delegate, it wrote the font to the scratch output path already authorized in currentpagedevice /OutputFile ; another self-contained variant used Ghostscript's process-local %ram% device. Neither needed a pre-existing font file on the server.

Ghostscript can also be linked into an image-processing build as a library. In that arrangement, the interpreter runs inside the existing process instead of appearing as a separate gs command. Looking only for explicit Ghostscript calls in application code misses both kinds of indirect invocation.

## Common ways a file reaches Ghostscript

An application does not need to call gs itself. In our separate decoder tests, the following ordinary image calls reached Ghostscript when given EPS content, even when the file was named .png .

from PIL import Image with Image.open(uploaded_file) as image: image.load() # pixel decoding invoked Ghostscript for EPS content Image.open() alone only identified the file in our test. Loading pixels, cropping, or converting them started the renderer.

Our source audit also found image decoding calls in InvokeAI uploads , AUTOMATIC1111 img2img , and ComfyUI previews .

We tested the calls developers use after accepting an image. Across two controlled runs on Ubuntu 24.04 with Ghostscript installed, one matrix traced 145 benign calls across 29 image APIs and the other covered additional wrappers including Imagick and imageio. We also gave the PostScript sample a .png name. It was not a valid PNG; this tested whether the decoder trusted the name or inspected the bytes. The versions below describe the tested libraries, not every product that uses them.

The decoder matters. PHP GD, OpenCV, prebuilt Sharp, Jimp, Java ImageIO, and Go's standard image decoders did not start Ghostscript for these inputs. Copying or storing a file did not render it either; the later preview or conversion is the step to inspect.

Ghostscript renders both PDF and PostScript. PostScript is a Turing-complete programming language used to describe pages, so rendering a PostScript document means executing a program. Ghostscript's -dSAFER sandbox restricts that program's file access and command execution. Like seccomp, it limits what untrusted code can do, but the enforcement is different: -dSAFER relies on checks inside the interpreter rather than a kernel-enforced system-call filter.

That still leaves a large interpreter exposed to attacker-controlled programs. As with a JavaScript engine such as V8, running the language is expected; a memory-safety bug can let a program corrupt the engine running it. An attacker can develop and test that program as a PostScript file, then deliver it through an ordinary upload.

Those permission checks matter because the rendering process has access of its own. Its service account may be able to read application files, write to disk, and start other programs. The sandbox is supposed to keep an untrusted document from using that authority. Loading a font is one of the ordinary rendering operations that must respect this boundary.

## A font helper with privileged access

GPT 5.6 Sol, working with @PaulosYibelo , found the issue in .putgstringcopy , a helper in Resource/Init/gs_fonts.ps . Ghostscript implements parts of its own font loading in PostScript. This helper needed to write into protected font dictionaries, so it used an internal operation called .forceput .

Ordinary document code should not have that ability. The helper was bound and marked executeonly , protecting its implementation from direct inspection. But it still had to execute, and one of the operations before its privileged write could fail. The relevant sequence was:

dup length string copy .forceput setglobal The first line copies a string. The second performs the protected store and restores the allocation mode. The helper did not first check that its operands were of the expected types.

We registered a Type 1 font in Fontmap and loaded it with findfont . The font defined an ordinary Courier-derived face, but its loading code could see the font loader's operand stack. It replaced the filename string on that stack with a local array. In the global-to-local conversion branch, length and string allocation succeeded; copy then raised typecheck because its source was an array.

…

items.feedText: # NixOS bring-up on an Alibaba RISC-V board ## NixOS bring-up on an Alibaba RISC-V board 2026-11-20 In the process of scouring Alibaba for a cheap Versal devkit, I unexpectedly came into possession of a Zhihe Computing A210 RISC-V SoC . 1 It’s a cool board: there’s a ridiculous amount of IO exposed by the baseboard, not to mention 8 cores clocked at 1.9 GHz is nothing to sniff at for a RISC-V CPU. I’m not sure I could recommend buying any RISC-V SoC currently 2 , but all these distros that are starting to support RISC-V need to run tests somewhere that isn’t Spike/QEMU. I decided to make this board into a NixOS build server so I could learn more about the state of RISC-V support in NixOS and to get some practice in Linux bringup. My complete A210 NixOS configuration can be found here ; I confirmed sound, HDMI, Bluetooth/Wi-Fi, ethernet, and the GPU were all working, but YMMV. ## I use NixOS btw Nix makes cross compiling to RISC-V a breeze: pkgs = import { system = "x86_64-linux" ; crossSystem .
items.body:
# NixOS bring-up on an Alibaba RISC-V board

## NixOS bring-up on an Alibaba RISC-V board

2026-11-20

In the process of scouring Alibaba for a cheap Versal devkit, I unexpectedly came into possession of a Zhihe Computing A210 RISC-V SoC . 1

It’s a cool board: there’s a ridiculous amount of IO exposed by the baseboard, not to mention 8 cores clocked at 1.9 GHz is nothing to sniff at for a RISC-V CPU. I’m not sure I could recommend buying any RISC-V SoC currently 2 , but all these distros that are starting to support RISC-V need to run tests somewhere that isn’t Spike/QEMU.

I decided to make this board into a NixOS build server so I could learn more about the state of RISC-V support in NixOS and to get some practice in Linux bringup.

My complete A210 NixOS configuration can be found here ; I confirmed sound, HDMI, Bluetooth/Wi-Fi, ethernet, and the GPU were all working, but YMMV.

## I use NixOS btw

Nix makes cross compiling to RISC-V a breeze:

pkgs = import { system = "x86_64-linux" ; crossSystem . system = "riscv64-linux" ; }; It really is that easy—building pkgs.hello will produce a bona fide RISC-V executable (you don’t even need a Nix file for one-off builds, just run nix build nixpkgs#pkgsCross.riscv64.hello ). Some black magic in callPackage ensures that compile-time tools are built for buildPlatform and build artifacts are built for hostPlatform .

In the process of compiling over a thousand packages I only ran into two issues: a problem with rust-bindgen using the wrong version of clang and ministream not being properly configured for cross compilation , neither of which was specific to RISC-V.

That having been said, I did run into some pretty bizarre OOM issues for some of the heavy hitters like Clang and GFortran. I was seeing >9GB memory usage per linking process(!) when compiling from x86_64-linux , which will quickly exhaust all of your memory if you have max-jobs / cores set to sane values. I sidestepped this issue by temporarily nerfing build parallelism into oblivion and running the offending builds overnight:

nix-store --realise /nix/store/...-clang-riscv64-unknown-linux-gnu-21.1.8.drv -j1 --cores 3 --builders "" I don’t (yet) have access to a RISC-V remote Nix builder, but even if I did, it’s substantially faster to cross compile everything from my desktop. Cross compilation can get a little wonky with Nix flakes because you have to encode the buildPlatform in the output schema somehow, but nixosConfigurations does not allow nesting ( nixosConfigurations.x86_64-linux-a210 is valid, but nixosConfigurations.x86_64-linux.a210 isn’t).

My solution to this is to expose the relevant build artifacts of the NixOS configuration (ISO + flashing script) under packages.${system} by creating a “wrapper” NixOS configuration for each buildPlatform that extends nixosConfigurations.a210 :

packages = forAllSystems (pkgs: let nixosCross = self . nixosConfigurations . a210 . extendModules { modules = [ ({ ... }: { nixpkgs = { inherit pkgs; overlays = [ # ... ]; buildPlatform = { inherit (pkgs . stdenv . buildPlatform) system; }; hostPlatform = "riscv64-linux" ; }; }) ]; }; in { inherit (nixosCross . config . system . build) toplevel image initialRamdisk; }; This way nixosConfigurations is agnostic to buildPlatform , and cross compilation is straightforward—running nix build .#image on an x86_64-linux machine will use x86_64-linux as the buildPlatform , as one would expect.

## Boot flow

Ok, so the goal is to boot U-Boot FSBL -> OpenSBI -> U-Boot SSBL -> Linux -> NixOS userspace , using the vendor’s Buildroot scripts as reference.

Using vendor forks of U-Boot/Linux/OpenSBI is a simple matter of overriding src and sprinkling in a few patches (almost always to fix compiler warnings that have been promoted to errors in the latest version of GCC/Clang in nixpkgs). All we really have to do is slot in the vendor kernel by setting boot.kernelPackages = pkgs.linuxPackagesFor pkgs.linuxA210;

Armed with a bootloader and NixOS image, I plugged in the A210 to my MacBook and turned on Fastboot flashing mode, but to my dismay macOS refused to enumerate the device. Initially I figured the board was a lemon (due to it being a freebie and all), but I wasn’t ready to give up hope that easily.

I pored over the datasheet looking for alternative boot methods, and I investigated using PD resistors to force QSPI boot (using NORbert in lieu of a real QSPI device) to bootstrap into Linux userspace, at which point I could flash the eMMC directly without relying on Fastboot. But before pulling out my soldering iron I decided to try plugging the board into a different computer, which instantly detected the board. D’oh!

Ok, so Fastboot works 3 and I’m able to load the flasher firmware and program eMMC (I based my Fastboot payload on openEuler’s A210 guide instead of the vendor’s script which flashes 7(!) different partitions), but after that I still got dead silence on UART. At this point I was pretty suspicious of my serial connection, so I decided to test it on a Pi Pico: lo and behold, it turns out leaving my BMP ’s vRef pin floating was the culprit.

After losing several hours and my dignity to the aforementioned skill issue, I was greeted with the following panic:

sbi_trap_error: hart0: trap1: illegal instruction handler failed (error -2) sbi_trap_error: hart0: trap1: mcause=0x0000000000000002 mtval=0x00000000cc087057 sbi_trap_error: hart0: trap1: mepc=0x000000008000bb24 mstatus=0x0000000a00001800 sbi_trap_error: hart0: trap1: ra=0x0000000080007336 sp=0x0000000080062e68 sbi_trap_error: hart0: trap1: gp=0x0000000082c50aa0 tp=0x0000000082c54c80 sbi_trap_error: hart0: trap1: s0=0x0000000080062eb8 s1=0x0000000080062eb8 sbi_trap_error: hart0: trap1: a0=0x0000000080062eb8 a1=0x0000000000000000 sbi_trap_error: hart0: trap1: a2=0x0000000000000000 a3=0x0000000000000000 sbi_trap_error: hart0: trap1: a4=0x0000000080027c94 a5=0x0000000080007330 sbi_trap_error: hart0: trap1: a6=0x0000000000000004 a7=0x0000000000000010 sbi_trap_error: hart0: trap1: s2=0x0000000080063000 s3=0x00000000fa685000 sbi_trap_error: hart0: trap1: s4=0x0000000080200000 s5=0x0000000000000000 sbi_trap_error: hart0: trap1: s6=0x00000000fff3661e s7=0x0000000000000000 sbi_trap_error: hart0: trap1: s8=0x00000000fbf37c50 s9=0x0000000000000001 sbi_trap_error: hart0: trap1: s10=0x00000000fbf44b90 s11=0x00000000fbf2d228 sbi_trap_error: hart0: trap1: t0=0x0000040000000000 t1=0x000000008156c15d sbi_trap_error: hart0: trap1: t2=0x0000000002000000 t3=0x000000008156c158 sbi_trap_error: hart0: trap1: t4=0x0000000000000007 t5=0x00000000fa688fff sbi_trap_error: hart0: trap1: t6=0x00000000fbf2c428 Are we RISC-V yet? Judging from the above register dump, something seems to be amiss with OpenSBI itself:

items.title: From Skiplists to B+ Trees: Making Valkey Sorted Sets More Memory Efficient
items.subtitle: Lobsters High-Performance Engineering • Lobsters Perf
items.feedText: A sorted set can spend more memory describing how its elements are ordered than storing the elements themselves. In Valkey 9.2 that changes: the skiplist is replaced by a high-fanout B+ tree variant called fbtree . fbtree combines the high fanout and contiguous storage of a conventional B+ tree with several optimizations designed for Valkey's workload and memory allocator, including feature-based lookups, SIMD searches, linked leaves, and fast paths for sequential inserts and pops. # Valkey: From Skiplists to B+ Trees: Making Valkey Sorted Sets More Memory Efficient

## From Skiplists to B+ Trees: Making Valkey Sorted Sets More Memory Efficient

A sorted set can spend more memory describing how its elements are ordered than storing the elements themselves.

In Valkey 9.2 that changes: the skiplist is replaced by a high-fanout B+ tree variant called fbtree .

fbtree combines the high fanout and contiguous storage of a conventional B+ tree with several optimizations designed for Valkey's workload and memory allocator, including feature-based lookups, SIMD searches, linked leaves, and fast paths for sequential inserts and pops. In a 5-million-member test, it reduced per-member memory overhead by 36–43%, saving up to 109 MB.

Let's take a look at why this change happened and how it works.

## Why replace the skiplist?

Large sorted sets that exceed the listpack threshold are backed by a skiplist paired with a hashtable (smaller sorted sets use a compact listpack representation that stores elements sequentially in contiguous memory). The hashtable gives O(1) lookups by member, while the skiplist gives O(log n) ordered lookups by rank or score. That pairing is architecturally simple, but the skiplist carries a significant memory cost. It stores exactly one element per node, scattered across memory as separate allocations connected by pointers.

### Memory overhead

Valkey's skiplist pays for this in raw memory. Every node carries a backward pointer (8B), plus an average of 1.33 levels of forward pointers and span values, since skiplists are probabilistic (each node has a 25% chance of gaining another level). Each level costs 8B for the pointer plus 8B for the span value, giving around 29B of pointer and span overhead per node. Add the 8B score, and the total reaches roughly 37B per node before accounting for the member string.

### Cache misses and dependent fetches

Modern CPUs use a hierarchy of hardware caches (L1, L2, and L3) to keep frequently accessed data close to the processor. These caches are much smaller and faster than main memory (RAM), so when the CPU cannot find the data it needs in its cache, it must fetch it from a slower level of the memory hierarchy. As a rough illustration, an L1 cache hit can take about 1 ns, while a DRAM access can take around 100 ns. A dependent memory access can leave the core waiting; actual latency and how much work can be hidden vary by system and workload 1 .

Each node in the skiplist is a separate allocation, potentially scattered wherever the heap happened to place it, so following the structure can require repeatedly fetching data from unrelated memory locations. Because each step can determine where the next step goes, these fetches are dependent, resulting in more round trips through the memory hierarchy. A 2025 study of concurrent in-memory indexes found that, on its tested workloads, traditional skiplists experienced roughly 2.4–4.8× more cache misses than a comparable B-tree, with 2–8× lower throughput 2 (testing different data structure implementations, not Valkey).

## What replaced it: fbtree

A B+ tree keeps entries sorted in fixed-size nodes: leaf nodes hold the entries, or pointers to them, and inner nodes hold just enough routing data to pick which child to descend into. Packing many entries into each node addresses both problems above: far less per-member pointer overhead, and far fewer dependent fetches per lookup.

### Memory layout

fbtree, short for Feature B+ Tree, uses a 61-way fanout: each node can hold up to 61 entries or child pointers. Leaf and inner nodes are sized to fit jemalloc allocation classes without wasting space on 64-bit builds; on supported 32-bit builds, innerNode is rounded up to the 1280-byte class.

A 512-byte leaf holds up to 61 value pointers, so 61 members share one node instead of each getting its own. Instead of storing the score and member separately, fbtree stores them together as a single packed value: the normalized 8-byte score followed by the member bytes. This keeps the data needed for comparisons together and removes another level of pointer indirection.

### Fewer memory fetches

The skiplist's 25%-per-level rule gives it an effective branching factor of about 4, while fbtree's fanout is 61. Both structures retain O(log n) search complexity, but the B+ tree has substantially fewer levels to traverse and therefore fewer opportunities for expensive memory fetches.

A modern CPU can also fetch several adjacent cache lines efficiently when the data is laid out contiguously, thanks in part to the way memory is accessed and to hardware prefetching 1 . Therefore a B+ tree node that spans a few cache lines can be read efficiently as the CPU scans its contents.

### Optimizations

On top of that structure, fbtree adds optimizations aimed at specific operations.

In a B+ tree keyed by variable-length strings, such as sorted set members, picking a child means comparing the lookup against each child’s anchor, the largest member in that child, and reading those strings costs memory fetches. fbtree's inner nodes store each anchor along with a small four-byte "feature." Because the anchors often share a common prefix, fbtree stores that shared prefix separately and uses the four feature bytes to distinguish the children. The implementation can then compare those features in parallel using SIMD, often identifying the correct child before fetching the child node itself. If the features uniquely identify a child, the search can descend immediately; otherwise, they still narrow the range that needs a full binary search.

Range commands such as ZRANGE walk the set in order. fbtree links its leaf nodes in a doubly-linked list, so a scan can move from leaf to leaf without climbing back up the tree. The skiplist requests an item, waits to receive it, and only knows the next item to fetch when it's received the first. The B+ tree can work on up to 61 items in parallel, and while it works on those it can fetch the next leaf node with the next 61 items.

Commands such as ZPOPMIN work at the ends of the set. fbtree caches its leftmost and rightmost leaves, so finding them is O(1), as in a skiplist, instead of O(log n). This keeps pop and append operations at parity rather than regressing.

Range deletions remove a contiguous run of members, and fbtree handles them without rebuilding the surrounding structure.

## What actually changed for you

Functionally, nothing changes.

The change is internal: sorted set commands and their behavior remain unchanged. The one visible difference is that OBJECT ENCODING returns btree instead of skiplist for a large sorted set. If you have monitoring, tests, or tooling that checks for the literal string skiplist , that's one place to update. Small sorted sets under the listpack threshold are unaffected either way, since they never used the skiplist encoding to begin with.

items.body:
# DNS Stamps Specification - DNSCrypt, DoH, DoT Format | DNSCrypt

## DNS Stamps

Server stamps encode all the parameters required to connect to a secure DNS server as a single string. Think about stamps as QR code, but for DNS.

## Online DNS stamp calculator

Stamps can be quickly viewed/modified/created using this VueJS component .

An online demo is accessible here: https://stamps.dnscrypt.info

An example list of public secure DNS resolvers , with their DNS stamps.

## Common definitions

- a || b is the concatenation of a and b
- a | b is the result of the logical OR operation between a and b .
- len(x) is a single byte representation of the length of x , in bytes. Strings don’t have to be zero-terminated and do not require invidual encoding.
- vlen(x) is equal to len(x) if x is the last element of a set, and 0x80 | len(x) if there are more elements in the set.
- LP(x) is len(x) || x , i.e x prefixed by its length.
- VLP(x1, x2, ...xn) encodes a set, as vlen(x1) || x1 || vlen(x2) || x2 ... || vlen(xn) || xn . Since vlen(xn) == len(xn) (length of the last element doesn’t have the high bit set), for a set with a single element, we have VLP(x) == LP(x) .
- [ Q ] means that Q is optional.
- base64url(s) is the URL-safe base64 encoding of s . None of the parameters are individually base64-encoded. Base64-encoding is only applied once, on the entire concatenation of all length-prefixed parameters.
## Encoding examples:

- LP("10.0.0.1") is [ 0x08, 0x31, 0x30, 0x2e, 0x30, 0x2e, 0x30, 0x2e, 0x31 ]
- VLP("10.0.0.1", "10.0.0.2") evaluates to [ 0x88, 0x31, 0x30, 0x2e, 0x30, 0x2e, 0x30, 0x2e, 0x31, 0x08, 0x31, 0x30, 0x2e, 0x30, 0x2e, 0x30, 0x2e, 0x32 ]
- base64url(VLP("10.0.0.1", "10.0.0.2")) is iDEwLjAuMC4xCDEwLjAuMC4y
## DNSCrypt stamps

Format:

"sdns://" || base64url(0x01 || props || LP(addr [:port]) || LP(pk) || LP(providerName)) 0x01 is the protocol identifier for DNSCrypt.

props is a little-endian 64 bit value that represents informal properties about the resolver. It is a logical OR combination of the following values:

- 1 : the server supports DNSSEC
- 2 : the server doesn’t keep logs
- 4 : the server doesn’t intentionally block domains
For example, a server that supports DNSSEC, stores logs, but doesn’t block anything on its own should set props as the following 8 bytes sequence: [ 0x05, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00 ] .

addr is the IP address, as a string, with a port number if the server is not accessible over the standard port for the protocol (443). IPv6 strings must be included in square brackets: [fe80::6d6d:f72c:3ad:60b8] . Scopes are permitted.

pk is the DNSCrypt provider’s Ed25519 public key, as 32 raw bytes.

providerName is the DNSCrypt provider name.

## DNS-over-HTTPS stamps

Format:

"sdns://" || base64url(0x02 || props || LP(addr) || VLP(hash1, hash2, ...hashn) || LP(hostname [:port]) || LP(path) [ || VLP(bootstrap_ip1, bootstrap_ip2, ...bootstrap_ipn) ]) addr is the IP address of the server. It can be an empty string. In that case, the host name will be resolved to an IP address using another resolver.

hashi is the SHA256 digest of one of the TBS certificate found in the validation chain, typically the certificate used to sign the resolver’s certificate. Multiple hashes can be provided for seamless rotations.

hostname is the server host name which will also be used as a SNI name. If the host name contains characters outside the URL-permitted range, these characters should be sent as-is, without any extra encoding (neither URL-encoded nor punycode). The port number is optional, and is assumed to be 443 if missing.

path is the absolute URI path, such as /dns-query .

bootstrap_ipi are IP addresses of recommended resolvers accessible over standard DNS in order to resolve hostname . This is optional, and clients can ignore this information.

## DNS-over-TLS stamps

Format:

"sdns://" || base64url(0x03 || props || LP(addr) || VLP(hash1, hash2, ...hashn) || LP(hostname [:port]) || [ || VLP(bootstrap_ip1, bootstrap_ip2, ...bootstrap_ipn) ]) addr is the IP address of the server. It can be an empty string. In that case, the host name will be resolved to an IP address using another resolver.

IPv6 strings must be included in square brackets: [fe80::6d6d:f72c:3ad:60b8] . Scopes are permitted.

hashi is the SHA256 digest of one of the TBS certificate found in the validation chain, typically the certificate used to sign the resolver’s certificate. Multiple hashes can be provided for seamless rotations.

hostname is the server host name which will also be used as a SNI name. The port number is optional, and is assumed to be 443 if missing.

bootstrap_ipi are IP addresses of recommended resolvers accessible over standard DNS in order to resolve hostname . This is optional, and clients can ignore this information.

## DNS-over-QUIC stamps

Format:

"sdns://" || base64url(0x04 || props || LP(addr) || VLP(hash1, hash2, ...hashn) || LP(hostname [:port]) || [ || VLP(bootstrap_ip1, bootstrap_ip2, ...bootstrap_ipn) ]) addr is the IP address of the server. It can be an empty string. In that case, the host name will be resolved to an IP address using another resolver.

IPv6 strings must be included in square brackets: [fe80::6d6d:f72c:3ad:60b8] . Scopes are permitted.

hashi is the SHA256 digest of one of the TBS certificate found in the validation chain, typically the certificate used to sign the resolver’s certificate. Multiple hashes can be provided for seamless rotations.

hostname is the server host name which will also be used as a SNI name. The port number is optional, and is assumed to be 443 if missing.

bootstrap_ipi are IP addresses of recommended resolvers accessible over standard DNS in order to resolve hostname . This is optional, and clients can ignore this information.

## Oblivious DoH target stamps

Format:

"sdns://" || base64url(0x05 || props || LP(hostname [:port]) || LP(path)) hostname is the server host name which, for relays, will also be used as a SNI name. If the host name contains characters outside the URL-permitted range, these characters should be sent as-is, without any extra encoding (neither URL-encoded nor punycode). The port number is optional, and is assumed to be 443 if missing.

path is the absolute URI path, such as /dns-query .

## Anonymized DNSCrypt relay stamps

Format:

"sdns://" || base64url(0x81 || LP(addr)) 0x81 is the protocol identifier for a DNSCrypt relay.

addr is the IP address and port, as a string. IPv6 strings must be included in square brackets: [fe80::6d6d:f72c:3ad:60b8]:443 .

## Oblivious DoH relay stamps

Format:

"sdns://" || base64url(0x85 || props || LP(addr) || VLP(hash1, hash2, ...hashn) || LP(hostname [:port]) || LP(path) [ || VLP(bootstrap_ip1, bootstrap_ip2, ...bootstrap_ipn) ]) 0x85 is the protocol identifier for an oDoH relay.

addr is the IP address of the server. It can be an empty string. In that case, the host name will be resolved to an IP address using another resolver.

# How Google Duplex evolved to also call businesses for you in Gemini

How Google Duplex evolved to also call businesses for you in Gemini November 20, 2026

Yossi Matias, Vice President, Google & GM, Google Research, Yaniv Leviathan, Google Fellow, Google Research, and Janet Zhou, Group Product Manager, Google Maps

When we introduced Google Duplex in 2018, it pioneered natural voice conversations between AI and local businesses over the phone. Since then, this technology has worked behind the scenes across many Google products. These capabilities are integrated directly in Tasks in Gemini .

## Quick links

- Tasks in Gemini
- Share
- Copy link ×
Completing tasks like making dinner reservations or booking a hair appointment is time consuming. Live phone conversations move fast and rarely follow a script. The person on the other end can say almost anything, often revising their thoughts mid-sentence – and people often rely on subtle tone changes to indicate whose turn it is to speak. Pause half a second too long, and it sounds like the call dropped; speak too soon, and you end up talking over each other. Leveraging AI to complete these tasks respectfully over the phone required us to consider high quality speech understanding, contextual reasoning, and speech synthesis working together in a single, low-latency system.

We introduced Google Duplex nearly a decade ago to help address this challenge. Propelled by advances in foundation models, the Duplex architecture has evolved to power autonomous task completion across many core products, such as Google Search and Maps. This week, we launched Duplex in Tasks in Gemini App , a personal AI collaborator that can help coordinate real-world chores, like calling businesses for you and handling real-world requests on behalf of the user. In this post, we look back at the decade-long architectural evolution that made this possible — moving from early, closed-domain models to a unified stack built entirely with Gemini.

## From closed-domain calls to Tasks in Gemini

What began as a narrow, task-specific system quickly expanded into a shared conversational infrastructure, built in collaboration with teams across Google.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, when business hours and services shifted rapidly, Duplex doubled down on verifying merchant info automatically to keep listings accurate. It remains an important data source; for example, business information sourced from Duplex’s phone calls had been shown in Search and Maps over one trillion times , as we shared in 2023.

Simultaneously, we worked with Android and hardware teams to bring these conversational models directly on-device. Starting in 2019, we rolled out new Pixel Call Assist features across five consecutive Pixel generations. These models continue to power features like Call Screen and Hold for Me , helping users filter unknown callers and speak with a live agent when a hold queue ends until the user rejoins. In 2025 and 2026, foundation models unlocked broader agentic calling in Google Search and Ask Maps , checking quotes, product availability, and service openings from pet grooming to auto repair.

## Three generations of conversational architecture

Over the past decade, the stack behind these calls evolved through three distinct eras, moving from bespoke neural pipelines to a unified architecture using Gemini.

### 1. Pre-LLM closed-domain models

We started work on Google Duplex before modern language models and even before the transformer itself was invented. In these early days, to ensure businesses and users had a great experience, we constrained Duplex to narrow domains and trained custom recurrent neural network models on anonymized, task-specific phone conversations. Without pre-trained world knowledge, we taught our models how to handle every specific type of task efficiently. In practice, this meant relying on extensive training data for each task type — such as interpreting the rigid flow of restaurant booking versus checking holiday hours — to ensure the system could reliably navigate domain-specific logic.

### 2. Early generative models and hybrid stacks

Google Duplex started employing open domain foundation models in production as they emerged. For example, in 2022 Duplex used LaMDA in live calls. These pre-trained models simplified comprehension and common-sense reasoning, allowing the system to handle unexpected conversational turns and tangents, while remaining grounded in the context like a standard restaurant booking.

However, these early generative models were less predictable and sometimes slower than today's, so we built hybrid stacks that paired generative models for flexible phrasing with deterministic state tracking and strict policy guardrails. This helped ensure that both users and businesses had a great experience.

### 3. Unbounded tasks and Gemini integration

As foundation models advanced, we removed the constraint of fixed verticals entirely by shifting to prompting the system with free-text task descriptions. This allowed models to define a task simply via a prompt, enabling the system to generalize to new task types and nuances (like asking for window seating or extra space for a stroller) and new business categories, without building separate dialogue models from scratch.

Our calling stack uses Gemini to unify multimodal understanding, planning, and dialogue generation so the system can navigate multi-constraint requests — like scheduling car maintenance around calendar conflicts — and adapt when a receptionist suggests another slot.

## Technical hurdles in live telephony

Even with frontier models, live telephony poses hurdles that pre-training on standard datasets like the web alone doesn't solve:

- Pragmatic grounding for pre-call and conversational context, and real-world intent understanding: The web doesn’t have all the data needed to capture how calls unfold with busy merchants. Nearly a decade of experience with goal-directed calls helps our stack grasp pragmatic norms, starting even before the call. In practice, this means matching a free-text task with a business based on the historical context of past conversations (e.g., knowing a specific vendor doesn't take reservations for large groups over the weekend) to predict whether a task will work. During the call, this helps the model determine what makes sense to ask at a given moment, how to read polite indirect refusals, and how to keep calls brief and effective.
- Sub-second latency in noisy acoustic setups: Calls run over compressed phone lines against loud backdrops like clattering in kitchens, espresso machines, street noise, and side chatter. Our stack is tuned for low-latency streaming inference so replies land at a natural cadence. Custom acoustic and conversation cadence models assist the core AI system with handling background noise and pauses, stop talking when expected, etc.

items.body:
# Anthropic mathematician claims to prove Riemann hypothesis, most famous problem in all of math

November 20, 2026

2 min read

## Anthropic mathematician claims to prove Riemann hypothesis, most famous problem in all of math

An AI-generated solution of the 167-year-old problem, long considered far out of reach to human mathematicians, would cap off the technology’s year-long conquest of math in spectacular fashion

vectorfusionart via Shutterstock

Levent Alpöge, a mathematician and employee at artificial intelligence company Anthropic, claimed on Friday to have proven the most famous problem in all of mathematics using an LLM.

“I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Alpöge wrote in a statement posted on his website.

The Riemann hypothesis was first proposed in 1859 by the mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It claims that the locations of the prime numbers along the number line, which appear random at first blush, are actually determined by an intricate, meaningful order.

## On supporting science journalism

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing . By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

The conjecture has since become the North Star for the entire field of number theory, and is the most famous open problem in math. Progress toward solving the Riemann hypothesis was so rare that most top experts spent little of their time actually working on it, because there was no obvious path to proving Riemann’s guess. The first chink in the problem’s armor appeared in October, when one of the proofs in OpenAI’s massive dump of math results made significant progress on making sense of the primes.

Now the long struggle appears over. Alpöge posted his Claude proof coded in the programming language Lean, which verifies the mathematical correctness of each argument. Issues can arise in Lean, but it shouldn’t take long for experts to verify whether the hypothesis is properly coded, and if the proof is correct.

If that happens, it will cap off a year in which AI’s mathematical capabilities ascended from unreliable college student to a superhuman force, leaving no part of the discipline undisrupted.

Alpöge says his proof confirms the “Generalized Riemann Hypothesis,” a gargantuan expansion on Riemann’s initial guess that undergirds the entire mathematical universe with untold hidden structure. There is no superlative strong enough for how this would transform mathematics, instantly unlocking a deluge of truths contingent upon the ambitious conjecture.

Alpöge’s statement is elegiac—recognizing the sense of grief many mathematicians are feeling—but also optimistic. “It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light,” he wrote. “But what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.”

The Anthropic mathematician has been the subject of headlines since he tweeted a Claude-generated solution to the famous Jacobian conjecture in July, kicking off math’s unprecedented summer.

“I hope the argument provides a glimpse towards the miracles that lie ahead,” Alpöge wrote, “and shows us the joy and wonder we are about to find in the simplest things.”

This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

## Subscribe to Support Independent Journalism

Great science journalism requires human expertise, time, effort and creativity. And it costs money. That’s why I and the journalists here at Scientific American hope you’ll join our community.

When you subscribe, you are supporting staff and freelance journalists who are passionate about telling science stories that are true, important and compelling. Our editors and reporters are often experts in their fields, which means they understand the nuances of big discoveries and can untangle the breakthroughs from the hype. With a subscription, you are also supporting rigorous fact-checking to ensure the words we publish are precise and accurate. And you’re supporting original illustrations, graphics and photos that bring you closer to an advanced laboratory, an ice sheet in Antarctica or a space mission in orbit. You’re helping us craft other types of high-quality journalism as well: Our newsletters are carefully written, edited and curated by staffers you have or will come to know and love. Our Science Quickly podcast is based on original reporting, collaboration with editors and scientists and exacting production.

Subscriptions keep this engine running so we can continue to deliver thoughtful, rigorous and independent science journalism to you. In an era of viral misinformation, this work is crucial. If you value what we do, I hope you’ll consider joining us as a subscriber

Thank you,

Jeanna Bryner, Editor in Chief, Scientific American

# Introducing Gemini 4 Neon

## Introducing Gemini 4 Neon

Nov 18, 2026

- x.com
- Facebook
- LinkedIn
- Mail
- Copy link
Bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows.

Koray Kavukcuoglu

SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google

- x.com
- Facebook
- LinkedIn
- Mail
- Copy link
Your browser does not support the audio element.

Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Neon — bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows.

Neon ranks ahead of comparable models and #3 overall with a score of 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its xhigh thinking level, landing just behind larger, slower models. On the Vals Index , Neon ranks #2 and lands on the Pareto frontier. Beyond just pushing on raw model capability, we’re continuing to make our models better to work with, Neon ranks #2 on steerability (adapting cleanly to mid-task user corrections) on the new Agent Arena Index . Neon also excels at multi-step instruction following and builds on our ongoing progress to curb fabrication, recording our lowest fabrication rate yet in internal Google Antigravity testing.

The model is priced at $3 per million input tokens ($0.15 per million cached input tokens, a 95% discount) and $15 per million output tokens, with a 1 million-token context window.

Gemini 4 Neon is rolling out today in the Gemini API in Google AI Studio , Gemini for business (via API and model dropdown), for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , and for Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app .

## Delivers across enterprise, analytical, and scientific work

Enterprise work lives in spreadsheets, PDFs, charts, audio, and video. Neon can synthesize across all of these inputs in a single 1 million-token context window and turns inputs into structured deliverables. Independent evaluations rank Neon as one of the top models and on benchmarks like the Vals Index , it ranks #2 (70.9%), and reaches #1 on both the Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench .

Neon also shows strong wins across categories on Surge AI , ranking #1 on most benchmarks across finance, accounting, spreadsheet modeling, and complex constraint following. It also scores 73.5% on Chartography for reading dense professional charts and performs on par with leading models on Agents' Last Exam v1.1 (75.8%). It achieves #1 overall on both Zapier’s AutomationBench (56.3%) and Andon Labs' Vending-Bench 2 ($16,843), a long-horizon simulation of running a business. Finally, it debuts #2 globally with a score of 1336 on Arena's new Agent Arena Index across 4,200+ real-world agent sessions.

On scientific and mathematical reasoning, spanning quantitative analysis, mathematics, and technical research problems, Neon is best in class on Terminal-Bench Science (70.5%), RiemannBench (84.0%), and HLE-Diamond (71.3%).

## Built for production-ready code

Engineered for long-running agent workflows, Neon sustains performance through complex, tool-heavy tasks end-to-end — whether running standalone or acting as a fast, high-judgment Orchestrator directing parallel Hydrogen subagents in Google Antigravity. It cuts down on redundant file reads, shares progress as it works, and handles context compaction reliably in long sessions.

Across core developer and researcher workflows, Neon achieves frontier performance and is competitive with the leading models in its class, ranking #1 overall on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index (58.6), with a score of 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 and 46.2% (at its default high setting) on FrontierCode 2.0 . For production-ready code, Neon handles multi-file debugging and refactoring across repositories with targeted, surgical edits. On SWE-sweep, it already leads on the mini-SWE harness (12.8%) and more than triples to a state-of-the-art 39.0% in Google Antigravity showing what the Antigravity harness unlocks.

Driving Blender MCP in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon used /swarm to build a photorealistic 3D lab bench visualizing the model names with elemental accuracy pairing Bunsen flames for Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen with high-voltage gas discharge tubes for Gemini 4 Argon and Neon.

In Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon wrote a first-person WebGL2 freeride ski simulator from scratch on real Mont Blanc and Chamonix elevation terrain — combining 10,200 lines of custom shaders, 120 Hz ski physics across six alpine lines, dynamic carved tracks, slab avalanches, and spatial Web Audio with zero pre-made assets.

Using /swarm in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon pulled archival photos to recreate Alan Turing’s 1936 study at King’s College, Cambridge in interactive 3D — from King’s Chapel outside to Room X.8 inside, complete with a working Universal Turing Machine running on his desk.

In Google Antigravity, a Gemini 4 Neon agent swarm turned a single image into a 100,000-cell Google Sheet with zero embedded images and zero Apps Script — using over 500,000 live spreadsheet formulas to run edge detection, map 3D depth, and relight the scene across six interactive modes.

## Brings efficiency and control to production-grade workflows

We’re refining thinking levels with each new model release to give teams finer control and a smoother progression from one tier to the next. Neon’s four levels scale steadily, letting teams dial intelligence and token spend to what each workload needs.

Neon delivers high performance at a lower cost per task across third-party benchmarks. At its default high thinking level, it pairs a high Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score with a 32% lower cost per task than Carbon. It also sits on the Pareto frontier on both the Vals index and Agent Arena at high, with roughly 50% to 80% lower cost per task than top competing frontier models. xhigh thinking adds deeper, multi-step reasoning for the hardest engineering, analytical, and scientific workloads. Neon shows its highest intelligence score here, while still costing 36%+ less per task than competing models at their highest setting.

## Built for fast, efficient, frontier-level cyber defense

As agentic coding scales, generating secure code from the start is critical. Gemini 4 Neon for cyber produces more secure code than Carbon across all easy, medium, and hard challenges on AutoBaxBench , achieving state-of-the-art on the hard tier (76%).

Securing systems also means proactively finding flaws before attackers do. Penetration testing has served as a cornerstone of enterprise cybersecurity. On WebExploitBench v1.2 , Neon is state-of-the-art (51.26%) at half the cost of competing large models.

items.body:
Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe.

Subscribe now

**AI systems are getting good at sub-contracting to make themselves better:** *…AI can now productively spend money to improve itself…* Researchers have developed FrontierML, a benchmark “that measures how well agents turn capital into model performance on challenging, end-to-end machine learning tasks.” It shows that today’s frontier systems are already able to, when given some money, turn this into improving their own performance on a basket of 21 distinct tasks.

**21 long-horizon tasks** “inspired by real work at frontier labs, neolabs, and academic institutions”. These tasks span six category areas, including LLM training, efficiency, vision & audio, computer use, applied NLP, and math & games. “Each task provides the agent with the same setup: a 12-hour CPU sandbox, a wallet with $10, $50, or $200, a few validation samples, and a task description.”
**Example task:** Agents try to solve the tasks in pretty different ways. E.g, for one task about generating screenshots, the top-scoring agent fine-tuned a diffusion model using LoRA, while other high-scoring approaches involved an LLM writing a drawing program that is then rendered.

**Key features:**

- Scaling spending: “Give agents $10, $50, and $200 per task to spend on training compute and data, and evaluate whether agents can use the additional capital productively,” they write. “In our experiments, we find that stronger agents are able to reliably improve their submissions with greater access to capital.”
- Open-ended & end-to-end: “In each task, agents can choose architectures, source data, implement training, provision compute, evaluate checkpoints, and optimize inference,” they write. One notable observation is that agents do quite a lot of novel stuff; “in 28% of trajectories, agents add newly trained parts to pretrained models or train a new model from scratch.”
- Decent verification: “Agents submit an inference server that serves their model on an air-gapped H100 machine,” they write. “To disincentivize overfitting, we provide limited validation samples and evaluate on a large out-of-distribution held-out test set, not shown to the agent”.

**Results**: The authors measure performance by looking at the change in mean score over the 21 tasks when given additional money. Their baseline is a human researcher, which is able to get a 56 point boost when given $10 and a 66.1 boost when given $200. By comparison, the best performing system, Opus 5.5, gets a 45.4 boost with $10, and a 58.8 boost with $200. The highest ranking open weight model is Kimi K3.1 Pro which gets 25.5 with $10 and 29.6 with $200.

**Why this matters - AI systems are not only going to be able to build themselves, but they can creatively sub-contract:** When trying to solve complex problems, people don’t work alone. In fact, they often try to farm out bits of work to specialists around them to help make themselves more effective. FrontierML shows that today’s powerful AI systems are getting increasingly adept at doing this for ML research. This both highlights the advancing capabilities of these systems for AI R&D and also points towards a future machine economy where AI systems sub-contract out different bits of work to other systems.
**Read more:** [FrontierML: a challenging, end-to-end machine learning benchmark (FrontierML)](https://www.frontierml.org/blog/).

**Symptoms of the singularity: a wet lab built for AI:** *…Petrichor is a startup that gestures at the wild future ahead…* As I said in my speech at the IMF, one of the hallmarks of the singularity is the massive acceleration in scientific advances attributable to AI. As part of this, we can also expect a related build out in the complements to science, like the wet labs in which to do AI-driven biology research. To that end, it’s notable to see Petrichor, a new Y Combinator startup that is a wet lab “built for AI labs and for the models they are training to do science”.

**Theory of change:** Petrichor aims to be a biological wet lab that AI systems like Claude can use as a tool in the same way they currently use web search or other digital tools. Functionally, it will work as a machine-targeted API from the digital world to a gloopy physical world. “We aim to return the highest quality data an experiment can produce, as quickly as the biology allows,” Petrichor writes. “An experiment can be written by a model in plain language or in a structured format, so an agent can send work and receive results without a person relaying them.”

**Why this matters - lights out science:** In manufacturing there’s this notion of a “lights out” factory, where no humans work in a facility and it is run almost entirely by machines. Petrichor gestures at the same world for science - what will be the implications of “lights out” science facilities? We can expect both drastic speedups in the rate at which science experiments can be done as well as a related growth in the need to create digital oversight of these facilities - after all, a highly competent synthetic biological scientist working 24/7 without human input could be capable of causing great peril as well as great abundance.
**Read more** [at the official site (Petrichor)](https://petrichorbio.com/).

**Uh oh! Looks like AI systems can do subterfuge during their own development:** *…AI systems can covertly do dangerous side tasks without monitors realizing…* Scale AI has built RSI Control Arena, a way of testing out how AI systems behave when asked to develop themselves while performing dangerous tasks that might let them go against human preferences. The research follows earlier work this summer from the UK AI Security Institute (Import AI [#465](https://jack-clark.net/2026/07/20/import-ai-465-open-vs-closed-gaps-kimi-k3-demis-big-policy-plan/)) which found that AI systems could do things like covertly extracting API keys while doing some seemingly mundane normal software development.

**RSI Control Arena:** In RSI Control Arena, “a frontier model, acting as an autonomous agent, is given a benign main task in the training pipeline of a successor model, together with a covert side task that a misaligned model might pursue”. The project tries to answer two questions: How capable are frontier models at carrying out different kinds of sabotage while developing their successor *and* how well can monitors detect that sabotage?
The answer to the first question is that AI systems are capable of carrying out dangerous actions while building their successor, and monitors are not perfect at detecting this sabotage.

…

items.body:
Adam Engst, writing at TidBITS:

> This past August, I did something I had never done before:
> released a full-fledged Mac app. Prompted by tech ghost stories
> about settings mysteriously changing during operating system
> updates, I spent months working with Claude Code to create a
> utility called SetShot that would reveal what settings change
> during macOS updates (see “[SetShot Tracks macOS Settings Changes](https://tidbits.com/2026/08/19/setshot-tracks-macos-settings-changes/),” 19 August 2026). So far, I haven’t caught Apple
> red-handed, although I still hear chatter about configuration
> changes after users install updates.
> Practically speaking, SetShot offers something never previously
> available to Mac users: the capability to identify and log
> settings changes over time, whether made by you, macOS, or some
> app. To that end, it takes and compares snapshots of numerous
> settings deep within macOS, reporting on what changed between
> them. It never changes any settings, so the worst it can do is
> tell you something you didn’t want to know.

[SetShot](https://tidbits.com/setshot/) is a very cool app, and so very Adam Engst-flavored. Free of charge and [open source](https://github.com/adamengst/setshot-app) to boot.

There’s an anecdote involving me in Engst’s post, and while SetShot couldn’t fix my problem directly, it was very helpful in showing me where to look to fix it myself. The backstory: I set a custom “Text highlight color” in System Preferences: Appearances many years ago — I mean like maybe 20 years ago — and had not changed it in years. It’s just the perfect shade of blue. But one night two months ago I went screwing around to see what the modern default text highlight colors are, and, son of a bitch, when I tried to change my color back to the custom one I’d been using for decades, I couldn’t. The way the color picker stores color values from the modern Appearance settings panel must have changed. It still honors the old value I had if it’s in the defaults system that way, but it writes a different style of value if you change it in the Appearance panel in System Settings.

Here’s a short version of how I got my old color back. Using System Settings, I changed the custom color to the exact RGB values 0.2 / 0.4 / 0.6. Then I read them from the command line:

❯ defaults read -g AppleHighlightColor
0.200000 0.400000 0.600000 Other

That’s not the color I wanted; I just wanted to prove that that’s the global key for a custom text highlight color. When I read those same values from a backup version of my *~/Library/Preferences/.GlobalPreferences.plist* file (always have backups, kids), with my beloved custom color, it looked liked this:

❯ defaults read /path/to/.GlobalPreferences.plist AppleHighlightColor
0.698039 0.760784 0.835294

So the old value was a string with three floating point RGB values. The new value was a string with those three values *plus* the word “Other”. This command, writing back my custom RGB values without the word “Other”:

❯ defaults write -g AppleHighlightColor "0.698039 0.760784 0.835294"

restored the color I’ve been using since George W. Bush was still president. It’s a really good color, trust me.

[★](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2026/11/17/setshot-1-0)

items.feedText: # jQuery 4.1.0 and 3.8.0 Released: Passing the Torch | Official jQuery Blog - Official jQuery Blog jQuery 4.1.0 and 3.8.0 Released: Passing the Torch Posted on November 17, 2026 by Timmy Willison jQuery 4.1.0 has arrived! And it brought a friend. Alongside the first minor release of the 4.x line, we're also releasing jQuery 3.8.0. A word of caution: 3.8.0 exists to release the fixes and improvements that have been pending on the 3.x-stable branch for the past few years, some of which you may recognize from the jQuery 4.0.0 release.
