items.body:
# Jquery 4 1 0 and 3 8 0 released passing the torch

# jQuery 4.1.0 and 3.8.0 Released: Passing the Torch | Official jQuery Blog - Official jQuery Blog jQuery 4.1.0 and 3.8.0 Released: Passing the Torch Posted on November 17, 2026 by Timmy Willison jQuery 4.1.0 has arrived! And it brought a friend. Alongside the first minor release of the 4.x line, we're also releasing jQuery 3.8.0. A word of caution: 3.8.0 exists to release the fixes and improvements that have been pending on the 3.x-stable branch for the past few years, some of which you may recognize from the jQuery 4.0.0 release. It is a send-off, not a comeback. Going forward, the 3.x branch will only receive critical security and bug fixes. If you haven't yet made the jump to 4.x, we encourage you to do so — we have an upgrade guide and the jQuery Migrate plugin ready to help, and most users will be able to upgrade with minimal changes. As usual, the releases are available on our CDN and the npm package manager. Other third party CDNs will probably have them available soon as well, but remember that we don't control their release schedules and they will need some time. Here are the highlights. In both 4.1.0 and 3.8.0 A few changes landed on both branches, so you get these no matter which version you're on. A new API for AJAX transport complete callbacks Custom AJAX transports have long received a completeCallback with positional arguments: function( status, statusText, responses, headers ) {} Transports can now instead invoke the callback with a single object: function( { status, statusText, responses, headers } ) {} This makes it possible for us to add new parameters in the future without relying on their order, and for transports to provide them selectively. In fact, 4.1.0 already takes advantage of it — see responseURL below. Selector: ReDoS fix in identifier matching The regular expression jQuery uses to match identifiers in selectors was vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking; a long chain of hex escapes followed by an invalid character — for example, in an attribute selector — could hang the page. The production now explicitly excludes digits & hex characters where the spec says it should, bringing us closer to spec and eliminating the ReDoS. Selector: loose document comparisons everywhere IE & Edge Legacy sometimes throw on strict document comparisons ( === ) but not on loose ones ( == ). We switched most of these comparisons years ago, but a few leftovers remained in the selector code. They've now all been converted, avoiding some rare crashes in those browsers. What else is new in 4.1.0 jqXHR gains responseURL jqXHR objects now expose responseURL — the final URL of the request after any redirects followed by the browser. Following the existing responseText / responseXML / responseJSON pattern, it is only set when the transport can report it: modern-browser XHR provides it, while IE 11 and the script & JSONP transports do not. Serialize form-associated custom elements Form-associated custom elements — custom elements registered with formAssociated = true — now serialize correctly with .serialize() and .serializeArray() . Elements that appear in form.elements are trusted to be submittable rather than being filtered out by a tag name check. CSS methods work in XML documents In non-XHTML XML documents, such as XSLT-transformed documents, elements created with document.createElement land in the XML namespace and have no style property, which broke jQuery's CSS support tests. jQuery now uses createElementNS with the XHTML namespace internally, so .css() and friends behave in these documents. querySelectorAll everywhere jQuery no longer uses getElementsByTagName or getElementsByClassName internally, relying on querySelectorAll instead. In today's browsers, qSA is on par with or faster than the old methods, and returns a static list rather than a live collection that we had to snapshot. The switch also fixes some long-standing bugs, including MathML elements not being found by lowercase tag names on cloned nodes in IE 11, selectors with leading combinators not working on document fragments, and selection by tag names containing less common symbols such as dots. Related selector work makes the quick selection paths stricter about what counts as a simple tag or class selector — with a fallback to regular selection when qSA throws — and invalid escape sequences in selectors are now decoded to U+FFFD, the replacement character, as the CSS specification requires. Faster uniqueSort jQuery.uniqueSort removes duplicates with a single-pass, two-pointer compaction instead of repeated splices, taking the duplicate removal from O(N²) time and O(N) extra space to O(N) time and constant space. Behavior and ordering are unchanged; large disconnected sets just get there faster. What's in 3.8.0 Again, most of what's in 3.8.0 has been sitting on the branch for a while, and much of it will look familiar if you read the jQuery 4.0.0 release post . But there are a few things specific to 3.x. Support for hidden="until-found" The hidden attribute used to be a boolean attribute, but it has since gained the until-found value. jQuery 3.x normalized boolean attributes in a way that clobbered that value; .attr( "hidden", "until-found" ) now sets it as-is. jQuery 4.x changed how boolean attributes are handled precisely to avoid this class of problem, so no change was needed there. Deprecations to smooth the road to 4.x Two sets of APIs that were removed in jQuery 4.0.0 are now formally deprecated in 3.x, which means the jQuery Migrate plugin can warn you about them before you upgrade: The push , sort & splice Array methods on the jQuery prototype. These were always meant for internal use and jQuery itself hasn't used them since Sizzle was inlined. If you need the same behavior, $elems.push( elem ) can be replaced with [].push.call( $elems, elem ) . - jQuery.expr[ ":" ] and jQuery.expr.filters , which have been documented as deprecated since 3.0.0 but never made their way into the deprecated module. Use jQuery.expr.pseudos instead. ### Backported fixes 3.8.0 also picks up a number of fixes that already shipped in jQuery 4.0.0, including support for self-removing scripts passed to .html() , a fix for jQuery.cleanData skipping elements during cleanup, correct dimensions for table elements, more robust native event handling in leverageNative , and support test fixes for pages under CSS zoom and initially hidden iframes.

items.body:
# How to Bypass Rust's Orphan Rule - Edmond Vong ## How to Bypass Rust's Orphan Rule ## What Is the Orphan Rule Actually Protecting Against? ## Why the Two Usual Workarounds Fall Short ### 1. Building it into the library ### 2. Wrap it in a NewType yourself ## Adding a Generic Slot to the Trait ## The Position of the Local Type Matters ## A Truly Standalone models Crate ## Real-World Example: How This Works in Kova How to Bypass Rust's Orphan Rule Contents What Is the Orphan Rule Actually Protecting Against? Why the Two Usual Workarounds Fall Short 1. Building it into the library 2. Wrap it in a NewType yourself Adding a Generic Slot to the Trait The Position of the Local Type Matters A Truly Standalone models Crate Real-World Example: How This Works in Kova Write Rust for long enough, and you are bound to run into error[E0117] . Take a simple, everyday scenario. You pull in a serialization library that defines a ToJson trait, along with a third-party type library like uuid . You want to turn a uuid::Uuid into JSON, so you naturally write: impl ToJson for uuid :: Uuid { fn to_json ( & self ) -> String { format! ( " \" {} \" " , self ) } } And the compiler immediately stops you: error[E0117]: only traits defined in the current crate can be implemented for types defined outside of the crate This is Rust's well-known Orphan Rule . Once people hit this wall, they usually either complain that the compiler is too rigid or dutifully wrap the type in a NewType. But if you look closely at how the Orphan Rule actually works, it is not a dead end. By design, it leaves a pretty wide door open. What Is the Orphan Rule Actually Protecting Against? Setting the jargon aside, the logic behind the Orphan Rule is simple: if you want a type to implement a trait, at least one of those two things (the type or the trait) must belong to your own crate. In plain English, you don't get to make rules for someone else's types. Suppose crate A implements ToJson for uuid::Uuid and outputs a hyphenated UUID string, while crate B also implements ToJson for uuid::Uuid and outputs 32 raw hex characters without hyphens. If a project depends on both A and B, the compiler has a problem when it sees uuid.to_json() : which implementation should it pick? To prevent this kind of global conflict, Rust enforces coherence , and the Orphan Rule is how it gets enforced. There is nothing wrong with the rule itself. It keeps the Rust ecosystem from turning into a mess as dependency trees grow. The catch is that real-world projects constantly run into a very common need: making a third-party type implement a trait from another third-party crate. Neither the type nor the trait is yours, yet gluing libraries together like this happens all the time. So what can you do? Why the Two Usual Workarounds Fall Short Right now, the Rust ecosystem mostly relies on two workarounds. Both appear to solve the problem on the surface, but because neither addresses the root cause, they get awkward fast. 1. Building it into the library Many foundational crates take this route: since users can't write the impl themselves, the crate provides it internally. Because ToJson is defined inside the crate, implementing it for any external type satisfies the Orphan Rule. Open up the Cargo.toml of one of these crates, and you will see a long list of feature flags: with-uuid , with-chrono , with-time , with-jiff , with-url , with-rust-decimal , and so on. It looks helpful at first, but it tries to enumerate an open, constantly changing ecosystem inside a single crate . That approach has clear limits, and the downsides show up quickly: You can never support everything. Today the community favors chrono , tomorrow people switch to jiff , and next week your team builds its own internal Money type. If the library doesn't have built-in support, you are stuck waiting for a release or opening a PR yourself. Version lock-in. When a third-party type crate bumps its major version, your whole dependency tree gets stuck until the trait crate publishes a matching update. Hardcoded behavior. Maybe the library serializes DateTime as an ISO-8601 string by default, while your API spec requires an integer timestamp in milliseconds. Because the implementation lives inside the library, you have no way to change it. 2. Wrap it in a NewType yourself When the library doesn't have built-in support, or its default behavior doesn't fit your needs, you fall back to the familiar NewType pattern: pub struct MyUuid ( pub uuid :: Uuid ); impl ToJson for MyUuid { fn to_json ( & self ) -> String { format! ( " \" {} \" " , self . 0 ) } } Wrapping one or two types is fine. The trouble starts when a moderately complex domain model mixes Uuid , Url , DateTime , HashMap , and custom domain types all at once. Once you wrap everything into MyUuid , MyUrl , and MyDateTime , your business logic gets littered with .0 , and you spend your time constantly wrapping and unwrapping values. It gets old very quickly. NewType is a genuinely useful pattern in Rust for expressing domain meaning, hiding internals, or enforcing invariants. The problem is that when you only use it to appease the Orphan Rule on types that didn't need a wrapper in the first place, your code bloats quickly. So is there a way to let users decide how third-party types implement a trait, without wrapping everything in NewTypes? Adding a Generic Slot to the Trait Let's go back to the rule: either the type or the trait must belong to the current crate. Many developers assume the compiler only looks at Trait and Type in impl Trait for Type . In fact, under Rust's Orphan Rule (RFC 2451), the trait's own generic type parameters are also part of the check . Put simply, in impl Trait

for Type , as long as a local type appears in the trait's generic parameters, and there are no uncovered type parameters before it, the compiler knows this implementation belongs exclusively to the current crate. No other crate can conflict with it, so the compiler lets it through. Take this example: impl ToJson < MyApp > for uuid :: Uuid { // ... } ToJson is a foreign trait, and Uuid is a foreign type, but MyApp is defined in the current crate. Because it sits in the trait's generic parameter position, this impl satisfies the Orphan Rule. Following this idea, a library author only needs to take one extra step when designing a trait: leave a generic parameter on the trait as an extension point for users . For example: pub trait ToJson < Ctx = ()> { fn to_json ( & self ) -> String ; } Notice that Ctx = () has a default type. When the library implements ToJson for basic types like i32 and String , it makes those implementations generic over any Ctx : impl < Ctx > ToJson < Ctx > for i32 { fn to_json ( & self ) -> String { self . to_string () } } impl < Ctx > ToJson < Ctx > for String { fn to_json ( & self ) -> String { format! ( " \" {} \" " , self ) } } This way, regular users never even notice Ctx exists. …

items.body:
I’m seeing some people object to these settings as being scarier “scare sheets”, and while I disagree, I think that’s a reasonable debate. But I think it’s indisputable that Apple put a lot of thought into these new settings and permissions. Again, you might disagree with their intentions and assumptions here, but given their stated intentions and assumptions — to wit: that many Mac users were granting Full Disk Access permissions to too many apps without realizing just how much access that entails — I think this is a very considered design. The previous settings for these permissions seem slapdash in comparison — like a lot of the “new” Mac System Settings panels.

Even this new support document seems very considered. A lot of times Apple doesn’t have support documents ready to go while the software is still in beta — here they have a good support document for the first beta with the new stuff.

*See Also:* * This [Apple Developer News article](https://developer.apple.com/news/?id=oqng0zjk), which states:

> Developers should be prepared to adjust how they onboard users
> and make sure their apps can gracefully handle having access to
> only a limited set of folders or apps when utilizing these APIs.
> Users will see these updates when approving new app permission
> requests. All app permissions previously granted by users will
> remain in effect.

So if you’ve already OK’d an app in MacOS 27.2 or earlier, you shouldn’t be prompted again after upgrading to 27.3.

> Paul Crowley, a cybersecurity researcher at Anthropic, is listed

> “designed to be spaces to … ignore the ‘nos’ of others.”
> Participants can use a safe word, “red,” to end an encounter but
> give “default consent” to “spanking,” “wrestling,” and “light
> pain” by entering the orgy, according to Red Means No’s
> [website](https://www.redmeansno.com/). More extreme actions, including “light electricity”
> and “moderate beatings,” are “permitted with negotiation,” though
> “body-shaming and race-shaming … are disallowed entirely.”
> The orgies have been known to attract a disproportionate number of
> employees at Anthropic and OpenAI, a dynamic critics say creates
> professional pressure for women in AI to attend. The criticism
> spilled into public view last month after an independent AI
> researcher, John Wentworth, said that he “absolutely [does]
> upgrade” his assessment of AI safety experts “if I find out they
> go to [Red Means No],” adding that attendance was a “strong
> signal” of free thought.

items.body:
[I wrote about David Sacks the other day](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2026/11/13/sacks), in the context of his being one of the Trump 2.0 gang that might get left holding the bag if this Jensen Huang/Nvidia scandal blows up the AI boom/bubble. Sacks *was* the administration’s “AI czar” — [until March](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/03/26/david-sacks-trump-crypto-ai-czar.html), when he announced his time was up. (His position as a “special government employee” was limited to 130 days. Sacks is definitely special.)

At the moment Sacks remains co-chair of the [President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology](https://www.whitehouse.gov/ostp/presidents-council-of-advisors-on-science-and-technology/) (PCAST), a [Legion of Doom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legion_of_Doom)-style committee of billionaire Trump backers, whose members include, in alphabetical order after the co-chairs:

- David Sacks — Co-chair
- Michael Kratsios — Co-chair
- Marc Andreessen (Andreessen Horowitz)
- Pam Bondi (fired as Trump attorney general [for insufficient cravenness](https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/5814055-pam-bondi-donald-trump-loyalty-firing/), no background whatsoever in science or technology)
- Sergey Brin (Google)
- Safra Catz (Oracle)
- Michael Dell (Dell Technologies)
- Jacob DeWitte (Oklo — nuclear power startup, fission)
- Fred Ehrsam (Coinbase — crypto)
- Larry Ellison (Oracle)
- David Friedberg (Ohalo — biotech)
- Jensen Huang (Nvidia)
- John Martinis (Qolab — quantum computing)
- Bob Mumgaard (Commonwealth Fusion Systems — nuclear power, fusion)
- Lisa Su (AMD)
- Mark Zuckerberg (Meta)

Not represented: anyone from Apple, Microsoft, or Amazon. There’s a game of reverse musical chairs here, and, amongst the multi-trillion-dollar tech Goliaths, it’s Nvidia, Google, and Meta who are still sitting in seats, soaking up the stench of a [historically unpopular president](https://time.com/article/2026/10/29/trump-approval-rating-midterm-elections-republicans/) — whose unpopularity is fueled first and foremost, [according to election exit polls](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-elections/exit-polls), by his abject corruption. Apple, Microsoft, and Amazon have seemingly made their [Irish goodbyes](https://www.dictionary.com/browse/irish-goodbye). Being associated with Trump now doesn’t just put you on the wrong side of popular party politics, but on the wrong side of being perceived as crooked.

Curiously absent from PCAST is Elon Musk, who I think got his licks in all at once with [the DOGE fiasco in Trump 2.0’s first year](https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2025/06/23/what-did-elon-musk-accomplish-at-doge).

[★](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2026/11/15/legion-of-pcast)

items.feedText: # Universal XSS in uBlock Origin from website-driven element picker Earlier this month I found a one-click universal XSS issue with uBlock Origin (the MV2 Firefox version, although a similar but less problematic issue also affected the MV3 version, uBO Lite), where a malicious website could trick the extension into adding arbitrary trusted filters. Trusted filters can inject JavaScript code into pages, and so the malicious website could create a trusted filter on another website and run arbitrary JS in the context of any site. This issue is fixed now; you can read the GitHub advisory for some more details. GPT-5.6 Sol did most of the hard work of finding the issue. I figured there might be some kind of UXSS from filter injection, so I asked it to take a look, and it found the issue. I then checked and verified the issue it proposed.
items.body:
# Universal XSS in uBlock Origin from website-driven element picker

Earlier this month I found a one-click universal XSS issue with uBlock Origin (the MV2 Firefox version, although a similar but less problematic issue also affected the MV3 version, uBO Lite), where a malicious website could trick the extension into adding arbitrary trusted filters. Trusted filters can inject JavaScript code into pages, and so the malicious website could create a trusted filter on another website and run arbitrary JS in the context of any site. This issue is fixed now; you can read the GitHub advisory for some more details.

GPT-5.6 Sol did most of the hard work of finding the issue. I figured there might be some kind of UXSS from filter injection, so I asked it to take a look, and it found the issue. I then checked and verified the issue it proposed. I wrote all of the prose in this post myself; Claude wrote most of the code for the PoC.

## The issue

uBlock Origin has an element picker that you can pull up by right-clicking on the page. You can use this to create a filter rule to block an element on the page without leaving the page.

The element picker is implemented by injecting an iframe to a URL like moz-extension://76b2331a-894c-4d25-8b89-fcce37e79cc4/web_accessible_resources/epicker-ui.html . That page can talk to the extension background script and tell it to add filters.

Basically the attack here is:

- Figure out the element picker URL
- Create our own invisible (opacity 0) iframe that embeds it
- Drive the picker to put the filter we want in it
- Position the invisible iframe to trick the user into pressing the invisible “Create” button
### Figuring out the element picker URL

On Firefox, the only information we needed to figure out was the extension internal UUID which is random per-installation.

On the default setup uBO has a lootdest.*##+js(no-fetch-if, adsbygoogle, war:googlesyndication_adsbygoogle.js) filter rule (from uAssets), which hooks fetch . From inside the fetch hook, it makes an XHR request to moz-extension://<extension UUID>/web_accessible_resources/googlesyndication_adsbygoogle.js and returns the response from that as the fetch body, instead of actually making the request. The filter rule is intended to replace a network request for JS from an ad server with a dummy script that has the correct API but doesn’t do anything.

But the attacker website can itself hook the XHR made from inside the no-fetch-if hook to extract the random extension UUID.

const origOpen = XMLHttpRequest . prototype . open ; XMLHttpRequest . prototype . open = function ( m , url , ... a ) { const e = /^moz-extension:\/\/[^/]+/ . exec ( url ); if ( e ) { e [ 0 ] // <- has the extension UUID! } return origOpen . call ( this , m , url , ... a ); }; Then the attacker website can run fetch('/adsbygoogle.js').catch(() => {}); to trigger the filter, and make their hooked XHR run. Note that there are several ways that the extension internal UUID could be leaked; it’s not just this one filter rule.

### Creating an iframe

Then you can use that to iframe the element picker. Given an iframe element in the page, you just set its src to `moz-extension://${origin}/web_accessible_resources/epicker-ui.html` .

### Sending messages to it

Now we can drive the element picker. We can create a MessageChannel and do iframe.contentWindow.postMessage({ what: 'epickerStart' }, '*', [ch.port2]); to send it to the picker iframe. Then we talk to it: it sends us a start message, we send it a showDialog message with a filter and a resultsetDetails message 1 to enable the create button and set opt .

Normally the picker restricts what filters you can enter, and doesn’t let you add scriptlet filters. But there’s a trick we can do to add arbitrary filters. There’s an opt field we set in the second message which is normally the type of network request to match (like image ), and gets appended to the filter with a $ if set, like $image . But since we control it, we can put a newline in it and make it "image\ngoogle.com##+js(trusted-rpnt, script, ...)" to inject an arbitrary trusted filter that injects a script. 2

This is where the main issue is - the element picker shouldn’t accept messages from the attacker. One of the fixes was having a secret password that the real element picker gets from the content script, that the element picker sends in the initial postMessage.

### Getting the click

I didn’t bother actually implementing this, but malicious websites could overlay stuff on top of the embedded element picker or make it invisible by setting the iframe opacity to 0. So as long as the website can get the user to click on the page, it can add arbitrary trusted filters for arbitrary domains.

Filters added by the element picker are always treated as trusted (at least until a recompile), which is why it can add a trusted filter. If the user later changes their custom filters it would cause a recompile, clearing the filter trust. But in practice the attacker could just immediately open the victim webpage, so this doesn’t help much.

- Originally I sent that message in reply to a dialogSetFilter message from the picker, but it turns out you can just send it right away instead of waiting to reply.  ↩︎
- Assuming the shown filter is a network filter.  ↩︎

items.title: Nix: Using the eval-profiler
items.subtitle: Lobsters High-Performance Engineering • Lobsters Perf
items.feedText: # Evaluation profiler - Nix 2.35.6 Reference Manual ## Using the eval-profiler Nix evaluator supports evaluation profiling compatible with flamegraph.pl . The profiler samples the nix function call stack at regular intervals. It can be enabled with the eval-profiler setting: $ nix-instantiate " " -A hello --eval-profiler flamegraph Stack sampling frequency and the output file path can be configured with eval-profile-file and eval-profiler-frequency . By default the collected profile is saved to nix.profile file in the current working directory. The collected profile can be directly consumed by flamegraph.pl : $ flamegraph.pl nix.profile > flamegraph.svg The line information in the profile contains the location of the call site position and the name of the function being called (when available). For example: /nix/store/2q71fdvr4h33g9832hiriwnf20fn630l-source/pkgs/top-level/default.nix:167:5:primop import Here import primop is called at /nix/store/2q71fdvr4h33g9832hiriwnf20fn630l-source/pkgs/top-level/default.nix:167:5 .

# Evaluation profiler - Nix 2.35.6 Reference Manual ## Using the eval-profiler Nix evaluator supports evaluation profiling compatible with flamegraph.pl . The profiler samples the nix function call stack at regular intervals. It can be enabled with the eval-profiler setting: $ nix-instantiate " " -A hello --eval-profiler flamegraph Stack sampling frequency and the output file path can be configured with eval-profile-file and eval-profiler-frequency . By default the collected profile is saved to nix.profile file in the current working directory. The collected profile can be directly consumed by flamegraph.pl : $ flamegraph.pl nix.profile > flamegraph.svg The line information in the profile contains the location of the call site position and the name of the function being called (when available). For example: /nix/store/2q71fdvr4h33g9832hiriwnf20fn630l-source/pkgs/top-level/default.nix:167:5:primop import Here import primop is called at /nix/store/2q71fdvr4h33g9832hiriwnf20fn630l-source/pkgs/top-level/default.nix:167:5 .

items.body:
I've long thought about how we're influenced by CPU architectures, and importantly, their ISAs.
In a discussion at a meetup, I brought up a topic that interested me for a while: how would an ISA that exposes memory and cache interactions in a more explicit way (because if you think about it, memory is very much I/O), as opposed to being smart and predictive on its own?

An obscure interest, of course. Nevertheless, I wanted to build a quick prototype after that.

What ended up transpiring was a bit larger. A multicore architecture with tiered stores, capabilities, a JIT'd emulator, Verilog RTL with a simulator, a small microkernel OS, UI, JIT Forth, an assembler in its own assembly, a bootstrapping C99 compiler, a few games, a visual debugger, and a few other things.

(This also shows just how far a directed LLM process can go in little time)

items.body:
WhatsApp verteilt auf dem iPhone erstmals Sticker, die beim Antippen einen Ton abspielen. Laut [WABetaInfo](https://wabetainfo.com/whatsapp-is-rolling-out-sticker-messages-with-audio-on-ios/) steht die Funktion mit der TestFlight-Beta 26.46.10.70 bereit, bei einigen Nutzern aber auch schon in der regulären Version aus dem App Store.

## Sticker aus eigenen Videos

Bisher waren Sticker bei WhatsApp entweder statisch oder animiert, blieben dabei aber stumm. Die neuen Sound-Sticker funktionieren wie animierte Sticker und bringen zusätzlich eine eigene Tonspur mit. Unter Android testet WhatsApp die Funktion ebenfalls, dort mit der Beta-Version 2.26.47.1 aus dem Google Play Store.

Wer einen Sound-Sticker erstellen möchte, tippt im Sticker-Bereich der Tastatur auf „Sticker erstellen“ und wählt ein Video aus der Mediathek. WhatsApp wandelt den Clip automatisch in einen animierten Sticker um. Über die neue Audio-Schaltfläche oben im Editor gelangt man anschließend in ein Menü, in dem sich die Tonspur festlegen lässt.

Enthält das Video bereits den passenden Ton, lässt er sich einfach übernehmen. Alternativ bietet WhatsApp vorgefertigte Effekte wie Grillenzirpen oder Katzenschnurren an. Wer etwas Eigenes möchte, importiert eine Audiodatei aus der Dateien-App oder nimmt direkt im Editor eine Sprachnachricht auf. Vor dem Erstellen kann man sich die Tonspur noch einmal anhören.

Im Chat ist ein Sound-Sticker an einem kleinen Audio-Symbol zu erkennen. Damit er Unterhaltungen nicht stört, bleibt er standardmäßig stumm. Den Ton hört der Empfänger erst, wenn er auf das Symbol tippt. WhatsApp spielt ihn dann dreimal hintereinander ab. Den Sticker und seine Tonspur überträgt WhatsApp Ende-zu-Ende-verschlüsselt.

WhatsApp schaltet die Funktion schrittweise frei, weshalb die Audio-Schaltfläche auch nach dem Update nicht bei jedem Tester sofort im Editor erscheint. WABetaInfo rechnet damit, dass in den kommenden Wochen weitere Nutzer hinzukommen.

items.body:
Come January 2027, everyday social media browsing in two of the country's largest states will look noticeably different. In California, AB 1709 (2026), AB 1043 (2025), and SB 976 (2024) are slated to take effect on January 1, 2027. Meanwhile, state attorney general regulations for New York’s Stop Addictive Feeds Exploitation (SAFE) for Kids Act take effect on January 25, 2027.

EFF has opposed these laws across legislatures, regulatory proceedings, and the courts. The core problem is simple: age-gating mandates trade away everyday user privacy and free expression under the guise of safety, while pushing platforms to gather even more personal data on users.

What California’s Rules Say

Three interlocking California laws take effect on January 1, 2027, reshaping how platforms handle age checks and design features for young users. First, SB 976 (2024) requires verifiable parental consent before platforms can offer algorithmic feeds or nighttime notifications to anyone under 18. Second, AB 1709 (2026) goes even further by outright banning "addictive features," including personalized recommendation algorithms, autoplay, and endless scroll, for users under 16, even with parental permission. Third, the Digital Age Assurance Act (AB 1043, 2025) mandates age-assurance checks across devices (operating systems) and apps, serving as the enforcement backbone for those restrictions. Together with the California Attorney General’s proposed rules on SB 976, which outline age-gating methods, accuracy, circumvention, and parental consent, these laws force platforms into a two-tier design that walls young people off from basic content-discovery tools, puts everyone's privacy at risk to prove their age, and has already drawn First Amendment lawsuits from social media companies against both SB 976 and AB 1709.

For example: rather than minimizing corporate surveillance and data collection by passing stronger privacy laws, the SB 976 regulations encourage companies to evaluate behavioral patterns, collected user data, digital interactions, and metadata to estimate age (Sec. 561(a)(2)), alongside location data collected for other purposes (Sec. 565). Good privacy laws should discourage collecting that information in the first place, not reward broader tracking.

At the same time, these age assurance rules build in steep error rates and weak safeguards. They acknowledge that age-verification tools can misclassify young people as adults, allowing false-positive rates of up to 8% for 16-year-olds and 15% for 17-year-olds (Sec. 561(c)(4)(iv)). Yet the rules set no benchmarks at all for false negatives, meaning adults (especially 18- to 20-year-olds) are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. They also recognize demographic bias in facial recognition, yet offer no concrete fix, vaguely telling companies to take mitigating measures like correcting dataset imbalances (Sec. 563(a)(6)). While users can appeal wrong age estimates, the rules set no firm deadlines, meaning mistakes can drag on without a prompt fix, blocking user access (Sec. 564). Worse, requiring platforms to let users report others they suspect are under the age of 18 (Sec. 567) invites targeted harassment by bad actors, while rules telling companies to account for users trying to “conceal or misrepresent” their California location (Sec. 565) risk penalizing everyday VPN users.

What New York’s Rules Say

Along the same lines as the California regulations, New York’s SAFE for Kids Act restricts personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (between midnight and 6am) without required consent, and mandates that platforms run age assurance and determine user location. If a user does not verify their age or is estimated to be under-18, they will either be relegated to an account with no personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (if the platform creates one), or prohibited from accessing the platform/service.

As we detailed in our December 2025 comments to the New York Attorney General, age-verification mandates inevitably chill access to online speech. And the final regulations introduce several troubling specifics.

The New York regulations use broad definitions for "age estimation," "age inference," and "age verification" (700.1(h)–(j)) that push companies to collect and retain more personal information from users. Even where privacy protections apply to that information, users cannot sue or enforce those rights themselves, since enforcement rests solely with the Attorney General (700.8). Worse, the rule’s definition of deletion appears to let companies "de-identify" age-assurance data and keep using it in that form, potentially feeding AI model training and creating re-identification risks if leaked or stolen. At the same time, platforms are required to hold onto records (including a user's age status and compliance data) for five years, increasing the risk of misuse or breaches (700.7(b)).

Echoing the problems in California, location and accuracy regulations bring further privacy and security risks. The regulations demand that operators must weigh all reliable location information and take reasonable steps to detect user efforts to “conceal or misrepresent” being in New York, which expands location tracking and threatens VPN use (700.2(d)(2)). On accuracy, the rules permit up to a 15% false-positive rate for 17-year-olds (700.1(b)), yet just like the California rules, say nothing about false negatives—meaning adults, especially 18- to 20-year-olds, are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. When that happens, the appeals process can take longer than 10 days, leaving misclassified adults locked out of standard features (or platforms altogether) for over a week.

What This Means for Users in NY and CA

Under both states' regimes, many users will be pressed to hand over personal information just to access standard features like personalized feeds or notifications, while social media companies are encouraged to monitor (and monetize) user behavior even more closely. Because these laws define "addictive feeds" so broadly that the label covers virtually every basic recommendation tool (including feeds built from who you follow, posts you like, or topics you say you are interested in), platforms face a stark choice: either build stripped-down versions of their apps without algorithmic feeds, likes, or notifications, or simply boot any account suspected of belonging to someone under 18. Either way, all users, and especially young people across both states, risk being shut out of major online spaces as they exist today.

items.body:
# Linke schliesst Emde aus: Eine Hürde weniger für Rot-Grün-Rot

## Linkenfraktion schliesst Vanessa Emde aus : Eine Hürde weniger für Rot-Grün-Rot

von Markus Gross

Vanessa Emde ist raus aus der Berliner Linksfraktion - und auf dem Weg zu Rot-Grün-Rot haben Linke, Grüne und SPD ein Problem weniger. Das letzte wird es wohl nicht bleiben.

Vanessa Emde wurde aus ihrer Fraktion ausgeschlossen. Sie war wegen ihrer Haltung zu Israel unter Druck geraten. Für die Regierungsbildung in Berlin ist es ein wichtiger Schritt.

Vor Raum 311 im Berliner Abgeordnetenhaus herrscht ein gewaltiger Medienrummel. Drinnen im großen Sitzungssaal diskutiert die Linksfraktion lebhaft über den Ausschluss von Vanessa Emde. Es scheint, als würde die halbe Republik auf ein Zeichen warten. Schafft es die Fraktionsführung, die aus ihrer Sicht widerspenstige Abgeordnete rauszuschmeißen?

Nach zweieinhalb Stunden steht fest: Vanessa Emde ist nicht mehr Mitglied der Fraktion Die Linke . 33 Abgeordnete stimmen für ihren Ausschluss, sechs stimmen mit Nein, es gibt vier Enthaltungen. Die nötige Mehrheit von 30 Stimmen wird erreicht.

- Umstrittene Abgeordnete: Vanessa Emde aus Berliner Linken-Fraktion ausgeschlossen
Sichtlich angespannt verkündet der Fraktionschef der Linken, Tobias Schulz: "Wir haben keine Möglichkeit mehr gesehen, mit Frau Emde weiter zusammenzuarbeiten." Sie habe sich nicht an Partei- und Fraktionsbeschlüsse zum Thema Antisemitismus gehalten. "Ihr Ausschluss ist folgerichtig", so Schulz weiter.

ZDF-Korrespondent Stephan Merseburger ordnet aus Berlin den Fraktionsausschluss Vanessa Emdes ein.

## Unterstützer empfangen Emde mit Jubel

Als Vanessa Emde den Fraktionssaal verlässt, wartet schon ein zwölfköpfiges Unterstützerkomitee auf sie. Es gibt Jubelrufe, als sie erscheint, Umarmungen und Zeichen der Solidarität. Emde bezeichnete ihren Ausschluss in einem Statement als Ergebnis einer "medialen Hetzkampagne".

Ihre Fraktion habe offenbar dem Druck von SPD und Grünen nachgegeben. Sie wolle ihr Mandat behalten. Ihre Unterstützer ruft sie dazu auf, sich zu "organisieren". Kämpferisch ihr Schlusswort:

> Wir sehen uns im Kiez und wir sehen uns am Streikposten! In diesem Sinne: Yalla, yalla, Klassenkampf, Freiheit für Palästina! „

Vanessa Emde

## Grüne und SPD sehen positives Signal

Die möglichen Koalitionspartner SPD und Grüne begrüßten den Ausschluss von Vanessa Emde. Werner Graf, Co-Chef der Grünenfraktion, gab sich zufrieden: "Die Entscheidung zeigt, dass für israelbezogenen Antisemitismus in einer rot-grün-roten Regierung kein Platz ist" . Steffen Krach, Co-Chef der SPD-Fraktion, der zuvor vehement einen Ausschluss Emdes gefordert hatte, ergänzte:

> Die Entscheidung der Linksfraktion ist eine gute Nachricht für die weiteren Koalitionsverhandlungen. „

Steffen Krach, Co-Chef der Berliner SPD-Fraktion

Die Berliner Linke hat die Abgeordnete Vanessa Emde aus ihrer Fraktion ausgeschlossen. Den Schritt hat man sich laut dem Fraktionsvorsitzenden Schulze nicht leicht gemacht.

## Antisemitismus-Vorwürfe gegen Emde

Vanessa Emde, mit über 46 Prozent direkt gewählte Abgeordnete in Neukölln, hatte zuvor mit ihren israelkritischen Aussagen immer wieder für Diskussionen gesorgt. Zuletzt hatte Emde in einem Instagram-Post das Existenzrecht Israels als jüdischer Staat angezweifelt. Ihre Kritiker werteten das als antisemitisch.

Der Zentralrat der Juden zeigte sich tief besorgt und forderte die Linke zum Handeln auf. Auch SPD und Grüne, die möglichen Koalitionspartner, waren verstimmt und machten den Ausschluss Emdes zur Bedingung.

- Schuster: Ausschluss von Emde "nur ein erster Schritt"
Bei den Grünen schaltete sich zuletzt sogar die Bundespitze ein. "Wenn das scheitert, kann ich allen nur abraten, in eine Regierung mit einer politischen Führung zu gehen, die in der eigenen Fraktion keine Macht hat" , hatte die Grünen-Co-Vorsitzende Franziska Brantner noch der "Frankfurter Allgemeinen Zeitung" vom Dienstag gesagt.

Die Berliner Linke hat die Abgeordnete Vanessa Emde aus der Fraktion ausgeschlossen. Was bedeutet die Entscheidung für die Partei und die Regierungsbildung in Berlin? ZDFheute live analysiert.

## Misstrauen bei SPD und Grünen bleibt

Mit dem Ausschluss Vanessa Emdes ist eine der größten Hürden auf dem Weg zu Rot-Grün-Rot in Berlin aus dem Weg geräumt. Doch Entwarnung bedeutet das nicht. SPD und Grüne bleiben misstrauisch. Der Vorwurf, in Teilen der Linken gebe es ein strukturelles Problem mit antisemitischen Tendenzen, ist längst nicht ausgeräumt.

Auch innerparteilich ist der Konflikt keineswegs beendet. Sechs Gegenstimmen und vier Enthaltungen zeigen, dass Emde weiterhin Rückhalt in der Fraktion hat. Wie sich ihr Unterstützerlager künftig positioniert, dürfte für die Koalitionsgespräche entscheidend werden. Der Politikwissenschaftler Thorsten Faas findet: "Der Ausschluss ist nicht so überzeugend, dass jegliche Diskussion innerhalb der Linken beendet ist." Das Bündnis bleibe in einem Schwebezustand.

Vorerst aber können alle Beteiligten aufatmen: Die Gespräche gehen weiter. Bis zum Jahreswechsel soll ein Koalitionsvertrag stehen. Anschließend müssen Linke und SPD noch ihre Mitglieder überzeugen. Doch bis dahin ist es ein weiter Weg - und das nächste Personalproblem womöglich nur eine Frage der Zeit.

Markus Gross ist Redakteur im ZDF-Landesstudio Berlin.

items.body:
After four years of work to build a browser engine from scratch, the [Ladybird](https://ladybird.org/) project released its first [downloadable alpha](https://ladybird.org/download/) on November 23, offering prebuilt versions for macOS and Linux. Previously, curious users had to compile the browser themselves from its source. Now it's an installable package with automatic updating.

Ladybird is most notable for what it isn't: another browser fork. Where Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Opera all run on Google's Blink engine, and Firefox depends on Gecko, Ladybird's rendering engine and its [LibJS JavaScript engine](https://ladybirdbrowser.github.io/libjs-website/) were written from scratch. "The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork," project lead Andreas Kling wrote in Monday's announcement. "The browser around it is modest, but functional."

## A fourth engine

Nearly the entire modern web currently runs on three browser engines. There's [WebKit](https://webkit.org/) (Safari), [Gecko](https://firefox-source-docs.mozilla.org/overview/gecko.html) (Firefox), and the biggest of them all, [Blink](https://www.chromium.org/blink/) (Chromium). Those limited options mean that web developers often end up optimizing sites for Chromium specifically, since that's where the majority of traffic is, and as a result, the whole web platform tends to follow suit toward whatever the dominant engine supports.

items.body:
**Gibt es eigentlich moderne Synthesizer-Klassiker – also Synthesizer von heute, über die man auch in 20 oder 30 Jahren noch sprechen wird? Wir glauben: ja! Hier sind sechs aktuelle Synthesizer, die das Potenzial haben, zu echten Klassikern zu werden.**

## Table of Contents

- Moderne Synthesizer-Klassiker
- Arturia PolyBrute 12: Ausdrucksstärkster Analogsynthesizer aller Zeiten?
- Moog Mother-Serie: Semi-modular für alle
- ASM Hydrasynth: Der digitale Rebell
- Groove Synthesis 3rd Wave: Kompromisslos gut
- Expressive E Osmose: Die Keyboard-Revolution
- Teenage Engineering OP-1 (Field): Synthesizer-Klassiker und Designikone

## Moderne Synthesizer-Klassiker

Wenn von einem **Synthesizer-Klassiker** die Rede ist, denkt man natürlich zuerst an die analogen Legenden der 1970er und 1980er wie den Minimoog, Odyssey, Jupiter-8, Prophet-5, CS-80 oder OB-X. Auch unter den digitalen Synthesizern gibt es echte Klassiker vom DX7 über D-50, [M1](https://www.gearnews.de/synthesizer-klassiker-korg-m1/) und Wavestation bis zum [Virus](https://www.gearnews.de/access-virus-alternativen/), JP-8000 und microKORG.

Aber was ist mit den **Synthesizern von heute**? Sind sie nicht immer wieder neue Aufgüsse der gleichen Ideen? Verblassen sie nicht ausnahmslos gegenüber den Meilensteinen vergangener Jahrzehnte? Gibt es überhaupt moderne Synthesizer-Klassiker?

Yamaha CS-80: Einer der großen Synthesizer-Klassiker vergangener Jahrzehnte · Quelle: Yamaha

Wenn man sich die Flut an Klonen und Nachbauten von **Vintage-Synthesizern** ansieht, die derzeit ganz oben in den Verkaufscharts rangieren, könnte man meinen, es gehe heute nur noch darum, das Erbe der Vergangenheit zu verwalten. Doch der Eindruck täuscht. Auch unter den Synthesizern von heute gibt es einige, an die man sich garantiert auch in 10, 20 oder 30 Jahren noch erinnern wird – sei es wegen ihrer innovativen Ideen, ihres tollen Sounds oder einfach ihrer großen Beliebtheit.

Einige Kandidaten, bei denen wir uns gut vorstellen können, dass man sie eines Tages als **Synthesizer-Klassiker** bezeichnen wird, haben wir hier zusammengestellt. Ob wir mit dieser Prognose Recht behalten werden, wird sich natürlich erst in einigen Jahrzehnten herausstellen …

## Arturia PolyBrute 12: Ausdrucksstärkster Analogsynthesizer aller Zeiten?

Angesichts der vielen bemerkenswerten Hardware-Synthesizer, für die Arturia heute bekannt ist, könnte man glatt vergessen, dass der französische Hersteller ursprünglich eine reine Software-Firma war. In den letzten gut zehn Jahren hat sich das gründlich geändert und Arturia hat mittlerweile mehr als einen Hardware-Synthesizer im Programm, der das Zeug zum Klassiker hat. Auf den **MiniFreak**am unteren Ende der Preisspanne trifft das meiner Ansicht nach durchaus auch zu, genauso wie auf den**MiniBrute**.

Der **PolyBrute 12**steht jedoch noch einmal auf einer ganz anderen Stufe. Das liegt in erster Linie an der unglaublich ausdrucksstark spielbaren**FullTouch-Tastatur**. Sie verleiht dem Synthesizer eine ganz neue Ebene der Expressivität, die man so bei kaum einem anderen Instrument findet – schon gar nicht bei einem Analogsynthesizer. Aber auch klanglich hat der PolyBrute 12 mit seinen Brute-Oszillatoren, den dualen Filtern und der umfangreichen Modulationsmatrix einiges zu bieten.

Arturia PolyBrute 12 · Quelle: Arturia

In unserem **[Angecheckt](https://www.gearnews.de/arturia-polybrute-12-test/)** schreibt mein Kollege Rob Puricelli: „Der Arturia PolyBrute 12 ist eine Zäsur. Eine Linie im Sand, könnte man sagen. […] Er ist ein Musikinstrument im wahrsten Sinn des Wortes.” Das dürfte reichen, um in ein paar Jahrzehnten als Meilenstein der Synthesizer-Geschichte und als Synthesizer-Klassiker zu gelten. Der Synthesizer ist bei [Thomann](https://www.thomann.de/de/arturia_polybrute_12.htm?offid=1&affid=84)* erhältlich.

## Moog Mother-Serie: Semi-modular für alle

Als Moog im Jahr 2015 den **[Mother-32](https://www.gearnews.de/news-moog-mother-32-moog-sound-fuers-eurorack/)**herausbrachte, betrat der Hersteller Neuland. Etwas Vergleichbares gab es damals nicht. Der**semi-modulare**und damals vergleichsweise günstige**Analogsynthesizer**war einfach zu bedienen, brachte seinen eigenen**Sequencer** mit und lieferte schon ohne Patch-Verbindungen einen satten Sound. Zugleich war er aber auch die perfekte „Einstiegsdroge” in die modulare Welt. Für unzählige Synthesizer-Fans wurde der Mother-32 zum Beginn einer modularen Leidenschaft. Praktisch, dass man ihn auf Wunsch direkt ins Eurorack einbauen kann!

Moog Sound Studio mit Mother-32, DFAM und Subharmonicon · Quelle: Moog

Später ergänzte Moog die Serie um den **[DFAM](https://www.gearnews.de/moog-dfam-limitierte-submutter-fuer-drums/)**, das eigenwillige**[Subharmonicon](https://www.gearnews.de/moog-subharmonicon-subharmonic-synthesizer/)**und schließlich den**[Labyrinth](https://www.gearnews.de/moog-labyrinth/)**und**[Spectravox](https://www.gearnews.de/moog-spectravox/)**. Im Team bilden die Synthesizer ein semi-modulares Klanglabor, das seinesgleichen sucht. Folglich gab es verschiedene Kombinationen der Synthesizer zeitweise auch als komplettes**[Moog Sound Studio](https://www.gearnews.de/moog-sound-studio-mother-32-dfam-subharmonicon/)** zu kaufen.

Man mag davon halten, was man will, aber dass die Synthesizer der Moog Mother-Serie mittlerweile von einem anderen Hersteller nahezu 1:1 kopiert werden, ist der beste Beweis für ihren Status als moderne Synthesizer-Klassiker. Die Serie ist bei [Thomann](https://www.thomann.de/de/search_AR_372745_430321_490371_592223.html?offid=1&affid=84)* erhältlich.

items.title: Digitalbank: Neuer N26-Chef: „Wir wollen unsere Kundenzahl bis 2030 mindestens verdoppeln“
items.subtitle: Mike Dargan spricht im ersten Interview als N26-Chef über seine Ziele und den Umbau der Digitalbank.
items.feedText: N26-Chef Dargan: „Wir müssen Dinge anders machen und uns als Organisation weiterentwickeln.“ Foto: Jan Philip Welchering für Handelsblatt Berlin. Hinter Mike Dargan liegen turbulente Monate. Seit April steht der Brite an der Spitze der Berliner Digitalbank N26 , die nach einer Investorenrevolte, dem Abgang der beiden Gründer und wiederholtem Ärger mit der Finanzaufsicht Bafin vor großen Herausforderungen steht. In seinem ersten Interview als N26-Chef spricht Dargan mit dem Handelsblatt über seine Umbauarbeiten, die Ziele bis 2030 sowie den Wettbewerb mit dem deutlich größeren Konkurrenten Revolut. items.body:
Take a look back at our main image again; see that in the background? That's the North America Nebula that I photographed with the Vaonis Vespera Pro 2 as part of my recent testing. I was massively impressed, both by its performance and the fact that this new smart telescope is currently on sale at its lowest-ever price for Black Friday 2026.

**You can buy the Vaonis Vespera Pro 2,** [on sale right now for $500 cheaper on Amazon in this early Black Friday smart telescope deal — now at its lowest-ever price.](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0GY1TH8QQ?plpRedirect=mhFallback&ref=clp_hp_h_pc)

I would expect this level of astrophotography from huge observatories and space telescopes, not from a consumer smart telescope. After setting up the Vespera Pro 2 for just an hour in my backyard, I was blown away by the resulting image.

**[Vespera Pro 2: was $2990 now $2490](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0GY1TH8QQ?plpRedirect=mhFallback&ref=clp_hp_h_pc)**
This is the second release of the Vaonis Vespera Pro. Just like the original, it has a 12.5MP sensor, 225GB internal storage, a built-in hygrometer and 11-hour battery life, but with some changes. The optical design has been upgraded to increase sharpness, direct USB-C file transfer and ships with an adjustable carbon fiber tripod.

We gave the original 4.5/5 stars in our [Vaonis Vespera Pro review.](https://www.space.com/stargazing/skywatching-kit/vaonis-vespera-pro-smart-telescope-review)

**Editor's note: ONLY 16 LEFT IN STOCK** [View Deal](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0GY1TH8QQ?plpRedirect=mhFallback&ref=clp_hp_h_pc)

Ahead of [Black Friday](https://www.space.com/best-black-friday-deals-sales) on Nov. 27, you can get $500 off possibly the [best smart telescope](https://www.space.com/best-smart-telescopes) for nebula and wide-field photography. We have just finished testing the Vespera Pro 2 and think it is at the top of its league, adding noticeable upgrades for professionals to the still amazing [Vaonis Vespera Pro.](https://www.space.com/stargazing/skywatching-kit/vaonis-vespera-pro-smart-telescope-review)

My first light with this telescope, the North America Nebula. Harry Bennett / Future

A section of the Heart Nebula, as imaged by the Vaonis Vespera Pro 2. Harry Bennett / Future

The Andromeda galaxy (M31), as imaged by the Vaonis Vespera Pro 2. Harry Bennett / Future

The Western Veil Nebula, as imaged by the Vaonis Vespera Pro 2. Harry Bennett / Future

The Eastern Veil Nebula, as imaged by the Vaonis Vespera Pro 2. Harry Bennett / Future

The Cygnus Loop, as imaged by the Vaonis Vespera Pro 2. Harry Bennett / Future

The Wizard Nebula, as imaged by the Vaonis Vespera Pro 2. Harry Bennett / Future

- Check out our [Black Friday page](https://www.space.com/best-black-friday-deals-sales), where we bring you the best deals of Black Friday 2026, including early telescope deals.
- We've also got you covered with reviews and rankings of the [best telescopes](https://www.space.com/15693-telescopes-beginners-telescope-reviews-buying-guide.html), [binoculars](https://www.space.com/26021-best-binoculars.html), [star projectors](https://www.space.com/best-star-projectors), [cameras](https://www.space.com/best-cameras), [drones](https://www.space.com/best-drones), [Lego](https://www.space.com/38810-best-lego-deals.html), [streaming](https://www.space.com/streaming-deals-guide) and more.

The Vespera Pro 2 is virtually identical to the first model apart from an upgraded interior. Harry Bennett / Future

The touch power button glows red when turned on. Harry Bennett / Future

The 50mm aperture remains the same but adds an upgraded optical design and internal light baffling. Harry Bennett / Future

Separate filters are available for the Vespera Pro 2 and I would highly recommend the dual-band filter for nebula imaging. Harry Bennett / Future

It's an impressive balance Vaonis have struck here between usability and premium astrophotography output. Prior to the pro-line of Vespera smart telescopes, I would have thought that this quality of astrophotography would require the highest levels of astronomy knowledge, alongside a pricey lineup of separate instruments. Don't get me wrong, the Vespera Pro 2 is not cheap but it really does have everything you need for capturing the wonders of the [night sky](https://www.space.com/stargazing/what-to-look-for-in-night-sky-november-2026)with ease.

Operation is controlled from the Singularity app on a smart device and setup takes minutes. After connecting the telescope, simply click on your chosen target to start automatic location and imaging. The app is intuitive and helpful for beginners, suggesting a range of night sky targets that are observable from your location and customisable plans that allow you to set a range of targets for automatic imaging throughout the night, so you can get some rest.

We wrote about an early [Black Friday deal](https://www.space.com/best-black-friday-deals-sales) on the the [Vaonis Vespera Pro](https://www.space.com/stargazing/skywatching-kit/vaonis-vespera-pro-smart-telescope-review) last week when it dropped in price, but Vaonis has now made both models of their Vespera Pro the same price. If you were thinking of getting a pro smart telescope for highly detailed [nebula](https://www.space.com/nebula-definition-types) photography, you may as well get the better version. It comes with a fully adjustable tripod, enhanced data transfer and an overhauled optical design for maximum performance.

The Dark Shark nebula, as imaged by the Vaonis Vespera Pro 2. Harry Bennett / Future

The Seahorse Nebula, as imaged by the Vaonis Vespera Pro 2. Harry Bennett / Future

This is a great model for expanding your knowledge of different types of objects in the universe. Do you know what a dark nebula is? I didn't until I decided to try and image one with the Vespera Pro 2. My attempts are not the best, but you can make out the clouds of dark dust that block out starlight behind them in the Dark Shark Nebula and the Seahorse Nebula. I'm sure that if I set these targets for "multi-night observation" in the app, those images would keep getting stronger and more detailed.

The Cygnus Loop, as imaged by the Vaonis Vespera Pro 2. (Image credit: Harry Bennett / Future)

On top of continuing observations from past sessions, the Vespera Pro 2 also offers mosaic mode for expanding your field of view on a certain target. This means that you can image vast expanses of the night sky without having to manually stitch together all the frames yourself. The Vespera Pro 2 does it for you. Here is my attempt at capturing the monumental supernova remnant, The Cygnus Loop. Again, it is fairly faint apart from the Eastern and Western Veil nebulas, but enabling multi-night observation will keep adding to this image whenever you get the chance to pick up where you left off.

items.body:
The New Scientist Book Club read Chris Beckett’s Dark Eden in November

Since starting the New Scientist Book Club in May 2023, I have aimed to vary our books as much as possible, moving between science fiction and popular science, older classics and the hottest new titles. Occasionally, though, I’m afraid I let the power go to my head and just choose one of my own personal favourites. That’s what I did in November, with Chris Beckett’s novel [Dark Eden](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2596432-read-an-extract-from-dark-eden-by-chris-beckett/), a book I’ve loved ever since it won the Arthur C. Clarke award in 2013.

Set on the planet Eden, a sunless world that drifts alone far outside the Milky Way, this follows the descendants of two astronauts who were marooned there over a century earlier. Now numbering 532 people, they tell each other stories of the world their ancestors came from, and struggle to survive on this dark, cold planet as they await the return of “one of those sky-boats with lights on them”. I think it is all wildly imaginative and original and exciting. So it was with some trepidation that I awaited the verdict of my fellow book club members on our [Discord](https://discord.com/invite/fn7m4NbSac) channel. I really wanted everyone else to love it, too!

Free newsletter

#### Sign up to Book Club

[Sign up to newsletter](https://www.newscientist.com/sign-up/bookclub/)

It started well. “I managed not to stay up all night reading, but the temptation was definitely there – I am hooked,” wrote Dee55. Les was similarly gripped. “Started it? I’ve only gone and finished it, haven’t I? It *really* got me in, and I found it a fascinating exploration of social anthropology and linguistics in a very small, isolated population. And the world-building was fascinating, too – *very* different flora and fauna.”

Several other members also cited the strength of the world-building in *Dark Eden*. I also love the lanternflowers and woollybucks of this planet, and was fascinated to learn, in an [essay](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2596453-in-dark-eden-i-imagined-how-life-might-exist-on-a-sunless-planet/) Chris wrote for book club members, that, when creating a world for a story, he doesn’t “usually seek to make the whole thing scientifically accurate, but I try to make it hang together in a way that feels coherent”. I think he definitely succeeds in that here.

[In Dark Eden, I imagined how life might exist on a sunless planet Dark Eden, the November read for the New Scientist Book Club, takes place on a rogue planet outside the Milky Way. Award-winning author Chris Beckett explains how he thought through the science behind this night world](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2596453-in-dark-eden-i-imagined-how-life-might-exist-on-a-sunless-planet/)

There were some excellent debates about the language these people have developed – they double up on words for emphasis, for example (“big big”; “cold cold”), use bastardised forms of our words (“Landing Veekle”; “leckytrickity”), and talk about Starry Swirl – the Milky Way they can see in their skies, a wonderfully evocative image.

“I think Beckett has done something really clever here. He’s created a language that feels familiar enough to read naturally, but is sufficiently different to remind us that this is an entirely separate culture that has evolved in isolation,” wrote Maria. “I enjoyed some of the language. Tom’s dick and Harry’s for instance,” wrote Matthew – referring to an exclamation the characters use for emphasis. “It’s contagious… yesterday I found myself saying Wow, it’s hot hot!” added leasabp. Dee55 also admitted to adopting some Edenisms: “My favourite bit of the language is ‘newhairs’! I am already using this for teenagers, but only to myself at present.”

The story’s protagonist is John Redlantern, a young man who decides there must be more to life than waiting for rescue around the Circle of Stones that marks the original astronauts’ landing point on Eden, and tries to spark an exodus from the Family’s small valley to explore the wider planet. John definitely drew some mixed opinions from readers.

“Problem is, I don’t much like our ‘hero’, he’s not a very sympathetic character, more Sméagol than Bilbo,” wrote Matthew. I chatted to Chris in an interview for book club members, and he was certainly aware of this: “He’s an awkward cuss, John, isn’t he? He’s not a particularly nice person,” he told me – before embarking on an enlightening discussion about why he chose to write from various viewpoints, and how hard it was describing the world of Eden from the perspectives of people who have never been anywhere else. “The discipline of just writing it from within the story is if I’m trying to describe the world to readers, I can’t use metaphors and analogies that refer to anything that’s outside of Eden. And that was quite tricky to do.”

Book club member Laura Akers, like others, said she “definitely enjoyed the story more when I realized that John, despite his own intentions, is not intended to be our ‘hero’”.

Overall, I think the book club mostly really enjoyed *Dark Eden* – I particularly appreciated leasapb’s comment: “Holy cow. Chapter 44!!!”, as I think the ending is fabulous – but one issue that was raised by a few people was the amount the characters have sex with each other. Incestuous sex.

“Certainly one of the odd things I found was the casual attitude to sex,” wrote Alan_P. Maria agreed. “I found the casual attitude towards sex quite unsettling too, particularly because the characters often seem almost childlike in their behaviour and understanding of the world, yet discuss sex so matter-of-factly. I honestly couldn’t bring myself to think too much about the incest!” And while Barbara Howe “loved the worldbuilding, and the story of John’s breakaway family’s trek to find a better place”, she found the “constant and highly unerotic sex… offputting”.

But given that at least some members have gone on to read the sequels, I think this was largely a popular choice – and a welcome change from the Earthly dystopias which seem to be dominating the big new sci-fi novels out this autumn (I’m looking at you, [Audrey Niffenegger](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2594474-theres-two-ways-of-doing-time-travel-right-says-audrey-niffenegger/) and [Emily St. John Mandel](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2595814-our-verdict-on-exit-party-by-emily-st-john-mandel-not-her-best-book/)).

items.title: DB Navigator: FlixTrain-Tickets ab Dezember direkt buchbar
items.subtitle: Wer mit der Bahn unterwegs ist, kann künftig auch Fahrkarten des Konkurrenten FlixTrain direkt im DB Navigator kaufen.
items.feedText:
Die Deutsche Bahn und FlixTrain haben eine entsprechende Vertriebsvereinbarung unterzeichnet. Ab dem 7. Dezember 2026 lassen sich über die iPhone-App und die Webseite bahn.de erstmals Tickets beider Unternehmen erwerben. Die Neuerung gilt für Fahrten ab dem 13. Dezember und damit passend zum Fahrplanwechsel. FlixTrain-Tickets erstmals direkt in der Bahn-App

Bislang wurden FlixTrain-Verbindungen zwar bereits in der Fahrplanauskunft der Deutschen Bahn angezeigt, eine direkte Buchung war allerdings nicht möglich.…
items.body:
Wer mit der Bahn unterwegs ist, kann künftig auch Fahrkarten des Konkurrenten FlixTrain direkt im DB Navigator kaufen. Die Deutsche Bahn und FlixTrain haben eine entsprechende [Vertriebsvereinbarung unterzeichnet](https://www1.deutschebahn.com/de/presse/pressestart_zentrales_uebersicht/deutsche-bahn-und-flixtrain-schliessen-vertriebsvereinbarung-14098862). Ab dem 7. Dezember 2026 lassen sich über die iPhone-App und die Webseite bahn.de erstmals Tickets beider Unternehmen erwerben. Die Neuerung gilt für Fahrten ab dem 13. Dezember und damit passend zum Fahrplanwechsel.

## FlixTrain-Tickets erstmals direkt in der Bahn-App

Bislang wurden FlixTrain-Verbindungen zwar bereits in der Fahrplanauskunft der Deutschen Bahn angezeigt, eine direkte Buchung war allerdings nicht möglich. Stattdessen mussten Reisende auf die Webseite oder App von FlixTrain wechseln, um ihre Fahrkarten zu kaufen.

Dieser Umweg entfällt künftig. Die Bahn übernimmt den Ticketverkauf innerhalb ihrer eigenen Buchungsoberfläche. Damit können Reisende direkt im DB Navigator nach passenden Verbindungen suchen, Preise vergleichen und Fahrkarten erwerben.

Die beiden Unternehmen bleiben dabei weiterhin eigenständige Wettbewerber. Fahrpläne, Preise und das jeweilige Zugangebot legen Deutsche Bahn und FlixTrain unverändert unabhängig voneinander fest. Laut Bahn sollen die Tickets zum gleichen Preis wie bei FlixTrain angeboten werden.

## ICE und FlixTrain in einem Buchungsvorgang

Besonders praktisch ist die Möglichkeit, Verbindungen beider Anbieter miteinander zu kombinieren. So lässt sich beispielsweise eine Reise planen, bei der zunächst ein ICE genutzt wird und anschließend der Umstieg in einen FlixTrain erfolgt.

Die dafür benötigten Fahrkarten können in einem einzigen Buchungsvorgang erworben werden. Das dürfte insbesondere bei längeren Reisen mit mehreren Umstiegen die Planung und den Preisvergleich erleichtern.

#### Der DB Navigator lässt bald auch Buchungen bei der Konkurrenz zu.

## Bei verpassten Anschlüssen bleibt Vorsicht geboten

Eine Einschränkung bleibt allerdings bestehen. Obwohl beide Tickets gemeinsam gekauft werden können, handelt es sich weiterhin um getrennte Fahrkarten. Die Buchung führt somit nicht automatisch zu einem durchgehenden Beförderungsvertrag.

Darauf weist auch der Fahrgastverband [PRO BAHN](https://www.presseportal.de/pm/177328/6397594) hin. Er begrüßt die Zusammenarbeit, fordert allerdings weitergehende Fahrgastrechte. Bei einem verpassten Anschluss zwischen zwei Anbietern sollte die Weiterreise ohne zusätzliche Kosten möglich sein. Bis dahin empfiehlt es sich, bei entsprechenden Verbindungen auf ausreichend Umsteigezeit zu achten.

In die umgekehrte Richtung funktioniert die Kooperation übrigens noch nicht: Fahrkarten der Deutschen Bahn lassen sich weiterhin nicht über die Buchungsplattformen von FlixTrain kaufen.

Der [DB Navigator](https://apps.apple.com/de/app/db-navigator/id343555245) ist kostenlos für iPhone und Apple Watch erhältlich. Zuletzt hatte die Bahn unter anderem die [Anmeldung per Passkey](https://www.iphone-ticker.de/db-navigator-anmeldung-jetzt-auch-per-passkey-moeglich-272359/) ergänzt. Die neue FlixTrain-Buchung soll ab dem 7. Dezember direkt über die bestehenden Vertriebskanäle zur Verfügung stehen.

[★ iPhone-Ticker bei Google bevorzugen ★](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=iphone-ticker.de)

Der Beitrag [DB Navigator: FlixTrain-Tickets ab Dezember direkt buchbar](https://www.iphone-ticker.de/db-navigator-flixtrain-tickets-ab-dezember-direkt-buchbar-291411/) Wurde zuerst auf [iphone-ticker.de](https://www.iphone-ticker.de) veröffentlicht.

items.body:
For many years, I have been frustrated by a simple question, one I ask myself all the time: what the hell did I do in my eight hours at work today? I’m a freelancer and micro-publisher, and my time may consist of moments spent each day across a thousand different tasks. This leaves me unable to recall comprehensively what I’ve done.

I finally have an answer in the form of [the Timing app](https://timingapp.com/): it offers app-driven, document- and dialog-level tracking. It’s not the first or the only such app, but it’s the first I’ve tried, found worthwhile, and stuck with. I now have many months of data about what I do, and it is truly revealing, particularly for the writing portion of my life.

Timing [1](https://sixcolors.com/post/2026/11/timing-review-let-an-app-track-what-you-do/#fn-42510-sponsor) tracks every context switch when you move from foreground app to foreground app, which includes the titles of windows and other identifying details. At the end of the day, I can see how much time I spent and most of what I did within each app.

Timing captures what you do by app using window titles, pathways, and more.

The reason Timing works for me? Powerful rules-based task filtering that, as I’ve set up over time, handles most of the work in letting me see what I’m doing without tediously categorizing pieces of time or individual documents and windows. I can mark time chunks manually or reassign them, but I rarely need to spend many of my precious minutes doing that.

This review isn’t exhaustive—the app has many features I never use, but the subset I describe below has a high value to me.

## Identifying what you’re doing

Timing records data about what’s happening in the foreground. While this has limitations, it has generally worked for me across many programs and types of work. Timing pulls titles from documents, tab titles from browser tabs, Terminal job information (often shown in a Terminal window’s title), people from Messages, channel names and DM names from Slack, and paths to files that are open. If you have Timing installed on multiple Macs, it syncs this data. You can manually start timers and edit information that’s been captured.

The Devices filter lets you include or exclude your linked devices for clarity.

While there’s no way for an iPhone or iPad app to extract document-specific usage, Timing Software extracts information from synced Screen Time data. The company notes that [this is a workaround](https://timingapp.com/help/screen-time), and Apple could break this method in the future. The company avoided iOS/iPadOS app development by [offering a web app](https://timingapp.com/help/web) for manual time recording that works on any platform.

Timing records data by app, with the details broken out. As data accrues, Timing sorts it in the Activities view. There are two other main views—Stats and Reports—which I have barely touched in nearly a year of using it. Most of what I need I find in Activities.

This report view may be useful to some people. It shows I have tracked 1856 hours of my time so far in 2026, starting in mid-January!

The three features that helped me use Timing effectively were:

The single-day view lets you get a densely layered graphical view of your work across all your devices.

- Time slicing: At the top of every view, there’s a time period button you can click to choose among presets, like the Past 30 Days, and custom ranges. If you choose Today or single day in Activities, you get a bonus graphical chronological view of the entire day’s behavior divided by platform, with some algorithm-generated text that defines the primary activity in that period.
- Projects: Create projects and sub-projects to organize what you’re doing. Because I have so many different things going on, I have my tiny publishing business, Six Colors, Take Control (books I write for royalties and books/consulting I do under contract), sites I’ve developed, and clients. I also set up projects for non-billable overhead stuff, which includes household work. (For clients, I don’t rely on Timing, but rather a separate timer-based accounting app that handles invoices and other tasks, too.)
- Rules: The most powerful feature, mentioned in the introduction, is Timing’s rules. The rules use pattern matching to assign an item identified in Activities to a project. You can create these rules automatically or by hand. For instance, I set up rules for specific paths for documents to always be part of a specific project, but I use automatic rule creation to add entries that don’t correspond to a path, like Safari windows that have a title that always starts with the same words.

The powerful rules editor includes all automatically created filters. Tweaking rules automates time tracking.

Those are the pieces; now I’ll tell you how I join them.

## Using dragging and rules to build the picture

To bring this all together, I start in the Activities view. All Activities shows everything that’s been tracked in the currently selected time period. Anything assigned to a project appears under My Projects. The Unassigned section has all the uncut gems you can work with to bring order to your tracking chaos. (I should note that Activities defaults to Unified, which shows tasks by apps. You can also use By Category—website, path, etc.—or Chronological.)

Depending on the app, you can drill down by clicking expansion triangles. So for Safari, I might click next to Safari, then Kickstarter, then find there are many different entries all related to a project I was working on. I can also hover over or click grouped or individual entries in the Today or single-day view at the right side of Timing, as shown above.

The Activities view set to a single day lets you reveal a lot of information about ranges of time, and assign them to projects.

In all these cases, I can assign tasks to a project, or drag windows, selections, or entire apps onto a project in the My Projects list.

If I’m sure I want to have that assignment stick—the document entry I’m dragging is always part of a given project—I can Option-drag, and Timing adds a rule. Over weeks and months, I have accumulated many rules and tweaked the entries by hand to make sure I was sweeping in the right documents.

For instance, I can review recent work on an update to *Take Control of Apple Wallet* by selecting the last 90 days as a time period, selecting the project name TCo Wallet in the sidebar, and then clicking Chronological. I can expand the time entries to make sure tasks were properly assigned, and look over the time I spent.

I can see exactly how much time I’ve spent on this book update.

My two greatest tips from using Timing are:

- I should be using tab groups in Safari more so that I have more discrete information when a Safari tab’s title tag lacks enough information for me to review later.
- Examine rules regularly to ensure you’ve got the right level of granularity to match what you want included in a project.

…

items.body:
When [Ableton](https://musictech.com/brands/ableton)’s Push 3 hit the market in 2023, it was framed as [a generational piece of kit](https://musictech.com/features/interviews/ableton-push-3-timeless-instrument-new-generation/). Not only did it ‘push’ the series into a new realm, able to operate as a totally standalone controller rather than a loyal [Ableton Live](https://musictech.com/tag/ableton-live) companion, but the Push’s third iteration also tightened things up. With a refined workflow, new modes like Autowarping, and a fresh grid of 64 expressive MPE pads, it was Ableton mastering the controller formula – and [it’s currently available for $360 off at Sweetwater](https://sweetwater.sjv.io/N9kLeN).

[deals ids=”42cf3ac6-66c1-439e-bd7d-86825d6cc3ba”]

To this day, the [controller](https://musictech.com/tag/controllers) continues to hold its own. And that’s because, alongside all the perks, Ableton’s design allows for the Push 3 to grow with you; the upgradable, modular system is built to last. Whether it’s a battery upgrade or processing update, Push 3 has the potential to keep up with even the freshest tech.

With that in mind, the Push 3 was never ‘just for Christmas’ – it’s a device you can invest in, knowing it would serve you well for years to come. That’s what makes Sweetwater’s current Black Friday even sweeter; for $1,439, you’ll get a quality controller that is an absolute powerhouse.

While the drop to $1,439 from $1,799 is already pretty nice, the deal only gets sweeter the more you consider it. Because it doesn’t just bag you a controller, but the ability to mix and edit without the need for Ableton Live. It’s a built-in audio/MIDI interface, making it a handy central hub for your entire rig.

However, if you know you’re someone who always plans to hook their controller up to their computer, there is also a deal on the Push 3 without a built-in processor. [The Push 3 Control Surface](https://www.sweetwater.com/store/detail/Push3--ableton-push-3) is exactly that, and it’s available at just $799, a $200 from its usual cost of $999. But, to reiterate, this option does require you to hook it up to a computer running Ableton Live.

**For more information, head to [Sweetwater](https://sweetwater.sjv.io/N9kLeN). If you’re interested in finding any other good deals, feel free to check out our full guide to[Black Friday](https://musictech.com/news/gear/best-black-friday-music-tech-deals/).**
