items.body:
Stepping back from the specifics of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) debate, I want to make a larger point about the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and its role in American public policy:

This law has “environmental” in its title, but in a critical respect it’s just not an environmental law at all.

Which is to say it does not set any kind of standards related to environmental quality. The Clean Air Act makes rules about air pollution. The Clean Water Act makes rules about water pollution. We could make stricter rules about microplastics or forever chemicals or something else. We also have parks and other kinds of wildlife and landscape conservation programs.

None of this is NEPA.

NEPA is a law that makes it harder to do certain classes of things by imposing various procedural requirements, and it creates a litigation attack surface for people who do not like these classes of things.

NEPA is entirely indifferent as to whether the proposed thing is good for the environment or bad for the environment. What’s more, unlike real environmental laws, NEPA does not govern private-sector economic activity. The key idea of NEPA is the “major federal action.” It burdens government activities relative to private-sector activities and it burdens “action” (doing something new) relative to the status quo.

If you want to cut taxes on business investment to encourage more data center construction, that’s not a federal action for NEPA purposes, even though common sense says that tax law is a very important facet of federal policy. Maintaining the regulatory status quo is not a federal action even if the status quo is bad for the environment. If you want to build a light rail line that’s partially financed with a Department of Transportation grant, that’s a federal action and you need to do your NEPA homework.

If requiring federal (but not private) actions (but not inactions) to meet a set of burdensome procedural requirements leads to better environmental outcomes than not doing this, that would have to be essentially by coincidence.

I think a lot of progressive analytical errors about the post-1970 history of the United States are downstream of not understanding this.

It’s not just that progressives overrate NEPA but that they have an essentially false narrative of why contemporary government is the way it is. There’s this view that something called “neoliberalism” happened and that now because of “neoliberalism,” all the Democrats do is hand out tax credits rather than being cool New Dealers who support a robust state. But guess what — a tax credit to buy electric cars is not a major federal action but a mass transit line is.

NEPA is not the only reason for the rise of what [Suzanne Mettler calls the “submerged state”](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0226521656?lv=shuf&channelId=500&plpRedirect=mhFallback) or what [Mike Konczal calls government by coupon](https://www.newamerica.org/insights/no-discount-comparing-the-public-option-to-the-coupon-welfare-state/), but it’s striking that progressives tend to neglect its existence while workaday bureaucrats are painfully aware of its relevance.

#### The bias toward inaction

When New York City was thinking about launching its congestion pricing program to reduce traffic in parts of Manhattan and raise revenue for mass transit, it was granted the grace of being allowed to comply with NEPA via an environmental assessment rather than the more burdensome environmental impact statement. That less burdensome document runs [868 pages](https://www.mta.info/document/93446) with a two-volume appendix. The first volume of the appendix has [1,966 pages](https://www.mta.info/document/93451) and the [second volume is 1,173 pages](https://www.mta.info/document/93456). Yes, that is 4,000 pages worth of environmental review under the *less* burdensome of the two NEPA tracks for a program that charges people money to drive cars and uses the revenue to fund mass transit.

The reason the report has to be so long is not because the question of whether this is bad for the environment is hard to answer.

[↗ slowboring.com](https://www.slowboring.com/p/nepa-is-not-an-environmental-protection)

items.body:
# Microduck Obstacle Avoidance: A Sim2Real Workflow with Isaac Lab and Newton

## a]:hidden"> Microduck Obstacle Avoidance: A Sim2Real Workflow with Isaac Lab and Newton

## TL;DR

Add local obstacle avoidance to Microduck while keeping its walking policy fixed. Build varied courses with reusable SimReady assets, model ToF sensing with Newton’s raycaster, and train a controller in Isaac Lab to adjust gamepad velocity commands around obstacles. This tutorial covers simulation training, evaluation, export, and real-robot deployment.

## Introduction

A walking policy can keep Microduck balanced, but it does not tell the robot how to steer around an obstacle in its path. In this workflow, we reuse the walking policy from our first Microduck tutorial and keep its weights fixed. This follow-up trains a separate avoidance controller using time-of-flight (ToF) sensing. You choose a direction with a gamepad; the controller adjusts the velocity command before passing it to the walking policy.

NVIDIA Isaac Lab is an open-source framework for training policies across thousands of GPU-parallel simulations and it provides the robot-learning environment. Newton simulates physics and the sensor’s depth measurements. We will cover the control architecture, train on varied obstacle layouts, evaluate the resulting policies, and prepare the interface for hardware testing.

## 1. Set Microduck obstacle avoidance in Isaac Lab

For simulation and training, prepare:

- A Linux system with a compatible NVIDIA GPU and driver. See the Isaac Lab installation guide for platform requirements.
- Git with Git LFS, and the uv package manager.
For physical-robot testing, prepare:

- A configured Microduck. Load the same backlash walking-policy export used by the navigation task.
- A supported ToF sensor with its configuration recorded.
- A paired gamepad and a level test area with obstacles.
### Quick install

Install uv if it is not already installed. Then clone the exp/microduck branch of the Isaac Lab repository and install its dependencies:

git lfs install git clone --branch exp/microduck https://github.com/isaac-sim/IsaacLab.git cd IsaacLab uv sync --frozen Once setup is complete, list the available Microduck environments and presets:

uv run isaaclab list_envs --keyword MicroDuck --show_presets Download the walking policy Download and export the upstream backlash walking checkpoint once before training. The obstacle avoidance task loads the exported walking policy automatically.

uv run isaaclab play \ --task IsaacContrib-Velocity-Rough-MicroDuck \ --rl_library rsl_rl --checkpoint pretrained \ --num_envs 1 --visualizer none \ --video newton_gl --video_length 1 \ presets=backlash 2. Build the obstacle course The environment combines simple primitives with OpenUSD assets available through SimReady Central on Hugging Face. We use a cardboard box , office bin , bedside cabinet alongside cones. From the IsaacLab repository root, download the pinned box, bin and cabinet packages into assets/simready.

uvx --from huggingface-hub hf download nvidia/simready-assets \ --repo-type dataset \ --revision 9d4556bfe80868c1d27a7a7ba1c2774e63e8cedd \ --include "box_cardboard_a01/*" \ --include "trashCan_office_black_a03/*" \ --include "table_bedside_b01/*" \ --local-dir ./assets/simready At each episode reset, the environment code automatically samples a layout, shuffles the props, and varies their placement and rotation. Most courses scatter obstacles ahead of the duck, with a smaller mix of clear paths, barriers and passages. The code also mirrors layouts and mixes aligned and staggered rows.

Goals start ahead of the duck. Movement commands guide it toward the goal while the policy adjusts them around obstacles.

Figure 1. Varied obstacle-course layouts with SimReady assets and primitive geometry.

## 3. Understand how ToF sensing guides the walking policy

The IsaacContrib-ObstacleAvoidance-Flat-MicroDuck task separates obstacle avoidance from balance. A navigation policy uses ToF sensing to adjust forward, lateral, and yaw commands at 50 Hz. The frozen walking policy then converts those commands into joint actions, allowing the robot to learn obstacle avoidance without retraining its walking behavior.

During training, the navigation policy’s actor receives ToF history and body and controller state available on the real robot. Its critic has access to additional simulation state to guide learning, but is not needed for deployment.

Rewards encourage progress toward the goal, safe arrivals, and movement around obstacles. Following a movement command earns credit only when the robot makes progress with sufficient clearance; risky approaches reduce that credit. Penalties discourage fast approaches, abrupt command changes, collisions, and falls.

The obstacle-avoidance task lives in isaaclab_tasks.contrib.microduck_obstacle . Its configuration is in obstacle_avoidance_env_cfg.py , ToF sensing is in sensors.py , and actions, commands, observations and rewards are organized under mdp/ .

### Model the ToF sensor

MicroDuckToFCamera extends Newton’s LegacyMultiMeshRayCasterCamera to model the VL53L5CX—a compact time-of-flight (ToF) sensor on the microduck that measures distance across an 8×8 grid at 15Hz. The simulated sensor has a 45° field of view and a 0.12–4 m range. It follows the duck’s head, with placement similar to the sensor on the real duck.

Real recordings informed the sensor placement and floor readings in simulation. Training adds noise, delays and missing measurements—including near the grid’s edges—to expose the policy to imperfect data. The excerpt below shows selected sensor settings already included in the task configuration. You do not need to edit or run this code separately.

# Selected settings; mount and raycast targets omitted. head_tof = MicroDuckToFCameraCfg( prim_path=MICRODUCK_HEAD_BODY_PATH, update_period= 1.0 / 15.0 , pattern_cfg=patterns.PinholeCameraPatternCfg( focal_length= 1.0 , width= 8 , height= 8 , horizontal_aperture=_TOF_APERTURE, vertical_aperture=_TOF_APERTURE, ), randomization=ToFRandomizationCfg( mount_pitch_degrees=(- 10.0 , 10.0 ), mount_height_m=(- 0.02 , 0.02 ), floor_validity_midpoint_offset_m=( 0.0 , 0.13 ), near_floor_edge_impairment_probability= 0.5 , ), data_types=[ "distance_to_image_plane" , "distance_to_camera" ], max_distance=TOF_MAX_RANGE, depth_clipping_behavior= "zero" , ) 4. Train the Microduck policy across parallel environments Train the navigation policy with PPO across 16,384 parallel environments for 1,500 training iterations. Its actor, critic, normalizers, and optimizer start fresh. The task configuration loads the fixed walking checkpoint, robot model, and obstacle assets.

items.body:
Rank the films inspired by Edgar Allan Poe, and several adaptations of [“The Fall of the House of Usher”](https://www.eapoe.org/works/tales/usherf.htm) will almost certainly come near the top. At first glance, that story of a man paying a visit to an old friend who lives with his twin sister in their family’s grand house — each of the latter three well advanced into a different process of deterioration — might seem too short, as well as too light on conflict to translate into a conventional screenplay. Yet it’s also full of cinematically irresistible images, from the somehow ruinous yet wholly intact titular mansion to the bloodily wretched sister throwing herself upon the terrified brother who entombed her alive while their ancestral home collapses around them.

Of the twenty or thirty versions of “The Fall of the House of Usher” so far made for the screen, the most celebrated remains the one Jean Epstein directed in 1928. [Officially designating it as one of the “great movies,”](https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/great-movie-the-fall-of-the-house-of-usher-1928) Roger Ebert calls that picture’s vision of the great hall “one of the most haunting spaces in the movies. Its floor is a vast marble expanse, interrupted here and there by an item of furniture that seems dwarfed by the surrounding emptiness. An odd staircase rises from one distant corner. It is not impossible that this vision, in one of the best-known French surrealist films, inspired the designers of the great hall of Xanadu in *Citizen Kane*.”

The avant-garde filmmaking duo James Sibley Watson Jr. and Melville Webber (in collaboration with e. e. cummings, who contributed to the script) could hardly manage the same scale of production design for [their own short adaptation of Poe’s story](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eh1Fnxctjsw), which happened to come out the same year.

But the resulting Expressionist take on the material has also been highly acclaimed, and through [this YouTube playlist of Poe films](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLGECP2JNbcRg), you can experience not just both of them, but also other adaptations of “The Fall of the House of Usher” by [idiosyncratic Czech animator Jan Švankmajer](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4f3ZxoLTHkk) and [B‑movie powerhouse Roger Corman](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EgktFwcVXCY). Sensitive to Poe’s sensationalist appeal and air of transgressive decadence, Corman ended up directing an eight-film “Poe cycle,” nearly all of which star Vincent Price.

It’s fair to say that no film actor is more closely associated with Poe than Price, a link Tim Burton [celebrated in animation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hD8uQzu0IL0) at the beginning of his career. Price even played the writer himself in [An Evening with Edgar Allan Poe](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZzyYzK94UU4&list=PLGECP2JNbcRg&index=7), a special from 1970 in which he recites “The Sphinx,” “The Cask of Amontillado,” “The Pit and the Pendulum,” and “The Tell-Tale Heart.” That last, the most screen-adapted Poe story of them all, also appears on [the playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLGECP2JNbcRg) in various forms: an [early D. W. Griffith feature](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=avB4bs4Q6DU), the [directorial debut of Jules Dassin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RW6fdqnN0E0), an [animated short narrated by James Mason](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WAXB2H3SsFg), a [British psychological thriller](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pXMZeSZS_-A), and a [transposition into modern-day New Orleans](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yWworPqU668). items.body: In October, U.S. President Donald Trump sold his eleventh-hour deal to secure diesel from Russian President Vladimir Putin—pausing sanctions that his own administration had imposed—as a boon for the negotiations to end the war in Ukraine. The arrangement, he wrote on Truth Social, was intended to keep Russia at “the bargaining table.” Of course, it was always obvious to observers that the gambit had as much or more to do with bolstering the U.S. economy and stemming a massive victory for the Democrats in this month’s midterm elections, and in that, it failed.Cynics have grounds for questioning all of Trump’s moves when it comes to Russia and Ukraine. He clearly dislikes Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and shows a marked preference for illiberal leaders, especially those willing to give him easy wins. Still, a stopped clock can be right twice a day. And concessions such as the fuel deal are exactly what might move Russia and Ukraine closer to peace, even if they are not wholly motivated by public-spiritedness.

items.title: Krebsmedikament erfolgreich in Tabakpflanze hergestellt
items.subtitle: Das Chemotherapeutikum Paclitaxel wird eigentlich aus Eiben gewonnen.
items.feedText: Zahlreiche Arzneimittel stammen ursprünglich aus der Natur und werden bis heute vollständig oder teilweise aus pflanzlichen Bestandteilen gewonnen. Dazu zählt auch das Chemotherapeutikum Paclitaxel, das gegen verschiedene Krebsarten zum Einsatz kommt, darunter gegen Brust-, Eierstock- und Gebärmutterhalskrebs sowie bestimmte Arten von Lungenkrebs. Isoliert wurde es ursprünglich aus der Rinde der Pazifischen Eibe (Taxus brevifolia). Allerdings werden große Mengen Eibenrinde für wenig Wirkstoff benötigt und die Pflanzen sterben nach der Ernte ab – eine nicht nachhaltige Strategie. Heute wird das Medikament stattdessen halbsynthetisch hergestellt, wobei Vorprodukte aus den Nadeln der europäischen Eibe isoliert und anschließend weiterverarbeitet werden. Zudem ist es bereits möglich, den Wirkstoff in Eibenzellkulturen zu produzieren.
items.body:
# Krebsmedikament erfolgreich in Tabakpflanze hergestellt

Zahlreiche Arzneimittel stammen ursprünglich aus der Natur und werden bis heute vollständig oder teilweise aus pflanzlichen Bestandteilen gewonnen. Dazu zählt auch das Chemotherapeutikum Paclitaxel, das gegen verschiedene Krebsarten zum Einsatz kommt, darunter gegen Brust-, Eierstock- und Gebärmutterhalskrebs sowie bestimmte Arten von Lungenkrebs. Isoliert wurde es ursprünglich aus der Rinde der Pazifischen Eibe (Taxus brevifolia). Allerdings werden große Mengen Eibenrinde für wenig Wirkstoff benötigt und die Pflanzen sterben nach der Ernte ab – eine nicht nachhaltige Strategie.

Heute wird das Medikament stattdessen halbsynthetisch hergestellt, wobei Vorprodukte aus den Nadeln der europäischen Eibe isoliert und anschließend weiterverarbeitet werden. Zudem ist es bereits möglich, den Wirkstoff in Eibenzellkulturen zu produzieren. Der vollständige Syntheseweg des komplexen Moleküls war allerdings bislang noch unklar. „Durch seine strukturelle Komplexität und seine geringe natürliche Häufigkeit ist die Herstellung von Paclitaxel nach wie vor kostspielig und ineffizient“, berichtet ein Team um Feiyan Liang von der Universität Kopenhagen in Dänemark.

## Eingeschleuste Gene

Nun haben Liang und ihre Kollegen erstmals sämtliche Schritte des Biosynthesewegs von Paclitaxel rekonstruiert und in eine artfremde Pflanze übertragen. Für ihre Studie schleusten sie die Baupläne für Enzyme, die in der Eibe an der Herstellung von Paclitaxel beteiligt sind, in die Blätter der Tabakpflanze Nicotiana benthamiana ein. Dazu nutzten sie Bakterien als sogenannte Genfähren. Die eingeschleuste DNA wird dabei nicht fest ins Erbgut des Wirts eingebaut, sondern bleibt nur einige Tage aktiv und wird während dieser Zeit in Genprodukte umgesetzt – in diesem Fall in Paclitaxel und seine Vorstufen.

Anhand der Modellpflanze konnte das Team die einzelnen Syntheseschritte detailliert nachvollziehen. „Dadurch haben wir offene mechanistische Unklarheiten systematisch beseitigt“, berichten die Forschenden. Wie sie feststellten, finden die verschiedenen Herstellungsschritte in unterschiedlichen Bereichen innerhalb der Pflanzenzellen statt. „Das erfordert einen gerichteten Transport der Zwischenprodukte zwischen den verschiedenen Zellorganellen“, erklären Liang und ihre Kollegen.

Auf Basis dieser Erkenntnisse gelang es ihnen, die ursprünglich sehr geringe Paclitaxel-Produktion in der Tabakpflanze um mehr als das 500-fache zu steigern, bis zu einem Wert von 61,05 Mikrogramm pro Gramm Trockengewicht. „Dieser Gehalt ist mit der Konzentration in der Eibenrinde vergleichbar“, berichten die Forschenden. Aus ihrer Sicht liefert die Studie den Nachweis, dass eine biotechnologische Produktion des Chemotherapeutikums in genetisch modifizierten Tabakpflanzen grundsätzlich machbar ist.

## Noch keine Konkurrenz zu bisherigen Methoden

Der praktische Nutzen dieser Methode ist zumindest für Paclitaxel jedoch begrenzt: Das neue Verfahren bietet in seiner bisherigen Form keinen Vorteil gegenüber den gängigen Methoden zur Herstellung des Chemotherapeutikums, wie der nicht an der Studie beteiligte Botaniker Heribert Warzecha von der Technischen Universität Darmstadt erklärt.

„Die Produktion in Eiben-Zellkulturen oder die Isolierung einer Vorstufe aus Nadeln und die anschließende chemische Modifikation zu Paclitaxel sind etabliert und kostenoptimiert“, erklärt Warzecha. „Damit sich der Aufwand der Umstellung auf eine neue Technik inklusive der notwendigen Anlagen lohnt, müsste der Ertrag zehn- bis hundertmal höher sein, oder die Kosten entsprechend niedriger, was hier nicht der Fall ist.“ Hinzu kommt, dass das neue Verfahren auf gentechnischen Methoden beruht, was die Zulassung komplizierter macht.

Doch auch wenn ein unmittelbarer praktischer Nutzen noch aussteht, trägt die Studie Warzecha zufolge entscheidend zum Verständnis der biochemischen Prozesse in den Zellen der Eibe bei, inklusiver aller notwendigen Gene und Enzyme. „Dass die Autoren durch ihre Methode in Tabakpflanzen vergleichbare Mengen an Paclitaxel erzeugen konnten, wie sie auch in der Rinde der Eibe vorkommen, ist ein großartiger Erfolg. Es zeigt, dass einige Verständnisfragen nun geklärt werden konnten“, sagt er. „Ob sich die Menge noch weiter steigern lässt, bleibt abzuwarten. Erst dann wäre die hier vorgestellte Produktionsmethode ‚konkurrenzfähig‘ zu etablierten Methoden.“

Denkbar wäre zudem, ähnliche Methoden für andere Arzneimittel anzuwenden, für die es bislang noch keine Zellkultursysteme gibt.

Quelle: Feiyan Liang (University of Copenhagen, Denmark) et al., Nature Chemical Biology, doi: 10.1038/s41589-026-02376-x

items.body:
The Guardian:

> Donald Trump made up to $15m (£11.5m) on his holdings of Nvidia
> stock after the US chipmaker’s share price soared on the surprise
> return of Jensen Huang as chief executive. [...] The US
> president’s financial disclosures to the Office of Government
> Ethics indicate he might have owned as many as 370,000 shares in
> Nvidia as of 30 September, the latest available data, in news
> first reported by the Financial Times.
> Nvidia’s shares rocketed by 31.5% on Monday, adding about $950bn
> to the company’s value.

This whole preposterous saga would reek to high hell even if Donald Trump didn’t own a share of stock in any public company. It’s [a national security farce](https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/2026/11/trump-huang-national-security-risk/689547/?gift=aQyUJR7AIw1mJWdQ6Ed6yMZXlDJkV7MdRh9tXNaeAe4&) and a full-throated embrace of “[state capitalism](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2026/11/24/nvidia-and-trumps-state-capitalism)” (per the well-known socialist sympathizers on the WSJ Editorial Board). But given that Trump *does* own stock in Nvidia, the corruption is prima facie. Who could possibly argue that this is *not* corrupt? The only possible defense is that everyone is corrupt and if everyone is corrupt, it’s OK when it’s your guy doing it.

This, after “corruption” was [the top issue on U.S. voters’ minds](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/23/corruption-midterm-election-cnbc-poll-trump.html) in this month’s election — an election in which Trump’s Republican Party took a historical drubbing. Huang’s reinstatement was obviously popular with a certain segment of investors and with [the AI-mania wing of the tech industry](https://x.com/gruber/status/2124214714825572861), but this whole abjectly corrupt affair is wildly unpopular with the electorate writ large.

[★](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2026/11/24/trump-nvidia-stock)

items.body:
arXiv:2611.31301v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Audio-video (AV) deepfakes can fake the face, the voice, or both. Most benchmarks only ask whether a clip is real or fake, so they cannot show whether a detector relies on the picture, the voice, or encoding traces. We present MOZAIC, a paired benchmark with a 4-way label in which every source clip is released in all four combinations of real or fake video and real or fake audio so each modality contribution can be measured directly. Fakes cover inner-face swapping, whole-frame video diffusion and voice conversion. MOZAIC has 137,745 clips from 15,014 source pairs and four tasks: T1 AV authenticity, T2 manipulation type, T3 identity verification and T4 explanation. We evaluate 12 AV multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), train four detectors and fine-tune MLLMs with LoRA. Overall, the best MLLM reaches only 35.6% on the four-way T1 and catches far more video-only fakes than voice-only fakes (43.6% vs 7.5%). Trained detectors reach 98.4% on T1, and LoRA fine-tuning raises explanation scores (OmniVinci 4.17 to 7.40, Qwen2.5-Omni 4.42 to 6.98), but the best T1 detector falls to 78.3% when the face-swap generator is held out of training, so generalization and explanation remain open. We release the dataset, the compact MOZAIC-SMALL split, the code and the prompts. https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mozaic/

items.feedText:
However all these are outshone by today’s twin title stories…

Jensen Huang is back. Eleven days after announcing his resignation, Nvidia announced his return as CEO, president and member of the Board of Directors. View post on X ↗

The board voted unanimously after more meetings with Jensen on Sunday and said it received input from senior U.S. officials (aka the Treasury Secretary and the President dialing into the board meeting). Colette Kress remains CFO, the independent directors’ investigation continues,…
items.body:
Congrats to Sierra on [tripling](https://x.com/sierraplatform/status/2124832956795539842?a=LMwTZcXTCy6VIdPRUb0&s=46) last year’s [$10B valuation](https://x.com/SierraPlatform/status/1963654362384724388), and to [Z.ai](http://z.ai/) for releasing [GLM 5.4](https://z.ai/blog/glm-5.4), their first looped transformer following Thinking Machine’s much smaller [Inkling Mini 2](https://x.com/miramurati/status/2123872534970208421) from last week. However all these are outshone by today’s twin title stories…

**Jensen Huang is**[back](https://x.com/aburducky/status/2124924846266277988/video/1?a=6-tbBZhGNaBzRNGkqhk&s=46)**.** Eleven days after [announcing his resignation](https://latent.space/p/ainews-jensen-huang-resigns-after-33-years-leading-nvidia/), Nvidia [announced](https://investor.nvidia.com/news/press-release-details/2026/NVIDIA-Board-Reinstates-Jensen-Huang-as-President-CEO-and-Board-Director/default.aspx) his return as CEO, president and member of the Board of Directors.

[View post on X ↗](https://x.com/alecqfong/status/2124938191761555517)

The board voted unanimously after [more meetings with Jensen on Sunday](https://x.com/lookner/status/2125067095113154824) and said it received input from senior U.S. officials (aka [the Treasury Secretary](https://x.com/CGasparino/status/2124899810314437062) and [the President dialing into the board meeting](https://x.com/rogoswami/status/2124881764535464261?a=wUcGlCxi-wvs1ZrGiJw&s=46)). Colette Kress remains CFO, the independent directors’ investigation continues, and Jensen’s Senate hearing is still due in 8 days. Nvidia also formed a board committee for national security and export control.

As [Matt Levine points out](https://www.bloomberg.com/opinion/newsletters/2026-11-23/jensen-s-candor-is-satisfactory-now?accessToken=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzb3VyY2UiOiJTdWJzY3JpYmVyR2lmdGVkQXJ0aWNsZSIsImlhdCI6MTc5NTQ3NDYxNSwiZXhwIjoxNzk2MDc5NDE1LCJhcnRpY2xlSWQiOiJUT1lWVEtSMjRVODkwMCIsImJjb25uZWN0SWQiOiI5MjgxRkY1M0M2N0Q0Qzg5QUQxNUQyMDNGMjlEOEEyRiJ9.xJ5NMXrrwB70YTBP2MCG1blRaX5XHxD7S0fAVzCB7Vw), with the firing AND the rehiring by this board with involvement from the government, the investigators are now being put in a position of having had the outcome somewhat predetermined for them, because both have demonstrated that they did not need to wait for any further evidence to come to light.

**OpenAI put its pretraining loss curve on the record.** In [Perplexity and Intelligence](https://openai.com/index/perplexity-and-intelligence/), Chief scientist Jakub Pachocki plotted base-model log-perplexity back to GPT-3.5 (on their [internal held-out coding dataset](https://openai.com/index/perplexity-and-intelligence/#citation-top-3)… which has [notable caveats](https://x.com/ziv_ravid/status/2124685987402182737)):

[View post on X ↗](https://x.com/merettm/status/2124549218995949967)

Think of it as how surprised the model is by the next token on a held-out dataset. Lower is better. GPT-3.5 was around 0.99 and GPT-4 around 0.91. When OpenAI put a model around 0.76 (GPT6 Astra) to work on open math problems, [hundreds of frontier math problems started falling quickly](https://latent.space/p/ainews-quasi-riemann-hypothesis-openai/). Pachocki extrapolates that another jump in capabilities could come around 0.68–0.70.

This is all in context of [pacing the frontier](https://latent.space/p/ainews-fearing-rsi-openai-anthropic/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv). Pachocki proposes that labs agree on a first limit to development and spell out what would let them cross it, such as a successor to chain-of-thought monitoring. Microsoft’s [Mustafa Suleyman](https://x.com/mustafasuleyman/status/2124663594449318173) gave the first win by cosigning and joining in, running MAI-2 Base on OpenAI’s evaluation set and reporting 0.819. We’d need at least a couple more top labs to join this effort for it to gather steam as a real self-regulatory limit, most notably of course, Anthropic.

items.body: BackgroundDelirium occurs in up to 52% of cardiac and vascular surgeries and is associated with long-term cognitive impairment and death. Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a delirium risk factor. In rodents, AKI induces systemic endothelial activation and, when combined with surgery, results in greater neuroinflammation than surgery alone. We hypothesized that systemic endothelial activation and blood-brain barrier BBB disruption are more strongly associated with delirium that occurs concurrently with AKI.MethodsWe performed a prospective study of 150 adults undergoing cardiac and major vascular surgery. We quantified intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1) and E-selectin, biomarkers of endothelial activation, and ubiquitin carboxy-terminal hydrolase L1 (UCHL1), a biomarker of neuronal injury and BBB permeability, in plasma collected after surgery. Delirium was assessed using the CAM-ICU tool. KDIGO serum creatinine criteria were used to assess AKI.ResultsPatients with AKI-associated delirium and those with non-AKI-associated delirium had similar clinical characteristics, delirium risk factors, and postoperative sedation scores. In multivariable models, ICAM-1 was not associated with delirium overall (p = 0.29). However, AKI modified the association between ICAM-1 and postoperative delirium (p = 0.01 for interaction between AKI and ICAM-1) such that when the interaction term was introduced, the estimated ICAM-1 OR was 0.57 [95% CI 0.37–0.87], p = 0.01. In post-hoc analyses, higher ICAM-1 concentrations were associated with decreased odds of non-AKI-associated delirium (OR = 0.48 [95% CI 0.28–0.81], p = 0.01) and increased odds of AKI-associated delirium (OR = 1.69 [95% CI 1.05–2.74], p = 0.03). E-selectin was not associated with delirium. Higher UCHL1 concentrations were associated with an increased odds of AKI-associated delirium (OR = 3.68 [95% CI 2.05–6.62], p < 0.001), but not non-AKI-associated delirium (p = 0.33). This association between higher UCHL1 and a greater odds of AKI-associated delirium was potentiated by increased ICAM-1 endothelial activation (p = 0.046).ConclusionDelirium occurring concurrently with AKI may represent a biologically distinct phenotype. Recognition of biologic heterogeneity within delirium populations may help explain inconsistent associations reported for delirium risk factors and biomarkers. Accounting for this biological heterogeneity may improve the identification of delirium biomarkers and therapeutic targets and should be considered in future delirium research. Future multi-center studies with larger and more diverse cohorts and extended cognitive assessment protocols are needed to validate these observations.

items.body: Adult fibromyalgia (FM) is characterized by altered functional connectivity between sensory, salience, and default mode networks (DMN), yet its early emergence and hierarchical organization remain unclear in Juvenile Fibromyalgia (JFM). We used stepwise functional connectivity (SFC) to detect early changes in the hierarchical integration of sensory signals toward salience and heteromodal networks in adolescents with JFM. Additionally, we assessed whether these alterations overlap with FM-associated gene expression from the Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA). Forty-six adolescent females with JFM (16.44-1.11 years) and forty-three healthy females (16.09-1.06 years) completed clinical questionnaires and underwent resting-state fMRI. Whole-brain voxel-wise SFC mapped connectivity patterns from primary sensory regions (visual, somatosensory, auditory) toward the DMN across increasing link-step distances. Regression models examined associations between symptom severity and SFC measures. Spatial overlap between functional findings and FM-associated gene expression profiles was also evaluated. Both groups showed a similar pattern, progressing from primary to secondary sensory regions, then to multimodal integration and salience areas, and finally to heteromodal DMN cortices. Greater symptom severity was associated with reduced second-step connectivity between secondary somatosensory cortices and the right anterior insula/operculum (T=5.11, pFWE<0.05). The neuronal transcription factor MYT1L showed relatively higher expression in AHBA in an overlapping region including the pars opercularis. Large-scale sensory-to-heteromodal functional architecture appears preserved in JFM. However, patients with greater symptom burden show reduced propagation of somatosensory information toward salience-interoceptive regions, suggesting altered multimodal processing. This disruption spatially overlaps with MYT1L expression, pointing towards a developmentally sensitive circuit vulnerability in severe patients.

items.body:
Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries:

With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library. It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians.

Here's the digitized sketchbook.

Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work.

Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue? Mark thinks it will be mild:

But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don’t chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. Humanity is thus something of a requirement for the production of historical literature.

items.title: How to Touch the Nothingness Behind Everything: Kahlil Gibran on the Seven Selves
items.subtitle: A self is an illusion, and yet it is the place where we live, the costume the naked soul wears to survive in the world.
items.feedText: A self is a forest. A self is a ship. Above all, a self is a sum of selves, contextual as a chameleon, conflicted as a parliament. Which self takes the reins of our character and conduct at any given time is a function of which animating passion takes possession of us. But though we may be governed by different selves at different times, our task is to discover — and to heed — the higher, truer self that hovers above them all like the shadow of a mountain, impervious to the passing winds, holding up the sky of l…
items.body:
A self [is a forest](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/11/09/pando/). A self [is a ship](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/03/08/plutarch-the-ship-of-theseus-ted-ed/). A self [is an illusion](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/10/21/iris-murdoch-unselfing/), and yet it is the place where we live, the costume the naked soul wears to survive in the world.

Above all, a self is [a sum of selves](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/04/10/parts/), contextual as a chameleon, conflicted as a parliament. Which self takes the reins of our character and conduct at any given time is a function of which animating passion takes possession of us. But though we may be governed by different selves at different times, our task is to discover — and to heed — the higher, truer self that hovers above them all like the shadow of a mountain, impervious to the passing winds, holding up the sky of life.

[Kahlil Gibran](https://themarginalian.org/tag/kahlil-gibran) (January 6, 1883–April 10, 1931), who thought deeply about [the art of becoming yourself over the sweep of life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/04/04/youth-and-age-kahlil-gibran/), takes up this question in one of his signature parable-poems found in his 1918 classic [The Madman](http://www.amazon.com/Madman-His-Parables-Poems/dp/0486419118/?tag=braipick-20) ([public library](http://www.worldcat.org/title/madman-his-parables-and-poems/oclc/242642&referer=brief_results) | [free ebook](http://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/5616)).

The poem unfolds as a taxonomy of the core animating passions we live with and suffer by — sorrow, ecstasy, infatuation, hate, longing, creative possession — each a trap, a cage, a dooming fate the sufferer yearns to rebel against. Then comes the seventh self, seemingly the most pitiable, for it is the self that appears to live in pointlessness, perpetually facing the void, but in the end the freest: Only the empty self that lusts for nothing can touch the essence of everything. (Gibran would have appreciated [the Japanese concept of ma](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/09/07/ma/).)

Kahlil Gibran

> THE SEVEN SELVES
> by Kahlil Gibran
> In the stillest hour of the night, as I lay half asleep, my seven
> selves sat together and thus conversed in whisper:
> First Self: Here, in this madman, I have dwelt all these years,
> with naught to do but renew his pain by day and recreate his sorrow
> by night. I can bear my fate no longer, and now I rebel.
> Second Self: Yours is a better lot than mine, brother, for it is
> given to me to be this madman’s joyous self. I laugh his laughter
> and sing his happy hours, and with thrice winged feet I dance
> his brighter thoughts. It is I that would rebel against my weary
> existence.
> Third Self: And what of me, the love-ridden self, the flaming brand
> of wild passion and fantastic desires? It is I the love-sick self
> who would rebel against this madman.
> Fourth Self: I, amongst you all, am the most miserable, for naught
> was given me but odious hatred and destructive loathing. It is
> I, the tempest-like self, the one born in the black caves of Hell,
> who would protest against serving this madman.
> Fifth Self: Nay, it is I, the thinking self, the fanciful self,
> the self of hunger and thirst, the one doomed to wander without
> rest in search of unknown things and things not yet created; it is
> I, not you, who would rebel.
> Sixth Self: And I, the working self, the pitiful labourer, who,
> with patient hands, and longing eyes, fashion the days into images
> and give the formless elements new and eternal forms — it is I, the
> solitary one, who would rebel against this restless madman.
> Seventh Self: How strange that you all would rebel against this
> man, because each and every one of you has a preordained fate to
> fulfill. Ah! could I but be like one of you, a self with a determined
> lot! But I have none, I am the do-nothing self, the one who sits
> in the dumb, empty nowhere and nowhen, while you are busy re-creating
> life. Is it you or I, neighbours, who should rebel?
> When the seventh self thus spake the other six selves looked with
> pity upon him but said nothing more; and as the night grew deeper
> one after the other went to sleep enfolded with a new and happy
> submission.
> But the seventh self remained watching and gazing at nothingness,
> which is behind all things.

Couple with Gibran on [silence, solitude, and the courage to know yourself](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/11/21/kahlil-gibran-prophet-talking/), then revisit Hermann Hesse on [discovering the soul beneath the self](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/02/18/hesse-soul/).

### donating = loving

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing *The Marginalian* (which [bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/10/22/brain-pickings-becoming-the-marginalian/) for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a [donation](https://www.themarginalian.org/donate/). Your support makes all the difference.

### newsletter

*The Marginalian* has a free weekly newsletter. It comes out on Sundays and offers the week’s most inspiring reading. Here’s [what to expect](https://mailchi.mp/brainpickings/janna-levin-rebecca-elson-anne-lamott-james-gleick). Like? [Sign up.](https://www.themarginalian.org/newsletter/)

items.body:
In March of this year, a flurry of emails and text messages from a half dozen reporters around the world disrupted my quiet Saturday morning. An Iranian news agency had aired a week-old video of what appeared to be a U.S.-made Tomahawk missile hitting a school. News reports claimed that the strike killed more than 175 people, most of them children. The U.S. president and military denied responsibility. In the age of generative AI and all things deepfake, everyone—including me—was skeptical of the video’s authenticity.

I get this type of request a lot. For the past three decades, I’ve been developing mathematical and computational techniques to analyze and detect manipulation in digital media. Over this time, I think it’s fair to say that I, like most people, have approached visual recordings with a “presumption of authenticity”: If a skeptic claims that a recording is fake, the burden of proof is on them.

In today’s world of generative AI, however, I think we need to shift this stance to a “presumption of fake.” That is, the burden is now on the creator to prove that their content is real. While this new stance may seem unfair to legitimate creators, I think it both reflects reality and points to a future where we will once again be able to trust that most online media is what it appears to be.

The Forensic Approach to Deepfake Detection

Even last March, I was already tilting toward a presumption of fake. My initial response to the reporters was something along the lines of, “I am suspicious of the video because the quality is low, it emerged weeks after the bombing, and it is only being distributed by an Iranian news agency with a less-than-stellar record of accurate reporting.”

Given the potential implications—if the video was indeed real, however, I resigned myself to spending my Saturday morning analyzing it.

I first reasoned that if the Tomahawk missile was digitally added to each frame of the video without taking into consideration the camera motion, we might see a physically implausible missile path. So I aligned the video frames using a stationary background landmark as a reference. In the updated video, the missile did, in fact, move in a nearly linear trajectory. (See the yellow dots in the composite shown below.)

I next asked if the size (in pixels) of the missile in the video was plausible. Under some reasonable assumptions, I estimated that the missile in the video corresponded to a 6-meter Tomahawk at a distance of approximately 100 meters. The distance seemed plausible from the scene and was also consistent with the delay of 0.3 seconds from visible impact to the sound of impact, given that sound travels at 343 meters per second.

A composite photo composed of frames from a video of the Tomahawk strike reveals the missile’s trajectory.Hany Farid; Source: Mehr News

Despite the mounting evidence, though, I struggled to refine my answer for the reporters.

My skepticism was fueled by a recent study I worked on with colleagues at the University of California, Berkeley, that showed how hard it is to distinguish real from fake videos. Observers are now so suspicious of videos in general that they have trouble convincing themselves that a video is real.

But after a few more hours and a few more analyses with the missile video, I finally decided that it was authentic, and I gave the reporters my updated view.

This analysis marked a turning point for me. I realized I was just like the participants in our study: The lack of artifacts was not enough to readily convince me a video is real. I had flipped from a presumption of real to a presumption of fake.

Signaling a Video’s Provenance

When the visual record is no longer reliable, what can we do?

The types of forensic analyses that I routinely perform do not currently operate at internet scale and speed. But provenance signals can. These signals include content credentials and watermarks that are inserted or embedded at the time of creation or recording.

Credentials that follow the C2PA standard, for example, attach a cryptographically signed manifest to a photo or video at the moment of capture; this metadata records the device, the time and location of the recording, and any subsequent edits. Because the manifest is signed, any tampering with either the content or its history can be detected later by machine. Watermarks, like Google’s SynthID, embed an imperceptible signal directly into the pixels or audio samples that identifies the content’s origin.

Apple recently took these ideas a step further. On some of its newest iPhones, the camera sensor can cryptographically sign the raw pixel data as it’s captured. That signed data is then developed into a reference image saved alongside the normal, editable photo. Anyone can then compare the two and see exactly what, if anything, was changed.

These provenance signals are often criticized as being only a partial solution or vulnerable to attack. This is true if we think of them as mechanisms for catching bad actors. But that’s not what they’re supposed to do. Their purpose is to let good actors prove that their audiovisual recording is what it claims to be.

Provenance signals thus need not be adversary-proof. Instead, these signals are part of a new reality in which consumers, journalists, and the courts must adapt to a presumption of fakeness. If enough good actors adopt these mechanisms, they can begin to drown out bad actors. In other words, we have to switch from a model of “catch the bad actors” to “empower the good actors.”

Real-Time Verification

This switch from trust to distrust of digital media has expanded to include routine video calls.

In September 2024, for example, Senator Ben Cardin (D-Md.), then chair of the Foreign Relations Committee, received a video meeting request from Dmytro Kuleba, who until a few weeks earlier had been Ukraine’s foreign minister. During the call, Cardin became suspicious when, out of character, Kuleba pressed him on whether the U.S. should allow Ukraine to fire long-range missiles into Russia. Cardin ended the call. Later, the State Department confirmed that Kuleba had never requested the meeting, and the Senate security office warned staff that foreign adversaries, possibly Russian, would likely try similar faked meetings again.

All it takes to conduct this type of impersonation is a face swap or avatar deepfake, along with voice conversion, both of which substitute the speaker’s face and voice for deepfaked versions in real time. These technologies are readily available in commercial products and open-source libraries and run on nothing more powerful than a modern laptop.

This video illustrates the current state of face-swap deepfakes.

Farid’s Company GetReal Shows How Real Deepfake Videos Look Today

Your browser does not support the video tag.
Firms that verify provenance have to move fast to detect real-time deepfakes. Hany Farid, GetReal

items.title: IP-Tracking (z.B. von Youtube) mit dem Mobilnetz umgehen
items.subtitle: Viele nutzen einen VPN, um sich gegen IP-Tracking zu schützen.
items.feedText: Aber gerade Youtube, wo sehr umfangreichen Verhaltensdaten entstehen, funktioniert über VPNs oft nicht – vor allem, wenn man Videos über Drittanbieter-Apps, Downloadtools oder mit Werbeblocker schauen will. items.body:
Viele nutzen einen VPN, um sich gegen IP-Tracking zu schützen. Aber gerade Youtube, wo sehr umfangreichen Verhaltensdaten entstehen, funktioniert über VPNs oft nicht – vor allem, wenn man Videos über Drittanbieter-Apps, Downloadtools oder mit Werbeblocker schauen will. In diesem Artikel stelle ich einen einfachen und kostenlosen Trick vor, mit dem man statt VPN eine neue IP über das Smartphone bezieht. Über die recht neue App »[5G Proxy Pro](https://f-droid.org/en/packages/com.tokyoxpa3.androidproxy/)« kann man diese IP auch in einem einzelnen Browser oder per Kommandozeile am Desktopcomputer nutzen. Am Ende des Artikel liste ich dann noch Ideen auf, um dauerhaft einen 5G-Proxy für Youtube im Einsatz zu haben. Der Trick hilft natürlich auch bei anderen Schutzmaßnahmen, die einen VPN benötigten.

**Nicht für Einsteiger**: Dieser Artikel ist für Fortgeschrittene. Die Tipps sind Bastellösungen, die für manche Personen möglicherweise nützlich sind, um eine Alternative für einen IP-Wechsel zu kennen. Damit ist nicht immer automatisch mehr Datenschutz erreicht. Probleme wie DNS-Leaks oder unbemerkte IDs von Apps müssen beachtet werden.

Gut zu wissen

### Das Problem mit manchen alternative Frontends

Nicht alle alternativen Youtube-Frontends und Apps schützen vor IP-Tracking. Vor allem die bekannten Android-Apps NewPipe, PipePipe und LibreTube fragen die Daten direkt bei Youtube ab. Das kann man teilweise in den Einstellungen ändern, zum Beispiel bei LibreTube. Andere Projekte nutzen „Piped“-Instanzen, so dass die IP geschützt ist. Aber wenn Piped-Adressen über das Terminal genutzt werden, können sie ebenfalls direkte Youtube-Verbindungen herstellen. Das Setup also besser einmal mit PCAPdroid oder einem Netzwerk-Sniffer oder über die DNS-Abfragen prüfen.

## 1. Warum man sich gegen IP-Tracking schützen sollte

Viele Websites geben deine IP-Adresse an Werbefirmen weiter, die dann Verhaltensdaten für einen Haushalt ganz ohne Cookies speichern können. Ausführlich habe ich das 2024 in diesem Artikel beschrieben: [IP-Haushaltstracking bei Google und Drittanbietern](https://www.kuketz-blog.de/ip-haushaltstracking-bei-google-und-drittanbietern-was-es-ist-und-wie-man-sich-schuetzt/). Wenn du Glück hast, wird das IP-Tracking über eingebundene Drittanbieter ausgeführt, die man mit einem klassischen Werbeblocker deaktivieren kann. So ist das beispielsweise bei Spiegel Online mit Einwilligung. Bei großen Plattformen wie Youtube passiert das aber serverseitig und man kann es nicht blocken. Die Technik wurde bis 2024 von Google auch ohne Einwilligung eingesetzt. Daher ist grundsätzlich Misstrauen angebracht, ob Google sich beim Haushaltstracking an die DSGVO hält.

Gut zu wissen

### Grundidee: Google/Youtube und andere IP-Tracker nur über eine zweite IP nutzen

Im Idealfall eines perfekt geschützten Haushalts könnte man das IP-Tracking durch Google, Shops oder Nachrichtenseiten einfach ignorieren: Man bekäme über Nacht eine neue IP-Adresse, eventuell erzwungen mit einer Zeitschaltuhr am Router beziehungsweise dem Flugmodus über Nacht am Smartphone. Wenn man alles perfekt konfiguriert hat, kann Google die Aufrufe aus dem Haushalt nur für jeden Tag zusammenknüpfen, nicht aber für einen längeren Zeitraum. Voraussetzung dafür wäre:

- Kein Browser im Haushalt speichert Cookies von Google
- Keine Apps im Haushalt senden eindeutige Installations-IDs an Google Firebase
- Keine smarten Geräte wie Fernseher senden IDs an Google
- Im ganzen Haushalt werden keine Websites, Apps oder Geräte mit Drittanbieter-Logins betrieben, die Anmeldeinformationen an Identitätsprovider weitergeben, beispielsweise über Zalando oder einen Cloudanbieter.

Da dieses Szenario aber im Alltag und mit mehreren Haushaltsmitgliedern sehr schwer oder gar nicht zu erreichen ist, besteht die Grundidee von VPN oder Proxy als Trackingschutz darin, gezielt problematische Seiten – also vor allem werbefinanzierte Seiten mit spezifischen Interessensdaten wie Youtube, aber auch Nachrichtenseiten, bei denen man eine Einwilligung geben muss – über eine zweite IP zu leiten. So minimiert man zusätzlich zum Werbeblocker das Risiko, dass sehr viele problematische Verhaltens- und Interessensdaten langfristig in einem Haushaltsprofil gesammelt werden. Das IP-Tracking wird also nicht verhindert, sondern abgetrennt.

## 2. Spontane Variante: Flugmodus-Trick mit googlefreiem Smartphone

Wer GrapheneOS oder ein ähnliches googlefreies Android installiert hat, hat gegenüber Stock-Androids den Vorteil, dass weder ein Google-Login noch eine Werbe-ID mit dem Smartphone verknüpft ist. Wenn man nun Wifi deaktiviert und dann einmal den Flugmodus an- und wieder ausschaltet, bekommt das Smartphone vom Mobilfunkprovider üblicherweise eine neue IP-Adresse. Das muss nicht sein, daher sollte man es zunächst testen: Einfach vor und nach der Neuverbindung eine der vielen IP-Serviceseiten aufrufen – leicht zu merken ist [ip.me](https://ip.me/) von Proton, werbefrei dafür [stat.ripe.net](https://stat.ripe.net) von der europäischen Internetregistry). Wenn ein solcher IP-Wechsel stattfindet, hat Google ein wichtiges Merkmal weniger, um die Youtube-Nutzung mit den vorherigen Aufrufen auf dem Smartphone zusammenzuführen. Vor allem wenn man trackingfreie Drittanbieter-Apps wie Newpipe oder einen Privatsphäre-Browser auf dem Smartphone nutzt, ist man so gegenüber den wichtigsten branchenüblichen Trackingmethoden geschützt.

Wenn man für diesen Trick ein eigenes **Profil** anlegt, hat man zwar einen etwas besseren Schutz, weil andere Apps oder Websites nicht versehentlich gestartet werden können.

Aber was viele nicht wissen: Apps, die im Eigentümer-Profil im Hintergrund laufen dürfen oder die anderweitig vom System aktiviert werden können (beispielsweise Signals Verbindungen zu Amazon AWS), **laufen auch bei einem Profilwechsel im Hintergrund weiter**. Also auch wenn beispielsweise Signal nicht im Zweitprofil installiert ist, laufen die Verbindungen aus dem Eigentümerprofil weiter. Andersherum ist das nicht der Fall: Die Apps aus Nebenprofilen laufen nicht weiter, wenn man zum Eigentümerprofil zurückwechselt. Daher nutze ich für mein Setup RethinkDNS, um vor dem Wechsel alle Apps im Eigentümerprofil abzuschalten, bevor man wechselt.

Das will man verhindern: Diese Netzwerkverbindungen öffnet mein Android, obwohl ich ins Zweitprofil gewechselt bin, in dem diese Apps nicht installiert sind. Sichtbar wird das nur mit einem externen Sniffer, den ich auf meinem Router laufen lasse. Die Datenverbindungen zu Signal sind im Eigentümerprofil weiter aktiv. Außerdem stelle ich fest, dass die Gopro-App aus dem Eigentümerprofil aktiv ist, obwohl sie dort keine Hintergrundrechte hat. Google Firebase erhält hier vermutlich eindeutige Installations-IDs. Eben weil es so viele Möglichkeiten gibt, wie Google eine dauerhafte ID aus dem Haushalt erhält, empfehle ich das umständliche Vorgehen mit einer extra IP, einem Zweitprofil und RethinkDNS im Eigentümerprofil.

items.title: What Happens When Elders Share Their Stories
items.subtitle: When I moved from the San Francisco Bay Area to a small, rural town in Vermont, I wanted to find a way to contribute to the local community.

items.body:
When I moved from the San Francisco Bay Area to a small, rural town in Vermont, I wanted to find a way to contribute to the local community. Knowing there was a significant senior population here, I reached out to the town librarian with hopes of helping elders share their stories.

The local historical society took interest in this idea, which led to an exhibit at the 159-year-old Tunbridge World’s Fair, and a book series entitled *Folk Life: Tunbridge Oral Histories*. The first two print runs sold out. The second collection of stories has just been published, and people are already asking who will be featured in the third.

What is it about life stories that strikes such a universal chord? And why is it important—and even imperative—to share our stories with others? I interviewed oral historians, teachers, and a digital storyteller to discover more about why the age-old tradition of recording oral histories continues to make such a significant impact for individuals and communities.

## Fostering connections and reflection

Storytelling is, according to scientific research, a biological shortcut to human connection. [Uri Hasson](https://blog.ted.com/what-happens-in-the-brain-when-we-hear-stories-uri-hasson-at-ted2016/) and fellow researchers at Princeton University discovered that the brains of the storyteller and listener physically sync up while a story is being told, promoting social connection, trust, and empathy.

The more emotionally affecting the story is, the stronger this connection becomes. As emotions and tension rise, hormones are released, including oxytocin, the “bonding hormone”; dopamine, which sharpens focus; and cortisol, which promotes attention and alertness as conflicts in the story arise. These hormonal responses enhance both the listener’s memory and connection to the storyteller.

For Erin Barnaby, a digital storyteller and 11th-generation Tunbridge native, oral histories create a connection not only to people, but also time and place. “My dad recently sold his house to my uncle, a house that he built on land that my grandfather had given to him. I love to hear him tell stories about the shifting of the land, from sheep farms to dairy farms and the shift from open pastures to forests.”

Even when the subject matter might not be instantly relatable, the process of listening to another’s stories still creates a profound interpersonal connection. Esther Ehrlich, who worked at [UC Berkeley’s Oral History Center](https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/visit/bancroft/oral-history-center) for six years before launching an oral history business of her own, experienced this sense of connection firsthand:

> I was assigned an interview with a former medical malpractice insurance guy, which initially didn’t interest me at all. And then lo and behold, after interviewing this man, I found him absolutely fascinating. What I came to discover was that by the time we were done, or even partway in, I came to love every single person I interviewed. I would feel connected to them and them to me.

## Providing unique perspectives

From that biological and psychological basis, oral histories make a critical social contribution.

According to the [Oral History Association](https://oralhistory.org/), “oral history is the oldest type of historical inquiry, stemming from the oral traditions of myriad cultures across the globe, predating even the written word.” These personal stories expand upon the narratives of history books, allowing people from varied walks of life to share their unfiltered experiences and perspectives. Indeed, many works by trained historians rely on oral histories.

The founders of [Voice of Witness](https://voiceofwitness.org/), a nonprofit dedicated to advancing human rights by amplifying unheard voices, believe that oral history “can democratize history, contribute to narrative change, and illuminate issues and events in a profoundly powerful way.” Enabling individuals to safely share their stories opens people’s minds to fresh perspectives and vantage points.

While oral histories are limited to an individuals’ memories and are by nature subjective, they remain incredibly valuable in their ability to paint a portrait of time and place. Plus, their narrative-driven format brings history to life in a more memorable way than date- and fact-focused textbooks.

Helen Marks, a former history teacher who has spoken to thousands of students about her experience as a hidden child in Belgium during World War II, has observed that when a person shares their stories, it brings that part of history to life:

> I am among the few surviving hidden children who are willing and able to talk about their experiences in the Holocaust. Reading numbers on a page does not create the same impact as someone standing or sitting in front of you describing a moment that was frightening or was so foreign they didn’t know what to do.... I think that when you connect a face, no matter what the face looks like, you get a wholly different reaction than when you read a page full of facts.

## Leaving a legacy

Throughout the interviews I conducted for *Folk Life*, the importance of leaving a meaningful legacy was a common theme. “That’s the reason we share our stories,” says Marsha Higgins, a history teacher for nearly 40 years. “It makes us feel like we matter.”

Higgins taught students to create personal narratives from a young age. Decades later, former students still express their thanks for her guidance in teaching them the importance of recording their experiences.

“I encouraged students to write down things that happened to them. It’s helpful to know at the time, you’re creating chapters in your life, that your story is just as interesting as anybody else’s.”

Like Marks, Higgins grew up around immigrants from Europe. “And they all had stories,” she says. “Whenever we got together, somebody would tell me a story. How do you make conversation without one? It’s just so much a part of who we are.”

“I think everyone wants to know that they have made a positive difference,” says Marks. “That they did some good, that their being here wasn’t just a fleeting moment of nothingness, but that they contributed something. They reacted to something. They gave something. So when you tell stories, that’s where you learn about people and what they value.”

## Gaining newfound awareness

Neal Allen, a coach and author (most recently of *Good Writing: 36 Ways to Improve Your Sentences* with his wife Anne Lamott), spent several years as a hospice volunteer. During that time, he helped a number of people share and record their stories.

“Every week I had one or two clients who were dying, and I spent time fluffing their pillows, listening to their stories and how they approach death. The funny thing is we were always asked, ‘Oh, isn’t that hard?’ It was quite the opposite. It was really quite extraordinary.”

…

items.body:
While my husband kept his eye on the light plastic kickball wavering indecisively in the air above, his arms upraised to catch it for the out, his feet scuttled side-to-side on the bumpy field, as he tried to position himself perfectly. It was his birthday, and we were playing a celebratory game with our extended family at his parents’ house an hour away from ours. After triumphantly catching the ball, he collapsed abruptly to the ground and, when we rushed over, he immediately told me to take him to the ER because he knew a bone had broken. I hate to admit that one of the first things I looked at—silently, selfishly—was which leg was hurt.

Right leg. Driving leg. At that moment, I knew that I was in for what my therapist friend would later call a “growth opportunity.”

Up until that point, my husband had done all of the driving for our family of four, us and our 13-year-old twins; I pinch-hit only when he went out of town. Living previously in Beijing, Brooklyn, and then downtown Boston had obviated most any need to drive, and my skills were basic anyhow, as my immigrant parents had severely limited my mobility as a suburban teenager. In the decade since moving to Cambridge and buying a car, my slight fear of being behind the wheel had deepened into a full-on phobia. The road seemed increasingly like a slippery sheet of ice, unpredictable and dangerous, and I clung to public transit, which is better in Boston than in most American cities though far from comprehensive.

I had always maintained that being terrified to drive in greater Boston was a rational response. Based on accident statistics, Allstate has ranked Boston as America’s worst city for drivers for eleven straight years. There is the running of red lights, the “banging” of “ueys,” the weaving through former-cow-path streets, the traffic jams, the rush hour daredevilry, the cutting off, the honking, the flicking off, the jaywalking, the lawless bicycling, the urgency, the rage, the tailgating. Indeed, it was this last behavior that set me off more than any other. I can picture it now: the heat in my rearview mirror, the voice inside my head that said, *You’re going too fuckin’ slow, you’re a pathetic driver, you need to get out of my way and off the road, you don’t deserve to be here—oh look, an Asian woman, of course.*

Unfortunately, the porous emotional boundaries that had served me well to date as a writer were terrible for a driver. Every time I got behind the wheel, I felt squeezed by the time-is-money capitalist python and crushed down by the country’s sexism and racism; the entire experience of being seen, judged, and honked at was psychologically harrowing. My cringing fear translated into a self-abasing timidity, and I let every single person who wanted to cut in front of me cut. Flash, flash; flash, flash.

After the ER trip that put my husband’s broken fibula in a temporary cast, I managed to pilot the car the hour home on the highway. After his surgery, he was ordered to keep weight off the foot for at least a month, and I prepared to take over the driving. Weekend drum and tennis lessons, weeknight capoeira lessons. I was finally going to learn to drive in Boston.

My instinct on my first drive was to flick loving-kindness at all the other drivers around me as I drove. *May you be happy—and you—and you—and you—and you.* This was a practice I’ve had on and off for the past two decades, ever since I sat my first weeklong silent retreat at the Insight Meditation Society, a loving-kindness focused program led by vipassana teacher Michele McDonald, who counseled us to take a light approach. If you’re sitting on the subway, you can just flick [metta](https://tricycle.org/magazine/metta-practice/) quickly at people, one by one, she said. You don’t have to make it something big and serious. I was living in New York at the time, and it was easy to feel barricaded or hostile or shrunken, especially when crammed into the tin can of the subway with strangers, and flicking loving-kindness at fellow riders shifted something in me—it expanded me, softened me, softened the space between me and others, woke me to the present. When I did the same while driving, it worked similarly, creating a radiant force field through which all the cars moved and related to one another. I could impute positive intentions to drivers I’d read earlier as only erratic, selfish, or terrifying. Even when confronted with impatience and rage, through the practice I learned that those feelings did not have to become mine. Each time I drove, my mind grew quieter.

Of all of the categories of people one can send loving-kindness to (self, benefactor, friend, neutral, difficult), I’ve always found the self the hardest, or at least I’ve found it hard to receive my own good intentions, but in this time of forced growth, I had to try. I returned to the [Metta Bhavana](https://dharmaseed.org/talks/3512/): *May I be safe, may I be peaceful.* In this mindset, when I had to make a turn, I realized that I didn’t have to peel out in front of oncoming traffic in a death-defying manner, no matter what the person behind me insisted. I could simply wait until there was a gap in traffic or someone let me go. And they did. There’s actually a lot of kindness out on the roads, in moments people do seem to understand that we’re suffering through this abominable system together and a little kindness can shift the whole system. These kindnesses, and my own, enabled me to enter the slipstream of humanity as an equal. Before, I used to flash my lights, urging others to turn out of terror, but slowly and through practice, I began to do it mainly to be part of the web of the road. I’ve become more confident about driving exactly how I want; after all, these roads are my roads too. And I admit that on some days I do hit the gas instead of flashing my lights because there are places I need to get to on time too.

…

items.body:
*A trained car mechanic who plays 150 BPM trance in a shirt and tie, and checks his tracks by dancing around his room. Meet Davyboi*.

In recent years, trance and its faster, more euphoric relatives have found a new generation of dancers across Europe. Among the DJs who have built a following on the back of that revival is Davyboi, a Munich-based DJ and producer with Polish roots. His sets usually sit between 148 and 155 BPM and draw on trance, eurodance, and hard house in equal measure.

Going out in a city where hard techno dominated, he wanted more melody and uplift than most nights offered, so he began playing the records he wanted to hear himself. That approach, delivered in his trademark shirt and tie, has since taken him to Gotec, Rotterdam Rave, and Into The Woods Festival.

We asked him to introduce himself for Introducing, our series on up-and-coming producers and DJs, many of whom have gone on to much bigger things.

## Who are you?

I’m Davyboi, a DJ and producer. I love fast music, big melodies and dancing just as much as the people in front of me. You’ll usually find me behind the decks wearing a shirt and tie.

## Where are you from?

I’m from Munich, Germany, with Polish roots.

## What do you sound like?

Mostly trance and eurodance, but I also love groove, gabber and makina. It’s fast and energetic, with plenty of melodies and vocals. I want people to dance, sing along and have a good time together.

"Your problems are someone else’s dreams"

## Why should we follow what you’re doing?

If you love dancing and getting a bit carried away with your friends, I think we’ll get along. That’s what I enjoy most about a night out, and it’s the feeling I want to share when I play. I’ve also got plenty of new music on the way that I’m excited for people to hear.

## Which of your tracks sums you up? Why?

“Discotheque,” my collaboration with Mika Heggemann. It’s a good introduction to the energy I like bringing to my sets. When I make music, I always ask myself whether I’d enjoy dancing to it if someone else played it. That’s a big part of why I chose this one.

## What have you got coming out in the near future?

My remix of BUNT.’s “I Need You” is coming, and I’ve been busy working on more tracks. There are a lot of ideas I’m excited about, but I want to give each release a little time before moving on to the next.

[quote align=right text="I don’t really feel like I’ve had to give anything up completely."]

## Who or what is your biggest influence, and why?

A lot of it comes from being on the dancefloor myself. Some nights really stay with you, especially when a DJ plays something you weren’t expecting, and it completely changes your mood. I still think about those experiences when I’m choosing music. I know how much a good night can mean to someone.

## How did you get into DJing OR producing to begin with?

I was going out a lot in Munich, where hard techno was very present. I enjoyed the energy, but I wanted to hear more melodies and uplifting tracks too. Eventually, I started putting together the kind of music I wanted to hear on a night out. Coming from the crowd still influences how I play today.

## What are three things on your studio shopping list?

A monitor, a height-adjustable desk and [Nexus](https://refx.com/nexus/) to use in [Ableton](https://www.ableton.com/shop/live/?affiliate=F4nlA735). A few things to make working on music a bit more comfortable and give me some new sounds to play with.

### Who or what have you sacrificed for your art?

I don’t really feel like I’ve had to give anything up completely. It’s more that fitting everything in has become harder. Seeing my friends in Munich takes more planning now that I’m away so often. I still want to make time for them, even when things get busy.

## What’s been your favourite place to play so far?

[Thuishaven](https://thuishaven.nl/) is a favourite. I really love playing for Dutch crowds, and that’s a place I’m always happy to come back to.

## Where can we hear your music?

Mostly on [SoundCloud](https://soundcloud.com/davyboii), where you can find my tracks and mixes. My releases are also on Spotify, Apple Music and the other usual platforms.

## What one song would feature on the soundtrack to your life?

“Tokyo Drift” by Teriyaki Boyz. I trained as a car mechanic and got into tuning cars quite early. That song reminds me of that time, which I look back on really fondly. It always puts me in a good mood.

## What motivates you?

Knowing that people have made an effort to come and see me. Some bring their friends, some travel quite far, and some have been looking forward to that night for a while. I really appreciate that. Seeing them enjoy themselves makes me want to keep improving and give them a reason to come back.

## Tell us an interesting fact about yourself.

I get up and dance to my tracks after working on them. It helps me hear things differently. Sometimes a section seems fine while I’m sitting at the laptop, but when I’m moving to it, I realise it goes on too long. So dancing around my room is actually part of the process.

## Complete this sentence: At heart I’m just a…

…raver who ended up behind the decks.

## What’s the best bit of advice you’ve received?

“Your problems are someone else’s dreams.” I take it as a reminder to appreciate what I get to do. It helps me keep some perspective.

## Where will you be in five years’ time?

I’d love to reach more people with my music and make something that means something to them, whether it helps them through a difficult day or becomes a song they share with their friends. Knowing that something I made could become a small part of someone’s life would mean a lot to me.

**Davyboi and DJ Cringey "Naughty" is out now. [Listen on Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/track/67MB3IlBzSxG6Q9SGh7qXF?si=3fcc2aea3dfb4851). Buy on Bandcamp.**

**Find Davyboi on [Instagram.](https://www.instagram.com/iamdavyboi/?hl=en)**

**Don’t have Ableton Live? Buy it [↗ ableton.com](https://www.ableton.com/shop/live/?affiliate=F4nlA735). Heads up, it’s an affiliate link. If you buy through them, we may earn a small commission (it doesn’t affect the price).**
