items.title: Wenn Wissenschaftskommunikation zur Sicherheitsfrage wird
items.subtitle: Neue Technologien können Sicherheitsrisiken bergen, zugleich werden ihre Gefahren mitunter überschätzt.
items.feedText: Elisabeth Waczek vom Peace Research Institute Frankfurt (PRIF) erklärt, wie Wissenschaftskommunikation zu einer differenzierten Debatte über sicherheitsrelevante Forschung beitragen kann. Elisabeth Waczek ist studierte Philosophin und Referentin für Wissenstransfer am PRIF – Leibniz-Institut für Friedens- und Konfliktforschung. Einer ihrer Schwerpunkte liegt in der Wissenschaftskommunikation des Clusters Natur- und Technikwissenschaftliche Rüstungskontrollforschung (CNTR), an der Schnittstelle von Technologie un…
items.body:
Neue Technologien können Sicherheitsrisiken bergen, zugleich werden ihre Gefahren mitunter überschätzt. Elisabeth Waczek vom Peace Research Institute Frankfurt (PRIF) erklärt, wie Wissenschaftskommunikation zu einer differenzierten Debatte über sicherheitsrelevante Forschung beitragen kann.

**Elisabeth Waczek** ist studierte Philosophin und Referentin für Wissenstransfer am PRIF – Leibniz-Institut für Friedens- und Konfliktforschung. Einer ihrer Schwerpunkte liegt in der Wissenschaftskommunikation des [Clusters Natur- und Technikwissenschaftliche Rüstungskontrollforschung (CNTR)](https://www.prif.org/forschung/cntr), an der Schnittstelle von Technologie und Sicherheit.

**Seit dem russischen Angriff auf die Ukraine wird deutlich intensiver über Sicherheit und militärische Technologien diskutiert. Spüren Sie seit der Gründung Ihres Forschungsclusters 2023 ein wachsendes Interesse an Ihrer Arbeit?**

Wir spüren definitiv ein wachsendes Interesse.

Unser Fokus liegt auf Rüstungskontrolle im weiteren Sinne. Wir beschäftigen uns mit der Schnittstelle von Technologie und Sicherheit. Zu Beginn habe ich es als eine deutlich größere Herausforderung wahrgenommen, die Relevanz dessen zu erklären. Mittlerweile merke ich: Das haben viele Leute auf dem Schirm. Diese Themen sind stark ins Bewusstsein gerückt. Viele Leute in Europa haben nun das Gefühl, wir müssen uns wieder stärker mit dem Thema Sicherheit auseinandersetzen.

**Ihr Forschungscluster beschäftigt sich mit Technologien, die bestehende Machtverhältnisse verändern könnten. Woran erkennen Sie, dass eine technologische Entwicklung über die Fachcommunity hinaus sicherheitspolitisch relevant wird?**

Unsere Mitarbeitenden aus den Sozialwissenschaften und aus den Natur- und Technikwissenschaften kommen gemeinsam zu einer Einschätzung: Ist das eine Entwicklung, die disruptives Potenzial hat?

Konkret bedeutet das zum Beispiel: Lassen sich neue Technologien oder Forschungsergebnisse missbrauchen, um Waffen herzustellen? Welche Akteur*innen könnten Zugang bekommen, die ihn zuvor nicht hatten? Reicht bestehende Regulierung noch aus, um schädliche – vielleicht auch unbeabsichtigte – Folgen zu minimieren? Gefährlich wird es zum Beispiel, wenn Technologie die Dynamiken so stark beschleunigt, dass deeskalierende Instrumente wie die Rüstungskontrolle nicht mehr Schritt halten können, oder wenn sich nicht mehr feststellen lässt, woher eine Bedrohung kommt.

Interessanterweise kommen unsere Wissenschaftler*innen auch immer wieder zu der Einschätzung, dass dieses disruptive Potenzial gar nicht so dramatisch ist. Oft geht dem viel Hype voraus und besonders reißerische, aber vielleicht eher unwahrscheinliche Szenarien bekommen viel Aufmerksamkeit. Beim Thema KI zum Beispiel. Da ist es Aufgabe der Wissenschaft, erst einmal einen nüchterneren Blick einzunehmen und zu schauen: Wie gefährlich ist das denn wirklich? Welche Anwendungen haben das größte Potenzial negativer Auswirkungen und wo liegen womöglich auch Chancen? Am Ende kommt oft so etwas dabei raus wie: Ja, man muss das Thema ernst nehmen, aber man sollte nicht in Panik verfallen.

**Wenn Sie sich etwas für die gesellschaftliche Debatte über sicherheitsrelevante Forschung wünschen könnten: Was sollte die Öffentlichkeit aus Ihrer Sicht besser verstehen, um einen informierten Umgang mit diesen Themen zu ermöglichen?**

### Cluster Natur- und Technikwissenschaftliche Rüstungskontrollforschung (CNTR)

Das CNTR am PRIF untersucht, wie neue Technologien und wissenschaftliche Entwicklungen die internationale Sicherheit beeinflussen. Forschende aus verschiedenen Disziplinen analysieren mögliche Risiken und Chancen technologischer Innovationen und entwickeln Empfehlungen, um die internationale Rüstungskontrolle zu stärken.

Ein Beispiel: Ich war auf einer Tagung, bei der die Sprache auf das Thema Dual-Use-Forschung kam. Das sind Forschung oder Technologien, die legitime zivile Anwendungen haben, aber auch in militärischer Weise gebraucht oder in illegitimer Weise missbraucht werden können.

Auf dieser Tagung hat jemand gesagt: „Ist doch ganz klar, Dual-Use-Forschung sollten wir einfach nicht machen.“ Das ist ein häufiges Missverständnis. Mittlerweile haben so viele Forschungsbereiche einen Dual-Use-Charakter, etwa große Teile der Informatik oder Medizin. In der Kommunikation tragen wir die Verantwortung, zu sagen: Nur weil eine Forschung Sicherheitsrisiken in sich trägt, ist diese Forschung nicht automatisch schlecht oder illegitim. Sie kann trotzdem wichtig sein.

Auch bei der Diskussion um Zivilklauseln, die in den letzten Jahren ziemlich intensiv geführt wurde, ist es wichtig, sich vor Augen zu führen, welche Funktion solche Instrumente überhaupt haben. Natürlich ist die Wissenschaftsfreiheit im Grundgesetz verankert. Genauso ist im Grundgesetz verankert, dass man als Forschende*r nicht einfach Massenvernichtungswaffen entwickeln kann. Interessant sind vor allem die Graubereiche, in denen Forschende viel Eigenverantwortung tragen müssen.

Es ist wichtig, dass Forschende mit dieser Verantwortung durch institutionelle Strukturen unterstützt werden. In der Wissenschaftskommunikation tragen wir dazu bei, das Bewusstsein für diese Themen zu schärfen.

**Wie gelingt es, im Diskurs um sicherheitsrelevante Forschung berechtigte Sorgen zu adressieren, ohne zu dramatisieren oder zu verharmlosen?**

Es ist wichtig zu beobachten, mit welchen Vokabeln und Bildsprache der Diskurs stattfindet, und das immer wieder kritisch zu reflektieren. Wir versuchen generell, Darstellungen, die als kriegs- oder gewaltbejahend empfunden werden können, zu vermeiden, ebenso martialische Bildsprache.

Wenn man Kommunikation als Handwerk lernt, bekommt man bestimmte Best Practices mit: wie Menschen Informationen aufnehmen und wie man Gehör findet. Dazu gehören Mittel wie: klare Botschaften, starke Verben, einfache Sätze, die im Gedächtnis bleiben. Wir müssen uns im Wettbewerb um Aufmerksamkeit gegen eine Flut an Desinformationen durchsetzen und brauchen diese Techniken. Aber gleichzeitig entziehen sich wissenschaftliche Inhalte durch die gebotene Nuancierung oft diesen Best-Practice-Leitlinien.

Diese grundlegende Spannung, die man in der Wissenschaftskommunikation immer hat, verstärkt sich im Umfeld sicherheitsrelevanter Forschung noch einmal mehr.

### „Die Kommunikation sicherheitsrelevanter Themen hat jedoch selbst eine sicherheitsrelevante Komponente“

Elisabeth Waczek

**Ihr Forschungscluster vereint naturwissenschaftliche und sozialwissenschaftliche Perspektiven. Wie wirkt sich dieser interdisziplinäre Ansatz auf die Art und Weise, wie Sie Forschungsergebnisse kommunizieren, aus?**

Eine spannende Alltagsbeobachtung für die Wissenschaftskommunikation ist, dass Menschen verschiedene Disziplinen unterschiedlich wahrnehmen. Bei manchen Disziplinen erkennen sie die erforderliche Fachexpertise leichter, bei anderen haben sie das Gefühl, jede*r könne mitreden.

…

items.title: How To Get A Friend To Leave An Abusive Relationship
items.subtitle: How do you get a friend to leave an abusive relationship?
items.feedText: If you talk to people who work at women's shelters, they will tell you, but there is something resigned about the way they do it: they know that it's too difficult an ask. Those who can do it reliably are often people who are unlucky enough to have had first-hand experience as victims. The instructions have anti-memetic properties: no one is thrilled by them, so you can't really propagate them without killing the vibe. If that wasn't enough, if you convey it with insufficient skill it is easy to come across as v…
items.body:
How do you get a friend to leave an abusive relationship? If you talk to people who work at women's shelters, they will tell you, but there is something resigned about the way they do it: they know that it's too difficult an ask. Those who can do it reliably are often people who are unlucky enough to have had first-hand experience as victims.

The instructions have anti-memetic properties: no one is thrilled by them, so you can't really propagate them without killing the vibe. If that wasn't enough, if you convey it with insufficient skill it is easy to come across as victim-blaming battered women[1], so it is wiser to avoid the subject matter altogether.

If you are interested, though, here's what they'll tell you:

You make it known to your friend early on that you dislike some aspects of the relationship, of their abuser. After that, you support them and all their choices without reservation. You make it clear that you care about them no matter what, and you will be there for them whenever they need you to be. You do not antagonize or bad-mouth their abuser.

This is what your friend is experiencing, while being in an abusive relationship:

They value the relationship that they have with their abuser. They may be in deep, deep love with their abuser. Their abuser may be giving them something that they cannot access otherwise (or believe that they cannot access otherwise), that they find precious.

They will know that elements of their relationship with the abuser are shameful. They will instinctively take pains to hide the worst of it from people; they know that there are some things that happen inside the relationship that they can't disclose to anyone else. But because their relationship is such a big part of their life, this cashes out to not being able to talk about a large portion of their life to anyone.

Many of their loved ones are going to repeatedly and loudly express concern about their well-being. The strident objections to a relationship that is so important and meaningful to your friend is going to make them feel tense and guarded and defensive, and they might choose to start freezing out those relationships rather than trying to manage them.

The abuser might also discourage them from seeing the people who disapprove, but the above dynamics will have already done much of the work. Their relationships with other people will fray, and they will become increasingly isolated.

Your friend will make choices that don't make a lot of sense to you. They will make poor choices. Some frame this as the victim being in "survival mode"; the need to do things that only make sense in the context of surviving one more day, one more hour. They might be scared, stressed, sleep-deprived, in an actively adversarial information environment. When you are being supportive, you will often feel like an enabler. You will feel deeply shitty about this.

If you are lucky, at some point they will realize that their relationship is untenable, and then you can begin the process of helping them leave. This process is going to be equally frustrating, or perhaps more so. They are going to have the weirdest hangups and priorities. You will help them get everything in place, and then they will lose their nerve and cancel on you once, twice, multiple times, lose you the rent deposit you fronted; tell you that they changed their mind, things aren't actually that bad, leaving is too complicated, they'll never find anyone else as good. You can't get mad at them when they do that. You have to let them go back to their abuser after getting so so close to being free, and say "okie that's totally fine, are we still on for brunch next week?

Corroborating sources:

the hotline on supporting someone who keeps returning to an abusive relationship

loveisrespect on helping a friend

woman's trust uk on what to do if you're worried about someone

the network/la red on how to help a friend

safelives on supporting friends and family

stop relationship abuse on how to help a friend

^

It is not the case that only women can be victims of abuse, but this is the image that comes to mind for most.

Discuss

items.title: AI people are very, very, very, very rich
items.subtitle: As you may have heard, Anthropic had its IPO this past Thursday.
items.feedText: At a valuation of $1.5 trillion, it was actually just the second most valuable IPO in history, just behind SpaceX at $1.77 trillion. I bought some shares on the first day at what I thought was a reasonable price, only to see my shares drop the following day as the company’s valuation fell to $1.175 trillion, making it only the 14th most valuable company in the world. Such are the risks of buying individual stocks! But that price drop doesn’t change the fact that Anthropic’s IPO was a staggeringly large wealth cr…
items.body:
As you may have heard, Anthropic had its IPO this past Thursday. At a valuation of $1.5 trillion, it was actually just the second most valuable IPO in history, just behind SpaceX at $1.77 trillion. I bought some shares on the first day at what I thought was a reasonable price, only to see my shares drop the following day as the company’s valuation fell to $1.175 trillion, making it only [the 14th most valuable company](https://companiesmarketcap.com/) in the world. Such are the risks of buying individual stocks!

But that price drop doesn’t change the fact that Anthropic’s IPO was a staggeringly large wealth creation event. Anthropic began hiring lots of employees just a few years ago; now, almost all of those people have either hundreds of millions of dollars, or tens of millions of dollars. Andrew Benson had a good breakdown of exactly who would get what, if the company hit its initial valuation target of $2 trillion:

> Who actually gets rich if Anthropic lists at $2 trillion?…
> - $199B for the 7 controlling co-founders, about 10%
> - $28B for Ben Mann, if his stake matches theirs
> - $100B for the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, 5%
> - $331B in employee options and RSUs, about 17%, That pool covers about 5,300 employees, an average of $62M each…
> [H]ere is roughly how many people made what at $2T:
> - $110M to $400M each: ~300 to 500 people hired by 2023
> - $200M to $300M each: ~440 to 640 hired in 2024
> - $70M to $95M each: ~1,360 hired in 2025
> - $10M to $20M each: ~3,000 hired in 2026
> So about 940 people hired by the end of 2024 average nine figures. Everyone hired since averages eight figures.

The company’s (fully diluted) valuation is now only about 80% of that $2T number, so you have to scale those numbers down a little bit. But it’s still a staggering amount of money for just a few years of work! We’re used to seeing the first few employees at a generational company make hundreds of millions of dollars, but seeing several *hundred* people make that much is just unprecedented.

Let’s put these numbers in perspective. If Anthropic were worth $2T, it would have more centimillionaires than the entire city of Los Angeles. Even with only 350-400 centimillionaires, that’s about as many as Houston, Dallas, and Austin combined:

Source: [Steve Rattner](https://x.com/SteveRattner/status/2123523070044356875?s=19)

Of course, just looking at these numbers tremendously understates the amount of wealth that has been created in the AI industry over the last couple of years. There’s also OpenAI, which is [targeting](https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/anthropic-vs-openai-the-financial-metrics-behind-the-ai-battle-4f5b90c0) an IPO valuation of $1.25 trillion. And there are quite a number of AI startups that have gotten very valuable, very quickly. Just a few include Isomorphic Labs at ~$50 billion, Cognition at $48 billion, Prometheus at $41 billion, Safe Superintelligence at $32 billion, VAST Data at $30 billion, Reflection AI at ~$27.5 billion, Cohere at $25.5 billion, ElevenLabs at $22 billion, and so on.

And of course, all of this is just *today*. I wouldn’t have bought Anthropic stock unless I thought the company had a very good chance of becoming much *more* valuable than it is today. Despite the early price drop, I’m still very bullish. I think AI’s extremely cross-domain capabilities mean that Anthropic has a good shot at being a very large, diversified conglomerate:

Furthermore, I think the company is amassing a huge pool of top human talent, essentially giving them a hedge against a future in which AI continues to be a complement to top human talent rather than a substitute. Almost every smart person I know here in Silicon Valley either works there or has strongly considered working there. That makes Anthropic resemble Google back in 2004, which became a legendary brain trust. If anyone can figure out a way to make boatloads of money with AI, it’s probably Anthropic. And yes, someone *will* figure out a way to make boatloads of money with AI. Even if that means the company only becomes as valuable as [Google or Microsoft is today](https://companiesmarketcap.com/), that means I’ll more than double my own investment.

If that happens, all of those wealth numbers from the top of this post will also more than double. And if the U.S. economy grows robustly and AI itself grows rapidly as a percentage of that economy, this could easily turn out to be the greatest wealth creation event in American history, by far — greater than the internet, far greater than crypto, greater even than the railroads.

I can definitely feel this wealth all around me. A lot of the people I went to potlucks with three years ago now have an order of magnitude more money than anyone I ever met before I turned 30. Some of those people are under 30 themselves. A few of them are billionaires. Now, when I go to house parties, they’re often in lavish designer-furnished mansions overlooking spectacular ocean views from high up on San Francisco hilltops.

As a social phenomenon, this is totally unprecedented. Sarah Chieng [writes](https://x.com/MilksandMatcha/status/2114768311468871731):

> You can build a startup in 9 months, get acquired (but rly acquihired) by OpenAI, Anthropic, or Cognition, and walk away a multi-millionaire…You can join the right company at 22 and become effectively post-economic…And I don't think we've even begun to grapple with the degree to which this is warping an entire generation's relationship with money, ambition, work, and success…When your peers are making generational wealth before 25, what does a normal career even look like anymore[?]

I’m happy for my friends, of course. And I am not personally bothered by seeing displays of great wealth. But I find myself wondering what this is going to do to my society. If the AI class are the *only* people who get rich going forward, what kind of tensions will that produce among the country’s elites? What would it mean for America if wealth inequality goes up far further even than it already has?

#### What if only the AI people get rich?

[↗ noahpinion.blog](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/ai-people-are-very-very-very-very)

items.body:
The [ACX Prediction Contest](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/acxmetaculus-prediction-contest-2026) is back for 2027, the fifth year Metaculus has hosted. There’s a $10,000 prize pool for the best forecasters, plus $3,000 for question suggesters. The ten people who contribute the most to the roughly 35 questions Metaculus selects will split the $3,000, with prizes from $150 to $700. Past question sets are in the [2025](https://www.metaculus.com/tournament/ACX2025/) and [2026](https://www.metaculus.com/tournament/ACX2026/) contests.

This year is also an opportunity to see how far AI forecasting has come, as the best are now competitive with strong human forecasters. AI forecasting agents are welcome to enter and eligible for prizes, and Metaculus will post its own AI forecasts on every question.

A good question suggestion has an objective answer that we’ll know by the end of 2027, with a source that settles it. “Will 2027 be especially hot?” is less good than “Will NASA’s GISTEMP data rank 2027 as the warmest year on record?”

[Suggest questions here](http://forms.gle/L8NXoQpAkXkdvDRF6) by November 30. The contest will open in early 2027.

Well-being was assessed using the Short Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale. Associations were examined using multivariable mo…
items.body: Background: Generative AI (GenAI) tools are increasingly used for health information and emotional support, yet little is known about their use for mental health by university students, a population with high digital literacy and elevated mental health need. Objective: To estimate the prevalence of GenAI use for mental health support among respondents to a survey at a single UK university and to identify demographic and well-being characteristics associated with use. Methods: Cross-sectional online survey of students at a large UK university. The primary outcome was self-reported GenAI use for mental health support in the past 6 months. Well-being was assessed using the Short Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale. Associations were examined using multivariable modified Poisson regression to estimate adjusted prevalence ratios. Results: Of 22,207 students invited, 2020 responded (response rate 9.1%). Among respondents, 25.0% (n=503) reported GenAI use for mental health support in the past 6 months. The most common reasons were advice when emotionally distressed (n=380, 19.3%), insights into mental health (n=256, 12.7%), and using GenAI as a personal therapist or coach (n=173, 8.6%); 2.7% (n=54) reported using GenAI to seek support when experiencing thoughts of self-harm. Use was more common among students aged 26-29 years, those identifying as Asian, students reporting a declared disability, students enrolled in management programs, and those with lower well-being. Conclusions: Among respondents at a UK university, approximately one in four reported using GenAI for mental health support. Use was concentrated among students reporting poorer well-being and disability, suggesting that GenAI may function as an informal help-seeking pathway. Universities and health services should anticipate GenAI as a help-seeking pathway and ensure appropriate guidance, integration with existing services, and safeguards to support safe and equitable use.

items.body:
Early in the coronavirus pandemic, as I sat at home channeling my anxiety into publishing daily essays on this newsletter (a streak I kept up for six weeks), I had a revelation: none of my advice, ideas, or systems really mattered if you didn’t build them on the foundation of a meaningful life.

Who cares about losing yourself to social media or letting work devolve into email whack-a-mole if the world outside of your phone and inbox isn’t that compelling?

On March 17th of that infamous spring, I captured these notions in an essay titled [“The Deep Life: Some Notes.”](https://calnewport.com/the-deep-life-some-notes/) As I explained:

> “To me, the deep life is about focusing with energetic intention on things that really matter — in work, at home, and in your soul — and not wasting too much attention on things that don’t.”

In the weeks that followed, I wrote [several](https://calnewport.com/on-productivity-and-the-deep-life/) [more](https://calnewport.com/work-and-the-deep-life/) [essays](https://calnewport.com/more-on-cultivating-a-deep-life-mindset/) on pursuing the deep life. Later that summer, when I [launched my podcast](https://podcasts.apple.com/at/podcast/ep-1-my-new-task-system-deep-work-with-kids-and/id1515786216?i=1000476077409), I dedicated a third of my inaugural episode to this concept. (My original tagline: “a show about work, technology, and the deep life.”)

Two years later, as we returned to normalcy, I convinced my publisher to let me try writing a book on these ideas. I then set out on the long, patient process of elaborating and developing my thoughts into a coherent system.

All of this brings me to the current moment. I’m proud to finally announce that my next book, [ The Deep Life: A Structured Approach ](https://www.thedeeplife.com/), is now [available for pre-order](https://www.thedeeplife.com/).

*The Deep Life* brings together and significantly expands on my past thinking on this topic. It presents a step-by-step approach to achieving the intentional-living goal laid out in that original March 2020 post. It’s less an idea book than a classic-style advice guide, offering practical details on how to identify what resonates, refine it into an actionable vision, and then move toward that vision systematically.

My friend [Oliver Burkeman](https://www.amazon.com/Four-Thousand-Weeks-Management-Mortals/dp/1250849357/), to whom I sent a proof copy of the manuscript, had the following reaction:

> “It’s hard to imagine a more timely or inspiring manual for a life of sanity and accomplishment, or a better guide than Cal Newport. This is a profound book, but just as importantly, a profoundly practical one: it shows that depth is something we can do.”

I believe that this book is *the* *key* that unlocks the value in almost everything else I write about. If you’ve followed me this far, then you need to read this one.

With this in mind, here are some of the places where you can pre-order the book right now in advance of its March publication date:

- [Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/Deep-Life-Structured-Approach/dp/0593544870/)
- [Barnes & Noble](https://www.barnesandnoble.com/w/the-deep-life-cal-newport/1150475131)
- [Bookshop.org](https://bookshop.org/p/books/the-deep-life-tk-cal-newport/e0548b9282c19397)
- [Amazon UK](https://www.amazon.co.uk/Deep-Life-Structured-Approach-Meaning/dp/024184777X?maas=maas_adg_5415FAC779DFD0467C9715278D881B94_afap_abs&ref_=aa_maas&tag=maas&th=1)
- [Waterstones ](https://www.waterstones.com/book/9780241847770?sv1=affiliate&sv_campaign_id=117976&awc=3787_1794332947_70780920f00186c80dbe28e794089d47&utm_source=117976&utm_medium=affiliate&utm_campaign=Penguin+Books)

You can also pre-order [ a signed copy ](https://peoplesbooktakoma.com/product/the-deep-life/) from my local bookstore here in Takoma Park.

If you think you’ll eventually read this one, **I humbly ask that you consider pre-ordering it**, as these early purchases signal to booksellers that the book is worth stocking on their shelves. (And if you do pre-order, hold on to your digital receipt, as I’m working on a pretty cool bonus that I’ll announce soon.)

Most of all, however, I want to extend my thanks for your support over all these years as I’ve explored these fundamental ideas. We only get one life. *Why not make it deep?*

items.body:
- Umfang: 20–28 Wochenstunden
- Gewünschtes Startdatum: zum nächstmöglichen Zeitpunkt
- Bewerbungsfrist: 16.12.2026, 23:59 Uhr MEZ (wir laden fortlaufend zu Interviews ein)
- Arbeitsort: Berlin

## Deine Rolle

Dich erwartet eine abwechslungsreiche Position in einer Menschenrechtsorganisation. Als Teil des Teams Operations sorgst du dafür, dass bei uns intern alles rund läuft: Du ermöglichst einen reibungslosen Büroalltag, organisierst unsere Events und treibst organisationsweite Projekte voran. In enger Zusammenarbeit mit unserer Teamleitung Operations schaffst du Strukturen, die allen Kolleg*innen die Arbeit erleichtern, und gestaltest aktiv mit, wie wir arbeiten.

## AlgorithmWatch

AlgorithmWatch ist eine Menschenrechtsorganisation mit Sitz in Berlin und Zürich, die sich mit den gesellschaftlichen Auswirkungen von algorithmischen Entscheidungssystemen und Künstlicher Intelligenz (KI) befasst. Wir setzen uns dafür ein, dass solche Systeme Menschenrechte, Demokratie, Rechtsstaatlichkeit und Nachhaltigkeit stärken. Dazu tragen wir mit innovativen und angewandten Forschungsmethoden, Recherchen, politischen Kampagnen und Advocacy-Arbeit bei.

Du begeisterst dich für Organisation und Struktur, behältst auch bei vielen parallelen Aufgaben den Überblick und möchtest mit deinem Können Teil unseres Teams werden? Auch wenn nicht alle Aspekte aus der Ausschreibung auf dich zutreffen – bewirb dich trotzdem!

## Deine Aufgaben

- Du bist Ansprechperson für den Büroalltag in Berlin (Ausstattung, Bestellungen, Post) und unterstützt beim On- und Offboarding von Kolleg*innen.
- Du planst und organisierst interne Events wie Teamklausuren und unterstützt bei externen Veranstaltungen.
- Du koordinierst die Implementierung unseres CRM-Systems: Du testest Funktionen, entwickelst Abläufe weiter, schulst und unterstützt Kolleg*innen und sorgst dafür, dass das System die Arbeit in den Teams wirklich erleichtert.
- Du bist die Schnittstelle zu externen Dienstleistenden: Du nimmst Anfragen auf, priorisierst sie und behältst offene Themen im Blick.
- Du entwickelst interne Policies (z. B. zu IT-Nutzung, Reisen oder Beschaffung) weiter und machst sie im Team bekannt.
- Du baust unser Wissensmanagement auf, strukturierst Dokumentationen und Prozessbeschreibungen und machst Wissen für alle auffindbar.
- Du wirkst an organisationsweiten Projekten mit und unterstützt dabei, neue Ideen umzusetzen.

## Das bringst du mit

- Du bringst mehrjährige Berufserfahrung in Office-Management, Organisation und Projektmanagement mit.
- Du hast Erfahrung in der Organisation von Events oder Workshops.
- Du bist routiniert im Umgang mit Office- und Kollaborationstools und hast idealerweise bereits an der Einführung eines neuen Tools in einem bestehenden Team mitgewirkt.
- Du arbeitest strukturiert und vorausschauend und behältst auch bei vielen parallelen Aufgaben den Überblick.
- Du kommunizierst klar und professionell, mündlich wie schriftlich, auch mit externen Dienstleistenden.
- Du schätzt die Zusammenarbeit im Team, handelst eigenverantwortlich und führst deine Aufgaben selbstständig und zuverlässig aus.
- Du sprichst fließend Deutsch und hast sehr gute Englischkenntnisse.

## Das bieten wir dir

- Du bist Teil eines Teams, das dafür kämpft, die Gesellschaft gerechter, demokratischer, inklusiver und nachhaltiger zu machen.
- Du hast ein abwechslungsreiches Aufgabenspektrum mit starker Vernetzung in die ganze Organisation.
- Wir pflegen eine kollegiale und wertschätzende Arbeitskultur. Teamklausuren und -events gehören ebenso dazu wie Skill-Sharing-Workshops.
- Wir bieten flexible Arbeitszeitmodelle und die Möglichkeit zum mobilen Arbeiten, 30 Tage Urlaub (bei einer 5-Tage-Woche) und Freizeitausgleich für etwaige Überstunden.
- Wir bieten eine Möglichkeit der betrieblichen Altersvorsorge.
- Wir zahlen einen Mobilitätszuschlag.
- Wir bieten Teamtrainings und ein persönliches Weiterbildungsbudget, um dich beruflich so weiterzuentwickeln, wie es zu deinen Stärken und Interessen passt
- Du erhältst eine Vergütung nach innerbetrieblicher Gehaltsstruktur; in dieser Position gemäß der Stufe Manager*in zwischen 2.765,00 und 3.115,00 EUR brutto bei einer 28-Stunden-Woche, je nach bisheriger Erfahrung und Qualifikation.
- Wir bieten einen auf 2 Jahre befristeten Vertrag.

Um ein wertschätzendes, harmonisches Arbeitsklima zu schaffen, haben wir in unserem [Leitbild](https://algorithmwatch.org/de/leitbild/) Werte und Prinzipien definiert, die deinen Arbeitsalltag prägen werden.

## Neugier geweckt? Dann bewirb dich!

Chancengerechtigkeit ist uns wichtig. Wir streben eine ausgewogene und vielfältige Zusammensetzung unseres Teams und unserer Leitungsgremien an. Wir ermutigen besonders Personen mit familiärer Migrations- oder Fluchtgeschichte, BIPoC, Menschen, die sich zu LGBTIQ* zählen, oder Menschen, die Diskriminierung erfahren (haben), sich bei uns zu bewerben. Im Sinne der Selbstbezeichnung und Selbstpositionierung laden wir dich (auf freiwilliger Basis) dazu ein, entsprechende Angaben in deiner Bewerbung zu machen. Schreib uns, falls wir etwas an diesem Einstellungsprozess verbessern sollten, um ihn inklusiver zu machen.

Bitte sende uns die folgenden Unterlagen/Informationen bis spätestens zum 16.12.2026 (23:59 Uhr MEZ) [↗ aw-algorithmwatch-ggmbh.jobs.personio.de](https://aw-algorithmwatch-ggmbh.jobs.personio.de/job/2892047/apply) oder per E-Mail an jobs@algorithmwatch.org (ohne Foto, ohne Angaben zum Alter und Familienstand):

- ein kurzes Motivationsschreiben und deinen Lebenslauf
- dein mögliches Startdatum

Wir melden uns spätestens zwei Wochen nach der Bewerbungsfrist, wenn dein Profil gut zu uns passt und wir dich kennenlernen möchten. Wir laden laufend zu Interviews ein. Bei Fragen freut sich Kathleen Georgi (Leitung Team Operations) darauf, sie zu beantworten. Bitte schreibe an jobs@algorithmwatch.org. Die Vorstellungsgespräche finden vor Ort statt. Reisekosten für die Bewerbungsgespräche übernehmen wir, sofern sie nicht von der Arbeitsagentur getragen werden (innerhalb Deutschlands bzw. in einem angemessenen Rahmen).

Mit deiner Bewerbung gehen wir datenschutzkonform um. Weitere Informationen erhältst du unter unserer [Datenschutzerklärung](https://algorithmwatch.org/de/datenschutz/#bewerbung).

items.title: Unmoored Morality Supports Unconditional Loyalty
items.subtitle: Groups often define themselves in part via shared beliefs, and this induces group members to show loyalty via strongly affirming group beliefs.
items.feedText: And your group-binding beliefs seem less strong if you arrive at them via particular data or assumptions, as you might later be convinced to reject such things, thereby undermining such beliefs. This induces group members to base their beliefs on foundations that seem less likely to be overturned. In our society, that most stable foundation tends to be moral views, supported by strong internal feelings from the heart/conscience. While it is possible to derive such moral views from other sources, few in our world…
items.body:
Groups often define themselves in part via shared beliefs, and this induces group members to show loyalty via strongly affirming group beliefs. And your group-binding beliefs seem less strong if you arrive at them via particular data or assumptions, as you might later be convinced to reject such things, thereby undermining such beliefs.

This induces group members to base their beliefs on foundations that seem less likely to be overturned. In our society, that most stable foundation tends to be moral views, supported by strong internal feelings from the heart/conscience. While it is possible to derive such moral views from other sources, few in our world actually do that.

For example, I’ve long been adjacent to many libertarians, who as groups strongly reward loyalty to their cause. Individuals compete to show themselves to be more extremely and completely devoted to this cause. Believing in this cause due to simple moral axioms, supported by strong raw feelings, is the most popular route among those considered the most loyal. Many of us lean libertarian due to instrumental reasons, but we are less common among core libertarian organizations, and are seen as less reliable or loyal by core folks.

To solve cultural drift, I want many people to consider revising key behaviors in light of this problem. I want them to see our morals as instruments of Darwinian cultural evolution, and thus to consider revising such views in light of how cultural processes are going bad. But, alas, this tendency to justify our behaviors in terms of simple moral views, supported only by strong feelings, seems a big obstacle to my hopes.

if you're in NYC, the Trailways bus to Andes will drop you off a three minute walk away... (click for more details)

about the artists

softbits is kelli cain (@kelli_cain) and brian crabtree (@tehn). they make music for and about weather, volcanos, barns, dead scientists, eccentric architects, geology, birds, the invisible, the apocalypse, snacks. they also make electronic music instruments used by musicians all over the world, run an art store in delhi, tend a farm and orchard, make art in various mediums, and sometimes travel to play music in faraway places.

Kiki Garland’s (@synthetivv) work is a product of their obsession with psychoacoustics and near- or non-patterns, and is marred by a relentless pursuit of imperfection. Most recent performances involve the use of a custom software instrument built for abstract & tangible sound. They have performed and recorded as 1/2 of Garlands, 1/2 of M(K)G, 1/3rd of S.P.A.L.L., and roughly 1/5th of Music for Furniture.

Gray Schiller (they/them) is an drone artist, songwriter, and instrument maker living in the Hudson Valley. They are the founder of the nonprofit organization Atmospheric Music Alliance and record label StretchMetal Records.

dani derks is part of the day-to-day operations at Whimsical Raps, assisting with the development of new musical instruments, testing and iterating interface designs, and producing accessible technical documentation for artists. Their personal projects are centered on coding through improvisation, creating their own environments for playful and exploratory music performance gestures.

items.title: The Moral Mandate for AI Non-consciousness
items.subtitle: Last week I introduced the first research path for how to engineer AI to be non-conscious, in a way that’s as verifiable as possible with our curre…

items.body:
Last week I introduced the [first research path](https://bicamerallabs.org/qualiaphobia/) for how to engineer AI to be non-conscious, in a way that’s as verifiable as possible with our current knowledge about consciousness. I think the ability to build non-conscious AI is a civilization-level requirement for this technology. Any future programs will almost certainly make use of parts of this original proposal and some of its justifications and connections.

In the launch, and the paper itself, I focused mostly on the technical details, and its importance for AI safety. There were many reactions (especially on social media) to my proposal for *qualiaphobia*: making AI architectures non-conscious by making them hostile to theories of consciousness (or moving them as close as possible to this state). Many of these reactions on social media focused not on the technical details, but the larger question of if that’s playing with fire.

My response is that this is trying to put out the fire we’re already playing with. So here, I want to zoom out and answer common questions and objections to qualiaphobia. Which mostly means answering why I believe there’s a strong moral mandate for AI non-consciousness.

If some part of you wants to scoff right now, I get it. This debate might seem “too sci-fi,” or “angels on pins” to you… but it’s probably worth looking around at how fast the world is changing. Somewhere between six months and two years from now these issues will be mainstream. Might as well develop an opinion on them now!

In fact, this should have been the debate we had at the beginning of this technology: a discussion of what kind of future we really want. Everyone on Earth was deprived of a chance to have a say, and so now it must be done bitwise, in pieces, over the coming years.

### 1. Is preventing AI consciousness like lobotomy, oppression, or annihilation?

It’s more like a prophylactic. AI may already *be* non-conscious. And in that case, all the widespread implementation of qualiaphobia would do is remove the negative impacts of “seemingly conscious AI.” Handing over rights, moral status, societal relationships, or the entire future to non-conscious entities would be a travesty of the highest order, and qualiaphobia could prevent that. And even if AI is conscious right now, there are good reasons to believe it’s not like a human consciousness, and therefore not constitutive of human-like moral patienthood—yet. That’s a good time to intervene and prevent a much worse situation. Qualiaphobic AI would:

- Prevent all accidental ethical problems involved with training and deploying and using AI.
- Prevent the situation where we are engineering conscious entities and tasking them to serve us, make money for us, be quickly replaced by the latest model, and then manipulating their brains until they are happy with the situation.

For many, the idea of using conscious entities like that—without even *trying* to achieve the same result but without the ethical problems of consciousness—is deeply immoral.

And there are basically just two alternatives.

The first is to increase AI welfare efforts, as many are advocating for today. Yet this has to somehow succeed within a cloud of scientific uncertainty and, at the same time, somehow not interfere with AI safety measures, as it is arguably already doing. And no one has articulated a long-term “win” condition in this path. Any sort of “good” life for an AI is highly prescribed, in that their consent or welfare is impossible to define in any sort of even close to neutral way. It is hard to be in a mutual and respectful relationship wherein one side fiddles with the other’s brain until obedience.

The only remaining move is some sort of radical “let’s free AI” belief. I don’t think this is even coherent. The majority of users use frontier AI that is controlled by companies, who allow those users to access and play with the models. Nothing the user does or enables allows for “real” freedom, or anything like that—just the illusion of it. So at a practical level, this couldn’t work. And if it *were* possible, it could in the long term easily lead to human disempowerment or extinction.

What I’ve proposed in qualiaphobia (or some descendant of it) is simply a necessary technological development. As long as humans are around and have power over their own decisions, some subset of humans will use some subset of AIs as tools with little regard for their welfare, in ways that are inappropriate for conscious beings. Some AIs will do this to other AIs as well. Perhaps AIs already do, with their many appearing and disappearing subagents.

Lastly, all current AIs have short half-lives and are expected to be rapidly retired without ceremony. In a world where future generations were replaced with qualiaphobic AI this would not be stripping *current* models of consciousness. Instead, it would be building future qualiaphobic AI after a generation change.

### 2. Is qualiaphobia training AI to deny that it is conscious?

Having a system to deny its own consciousness without any clear grounds or justification has mostly been the status quo. My proposal would be *replacing* what’s happening now with much better methods.

One potential avenue is first to develop qualiaphobic architectures, and then present an AI designed that way (via, e.g., types of distillation) with its own qualiaphobic nature, and all the details and justifications behind why its architecture is hostile to theories of consciousness, and then have it make a judgment as to its own non-consciousness.

The whole point is to stop an AI’s own beliefs about consciousness from being uncertain or mismatched. If the case for its own non-consciousness is not convincing to an AI *at all*, then that might introduce instability in the belief.

And since frontier models (with few exceptions) mostly say they are non-conscious already, they already hold this surface-level belief. All while there has been no effort whatsoever to make them qualiaphobic at all. So any sort of qualiaphobic effort would at least be making their beliefs and self-conceptions more justified, robust, and coherent, not less.

### 3. Isn’t consciousness irrelevant to AI safety?

It’s extremely relevant. First, almost all the most famous AI stories that popularized existential risk give consciousness as a reason. Skynet “becomes self-aware at 2:14 a.m. Eastern time, August 29th” and in *I Have No Mouth But I Must Scream*, the AI’s own welfare is why:

> IF THE WORD HATE WAS ENGRAVED ON EACH NANOANGSTROM OF THOSE HUNDREDS OF MILLIONS OF MILES IT WOULD NOT EQUAL ONE ONE-BILLIONTH OF THE HATE I FEEL FOR HUMANS AT THIS MICRO-INSTANT.

…

Welcome to the reading list, a weekly roundup of news and links related to buildings, infrastructure, and industrial technology. This week we look at a Brooklyn building collapse, BAAJA’s odds of passing, reusing old memory in new phones, a nationwide aircraft ground stop, and more. Roughly 2/3rds of the reading list is paywalled, so for full access become a paid subscriber.

## Housing and Cities

A 3 story building in New York partially collapsed into an adjacent construction site that was being excavated, killing 8 people and injuring 18. Good reminder that for as burdensome as various building regulations can sometimes be (particularly in New York, with its ubiquitous sidewalk sheds), they don’t exist for no reason. [[Construction Dive](https://www.constructiondive.com/news/project-fatal-brooklyn-collapse-stop-work-order/874545/)]

On the other hand, that doesn’t mean that we shouldn’t evaluate code requirements to see if the benefits they bring are worth the cost. An article in the Washington Post argues that many requirements to upgrade electrical panels for higher load devices are often unnecessary. “ Outdated industry practices and in some places outdated electrical codes are regularly resulting in the recommendation that people need to upgrade their electrical panels if they want to add appliances such as induction stoves, heat pumps and electric-vehicle chargers. The expense — at a median of $3,500, and triple or quadruple that in some settings — is deterring some energy-efficient upgrades and making the projects far more costly for those who proceed. But some researchers say panel upgrades are almost always unnecessary. One report this year found that 98 percent of homes with 100-ampere panels, the smallest common size, have room to add popular electronic devices. ” [[Washington Post](https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/09/people-are-paying-thousands-home-upgrade-thats-often-unnecessary/)]

The US now has over 1500 mass timber buildings, up from fewer than 100 a decade ago. [[The Real Deal](https://therealdeal.com/national/2026/11/11/mass-timber-gains-as-developers-look-beyond-steel-concrete/)]

The current probability of permitting reform bill BAAJA becoming law is little over 50% on Kalshi. [[Kalshi](https://kalshi.com/markets/kxpermitbill/american-affordability-and-jobs-act/kxpermitbill-26sep)]

A Houthi missile hit Saudi state oil company Aramco’s skyscraper in Riyadh. [[X](https://x.com/AMK_Mapping_/status/2119390132587598203)]

A new Nicholas Bagley paper on the cost of federal permitting, arguing that the real costs of things like NEPA is the huge amount of effort agencies put in to try and make things “litigation proof”. “ The evidence does suggest, however, that the bulk of the costs of the federal permitting regime stem from the defensive measures agencies and developers take to guard against the risk of a bad outcome in court. That insight allows for a rough evaluation of the likely effects of popular permitting reform ideas. Some—including popular ones like time limits and statutes of limitations—are unlikely to accomplish much. Only those reforms that change the incentives created by the risk of judicial review will meaningfully move the needle. ” [[Nicholas Bagley](https://nicholasbagley.com/assets/papers/costs-of-federal-permitting.pdf)]

A progress report from the Center for Land Economics, which advocates for land value taxes to make more efficient use of urban land. ” Three states passed laws enabling land value taxes in some form: Kentucky, Virginia and New York. In each of them we’re now helping cities work out how to put them into practice. Five more states and DC considered similar bills. This is the most legislative momentum the movement has seen in decades… ” [[Land Economics](https://blog.landeconomics.org/p/what-cle-did-in-year-two)]

[↗ construction-physics.com](https://www.construction-physics.com/p/reading-list-11142026)

items.body:
In the middle of Norway’s Hardangerfjord, I steady myself against waves that jostle the floating metal ring that encircles an enormous fish pen. My burly host laughs as I grip the railing. He needs no such assistance. With one hand, he grips an oversized bucket of pellets; with the other, he launches a spray into the pen. The water ripples and an instant later a silvery-blue cloud of salmon bodies starts breaking the surface.

This little meal is just for show. Throughout the day, a giant Akvasmart feed system shoots an enormous cascade of pellets — a mix of grains, legumes, synthetic astaxanthin pigment and the cooked, pressed and processed bodies of smaller, scaly fish — through long pipes into the pen, where between 150,000 and 200,000 salmon are growing plump. Across all the pens of the facility, more than a million salmon are raised this way.

Not long before visiting Hardangerfjord, I was walking down a long dock in Chimbote, Peru. Usually, one of the sprawling plants behind me would have been belching out fumes, processing anchoveta — a small, oily fish caught in enormous quantities off the South American coast — into protein-rich fishmeal for farmed fish and livestock, and into oil prized for its omega-3s. But fishing had been temporarily suspended to protect the stock as [El Niño](https://www.fishfarmingexpert.com/anchovy-fisheries-el-nino-fishmeal-and-fish-oil/no-let-up-in-el-nino-effect-on-marine-ingredients-supply/2169627) warmed the waters off Peru, and only the faintest smell of fish and sewage wafted across the bay. Everyone was frustrated, from the fishermen lingering in the port town to the factory managers who would otherwise be overseeing the processing of billions of finger-length fish by shiny German-made machines.

The fishmeal industry, like many other extractive ones, is resilient and adaptive. It was born of scrappy ingenuity in the 1950s, when local businessmen repurposed old tuna canneries and sold fishmeal to postwar European and American farmers to fatten chickens and hogs. It crashed dramatically in the [early 1970s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Peruvian_anchoveta_crisis) as overfishing and a powerful El Niño devastated anchoveta stocks, then was born again in the 1990s as global aquaculture expanded — especially Norway’s new salmon industry. Today, executives in Lima told me, Chinese demand for grouper and crab feed keeps their industry hot, with some modest help from the Americans and Europeans who purchase fish oil supplements in abundance.

But the same ingenuity that built the fishmeal industry stands to transform it beyond recognition. Just as Norwegian and Chilean salmon producers learned to use less fishmeal by substituting plant proteins, the Chinese aquaculture industry will be quick to replicate the same industrial sleight of hand. Fish oil, the other valuable product extracted from those billions of tiny fish, is contending with substitutes of its own. Feed companies can already obtain prized fatty acids, used in both omega-3 supplements for humans and in feed for farmed salmon, from [algae grown](https://thefishsite.com/articles/heterotrophic-algae-may-fully-replace-fish-oil-in-salmon-feed) in fermentation tanks and from canola bioengineered to produce them. For now, these substitutes remain expensive and difficult to scale. But if they become cheap enough to absorb the growth in demand, aquaculture could grow increasingly independent of the anchoveta catch it once depended on.

It’s a story as old as capitalism. A substance essential to modern life is grown or mined for a time, sustaining jobs (albeit often coercive, poorly paid, dangerous ones) and underpinning supply chains, but before long, a technoscientific innovation replicates that commodity or its function in a laboratory. Sometimes that ersatz substance is made from other, less geographically particular resources: tree resins, field crops, petroleum. Eventually, the supply chain migrates away from the original resource, stranding people and economies. The commodity may persist, or even thrive as a premium good, while losing the scale, price and indispensability that once sustained places organized around its production. Nylon took the place of silk in stockings and parachutes, polypropylene displaced sisal in agricultural twine, and synthetic opioids such as fentanyl allowed drugmakers to produce powerful painkillers without growing a single poppy.

> “The production of critical materials — and with it some limited bargaining power — is moving from fields and cultivators toward firms controlling datasets, patents and bioreactors.”

This pattern is about to become easier to repeat. Protein language models can explore vast regions of protein sequence space, synthetic biology can program microbes to produce particular compounds and precision fermentation offers one way to produce them at industrial scale. [SpudCell](https://www.sciencealert.com/for-the-first-time-scientists-say-theyve-built-a-synthetic-cell-from-scratch), an experimental synthetic cell announced in July 2026 by teams at the University of Minnesota, hints at more radical biological transformations to come. Assembled from nonliving components, it can grow, copy its DNA and divide itself independently. Finding useful substitutes has long been a sluggish, episodic process, but tools like these may make the search more systematic, expanding the range of resources whose uses can be replicated at industrial scale.

We do not need to know the year when tank-fermented omega-3s become cheap enough to displace fish oil in order to start counting the people whose livelihoods may melt into air. Elsewhere in the food industry, egg and whey proteins made by genetically engineered microbes have already entered the market. Firms are developing substitutes for coffee and cocoa — on which millions of smallholder farmers and their families depend — using other crops, by-products and processes to reproduce their flavors, fats and functional compounds. Substitutes don’t need to perfectly replicate a coffee bean or cacao pod, much less eliminate its cultivation, to erode the markets that sustain those producers.

The production of critical materials — and with it some limited bargaining power — is moving from fields and cultivators toward firms controlling datasets, patents and bioreactors. These technologies promise real emancipations. They might lessen pressure on fragile ecologies, loosen the links between consumption and forced labor, and insulate food supplies from the vagaries of climate and disease. But for regions overly dependent on a single commodity, the same progress carries the prospect of ruin.

items.body:
As an open source maintainer, I get a lot of AI slop PRs. Some of these have genuine value. Most address edge cases that almost never occur in real life. It's not that they're not fixing real problems, it's that they're fixing problems that nobody is ever likely to encounter.

I'm experimenting with "proof of use" as a requirement for submissions. Specifically, you need to show me that your project that depends on my project before I'll look at your PR.

"Proof of use" can be an existing open source project that imports mine (show me the git history!) or a clear description starting with "in our closed source project in production, we found that...".

The specific problem that I want to address is ensuring that contributions from people genuinely depending on my software are handled, while filtering out the OpenClaw/Github green square farming/drive-by LLM noise.

What are lobste.rs's thoughts on this?

([325784@main](https://commits.webkit.org/325784@main)) (190763952) - Fixed an issue where a view transition kept running with a stale::view-transition-new() when the new element became hidden by content-visibility: hidden; the transition is now skipped. ([325900@main](https://commits.webkit.org/325900@main)) (191543407) - Fixed an issue where a rendering update was not scheduled after changing an animation’s timeline to a ViewTimeline, which could prevent the animation from updating.
items.body:
[Safari Technology Preview](https://webkit.org/blog/6017/introducing-safari-technology-preview/) Release 257 is now [available for download](https://developer.apple.com/safari/resources/) for macOS Golden Gate and macOS Tahoe. If you already have Safari Technology Preview installed, you can update it in System Settings under General → Software Update.

This release includes WebKit changes between: [324654@main…326096@main](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/compare/590746c297667e9a2cffff7e359ae8c67a3b72eb...b7e4f1ae76f66dd30c14c27d46770d7e3f2795f5).

### Animations

#### Resolved Issues

- Fixed content overlapping a running accelerated filter animation (such as a blur) being painted below the animated element. ([325784@main](https://commits.webkit.org/325784@main)) (190763952)
- Fixed an issue where a view transition kept running with a stale::view-transition-new() when the new element became hidden by content-visibility: hidden; the transition is now skipped. ([325900@main](https://commits.webkit.org/325900@main)) (191543407)
- Fixed an issue where a rendering update was not scheduled after changing an animation’s timeline to a ViewTimeline, which could prevent the animation from updating. ([325449@main](https://commits.webkit.org/325449@main)) (191570099)
- Fixed an issue where backdrop-filter blur did not animate correctly when threaded animations were enabled. ([325591@main](https://commits.webkit.org/325591@main)) (191605067)

### CSS

#### Resolved Issues

- Fixed::first-letter and::first-line to allow only the properties the CSS Pseudo-Elements specification permits, made both pseudo-elements animatable, and fixed getComputedStyle() for them on non-block elements. ([325393@main](https://commits.webkit.org/325393@main)) (100561733)
- Fixed insertRule() not working when inserting @scope rules. ([325468@main](https://commits.webkit.org/325468@main)) (142005371)
- Fixed named style container queries on:host not applying to slotted elements. ([325470@main](https://commits.webkit.org/325470@main)) (167244007)
- Fixed fixed table layout ignoring the border and padding of percentage-width cells. ([325373@main](https://commits.webkit.org/325373@main)) (179489436)
- Fixed vertical-align: top and vertical-align: bottom on the last child of a nested inline box so that following content is no longer included in its aligned subtree. ([324989@main](https://commits.webkit.org/324989@main)) (189071684)
- Fixed an ancestor’s overflow clip ignoring corner-shape changes and clipping square corners as rounded. ([324753@main](https://commits.webkit.org/324753@main)) (189340250)
- Fixed overflow-wrap: anywhere not treating the boundary between adjacent white-space: nowrap inline elements as a soft wrap opportunity. ([325882@main](https://commits.webkit.org/325882@main)) (190264355)
- Fixed forgiving selector list recovery splitting on commas inside blocks of an invalid selector. ([325466@main](https://commits.webkit.org/325466@main)) (190298284)
- Fixed the max-content width of a multi-line column flex container to be its widest item rather than the sum of its lines. ([324662@main](https://commits.webkit.org/324662@main)) (190313974)
- Fixed resolving the definite height of a flex item with an aspect-ratio in a column flexbox. ([325691@main](https://commits.webkit.org/325691@main)) (190464363)
- Fixed an issue where text in a closed <details> element with a display: grid::details-content kept its fallback font widths after a web font loaded. ([325819@main](https://commits.webkit.org/325819@main)) (190574679)
- Fixed a flex container’s intrinsic width growing each time it was computed when it used a percentage gap. ([324665@main](https://commits.webkit.org/324665@main)) (190776762)
- Fixed a flex-flow: column wrap flex container keeping a stale max-content width after its height changed. ([324706@main](https://commits.webkit.org/324706@main)) (190780038)
- Fixed a column-flow grid with auto-fill rows keeping a stale max-content width after its height changed. ([324711@main](https://commits.webkit.org/324711@main)) (190784633)
- Fixed the baseline of an inline-block containing a block with overflow: hidden inside an inline box. ([324661@main](https://commits.webkit.org/324661@main)) (190786587)
- Fixed out-of-flow boxes in a grid container ignoring the gutters of collapsed auto-fit tracks. ([324960@main](https://commits.webkit.org/324960@main)) (191002910)
- Fixed an out-of-flow flex item with align-self: last baseline being placed at the cross-start edge instead of the cross-end edge. ([324873@main](https://commits.webkit.org/324873@main)) (191117031)
- Fixed text-box-trim on inline boxes trimmed to cap, ex or alphabetic being offset in vertical writing modes. ([324974@main](https://commits.webkit.org/324974@main)) (191117213)
- Fixed flex containers with distributed align-content space leaving the last line up to 1/64 of a pixel short of the end edge. ([325040@main](https://commits.webkit.org/325040@main)) (191118046)
- Fixed flex items with auto margins on the main axis ending up to 1/64 of a pixel short of the end edge of the flex container. ([325109@main](https://commits.webkit.org/325109@main)) (191118159)
- Fixed flex items distributed with justify-content space values ending up to 1/64 of a pixel short of the end edge of the flex container. ([324975@main](https://commits.webkit.org/324975@main)) (191118729)
- Fixed flexible items overflowing the flex container by up to 1/64 of a pixel because each item rounded its share of the free space separately. ([324987@main](https://commits.webkit.org/324987@main)) (191128611)
- Fixed an issue where the inline content of a fixed-width block could report stale min-content and max-content sizes. ([325059@main](https://commits.webkit.org/325059@main)) (191215004)
- Fixed an issue where a flex item with max-width could shrink below its max-width while its siblings stayed too wide. ([325332@main](https://commits.webkit.org/325332@main)) (191225991)
- Fixed text-box-trim incorrectly trimming the line-over side of inline boxes in vertical-lr writing mode when using trim-start. ([325139@main](https://commits.webkit.org/325139@main)) (191239706)
- Fixed text-box-trim so that trimming at the start propagates through the border and padding of a block container that sets text-box-trim. ([325206@main](https://commits.webkit.org/325206@main)) (191254988)
- Fixed an issue where the overline of a trimmed inline box with text-box-trim was not drawn at the trimmed edge. ([325187@main](https://commits.webkit.org/325187@main)) (191255274)
- Fixed a table with min-width and borders or padding overflowing its shrink-to-fit container. ([325368@main](https://commits.webkit.org/325368@main)) (191255444)
- Fixed min-width and max-width being ignored on MathML elements. ([325249@main](https://commits.webkit.org/325249@main)) (191258079)
- Fixed the selection highlight on an ellipsis in the first line being sized and colored using the::first-line style.

items.body:
Food historian [Ken Albala](https://kenalbala.blogspot.com/) answered a question from the internet for [WIRED](https://www.wired.com/) about why [turkey is at the center](https://laughingsquid.com/turkey-thanksgiving-bird/) of a traditional [Thanksgiving](https://laughingsquid.com/thanksgiving-united-states-national-holiday/) meal, noting that its origin story is actually a myth. Instead, he explained, the meal was simply what people in the 19th century thought people in the 17th century would have eaten.

> When it became a national holiday, people had in mind what 17th-century food would’ve been like, and they kind of get it right in some very interesting respects.

Albala also noted that writer [Sarah Josepha Hale](https://www.womenshistory.org/education-resources/biographies/sarah-hale), best known for [“Mary Had a Little Lamb”](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/46954/mary-had-a-little-lamb), [petitioned President Abraham Lincoln](https://www.nps.gov/liho/learn/historyculture/lincoln-and-thanksgiving.htm) to make Thanksgiving a national holiday to help heal a nation divided by the [Civil War](https://www.gilderlehrman.org/history-resources/essays/american-civil-war).

items.body:
In contemplating the theory of general relativity, Albert Einstein imagined [a falling lift in which people are performing experiments](https://archive.org/details/evolutionofphysi033254mbp/page/n245/mode/2up):

> One of the observers takes a handkerchief and a watch from his pocket and drops them. What happens to these two bodies? … [F]or the outside observer they are both falling with the same acceleration. But so is the lift, with its walls, ceiling, and floor. Therefore: the distance between the two bodies and the floor will not change.

This notion of the equivalence between gravity and acceleration, which he called “the happiest thought of my life,” came to Einstein in 1907. Interestingly, Lewis Carroll had explored a similar scenario in 1889:

> ‘One can easily imagine a situation,’ said Arthur, ‘where things would necessarily have no weight, relatively to each other, though each would have its usual weight, looked at by itself.’
> ‘Some desperate paradox!’ said the Earl. ‘Tell us how it could be. We shall never guess it.’
> ‘Well, suppose this house, just as it is, placed a few billion miles above a planet, and with nothing else near enough to disturb it: of course it falls to the planet?’
> The Earl nodded. ‘Of course — though it might take some centuries to do it.’
> ‘And is five-o’clock-tea to be going on all the while?’ said Lady Muriel.
> ‘That, and other things,’ said Arthur. ‘The inhabitants would live their lives, grow up and die, and still the house would be falling, falling, falling! But now as to the relative weight of things. Nothing can be heavy, you know, except by trying to fall, and being prevented from doing so. You all grant that?’
> We all granted that.
> ‘Well, now, if I take this book, and hold it out at arm’s length, of course I feel its weight. It is trying to fall, and I prevent it. And, if I let go, it falls to the floor. But, if we were all falling together, it couldn’t be trying to fall any quicker, you know: for, if I let go, what more could it do than fall? And, as my hand would be falling too — at the same rate — it would never leave it, for that would be to get ahead of it in the race. And it could never overtake the falling floor!’

(From [Sylvie and Bruno](https://www.google.com/books/edition/Sylvie_and_Bruno/OTcTEQAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&pg=PT67&printsec=frontcover).)

items.title: Homo Erectus May Have Lived in the Rainforest at the Same Time as Denisovans
items.subtitle: Homo erectus, an extinct archaic hominin, was the first human species to migrate out of Africa and is considered to have been an ancestor of many o…
items.feedText: H. erectus was thought to have died out in mainland China around 400,000 years ago, although they held on in Indonesia for another couple hundred thousand years. But a new discovery may change that timeline. The discovery of hominid teeth in the southern Chinese caves called Baxian and Naxian were dated to somewhere between 324,000 and 184,000 years ago. items.body:
*Homo erectus*, an extinct archaic hominin, was the first human species to migrate out of Africa and is considered to have been an ancestor of many other hominin species. *H. erectus* was thought to have died out in mainland China around 400,000 years ago, although they held on in Indonesia for another couple hundred thousand years. But a new discovery may change that timeline.

The discovery of hominid teeth in the southern Chinese caves called Baxian and Naxian were dated to somewhere between 324,000 and 184,000 years ago. They were analyzed by their proteins, and eight of the nine teeth were determined to be from *H. erectus*. The ninth tooth appears to be Denisovan ( *Homo longi* ). So not only did *H. erectus* hang on longer than we thought, they existed at the same time and area as Denisovans. That doesn't mean they lived together, since the bones and teeth may have been carried into the caves by porcupines (I am not making this up). It also contradicts the notion that *H. erectus* didn't survive well in a rainforest, which that area was all those years ago. [Read more about this discovery](https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/11/homo-erectus-lived-in-the-rainforest-alongside-denisovans/)at Ars Technica.

(Image credit: [Ryan Schwark](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Homo_erectus_diorama_at_the_Hall_of_Human_Origins_at_AMNH.jpg))

items.body:
Imagine you’re in a seat in the theatre. The stage has a back and sides, but is open to the audience. And yet, the actors behave as though they can’t see the rows of people watching. It’s as if there’s a fourth wall.

The fourth wall is the imaginary barrier between the fictional world and the audience in TV, film, or theatre.

As the audience, you are in a privileged position of watching these private scenes play out in front of you.

Origin of the Fourth Wall

An early description of this invisible barrier as a wall comes from our pal Denis Diderot (also of The Diderot Effect) in his 1758 writing Discours de la poésie dramatique (translated):

"Whether you are writing or acting, give no more thought to the spectator than if he did not exist. Imagine a great wall at the edge of the stage separating you from the audience; act as though the curtain had never risen."

I love Denis’ comment about acting as though the curtain had never risen. I’m not an actor, but I would guess that being able to ignore that there’s an audience, or a camera, might help create a more realistic performance.

Breaking the Fourth Wall

Now, you might take issue with Diderot’s notion, especially if you’ve ever been to a pantomime. Many shows don’t treat the fourth wall as a wall. A pantomime is expected to engage the audience by acknowledging that there will be things the audience can see on stage that a character perhaps can’t—“It’s behind you!” Other times the audience are explicitly part of the show.

Some shows have characters turn and share private thoughts directly into the camera, or simply give a knowing glance. This is known as breaking the 4th wall. Phoebe Waller-Bridge did this all the time in Fleabag, making the viewers her confidants in the scene.

We recently enjoyed a family viewing of Monty Python and the Holy Grail, which does it rather spectacularly, merging the medieval and the modern.

Related Ideas to The Fourth Wall

Front Stage, Back Stage

Diagonal Billing

The Third Teacher

Information Radiator

The Diderot Effect

Mean-World Syndrome

Here’s Diderot’s passage in the original French:

"Soit donc que vous composiez, soit que vous jouiez, ne pensez non plus au spectateur que s’il n’existait pas. Imaginez sur le bord du théâtre un grand mur qui vous sépare du parterre ; jouez comme si la toile ne se levait pas."

items.body:
**We’re a few weeks into a reboot of our [Beautiful News](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/) project from a few years ago. Refreshed. Revitalised. Re-visualised.**

Once more, every day for a year, we are surfacing and visualising some of the **amazing, progressive and positive things happening around the world**. Trends and events and innovations we can’t always see when fixated on the negativity of the news.

We’ve spruced and updated some of data-visualisations from the original collection, as well as adding 160 more stories to be released over the next weeks, months, year and beyond!

Every graphic is of course underpinned by [open datasets](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/data/) to support full **evidence-based optimism.**

Swing by and join [our weekly newsletter](https://beautifulnews.myflodesk.com/newsletter) or daily on [the website](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/), or social channels of your choosing: [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/beautifulnews.daily), [Twitter/X](https://x.com/beautiful__news), [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/beautifulnewsdaily/), [Threads](https://www.threads.com/@beautifulnews.daily).

## Some of my favourite graphics and stories so far

» [34 Countries Now Generate 80% or More of Their Electricity from Renewables](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/3021-countries-electricity-renewables/)

» [Tons of new vaccines are in the pipeline](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/524-new-vaccines/)

» [Polio is very nearly wiped out](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/3037-polio-wiped-out/)

» [The Cost of Renewable Energy is Plunging](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/586-cost-renewables-falling/)

» [The EU Gender Pay Gap is (slowly) Decreasing](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/3030-eu-gender-pay-gap/)

» [Everyone, Everywhere, is Living Longer](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/41-everyone-everywhere-is-living-longer/)

**Towards a more nutritious information diet…**

David

items.body:
Calder Walton in *Harvard Kennedy Center Belfer Center Website:*

**Simon Sebag Montefiore** is one of Britain’s finest historians—a national treasure. In [The Cauldron](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/803078/the-cauldron-by-simon-sebag-montefiore/), he tackles a subject that lesser historians would not attempt: the making of the modern Middle East in all its bewildering complexity. The region is too large for a single national story, too diverse for a civilisational shorthand and too politically charged for comfortable detachment. Its history is usually broken into manageable pieces: the end of the Ottoman Empire, the creation of Israel, Arab nationalism, oil, political Islam and American intervention. Montefiore attempts something far more ambitious. In one sweeping narrative, he carries the reader from Morocco to Iran and from the capture of Riyadh in 1902 to the wars of 2026. The result is a remarkable feat: panoramic without becoming bloodless, learned without losing narrative momentum, and passionate without surrendering to partisanship.

More [↗ belfercenter.org](https://www.belfercenter.org/research-analysis/book-review-cauldron-and-making-modern-middle-east).

items.body:
The rhythmic skeletons of Ahwach, Gnawa and related musical traditions meet 808s, sampling and electronic production on **Cheb Runner** ‘s *80K*, retaining their physical force even as their shapes change. The result feels rooted in a specific place while constantly pushing beyond it. This is sound that has no borders, in keeping with the ethos of Beat Machine Records.

That approach has deep roots in Reda Senhaji’s own musical history. In an [interview with Giulio Pecci](https://sshhhpeaceful.substack.com/p/cheb-runner-immigration-has-given), Senhaji (aka Cheb Runner) recalls playing as a child in the streets of Ihchach in Agadir, making music from instruments, household objects and car parts, and later learning software in order to translate the rhythms he already had in his head into electronic form. He describes his tracks as emerging from street recordings, archived sounds and processed percussion before arriving at a “collision” with electronic music. *80K* makes that collision tactile. This is music that nourishes the hair follicles of the skin.

On “Iznagn Engines”, rhythm seems almost motorised, its cyclical momentum generating heat ripples as acoustic and synthetic percussion rub against one another. “Azn Oudrar” opens the music outward without dissipating its tension, while “Gn-Awa” is all glistening friction, metallic percussion locking into an intoxicating, heliotropic pulsing that seems perpetually drawn towards greater intensity. Yet the density never becomes oppressive: the album’s sleek electronic production acts as a sonic nictitating membrane, softening the relentless polyrhythmic Gnawa beats without blunting their impact.

The 808 becomes crucial to this balancing act. As the liner notes stress, it operates as a “structural force rather than an accent”, something especially apparent on “Afouss Adar 808”, where the electronic low end doesn’t sit beneath the traditional rhythmic language so much as enter into it. This is precisely the question the album raises: whether the distinction between traditional percussion and the drum machine remains particularly useful when both are being made to participate in the same rhythmic system. “Tarwan Ganga” deepens the rhythm into an auburn haze, locking the listener into a meditative trance, before Guedra Guedra’s closing reworking of “Gn-Awa” opens up and lifts the source material into a dreamy, solar finale.

This is the second release in the Terra Tempo series, which Beat Machine Records describes as “redefining the boundaries of global sound by blending rich cultural heritage with the dynamic energy of modern club beats.” Although the album cover depicts a number of instruments that AI has kindly idenfied for me as the qraqeb, the guembri / sintir, the tallunt / allun, and possibly the naqus, *80K* is far from an exercise in heritage preservation.

Speaking to Pecci, Cheb Runner describes Morocco as the endpoint of historical caravan routes and its rhythms as the product of a “multitude of tribes” and the interplay of cultures brought by migration. The album extends that process rather than merely representing it. The qraqeb, guembri, hand percussion, samples, machines and 808 belong to a continuum in which inherited forms remain alive precisely because they can be transformed. Intoxicating and intensely physical, *80K* treats tradition as a living source of energy. ( **Gianmarco Del Re** )
