items.body: AI and multiomics can describe therapeutic cell and extracellular-vesicle (EV) products and the postischemic environment, but a molecular signature matters only if it changes a defined development or treatment decision. Existing reviews address stroke single-cell and spatial biology, AI in stem-cell multiomics, or AI-enabled regenerative engineering. This critical narrative review connects those topics through three decisions: whether a finished product has reproducible activity, which host conditions permit that activity, and whether a patient gains benefit attributable to treatment. We compare integration methods by their assumptions for paired, unpaired and mosaic data; distinguish Geneformer, scGPT, scFoundation and universal cell embeddings by input encoding and learning objective; and examine why larger pretraining has not produced consistent gains over simpler baselines. A worked EV-potency task specifies candidate functional labels, independent training units, controls and external validation. Representative stroke studies are mapped from molecular description through experimentally tested mechanisms to prediction of unseen product lots and controlled clinical benefit. The reviewed stroke and adjacent cerebrovascular literature includes AI-assisted molecular prioritization, computational graft-host analysis and automated behavior quantification, but does not establish an externally validated AI predictor of finished-product potency or treatment-attributable patient benefit. Cross-scale virtual-cell and heterogeneous protein representations offer transferable methods, not validated ischemic-repair models. The framework identifies the experiments needed to turn molecular associations into decisions with measurable biological value.

items.body: Memory consolidation during sleep is thought to build on processes initiated during encoding, but how encoding-related brain activity affects individual memories during sleep is unknown. Using targeted memory reactivation (TMR), we tested whether auditory cues elicit memory-related responses during sleep, whether encoding theta and delta power predict these responses, and whether encoding- and sleep-related measures predict long-term retention. Eighty-one healthy young adults learned sound-associated item-face/place pairs during electroencephalography (EEG). Memory was tested before sleep, 12 hours, and 5 days after encoding. During non-rapid eye movement sleep, a subset of learned sounds and novel control sounds were replayed. Item-level mixed-effects models assessed behavioural and EEG predictors of retention success, and item-level correlations related encoding to cue-induced power during sleep. Pre-sleep memory strength and encoding vividness predicted retention, with the vividness effect depending on encoding theta power. TMR did not improve memory and was associated with poorer retention of initially weak memories. Learned cues elicited stronger delta responses than novel sounds during sleep, yet cue-induced delta, theta, and sigma power did not predict retention. Encoding and sleep EEG power were unrelated and showed distinct scalp topographies. In a large item-level dataset, the sleeping brain distinguished learned from novel cues, but this processing did not translate into durable retention, which was instead determined at encoding. Encoding-related oscillations did not relate to memories preferentially reactivated or strengthened by sleep cueing. These findings caution against treating cue-induced sleep oscillations as markers of successful reactivation or consolidation.

Release: datasette-charts 0.2a0

I introduced this new charting plugin for Datasette yesterday. Today it's gained integration with Datasette Agent, so now you can ask chat for a chart and it will create one for you using the same underlying chart suggestion and generation tools.

Here's a demo video, recorded on agent.datasette.io where you can sign in with GitHub to try the plugin yourself:

Download the video (MP4)

I prompt Datasette Agent to "Use #stats to show sqlite-utils downloads over time as a chart" - where typing "#stats" opens a table search box. It shows me a chart inline in the chat, and when I click "Open in the chart builder" it opens the chart in a panel along with the table page. I use the table page to switch to a chart of "datasette", then when I ask the agent "what does the chart show?" it notices that I changed the content in the panel and describes the new Datasette chart to me.

Here's a Markdown export of the chat from the video.

We have had many words for heretics over the epochs — rebels, radicals, freethinkers — but they have always been the ones to dislodge humanity from the stagnation of the status quo, to illuminate our blind spots, dismantle our unexamined biases, and jolt us out of ou…
items.body:
### “If we are to be true and worthy heretics, we need not only new heads, but new hearts, and, most of all, that new emotional imagination… begotten of enlarged sympathies and a more sensitive habit of feeling.”

**UPDATE 2025: This book is now [back in print](https://www.amazon.com/Alpha-Omega-Jane-Ellen-Harrison/dp/1961341417/?tag=braipick-20) as the third title in [Marginalian Editions](https://www.themarginalian.org/editions/). When the Inquisition persecuted Galileo for advancing the rude truth that Earth is not the center of the universe, the charge against him was heresy — the same charge on which Joan of Arc was burned at the stake for her crusade for political reform. We have had many words for heretics over the epochs — rebels, radicals, freethinkers — but they have always been the ones to dislodge humanity from the stagnation of the status quo, to illuminate our blind spots, dismantle our unexamined biases, and jolt us out of our herd mentality. Without those devoted to seeing reality more clearly and possibility more wildly, we would still live in a world haunted by superstition and governed by dogma. The power and dignity of this most courageous human mindset is what the pioneering classicist Jane Ellen Harrison** (September 9, 1850–April 15, 1928), who brought the culture of Ancient Greece to the modern world, explores in her magnificent essay “Heresy and Humanity,” found in [Alpha and Omega](https://www.amazon.com/Alpha-Omega-Jane-Ellen-Harrison/dp/1961341417/?tag=braipick-20) ([public library](https://www.worldcat.org/title/769418)) — the out-of-print essay collection that gave us Harrison on [the art of growing older](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/09/10/jane-ellen-harrison-crabbed-age-and-youth-alpha-and-omega/), published just as humanity was being dehumanized by its first World War.

Jane Ellen Harrison

Harrison writes:

> The word “heretic” has still about it an emotional thrill — a glow reflected, it may be, from the fires at Smithfield, the ardours of those who were burnt at the stake for the love of an idea.
> Heresy, the Greek hairesis, was from the outset an eager, living word. The taking of a city, its expugnatio, is a hairesis; the choosing of a lot in life or an opinion, its electio, is a hairesis; always in the word hairesis there is this reaching out to grasp, this studious, zealous pursuit — always something personal, even passionate… To be a heretic today is almost a human obligation.

In a sentiment Bertrand Russell would echo in [timeless manifesto for freedom of thought](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/05/18/bertrand-russell-free-thought-propaganda-doubt/), Harrison adds:

> The gist of heresy is free personal choice in act, and specifically in thought — the rejection of traditional faiths and customs.

Art by Olivier Tallec from [Louis I, King of the Sheep](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/10/14/louis-i-king-of-the-sheep-olivier-tallec/)

A century and a half after Emerson inveighed that [“masses are rude, lame, unmade, pernicious in their demands and influence,”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/05/04/emerson-masses/) she considers what makes heresy so difficult yet so necessary to the health of society:

> All traditional views are held with such tenacity, such almost ferocity, because they belong to the class of views induced, not by individual experience, still less by reason, but by collective, or, as it is sometimes called “herd,” suggestion. This used to be called “faith.” The belief so held may or may not be true; collective suggestion is not in the least necessarily collective hallucination. Mere collective suggestions — that is the interesting point — have the quality of obviousness; they do not issue from the individual, but seem imposed from outside, and ineluctable; they have all the inevitableness of instinctive opinion… Hence they are held with an intensity of emotion far beyond any reasoned conviction. To doubt them is felt to be at once idiocy and irreverence. Inquiry into their rational bases is naturally, and in a sense rightly, resented, because they are not rationally based, though they may be rationally supported. It is by convictions such as this that a society of the homogenous kind — a society based on and held together by uniformity — lives and thrives. To attack them is to cripple and endanger its inmost life.

Observing that the development of science is what pivoted heresy from damnable to desirable in society, Harrison contrasts sensemaking by empiricism with sensemaking by authority:

> Science classifies, draws ever clearer distinctions; herd-suggestion is always in a haze. Herd-suggestion is all for tradition, authority; science has for its very essence the exercise of free thought. So long as we will not take the trouble to know exactly and intimately, we may not — must not — choose… We must follow custom; we must accept the mandates of [those] who enforce tradition.
> […]
> Science opens wide the doors that turned so slowly on tradition’s hinges, and opens them on clean, quiet places where we breathe larger air… It is well to remember our debt to science — our inward and spiritual as well as material debt.

Art by [Rockwell Kent](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/02/15/rockwell-kent-wilderness/), 1919. (Available as [a print](https://society6.com/product/the-star-lighter-by-rockwell-kent-1919_print?curator=brainpicker) and as [stationery cards](https://society6.com/brainpicker/cards?sort=new?curator=brainpicker).)

And yet, Harrison argues, the heretic needs more than science — the heretic needs humanity. She writes:

> Science broke the binding spell of herd-suggestion. For that great boon let us now and ever bless and praise her holy name. She cleared the collective haze, she drew sharp distinctions, appealing to individual actual experience, to individual powers of reasoning. But by neither individual sense — perception nor ratiocination alone do we live. Our keenest emotional life is through the herd, and hence it was that, at the close of the last century, the flame of scientific hope, the glory of scientific individualism that had blazed so brightly, somehow died down and left a strange chill. Man rose up from the banquet of reason and law unfed. He hungered half unconsciously for the herd. It seemed an impasse: on the one side orthodoxy, tradition, authority, practical slavery; on the other science, individual freedom, reason, and an aching loneliness.
> […]
> We live now just at the transition moment; we have broken with the old, we have not quite adjusted ourselves to the new. It is not so much the breaking with the old faiths that makes us restless as the living in a new social structure.

Art by Olivier Tallec from [Louis I, King of the Sheep](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/10/14/louis-i-king-of-the-sheep-olivier-tallec/)

…

items.body:
Many farmers and ranchers in eastern Colorado are curious about artificial intelligence, but they don’t have a local tech-savvy person to show them how to use it. Xue “Alice” Dong has made that her job.

Dong, an IEEE senior member, is an extension regional specialist with the Colorado State University Extension, CSU’s outreach arm. She works in Logan County and serves a 10-county farming area in Colorado’s northeast corner. Her job is to turn university research into practical help for the people who live there.

Xue “Alice” Dong

Employer

Colorado State University Extension in Logan County

Title

Extension regional specialist

Member grade

Senior member

Alma maters

Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global

She built the AI-Powered Agritourism Chatbot (AgriTourismAI.com), which helps farmers and ranchers launch and run “agritourism” businesses. Agritourism is when farmers open their property to visitors for fun, education, or shopping events. Familiar examples include pick-your-own fruit orchards, lessons on how to grow vegetables, and sales of handmade products.

Dong also teaches workshops where she shows farmers and ranchers how they can use AI tools to help grow and manage their business.

She says she sees herself as a link between the university and the countryside.

“We [extension specialists] act as a bridge,” she says. “We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”

Many farmers and ranchers are older, and they typically have no technical training. Often their children and grandchildren have left the farm to work in a city or otherwise aren’t around to teach them about new tools. Without help, the benefits of AI could pass the farmers by. Dong’s workshops give them a way in.

Dong was named a finalist in the 2026 GenAI for Good Challenge for her AgriPivot AI Agent. The challenge was organized by IEEE Humanitarian Technologies and theU.N.’s International Telecommunication Union, and her project was selected from 318 teams across 79 countries. She also won the 2026 Award for Innovation from the National Extension Technology Community (NETC), and both the 2025 national and Western regional Educational Technology Awards from the National Association of Community Development Extension Professionals (NACDEP).

She has secured seven competitive grants totaling more than US $250,000 as principal investigator or co-principal investigator, including funding supported by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture.

An early love of design and problem-solving

Dong was born in Beijing. Both her parents are doctors.

As a child, she liked drawing new and inventive things. Sketching, she says, lets her picture solutions to problems in her head and put them on paper as practical designs.

That habit grew into a way of relating to her surroundings.

“I’ve always had a passion to create something tangible that can solve problems in the real world,” she says.

She doesn’t credit a single mentor for the direction her life has taken. Instead, she says all her teachers helped lay the groundwork for her career.

She attended the Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot, an institution that trains teachers. She earned two bachelor’s degrees there in 2013—one in geographical science and one in education.

She then earned a master’s degree in curriculum and instruction from Beijing Normal University in 2016.

That year, she moved to the United States to continue her graduate studies at the State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse. She earned a master’s degree in environmental biology in 2020.

From outreach to extension work

After earning her second master’s degree, she joined Paul Smith’s College, in Paul Smiths, N.Y., as an education and outreach coordinator.

She managed several national watershed projects to protect rivers, lakes, and aquifers. Watersheds are areas of land from which water drains into bodies of water.

She also undertook invasive-species-prevention projects, wrote grants to secure project funding, and designed two educational websites and several outreach publications. One website, Maintain the Chain, helps lake residents, boaters, and visitors from around the world keep invasive species out of the Fulton Chain of Lakes in New York’s Adirondack Park.

In 2022, she joined Stewards of the Coast and Redwoods as program manager. The nonprofit, based in Guerneville, Calif., works with California State Parks to protect, restore, and educate the public about the parks along Sonoma County’s coast and the Russian River area. The region is known for its redwood forests, wineries, and resort towns.

She left in 2023 to join the CSU Extension as a regional specialist, a title she still holds.

Her employer is part of the Cooperative Extension System, a nationwide network run by land-grant universities, schools founded with federal grants to teach farming and other practical subjects. Extension faculty and staff share what researchers at their universities learn with the citizens of those states.

The cooperative system operates on three levels. It is overseen federally by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture, managed statewide through land-grant universities, and delivered locally by county offices and Extension agents across more than 3,000 counties.

The work goes well beyond farming, Dong says, also covering community and economic development, health initiatives, and the 4-H program, which teaches children hands-on skills in agriculture, science, leadership, and citizenship.

Extension faculty members’ performance is judged on their research, teaching, and service to the community, Dong says—similar to the way professors in academia are evaluated. The difference, she says, is the audience: Professors teach students; most extension specialists teach adults, including farmers, ranchers, and community leaders. The setting is different, too. Dong doesn’t commute from the campus to the countryside; she lives and works in it. Her office is in Sterling, a small rural town. But her projects serve the whole state, and many of the people she helps live one to four hours’ drive away. So, most of her work with farmers and ranchers happens by email, phone, and virtual meetings. County fairs, farmers markets, and agricultural events give her chances to meet large groups of them in person.

She can’t just hand Colorado residents research findings and expect them to figure out the information they need, she says.

“We need to translate that research into something more practical, and easier to use, that farmers and ranchers can understand immediately,” she says.

items.body:
## Re-Design

Wer den Kuketz-Blog in den vergangenen Wochen regelmäßig besucht hat, dürfte es bemerkt haben: Hier hat sich einiges verändert. Was ursprünglich mit ein paar kleineren Anpassungen begann, ist schließlich zu einer umfassenden Überarbeitung des gesamten WordPress-Themes geworden. Sowohl auf dem Smartphone als auch auf dem Tablet und Desktop präsentiert sich der Blog nun in einem neuen Gewand.

Dabei ging es mir nicht einfach darum, alles etwas moderner oder schicker aussehen zu lassen. Im Mittelpunkt stand die Frage, wie sich die vielen Inhalte übersichtlicher, angenehmer und möglichst ohne unnötige Ablenkung darstellen lassen.

## Weniger Ballast, mehr Übersicht

Die [Startseite](https://www.kuketz-blog.de/) wurde grundlegend neu gestaltet. Kurzbeiträge und ausführliche Artikel sind nun deutlicher voneinander getrennt und werden in einer übersichtlichen Kachelansicht präsentiert. Auch die Navigation, die Suche, die Darstellung einzelner Beiträge und zahlreiche kleinere Elemente wurden überarbeitet. Wer lieber chronologisch stöbert, findet sämtliche Veröffentlichungen weiterhin in der [Sitemap](https://www.kuketz-blog.de/sitemap/).

Auf größeren Bildschirmen ist die bisherige Seitenleiste verschwunden. Stattdessen bekommen die Inhalte mehr Raum. Auf mobilen Geräten wurde die Darstellung ebenfalls umfassend angepasst. Alles soll besser zusammenpassen und unabhängig von der Bildschirmgröße ein möglichst einheitliches Erscheinungsbild bieten.

Auch unter der Haube hat sich einiges getan. Zahlreiche Altlasten wurden entfernt, bestehende Funktionen vereinfacht und der Code aufgeräumt. An einem Grundsatz halte ich dabei weiterhin fest: Das Theme kommt ohne JavaScript aus. Für eine gut funktionierende Webseite braucht es schließlich nicht für jede Kleinigkeit ein zusätzliches Skript.

## Über Geschmack lässt sich streiten

Natürlich ist mir bewusst, dass ein neues Design nicht jedem gefallen wird. Manche mochten die bisherige Darstellung, andere werden sich erst an die neue Aufteilung gewöhnen müssen. Das ist völlig in Ordnung. Gestaltung ist immer auch Geschmackssache, und Veränderungen brauchen manchmal etwas Zeit.

Mir war vor allem wichtig, dass der Blog seinen Charakter behält. Er soll kein überladenes Nachrichtenportal werden, sondern ein Ort, an dem Inhalte im Mittelpunkt stehen. Mit möglichst wenig Ablenkung, einer klaren Struktur und einer angenehmen Lesbarkeit.

Ob mir das gelungen ist, müsst letztlich ihr entscheiden.

## Fertig – aber Feedback ist willkommen

Die Überarbeitung ist inzwischen abgeschlossen. Das neue Design steht und ich bin mit dem Ergebnis zufrieden. Trotzdem kann sich bei einer so umfangreichen Umgestaltung natürlich irgendwo noch ein kleiner Fehler eingeschlichen haben. Gerade unterschiedliche Browser, Geräte und Bildschirmgrößen bringen manchmal Überraschungen mit sich.

Deshalb freue ich mich über eure Rückmeldungen. Was gefällt euch? Was könnte besser sein? Und falls euch Darstellungsfehler oder andere Probleme auffallen, gebt mir gerne über die [Kontaktseite](https://www.kuketz-blog.de/kontakt/) Bescheid. Besonders hilfreich sind konkrete Hinweise, möglichst mit einem Screenshot.

Auch kritische Rückmeldungen sind ausdrücklich willkommen. Schließlich soll der Blog nicht nur mir gefallen, sondern vor allem für euch gut funktionieren.

Eines bleibt bei aller Veränderung unverändert: Der Kuketz-Blog steht weiterhin für unabhängige, kritische und möglichst verständliche Beiträge rund um IT-Sicherheit, Datenschutz und digitale Selbstbestimmung.

Die Verpackung ist neu. Der Anspruch bleibt derselbe.

Viel Freude beim Lesen und Stöbern!

👇

items.body:
On a summer day at UC Berkeley, four teenagers jostled at a whiteboard, vying to write down their solutions to an important public health concern. They were having fun even as they took on a heavy task: helping researchers design programs to reduce the skyrocketing suicide rate among Black youth.

In the United States, deaths by suicide have been surging among Black kids and teens for decades. For those between 10 and 17 years of age, the suicide rate [rose 144% from 2007 to 2020](https://publichealth.jhu.edu/sites/default/files/2023-08/2023-august-still-ringing-alarm.pdf). What’s more, Black boys die by suicide more than twice as frequently as Black girls, although the suicide rate for Black girls [increased by 182% between 2001 and 2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10900-019-00678-x).

As the teenagers brainstormed, [Jasmin Brooks Stephens](https://psychology.berkeley.edu/people/jasmin-brooks-stephens), a Berkeley assistant professor of psychology, watched nearby. The moment was a highlight in research she was conducting with the Homeless Children’s Network on improving mental health outcomes for Black youth. Brooks Stephens believed that teens themselves have meaningful ideas to share, and she had worked for eight weeks with these particular teenagers, who were part of the network’s [Jabali Youth Advocacy](https://www.hcnkids.org/jabali-youth-advocacy) organization, culminating in their trip to campus.

“One of the most exciting things was seeing them all jump up and say, ‘Wait, we can make a program for making us feel better? We have the power to do that?’” Brooks Stephens recalled. “Seeing them find and discover that sense of agency in themselves—that was invaluable to me.” It also was one of the few times any of the teens had visited a college campus, she said, an added bonus. In future work, Brooks Stephens plans to translate the results of her study for clinicians and policymakers who are trying to improve suicide prevention for Black youth.

The ongoing project is just one example of how Brooks Stephens is working to address rising suicide rates among Black youth by engaging them in participatory research—an unusual and hopeful approach in suicide prevention studies. “This summer I had the incredible opportunity to work alongside young people to design a program that would help other young people want to live,” she said. “Rather than waiting until a young person is already in crisis, I’m interested in understanding what helps youth thrive—what gives them hope and a sense of possibility and helps them recognize the brilliance they have inside them.”

## A pathway to hope in the face of racism

Despite the growing crisis among Black youth, [suicide rates are dropping for adolescents in the U.S. overall](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt57150/2025-nsduh-annual-national-report.pdf). Brooks Stephens finds these statistics revealing: “To me, that suggests that the approaches we have relied on have not adequately addressed the conditions driving suicide risk in Black communities,” she said.

It’s easy to talk about [structural racism](https://news.berkeley.edu/2025/08/14/watch-berkeley-scholar-explain-structural-racism/) as an abstract concept, or personal encounters with racists as disturbing but bounded moments. But grappling with racism heavily impacts Black youth and increases their suicide risk, according to a 2023 report from the [Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health](https://publichealth.jhu.edu/sites/default/files/2023-08/2023-august-still-ringing-alarm.pdf). Indeed, Brooks Stephens has published work documenting how racial discrimination and the COVID-19 pandemic, which disproportionately harmed Black Americans, together [worsened suicide risk for Black young adults](https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2025-01327-001).

Brooks Stephens’s work is informed by both her research and her own experience of how race can shape young people’s sense of self. “I became aware very early on that Black children are often navigating expectations about who they are supposed to be before they have even had the opportunity to figure out who they are for themselves,” she said. “That has stayed with me—the importance of creating space for Black young people to define themselves, recognize their strengths, and imagine who they want to become.” At the same time, she saw how the stigma surrounding mental health could make it harder for Black youth and families to seek support, even as racism and other chronic stressors were impacting their well-being.

When she took an African American psychology class as an undergraduate at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, with Enrique Neblett, a renowned scholar of race and health who became her mentor, Brooks Stephens saw the connection between those experiences—and found her passion. “I realized that there was an entire field devoted to understanding how racism affects mental health and how Black children come to understand themselves and their racial identity,” she said.

Later, during her doctoral research at the University of Houston, Brooks Stephens worked with Rheeda Walker, an expert on suicide science and African American adult mental health research. Brooks Stephens noticed that there was very limited discussion about building upstream resilience in suicide prevention research—an approach that focuses on child well-being and happiness before the development of a mental health crisis.

“We’re studying why people choose to end their life without understanding what makes people want to live,” she said. For Brooks Stephens, that realization opened up a different way of thinking about suicide prevention, one that made room for the strengths that were often absent from traditional models, such as racial identity, spirituality, family connection, belonging, or hope.

## Focusing on strengths to prevent suicide

Brooks Stephens knows she can’t single-handedly eliminate the racial traumas faced by young Black people. Nor can she end other factors that lead to higher suicide rates in her community, such as systemic injustice or poverty. Instead, she’s focusing on where she can make a difference through her research.

“While I may not be able to eradicate racism, I can help build programs that change how Black young people see themselves and their futures—programs that help them feel grounded in their identity and able to imagine a life that feels worth living,” she said.

*Brooks Stephens and her colleagues identified six positive factors that reduce suicidality among Black youth (courtesy of Jasmin Brooks Stephens).*

items.body:
For poet Chase Twichell, Zen practice and writing have long been deeply intertwined. “Zen is said to be a ‘mind-to-mind transmission,’” she told the [Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/chase-twichell). “The best poems are exactly that: They leap from one mind to another without stopping to explain exactly how they did it.... In our culture, out of necessity, we’re used to living in a mostly literal mind, and poetry demands that we enter it with another kind of mind.”

Her latest collection, [The World It Was](https://www.coppercanyonpress.org/books/the-world-it-was-by-chase-twichell/), offers one such opportunity to access another kind of mind—one carefully attuned to grief, transience, and environmental destruction. Composed in the wake of the Covid pandemic, the collection consists of restrained, nearly skeletal elegies—for her late husband, for her aging body, and for the Earth itself—that look directly at suffering and ask how to live in the face of seemingly all-pervasive loss (or, as the book’s description states, “being fully alive inside the brief body and the dying world”).

Though this question is of course unanswerable, the poetic worlds that Twichell builds suggest that [attention](https://tricycle.org/magazine/attention-means-attention/) plays a key role in figuring out a way forward. “Zen and poetry have both taught me that the quality of attention we pay to the world is crucial,” Twichell[said in a 2016 interview](https://ashberyland.com/2016/11/19/poetry-and-life-an-interview-with-chase-twitchell/). “Of course there are many ways to make people see the damage we’ve done, and poetry is only one of them. But to me, it’s the arrow that most deeply pierces my consciousness.” *The World It Was* presents sixty-seven such arrows: invitations to embody a different kind of mind, and, in the process, relearn what it means to exist fully in a world defined by impermanence.

*–Sarah Fleming, senior editor*

## The World It Was

I was a kid transfixed by

the endlessly mutating

gloomy rooms among the trees,

and I wandered far.

At seventeen, I married thunder

and wind and snow. I took vows.

I pledged to be only half human,

so only half guilty of our crimes

against Earth and all its beings.

Wherever I am, I visit Earth’s memorial.

Sometimes I leave a few words

in the dirt on a car.

The memorial surrounds us.

Earth’s body is also its grave.

## Death’s Hors d’Oeuvres

A school of dead gray fish drifts

across my vision—floaters.

No names come when I call.

Is this what old age will be like?

No, this is old age now.

I like to take little sips of the horror,

morsels of poisoned meat,

each taste a foretaste.

I’m preparing for future pain,

not this pain.

That’s the lie I tell myself.

## I Can’t Make Sense of It

In one of these many centuries,

my words fell briefly through the air.

A flurry, among many flurries.

I can’t make sense of it:

the word-bearing trees

grew older, bore less and less fruit.

Birds carrying the twigs of poems

still fly in from time to time

but they don’t nest here anymore.

## Flower of False Starts

It’s a strange flower,

the flower of false starts.

I dress in its withered petals.

Each knob on the stem

is the scar of a flower

that never fully bloomed.

Or it bloomed, but the flower

was not the flower I dreamed.

It’s almost all stem now.

Withered petals—pretty dress.

The flower is nearing

the end of its life.

Each poem leaves a scar.

## Solitaire

When Russell was dying

I sat beside his bed

playing solitaire on my phone,

practicing his not being there.

I liked the way the cards came

in quick cold cascades of numbers,

clusters of luck,

and I could visit that bright flow

day or night.

I liked the way the game was

always starting over, always

not quite daybreak on the screen,

the longest time until dark.

♦

*“The World It Was,” “Death’s Hors d’Oeuvres,” “I Can’t Make Sense of It,” “Flower of False Starts,” and “Solitaire” from* [The World It Was](https://www.coppercanyonpress.org/books/the-world-it-was-by-chase-twichell/) *, copyright 2026 by Chase Twichell, used by permission of Copper Canyon Press.*

items.subtitle: As Rane turns 45, Rick Jeffs tells the story of the Steelworkerz, the TTM 54 and the magnetic crossfader, and gives his view on AI in DJing.

items.body:
*As Rane turns 45, Rick Jeffs tells the story of the Steelworkerz, the TTM 54 and the magnetic crossfader, and gives his view on AI in DJing.*

Rane was founded in 1981 and released its first DJ mixer in 1986 at the request of Richard Long, the sound designer for [Studio 54](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_54), among many other clubs. This was the beginning of what is now 40+ years of innovation for the DJ market, a CV that includes milestones like the world’s first magnetic crossfader, dual USB connectivity for seamless multi-laptop handoffs, and much more.

As Rane celebraes 45 years in the business, we spoke with Rick Jeffs, Principal Design Engineer at Rane, to get the inside scoop behind Rane’s biggest technical achievements. This interview has been edited for brevity and consistency.

**Attack: Rane began in 1981 and released its first DJ mixer, the [MP 24](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/mp24evo.html), in 1986. Technologically, what are the biggest changes in the world of mixers since then? **

Rick Jeffs: The MP 24 came from a very different time. It was a purely analog design built with little more than op-amps, resistors, and capacitors. There was no firmware to write, no software applications to support, and no computer drivers to maintain. If a DJ wanted to play a song, they needed the vinyl record in their hands.

Today, nearly everything has changed. Modern mixers digitize audio as it enters the product, perform most processing in the digital domain, and convert the signal back to analog at the outputs. Digital processing eliminates many of the limitations and tolerances of analog circuitry while making advanced features practical and affordable. Controls are monitored by MCUs, enabling more precise operation and far greater flexibility.

The biggest change may be the connection between the mixer and the computer. Dual USB ports allow two DJs to connect simultaneously, while software platforms such as Serato and Engine provide access to enormous music libraries, streaming services, real-time effects, and advanced performance tools. DJs no longer need to transport hundreds of pounds of vinyl to every gig. Instead, virtually unlimited amounts of music can travel on a laptop, SSD, or media stick.

Rick Jeffs, Principal Design Engineer at Rane

**Let's talk about how Rane became associated with turntablism. The story goes that a group of New York turntablists sent you a hand-drawn diagram for a new mixer, and Rane engineers flew to New York to meet them. What happened that day?**

Rane has always been involved in the DJ market, with early products such as the X3000 Isolator, X5000 Equalizer, and MP 24 mixer.

The Steelworkerz DJ crew approached Rane with an ambitious idea: build the ultimate scratch mixer. Intrigued by the opportunity, we flew to New York to meet with them and explore what such a product might look like. Our first meeting took place at a Tableturns event in lower Manhattan, an open-format competition where local DJs showcased their creativity, technical ability, and performance skills. The Steelworkerz crew included Brian Lane (Big Wiz), Doug Coen (Sugarcuts), Marz1, and Peter Parker.

The experience was unlike anything I had encountered before. Our taxi dropped us off in a dark alley in front of a large steel door. When we knocked, a massive bouncer opened the door, looked us over, and said, “You don't belong here.” After we explained that we had been invited by the Steelworkerz to discuss a new mixer project, his expression immediately changed, and we were warmly welcomed inside.

That evening was my first introduction to true performance scratch mixing and turntablist culture. What I witnessed was far beyond simply playing records. The DJs were using turntables as musical instruments, combining technical precision, creativity, and showmanship in ways I had never seen before. The following night, we met with members of the Steelworkerz in an apartment in the South Bronx, where we sketched ideas and discussed what they believed the ideal battle mixer should be.

Rane recognized an opportunity. The turntablist community was growing rapidly, yet the available mixers often lacked the features DJs were requesting and frequently suffered from durability issues under the demands of competition-style performance. The result was the [TTM 54](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/pdf/old/ttm54man.pdf), which delivered many of the features turntablists had been asking for.

The TTM 56 followed and introduced what would become one of the most significant innovations in DJ mixer design: **the industry's first non-contact magnetic crossfader**. Combined with improved full-cut channel faders, the magnetic design delivered dramatically better reliability, consistency, and performance than traditional contact-based faders.

The innovations did not stop there. Later Rane products introduced dual USB connectivity, allowing two DJs to remain connected simultaneously and perform seamless handoffs between laptops without interrupting the music. Like the magnetic crossfader before it, dual USB support would eventually become a widely adopted feature throughout the DJ industry.

Looking back, that trip to New York marked the beginning of Rane's transformation from a company known primarily for professional audio products into a leader in the emerging performance DJ market.

[quote align=right text="The DJs were using turntables as musical instruments, combining technical precision, creativity, and showmanship in ways I had never seen before."]

The Steelworkerz crew

**The magnetic crossfader is an important design in Rane's history. How did you settle on magnetism as a method? **

Several technologies were considered, including resistive, inductive, optical, and magnetic sensing. I chose the magnetic approach because it offered the best combination of robustness, performance, and simplicity. It was largely immune to the environmental contamination that often affected conventional faders, while avoiding the complexity associated with optical systems.

Over time, we continued to refine the design, eventually implementing more advanced magnetic sensing methods with improved linearity and resolution. What began as a solution to a reliability problem ultimately became one of the defining technologies of the TTM series and helped establish a new performance standard for DJ mixers.

**Is it correct that modern mixers don't pass audio through the faders/crossfaders, but instead use them to send signals that control the amplifier, which is why there can be different fader curves, reverse control, etc.? Why is this better? **

items.body:
Eine „Wissenschafts-NATO“ gegen politische Eingriffe, Kritik an einem Impulspapier des Wissenschaftsrats und eine Studie zu überlasteten Forschenden: Das Wisskomm-Update gibt alle 14 Tage einen Überblick über aktuelle Themen, Debatten und Trends.

### Was gibt’s Neues?

**Angela Ittel wirbt für eine „Wissenschafts-Nato“**

Die Präsidentin der TU Braunschweig, Angela Ittel, spricht sich für einen länderübergreifenden Beistand zum Schutz der Wissenschaftsfreiheit aus. Anlass sind Pläne der AfD, die Gleichstellungsarbeit an Hochschulen einzuschränken und Mittel für die Geschlechter- und Klimaforschung zu kürzen. Sollten die Gleichstellungsbeauftragten in Sachsen-Anhalt aus dem Hochschulgesetz gestrichen werden, erwartet Ittel von anderen Hochschulen und der Allianz der Wissenschaftsorganisationen öffentliche Rückendeckung und konkrete Unterstützung. Das sagte die Universitätspräsidentin [im Interview mit Anna-Lena Scholz](https://www.zeit.de/2026/48/gleichstellung-hochschulen-angela-ittel-afd?).

Den weiterhin großen Bedarf an Gleichstellungsarbeit begründet Ittel mit dem sinkenden Frauenanteil über die wissenschaftlichen Karrierestufen hinweg. In der Medizin liege der Anteil der Studentinnen teils bei 70 Prozent, während nur jede zehnte Professur mit einer Frau besetzt sei. 126 Hochschulen hätten 2024 eine Selbstverpflichtung der Hochschulrektorenkonferenz für Gleichstellungsmaßnahmen unterzeichnet. Nun würde bei Berufungen dokumentiert, wie viele Frauen sich bewerben, eingeladen werden und eine Stelle erhalten. Die Wirksamkeit einzelner Maßnahmen werde derzeit untersucht.

**NaWik-Trialog: Wie kommt Wissenschaft in die Politik?**

Wie arbeiten Wissenschaft und Politik optimal zusammen und welche Kompetenzen benötigen Wissenschaftler*innen, um ihre Erkenntnisse in die Politik zu tragen? Über diese Fragen diskutierten Armin Grunwald, Katrin Rehak-Nitsche und Richard Fuchs am 4. November beim [NaWik*-Trialog](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hj8qquMHEtU) „Politik & Wissenschaft“.

Dass politische Entscheidungen wissenschaftlich fundiert sein sollten, darüber waren sich alle drei Diskutant*innen einig. Doch wie gelingt es Wissenschaftler*innen ihre Expertise einzubringen? „Gute Politikberatung ist eine Langstrecke“, sagt Fuchs, Wissenschaftsjournalist, Medientrainer und Berater für Wissensorganisationen. Politische Autorität müssen sich Wissenschaftler*innen erarbeiten. Zunächst sollten sich Forschende klarmachen: „Wissenschaft und Politik ticken anders“. Wissenschaftliche Projekte hätten häufig einen langen Vorlauf, während Politik schnelle Ergebnisse wolle. Das könne für Wissenschaftler*innen frustrierend sein. Für eine erfolgreiche Politikberatung sollten Forschende die Arbeitsweise, Bedürfnisse und zeitlichen Zwänge politischer Entscheidungsträger*innen verstehen.

Grunwald, der das Institut für Technikfolgenabschätzung und das Büro für Technikfolgenabschätzung beim Bundestag am Karlsruher Institut für Technologie (KIT)* leitet, findet es zudem wichtig, die verschiedenen Rollen zu verstehen: „Wir wollen nicht, wir können nicht, wir dürfen nicht die besseren Politiker sein wollen.“ Forschende könnten Politiker*innen nur bei ihrer Entscheidungsfindung unterstützen. Dafür ist laut Fuchs ein Perspektivwechsel wichtig. Forscher*innen müssten sich überlegen, was Politiker*innen von ihnen benötigen.

Laut der Politikerin und Landtagsabgeordneten aus Rheinland-Pfalz, Rehak-Nitsche, werden vor allem konkrete Handlungsoptionen und Lösungsvorschläge benötigt. Forschende sollten dafür gezielt auf fachpolitische Sprecher*innen, Ausschüsse oder auch lokale Abgeordnete zugehen. Dabei sollten ihre wissenschaftlichen Ergebnisse aber realistischen Erwartungen entsprechen. Die Diskutierenden kritisierten überzogene wissenschaftliche Versprechen, da diese die Glaubwürdigkeit schmälern. Außerdem sollten die Ergebnisse priorisiert werden, zum Beispiel mit einer zentralen Botschaft pro Studie. Diese sollten Forschende verständlich kommunizieren können.

Wie das in der Praxis aussieht? Das lest ihr in unserem [Interview mit dem Politikwissenschaftler Daniel Wiesner](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/wie-politik-wissenschaft-in-debatten-einsetzt-101497/) über wissenschaftliche Inhalte in österreichischen Parlamentsdebatten.

**Kritik am Impulspapier des Wissenschaftsrats**

Welchen Beitrag kann und soll Wissenschaft zur freiheitlich-demokratischen Gesellschaft leisten? Anfang November hat der Wissenschaftsrat zu dieser Frage ein [Impulspapier](https://www.wissenschaftsrat.de/SharedDocs/Pressemitteilungen/DE/PM_2026/PM_2426?nn=68873b8321233a04bb97cedd&wt_zmc=nl.int.zonaudev.112331552451_555074179233.nl_ref) veröffentlicht. Zu den Impulsen zählen Fragen zur Balance zwischen wissenschaftlicher Selbstbestimmung und gesellschaftlichen Erwartungen sowie zu Werten und Wertekonflikten in der Wissenschaft. Der Rat sieht den Anlass darin, dass demokratische Institutionen und der gesellschaftliche Zusammenhalt zunehmend unter Druck stünden: „Wissenschaftliche Erkenntnisse werden infrage gestellt, einzelne Wissenschaftlerinnen und Wissenschaftler bedrängt und angefeindet.“

Der Wissenschaftsrat versteht das Impulspapier als „Plädoyer und als Anstoß zur Debatte“, um Thesen, Anregungen und Spannungsverhältnisse offenzulegen. Diese sollen gemeinsam mit Wissenschaft, Politik und Gesellschaft erörtert werden. Gelegenheit dazu soll unter anderem ein gemeinsames Symposium im nächsten Frühjahr bieten. Bei [Table Media](https://table.media/research/thema-des-tages/wissenschaft-und-die-demokratie-welche-diskussionen-der-wissenschaftsrat-anstossen-moechte) bemängeln teils anonyme Kritiker*innen, dass das Papier vor allem Fragen stellt, wo längst Entscheidungen und Reformen gefragt wären. Johannes Vogel, Direktor des Naturkundemuseums Berlin, [fordert](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/m-weisskopf_wissenschaft-demokratie-symposium-share-7524013244613603328-UDsU/?utm_source=share&utm_medium=member_desktop&rcm=ACoAABrhP4ABM9rIpbs8S5tg0GHwDJPz18tv5aQ) etwa: „Die Diskussionen zu den genannten Themen führen wir teilweise seit zehn Jahren oder noch länger.“ Es sei nun keine Zeit mehr für teils systembewahrende Debatten, sondern für Experimente, Lernen, Mut und Handeln.

### Und sonst?

Ein KI-basiertes Tool könnte zukünftig Creator*innen beim **Factchecking** ihrer Inhalte unterstützen. Dabei würden Informationen eine Art „Nutri-Score für Social Media“ erhalten, die ihren Wahrheitsgehalt signalisieren sollen. [Im Podcast](https://www.podcast.de/episode/709350253/nutri-score-fuer-social-media-wer-bestimmt-kuenftig-was-im-feed-als-vertrauenswuerdig-gilt) spricht Journalist Martin Fehrensen mit der Gründerin Malina Wiethaus über das Tool „TrustScored“.

items.body:
This is a weird moment. I have a hunch that we'll look back later and tell ourselves stories in which it seemed obvious where things were going. So I wanted to lay down a little time capsule and register just how confusing everything felt at the time. This is a personal view from the trenches.

1.

If you're a normal person, you may feel that AI has been good at math for a long time.[1]But for "real" math, this is roughly what it felt like:

When

Feeling

2024

LLMs are toys

Summer 2025

LLMs are interesting toys

Early Autumn 2025

LLMs can do useful stuff sometimes

Mid Autumn 2025

…a lot of stuff

Late Autumn 2025

…a lot

Early 2026

holy god

Even having been astonished by AI progress in the past, it was still astonishing to see AI move in a matter of months from a mildly-useful toy to something that many people now consider almost impossible to do without.

2.

Personally, I'd say that current AI makes me around 50% more productive at "doing math". That's despite the fact that AI can now often do in a few minutes things that would have taken me hours to do myself.

The main reason is that my concept of "doing math" involves various steps, like coming up with ideas for theorems, trying to prove them, writing things down, reorganizing everything to make it more clear, and so on. AI is good at some parts of this, but still pretty bad at others, so the overall speedup isn't as high as you might expect.

(Even if planes could go 10× faster, your door-to-door travel time from your apartment in London to your friend's place in Rome wouldn't decrease that much, because you still have to get to the airport and wait to board.)

3.

But then, I'm still (sort of; more on this later) trying to follow my old "doing math" workflow, just automating certain parts of it. That can't be right, can it?

If we found a way to make batteries at 1% of the current cost, we wouldn't just say, "cool, batteries are cheap now". We'd find all sorts of new ways to use batteries that didn't make sense before, and change the ways we generate power to account for all these new batteries. Probably our whole energy system would end up transformed. Analogously, AI being good at proofs should lead to a very different equilibrium. But what is that?[2]

4.

It seems healthy, at the moment, to maintain a fluid view of what "doing math" means. But at bare minimum it surely involves understanding the math that "I" am "doing". So long as that's part of the workflow, it would seem to impose a limit on how quickly "I" could "do" math, no matter how good AI is.

One obvious conclusion would be that my tiny organic brain should be removed from the workflow entirely. Maybe! But it's interesting to speculate about how much faster things could go while still keeping a human brain in the loop. I think the answer is: A lot.

5.

Contrary to what you may have heard, humans are not obsolete for math. Not yet. The most obvious reason is that AI is still bad at writing.

People often complain that AI writing overuses various patterns or lacks a unique voice or whatever. I don't disagree, but I always felt like there was a deeper issue that I couldn't quite put my finger on. With math, this becomes very clear: The problem is it doesn't make any goddamned sense.

Really, I think it's deeper than being bad "at writing". It seems like AI is bad at thinking in certain ways that manifest as bad writing.

6.

When novices do math, they often create "spaghetti-code math": Imagine a long document with lots of equations, but if you point at any one equation, it's hard to say what assumptions underpin it, or how it fits into the bigger picture. Any random idea that was mentioned 17 pages ago might be used again at any time with no warning. With experience, people learn to break complex arguments down into modular pieces with a good "API", in the sense that the assumptions and conclusions for each part are relatively simple.

Somehow, AI has developed these amazing technical skills, while still being bad at creating abstractions So the arguments it gives are long and tangled and bewildering. This is what makes AI math seem so alien.

7.

Now I know what you're thinking. Maybe AI isn't bad at creating abstractions. It's just bad at creating abstractions that work for you, human with tiny organic brain.

From a distance, that seems plausible. And it might be true to some degree. I have high-bandwidth access to a human brain. It's not crazy to imagine that this gives me an advantage in predicting how a human brain would react to a given presentation of ideas. But still, I claim that current AI is objectively bad at creating abstractions, regardless of if the consumer of those abstractions is human or artificial.

Here's why: If I ask AI to prove something hard, it will produce a proof that starts simple and gradually descends into a rampage of complexity. If I tell it to break that proof down into self-contained pieces, it will produce lemmas that each take a full page just to state. If I ask, "Why? Why have you done this to me?", the AI will say, "This is as simple as it gets. It's not that bad. What's your problem?"

But if I argue with the AI for a while, I can start to understand the basic contours of the argument. And I'll ask, "Why don't you first just try to prove blah using only assumptions blahblah, without worrying about blahblahblah? Wouldn't that be easier?" Often, this doesn't work, either because my idea was bad, or because the AI isn't smart enough to do it. (Which one? Who knows!) But after a few attempts, I can usually find something that that works, and the AI can use it to re-write the proof in a somewhat simpler way. If I repeat this many times, I can gradually chip away at the complexity.

But maybe that's still just making the proof easier for humans to understand? No! For one, this usually makes the proof shorter, and sometimes dramatically shorter. More importantly, during this process, someone (maybe me, maybe the AI) will often realize that there's a different proof strategy that gives a stronger result. Instead of proving x , now we can prove x . Thus, artisanal human abstractions are "objectively" useful.

8.

Some people might claim that it's already possible to automate some of what I'm doing with some multi-agent Rube Goldberg thing. I'm not sure, because my experience has been that investing lots of time into clever AGENTS.MD or custom skills or harnesses isn't a great use of time. That stuff is somewhat helpful, but things are changing so fast that the knowledge has a short half-life. Also, the majority of information about these tricks seems to come from people who are excited about the technology itself.

On the other hand, the automator told me to try typing, "ask independent agents for an adversarial review", and I've found those seven words to be quite helpful. I wish I could find a source with boring best practices for people who are happy to stay away from the bleeding edge.

9.

items.body:
Vernor Vinge is possibly my favorite science fiction author of all time.1 The Singularity, which he famously predicted would happen somewhere between 2005 and 2030, features heavily in most of [his stories](https://www.amazon.com/stores/Vernor-Vinge/author/B000APOW0E?ref=ap_rdr&shoppingPortalEnabled=true&ccs_id=8c9a5a85-687e-4609-8f62-c647a22cfbe5). It usually happens the same way: an Intelligence Explosion, of the type envisioned by [I.J. Good](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I._J._Good) — the smarter AI gets, the faster it’s able to make itself even smarter, meaning that AI becomes godlike nearly instantaneously once it reaches a certain threshold of capability.

Almost every discussion about AI safety that I hear in San Francisco or read in the tech blogosphere centers around this sort of event. The discussions are all about whether recursive self-improvement (RSI) is near, and whether we should “pace the frontier” — i.e., deliberately slow down or pause AI progress — to stop RSI from creating an intelligence explosion.

As I’ve listened to these arguments, I’ve grown increasingly skeptical that this is the right discussion we should be having. But before I explain why, let me quickly summarize the debate itself, to give an idea of what the arguments look like.

#### The intelligence explosion debate, in brief

In fact, I’ve published some pieces of that discussion on this blog. Back in September, Ramez Naam wrote a guest post arguing that an intelligence explosion is not imminent:

His basic arguments were:

- OpenAI data show that AI is still only able to automate short chunks of the AI research process.
- AI research is subject to diminishing returns, so that each increase in AI capability should buy less of a speedup in the pace of automated research.
- Diminishing returns also mean that accelerating AI progress will require exponentially more of other resources, such as compute and money.
- There’s no sign yet of an acceleration in the rate of AI progress.

In [a follow-up post](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/can-a-million-ai-agents-create-superintelligence), Ramez did a deeper dive on the topic of agent swarms, arguing that they’re not as effective as many people believe.

Theo Jaffee [echoed these arguments](https://x.com/theojaffee/status/2123231377177157992), noting that OpenAI’s data shows that AI hasn’t even been able to fully automate smaller research tasks yet:

Source: OpenAI via [Theo Jaffee](https://x.com/theojaffee/status/2123231377177157992)

Luis Garicano and Alex Imas also wrote a post downplaying the likelihood of an intelligence explosion:

[Silicon Continent Are we approaching an intelligence explosion? (Dear reader: this is an unusual post; it gets a bit technical. Alex and I are trying to do something hard here: look at the data and try to understand what they tell us about the intelligence explosion. There is math, Greek letters, and two models. So please bear with us, and if you are bored, apologies. We think it is worth making an exception here… Read more 12 days ago · 65 likes · 13 comments · Luis Garicano and Alex Imas](https://www.siliconcontinent.com/p/are-we-approaching-an-intelligence?utm_source=substack&utm_campaign=post_embed&utm_medium=web&embedding_publication_id=35345)

Their arguments are more economic in nature. They show that although AI progress has accelerated, it also shows diminishing returns in terms of research spending, meaning that every unit of progress has come with a higher price tag:

Source:[Garicano and Imas](https://www.siliconcontinent.com/p/are-we-approaching-an-intelligence)

They also estimate an economic model of RSI,2 and conclude that ideas in AI research are probably getting harder to find, reducing the likelihood of an intelligence explosion.

On the other side of the debate, we have [the recent METR report](https://metr.org/blog/2026-11-05-anthropic-ai-rd-acceleration-assessment/) about Anthropic’s internal progress in automating AI research. The report uses Anthropic’s own internal measure of AI capability, AECI, rather than the better-known public ECI. It also relies on data that aren’t public, meaning that deciding how much of the report to believe requires a lot of guesswork and assumption-making. But the basic story METR tells is that Claude is already speeding up Anthropic’s research process by a lot:

> As we describe below, we were able to confidently determine that the acceleration [of AI progress in late 2025] was not due to an acceleration in the rate of growth of training compute…We guess that a majority (perhaps ≈80%) of the current…acceleration is due to AI.

Dwarkesh Patel, meanwhile, argues that AI research isn’t that different from math, and that the same factors that made AI suddenly go from useless to godlike at math will happen soon with AI’s own self-improvement:

[Dwarkesh Podcast The avalanche that hit math is coming for AI development Read more 12 days ago · 547 likes · 103 comments · Dwarkesh Patel](https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/rsi?utm_source=substack&utm_campaign=post_embed&utm_medium=web&embedding_publication_id=35345)

He writes:

> It’s crazy how fast we went from, in 2023, “This model can’t reliably add four-digit numbers,” to…about a month ago, “Okay, it fucking [solved a Millennium Prize problem](https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution/) in 88 hours.”…
> AI research is actually surprisingly similar to the type of mathematical progress that current AIs are disproportionately good at: unlocking a ton of low-hanging fruit by applying a combination of incredible persistence and a superhuman capacity to connect ideas from lots of adjacent domains…In every domain where we can check answers and give AIs thousands of rounds of practice—for example, competitive programming contests, or well-scoped open math problems—they’ve gone from worse than most humans to better than the best humans within a few years…AI research has those same verifiable properties…
> Once AI is as good as the best humans at AI research, algorithmic progress will get radically faster…Today’s AIs already do work at about 10 times human speed. And automated researchers would also be working around the clock, nights and weekends included. As a result, each individual automated researcher will be cramming in roughly 50x more work every calendar week than a human researcher can do…During the intelligence explosion, automated engineers will build tens of thousands of times more [reinforcement learning] training environments than we have currently.

So that’s the debate. Basically, it depends on whether ideas get harder to find faster than AI gets better at finding ideas, and only time will tell which one wins.

But as I said, while this debate is intellectually interesting, I’m not sure how much it matters.

items.body:
AI forecasters now equal or beat top human performance at traditional forecasting questions (eg [ForecastBench](https://forecastingresearch.substack.com/p/ai-models-have-likely-reached-parity), the [Metaculus Cup](https://www.economist.com/science-and-technology/2026/09/16/artificial-intelligence-now-beats-some-of-the-best-human-forecasters)).

These are usually specialized AIs with forecasting harnesses, created by forecasting startups (eg [FutureSearch](https://futuresearch.ai/), [Mantic](https://mantic.com/), [Preseen](https://preseen.com/)), but foundation models like ChatGPT and Claude are only about six months behind the specialized models, so by the end of the year they’ll match top humans too.

In the past, the options for getting top-human-level forecasts were slim and inconvenient. You could hire a team of superforecasters to work on the problem, but this would cost thousands of dollars and take weeks. Or you could check prediction markets (or Metaculus), but they only have a small sample of general-interest questions and are constantly trying to screw you over by gaming resolution criteria.

The rise of AI forecasters solves these problems more cleanly and comprehensively than almost anyone thought possible just a year ago. The “science of forecasting”, which only recently felt like trying to pick the least-bad of various bad options, now faces tasks more like “what kind of magnifying glass should we use to inspect our giant novelty lottery check as we confirm that it’s real?” and “how do we spend our winnings?”

Specifically: AI forecasters now equal or beat top human performance at traditional forecasting questions. We need to learn how this success decays as we move to different types of non-traditional forecasting questions.

I recently got to talk to some people at the [Forecasting Research Institute](https://forecastingresearch.org/), one of the leaders in this field. Here’s my impression of the remaining challenges:

**1: Can AI do conditional forecasts?**

A traditional forecasting question asks something like: will the Democrats win the next election?

A conditional forecasting question is more like: *if* the Democrats win the next election, how will that affect the chances of a stock market crash?

Conditional forecasting questions are more exciting than traditional ones because they directly speak to policy outcomes. If we defund the police, how will that affect crime rates (compared to the counterfactual where we hold police funding constant)? If we mandate COVID vaccinations, how will that affect COVID mortality and myocarditis mortality (compared to the counterfactual where vaccines are voluntary / banned)?

Prediction markets have been slow to experiment with these, partly because of annoying logistical issues (you have to refund people’s money if the condition doesn’t come true) and partly because they entice fewer customers than new forms of degenerate sports gambling. AI forecasters don’t have this problem; you can ask an AI forecaster any of those questions above right now, and the big companies ([FutureSearch](https://futuresearch.ai/docs/forecast-conditional-scenarios/), [Preseen](https://blog.preseen.com/p/predicting-science-and-technology), [Mantic](https://blog.mantic.com/p/friday-forecasts-2)) have it as an explicit feature.

What remains is to prove that AI forecasters’ great performance on traditional questions carries over to conditional questions. About a year ago, FRI tested this and found that it didn’t - the AIs of the time did significantly worse on conditional questions. It seemed like some kind of weird misunderstanding where the AI didn’t entirely understand the concept.

Will this flip like a switch? At some point, the AI is smart enough to fully grasp conditionals, and it becomes exactly as good at conditional forecasting as the regular type? The experts I talked to thought no - as it gets smarter, its conditional forecasting ability will improve gradually. Where is it now? The experts weren’t willing to hazard a guess on whether it was better or worse than the average smart human, although they did think it was still worse than top superforecasters. They’re working on a benchmarking experiment that should give us a better measure of this in a few months.

**2: Can AI do truly causal forecasts?**

There’s a known flaw in standard conditional forecasting. When we ask “if the Democrats win the next election, will the economy go down?”, what we really want to know is a causal question - does voting for Democrats hurt the economy?

But that’s not what we asked. Suppose we’re wondering this in 2025, so we ask “If the Democrats win in 2026, is the economy more likely to be bad in 2027?” But maybe the Democrats will win in 2026 because there’s a already a bad economy (eg the Republican president implements tariffs and declares war on Iran, raising prices and making him historically unpopular), and then that bad economy continues into 2027. So the answer to the question “If the Democrats win in 2026, is the economy more likely to be bad in 2027?” is yes, but we still don’t know whether voting for Democrats in 2026 is good or bad for the economy.

Prediction markets can’t answer this question, because they can only be used to predict observable events that let us give payouts to successful gamblers. Might AI superforecasters succeed where the markets fail? Could you just prompt them with “please answer the unobservable causal question, instead of the easily-resolved conditional one”?

The experts I talked to weren’t excited about that particular prompt, but they did point out that a causal forecast is basically a combination of conditional forecasts. That is, if your original conditional forecast implicitly considered the four different combinations of two variables - that is:

- p(Democrats win & economy good)
- p(Democrats win & economy bad)
- p(Republicans win & economy good)
- p(Republicans win & economy bad)

…then things like “the previous economy was good” or “we’re at war with Iran” are just more variables you can add to the stew. It would be crazy to ask humans to forecast 2^10 branches so you could combine ten variables, but for AIs that could just mean a bit higher API spend. If you capture enough relevant variables in your “conditional” forecast, and find that the economy is still worse when the only one you’ve changed is whether or not the Democrats win, that’s a causal forecast. At least one company already tries something like this, though there are no studies of how well it works.

items.body:
Most people find information on the internet through online search engines. On these platforms,
AI-generated responses increasingly replace the known lists of links, and original sources become less visible. In addition, the number of people turning directly to chatbots to look up information is rising. With these AI systems, it often remains unclear how a response is generated, what sources support it, and how reliable it is.

This development is problematic for several reasons. It weakens independent critical thinking, as users read a supposedly comprehensive generated answer instead of visiting the original sources themselves. At the same time, it jeopardizes the information ecosystem: When users visit media websites less frequently, the media’s ability to generate revenue comes under pressure. However, AI systems rely on media outlets and other sources to publish trustworthy information so that they themselves can provide high-quality answers. In the long run, this can jeopardize people’s access to information – which is a key prerequisite for a functioning democracy.

## Our Studies

Since 2023, AlgorithmWatch has been using regional elections for case studies to investigate how reliably AI systems answer political questions and what risks this poses to democratic opinion-forming. In three studies, we examined Microsoft Copilot (formerly: Bing Chat), Google Gemini, models from OpenAI, and Google’s AI Overviews.

[2026 Developing Political Views with AI: What Election-Related Information Do Google’s AI Overviews Provide? A brief analysis in the context of the state elections in Saxony-Anhalt, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, and Berlin in 2026.](https://algorithmwatch.org/en/google-ai-overviews-state-elections/)[2024 Large Language Models Continue To Be Unreliable Concerning Elections Our research has significantly improved the effectiveness of the safeguards in the Microsoft Copilot chatbot against misinformation about elections in Germany.](https://algorithmwatch.org/en/llms_state_elections/)[2023 AI Chatbot produces misinformation about elections Final report by AlgorithmWatch and AI Forensics on Bing Chat’s responses regarding elections in Bavaria, Hesse, and Switzerland in October 2023.](https://algorithmwatch.org/en/study-microsofts-bing-chat/)

items.body:
We moderns tell ourselves that while the ancients were transparently and strongly dominated by elites, we hold our leaders far more accountable, such as via law, media, and democracy. But we allow our elites many easy ways to use money or political connections to gain far more favorable treatment from media and law. And we use democracy much more to fight each other via coalition politics than to hold leaders accountable. That is, we much more submit to the leaders we vote for, than we defy the leaders we don’t.

Consider 18 ways we now block holding our leaders accountable:

- We make [blackmail](https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/checkmate-on-blackmailhtml) illegal, so they are less penalized for misbehavior.
- We don’t arrange to try to secretly and randomly bribe officials.
- We don’t expect leaders to post bonds they forfeit if not keep promises.
- We mostly pick leaders on recommendation of other leaders.
- We rarely collect track records re their performance outcomes, or predictions.
- We rarely use prediction/decision markets to check leader prediction/decisions.
- We let firms pick their own auditors, and audits are rarely randomized.
- Evaluators usually can’t see leader decision internal records.
- Old leaders are not given regular tests re dementia.
- We don’t much protect or reward whistleblowers.
- Leader evaluations are rarely blinded.
- 360 reviews are rare and toothless.
- Only for-profit leaders have much cash performance incentives.
- We give police, prosecutors, and govt officials have legal immunity.
- Police internal affairs reports to police chief, not mayor.
- Firms use poison pills to block takeovers, and we vilify short sellers.
- Golden parachutes and option price resetting cushion CEO losses.
- We let CEOs pick who is on their boards.

Many excuses are offered for each of these patterns, but the obvious explanation here is that we are far more like the ancients than we like to think. We are eager to submit to the powerful, and show them our fealty, and are wary of endorsing positions by which we might seem to challenge or defy their power.

This is a big problem with two of my solutions to cultural drift, which require at least some of our groups to adopt much more competent forms of governance, forms that induce leaders to actually achieve identified goals. Our world now far less achieves most of the goals we give our leaders, due to our using pretty bad governance mechanisms. But we each prefer that to risking our seeming less loyal to our elites.

items.body:
Ridgeline subscribers —

A little note to begin:

A buddy of mine, Nick Dwyer, is running a Kickstarter campaign for his A Century in Sound documentary. He’s looking at 100 years of Tokyo history through its music cafés (classical, jazz, rock, noise, etcetera). He’s collaborated with photographer Lee Chapman on a companion book. I am a backer. Nick handed me the book in person last week — it’s stunning. They nailed it. What makes this project extra special is that Nick has truly put in the shoe leather for cultivating intimate relationships with all the shops they feature. He’s been working on this documentary series for a decade. The shop owners adore the hell out of him. (I’ve seen it in person.) I also got a sneak peek at half of the doc in August — it’s fabulous, and deserves to be seen all over. Consider giving it a back and grabbing the book. It’s a good’un. Six days left, and they’re almost at their goal.

items.body:
Hello everyone,

I’m delighted to announce the release of Silver Bough, the third album from my wyrd folk / medieval ambient / experimental Celtic music project Glamourie:

Since the previous album whose production process was described in a topic entitled Otherworldly music for futuristic Middle-Ages, my set-up has slightly changed. I have switched from processing effects in series to processing them in parallel, which has allowed me to preserve the sound of the acoustic instruments I use (hammered dulcimer, flutes, percussions) in a much drier form. I’ve also had a bit of fun with some subtle feedback loops in the effects, which add a bit of shimmer and movement to the sound.

I continued my exploration of modal scales, which I was able to expand upon with the arrival of a C-tuned low whistle, and I read many more medieval texts and anthropological publications, which enriched my knowledge base in terms of themes and scholarly allusions to Celtic folklore and Arthurian mythology.

For the first time as part of this project, I also collaborated with an Irish singer who came to record her vocals for a contemporary arrangement of an old sean-nós about fairies.

I’ve left a few codes here for you in case you’d like to download the album from Glamourie

items.title: Introducing: Qualiaphobic AI
items.subtitle: We are in a drought of good futures.
items.feedText:
AI capabilities keep increasing—spikily, yes, but they are—and the ability to articulate good futures where AI progress continues has been… less than inspiring. So this past month I’ve been away developing a plan, one that I think solves some of the thorniest issues in AI safety and gets us a lot closer to ensuring a good future for all of humanity.
