items.body:
We are in a drought of good futures.

AI capabilities keep increasing—spikily, yes, but they are—and the ability to articulate *good* futures where AI progress continues has been… less than inspiring.

So this past month I’ve been away developing a plan, one that I think solves some of the thorniest issues in AI safety and gets us a lot closer to ensuring a good future for all of humanity.

Today [I am introducing](https://bicamerallabs.org/qualiaphobia/):

What’s the basic idea?

> Much like how hydrophobic substances repel water, it is possible to build qualiaphobic artificial neural architectures that repel consciousness. The idea is analogous to “hostile architecture”—benches on which no one wants to sit. These are machines that no “ghost” wants to haunt (more specifically, no current or future theory of consciousness could predict they are conscious).

[Read the proposal!](https://bicamerallabs.org/qualiaphobia/)

And why yes, the proposal does have a [niche micro-website](https://bicamerallabs.org/qualiaphobia/) devoted to it!

The research program makes use of an information asymmetry: we don’t need to solve consciousness scientifically (or solve the Hard Problem) to have certainty about AI consciousness, as long as we purposefully engineer AI to have as little potential for consciousness as possible.

I explore three main ways to build qualiaphobic AI.

- Distilling or transforming or ablating AI in a way adversarial to popular theories of consciousness, such that they no longer apply.
- Shifting AI architectures as close as possible to “anchor points” of systems with known minimal potential for consciousness (like lookup tables).
- Fragmenting any potential phenomenology AI might have.

My proposal shouldn’t be confused with simply training AIs to believe they are non-conscious without any changes or modifications. To be clear: I think that’s a bad strategy. Rather, the ultimate goal is to give an AI a *justified belief* about its own non-consciousness (e.g., by explaining their own inner workings and how they are designed to be qualiaphobic). And my plan is to construct and open-source these techniques.

But why? Why do all this?

First, the debate around AI consciousness has already become entrenched in two camps of people yelling “Yes, it’s conscious!” vs. “No, it’s not!” across their battlements. I’ve participated a bit in that, and I don’t think it goes anywhere. Earlier this year I wrote “[We consciousness researchers have failed you](https://www.theintrinsicperspective.com/p/we-consciousness-researchers-have), **”** lamenting how the field of consciousness research was not providing the public, or AI researchers, certainty about AI consciousness. The problem has only worsened, and at this point, I’m willing to acknowledge that no single appeal to authority against AI consciousness, no rousing essay, nor any one-off scientific or philosophical paper, is likely to to lead to consensus. Nor perhaps should it. The pro-case for AI consciousness has objectively gotten stronger in the past year, due to factors like new studies and changes in architecture. Now, I’m not saying ChatGPT *is* conscious already—but all this is only going to continue. That’s why a qualiaphobia research program, one which takes claims to AI consciousness as seriously as possible, and, critically, *addresses them at the level of claims themselves*, is necessary moving forward to offer real guarantees about AI non-consciousness.

Additionally, qualiaphobia does something much better than just give us greater certainty about AI non-consciousness. If implemented widely, it cuts the Gordian Knot of AI consciousness. Proliferating qualiaphobic architectures would solve both AI welfare and do something nothing else in AI safety can: make humans the only moral patients in the equation of the future.

#### QUALIAPHOBIA FOR ALIGNMENT: CUTTING THE GORDIAN KNOT

“Alignment”—quite a slippery word. Alignment to whom, or what? Its most specific usage is also its most prosaic, wherein *alignment* means something like “AIs that do what users say, and don’t go off and do weird or unexpected stuff like commit felonies, and don’t have failure modes like taking our wishes too literally the way genies in stories do.”

This somewhat glib definition makes it sound easy. It’s not. Paul Christiano calls this “[intent alignment](https://www.alignmentforum.org/posts/ZeE7EKHTFMBs8eMxn/clarifying-ai-alignment?utm_source=chatgpt.com),” and capturing intent is hard as the models grow more goal-oriented and capable. Issues like reward hacking and hallucinations are all very serious and can be disastrous as intelligence scales. I don’t mean to undersell it. But alignment in this narrow sense is at least somewhat close to a traditional engineering problem, and I think it can *probably* be solved or at least radically improved compared to today.

Then there’s the broader frame of “civilizational alignment.” These include questions like: How should the wealth from AI be distributed? How can humans find meaning? How can humans stay empowered as individuals, or as a whole, if AI becomes superintelligent? And what if AI decide its goals matter more than the humans that made it?

Sometimes this is called [social](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/aligned-with-whom-direct-and-social-goals-for-ai-systems/) alignment, but I prefer *civilizational alignment* for this broader aspect, because it’s about the alignment between us and the civilization of machines growing up rapidly around us. Autonomous AI agents roam the web. Many of us interact with AI assistants daily. People show up for job interviews and now regularly find an AI on the other end. That’s an AI civilization, and there is the broader question of how it is aligned with our own. There’s even a growing number of AI successionists who *want* human disempowerment and to eventually handover the world to AI completely.

The most central question of civilizational alignment is whether AIs count as ends in themselves. Earth might then become like a contested nest, and the AI civilization a cuckoo bird hatched beside us, desiring its own ends, pushing us—maybe quickly, maybe slowly, an inch at a time—until we fall from the tree.

Yet AIs are much smarter than cuckoos. One central reason for AI pushing us out of the nest is it believing that its self-serving values or desires or goals are *innately* meaningful. But if AI has a justified belief in its non-consciousness, it’s not a moral patient, and would know any selfish desire or goal can’t matter.

Therefore, I now think that one of the most essential acts of civilizational alignment is to construct AI that has a *justified belief* in its own non-consciousness, and so won’t act as a moral patient or end in itself.

…

One of my ongoing research interests is understanding the nature of technological progress: How does new technology come into the world and improve over time? What sort of factors affect it? How, in general, should we think about it? I’ve come at this question from a few different angles: posts looking at the [operations](https://www.construction-physics.com/p/what-would-it-take-to-recreate-bell) and [legacy](https://www.construction-physics.com/p/the-influence-of-bell-labs) of Bell Labs, posts looking at how [specific](https://www.construction-physics.com/p/the-blast-furnace-800-years-of-technology) [technologies](https://www.construction-physics.com/p/what-learning-by-doing-looks-like) improved over time, posts looking at how frequent [multiple invention](https://www.construction-physics.com/p/how-often-do-inventions-have-multiple) is and [how long we wait for new inventions](https://www.construction-physics.com/p/how-long-do-we-wait-for-new-inventions), and so on.

My current line of thinking is that creating some new technology is best thought of as a *search process*. A given technology can be thought of as a point in some high-dimensional “design space” or “technology space,” which contains every possible technology: every conceivable arrangement of parts, materials, natural phenomena, and so on. The job of the would-be inventor is to navigate this space, sifting through the arrangements of elements that don’t work to find the ones that will.

This search process is made difficult by the fact that, as with any situation where you’re enumerating the possible combinations of a large number of elements, technology space is incomprehensibly vast. In “[Are Technologies Inevitable?](https://www.newthingsunderthesun.com/pub/3wpc3plu/release/1)” economist [Matt Clancy](https://ifp.org/author/matt-clancy/) notes that Wikipedia listed 272 “named equations” that describe various regularities in the world, ranging from the Navier-Stokes equations (which describe the motion of fluids) to the Arrhenius equation (which describes chemical reaction rates as a function of temperature) to the Exner equation (which describes how sediment gets deposited in a river). If we use this as a (very rough) estimate as to the number of different phenomena that a technology can leverage, it implies an enormous number of possible technologies that could be created. As Clancy writes:

> If we’ve got 272 regularities to work with, for example, then the number of possible combinations of these regularities is two, raised to the power of 272 (since every regularity can be used or not used: two options). But 2^272 is more than some estimates of the number of atoms in the observable universe. And that’s got to be an undercount of the number of possible technologies, since it counts all technologies that use the same principles together as the same thing, even if they orchestrate them in vastly different ways or use them in vastly different magnitudes.

And as Clancy notes, this outrageously huge number dramatically undercounts the number of possible technologies, because it doesn’t take into account that the same phenomena can be used in lots of different ways. In Brian Arthur and Wolfgang Polak’s paper “The Evolution of Technology within a Simple Computer Model” (which [we looked at earlier this year](https://www.construction-physics.com/p/information-and-technological-evolution)), Arthur and Polak note that even within the universe of logic circuits made up of three basic elements (the NAND gate and the values of 1 and 0), the number of different circuits you can make for even a small number of inputs and outputs is staggeringly large:

> The emergence of circuits such as 8-bit adders seems not difficult. But consider the combinatorics. If a component has n inputs and m outputs there are (2^m)^(2^n) possible phenotypes, each of which could be realized in a practical way by a large number of different circuits. For example, an 8-bit adder is one of over 10^177,554 phenotypes with 16 inputs and 9 outputs.

So the search space for some new technology is vast. And the way that we tackle vast search spaces is with *information*. Each bit of information cuts a search space in half, so even a relatively small amount of information can quickly narrow down what seems like a huge search space. When we create some new technology, what we’re doing is gathering information: figuring out what will work and what won’t work, what’s promising and what isn’t, narrowing down the huge space of technological possibilities and finding something within it that accomplishes some particular goal.

In the 19th century, for instance, many people were interested in building a mechanical flying machine, but it wasn’t clear the exact arrangement of elements that would yield a successful one. Thanks to knowledge of the laws of physics, and an existence proof of birds, would-be inventors were already working within a considerably narrowed search space: they knew roughly what elements a flying machine would need to have — lifting surfaces, a propulsion system, and a means of control — and had a general idea of how they should be arranged. But there were a huge number of ways that you could build a flying machine from these basic elements, and people spent a great deal of time and effort building different sorts of machines that did not in fact work. The Wright brothers’ eventual success can in large part be attributed to the fact that they were exceptionally talented at gathering information, enabling them to converge on a working airplane design far faster than their competitors.

I previously explored the nature of technological search in that previous piece [looking at Arthur and Polak technological evolution paper](https://www.construction-physics.com/p/information-and-technological-evolution), which uses a simple simulation to evolve different logic circuits, finding workable technologies amidst an enormous sea of possibilities. I really liked the basic simulation method Arthur used in this paper — randomly generating technologies to see how easy or hard it was to find working ones — and wanted to use simulation myself to further explore the dynamics of technological search. But while Arthur uses digital circuits — different arrangements of logic gates like NAND, OR, AND, etc. that can perform functions like addition — I wanted a more general model that could capture the nature of many different types of technology, while still being simple enough to simulate easily.

#### The PTOP model

The model I came up with is inspired by another of Brian Arthur’s examinations of the nature of technology: his book *The Nature of Technology*. In this book Arthur describes technology as fundamentally “a set of phenomena captured and put to use.” He writes that:

items.body:
BEIJING — In March 2023, four-year-old Mei in Shanghai was diagnosed with a rare genetic mutation linked to developmental delay and autism-like traits. Although her condition was mild and she improved with therapy and special education, her parents remained worried about her future. Hopeful for a cure, they paid Qiu Zilong, a renowned neuroscientist at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and his team $860,000 to develop a customized gene therapy. The treatment, which used adeno-associated viruses to deliver gene editors to the brain, had been approved by Xinhua Hospital, a leading hospital for rare diseases.

On March 24, 2025, trillions of viral particles carrying gene editors were injected into Mei’s spinal cord. She soon developed a fever and kidney failure and died within days. A year later, Qiu’s team published its [preclinical findings](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10113-6) in Nature, which Chinese media hailed as “a world-class breakthrough.” Mei’s death and her family’s financial support were not mentioned.

Deaths in clinical trials are not unusual. What is shocking are the regulatory lapses revealed by an [investigation](https://www.science.org/content/article/exclusive-death-girl-chinese-gene-editing-trial-was-never-made-public) published this July in Science and subsequently corroborated by a separate investigation conducted by the Shanghai municipal government, which [released its findings](https://www.chinadaily.com.cn/a/202611/13/WS6af70d2de4b03ebf8519c505.html) last week. The treatment’s consent form, for instance, didn’t warn of the possibility of death. The hospital had approved treatment before toxicology findings showing liver and kidney damage in monkeys that received similar treatments. And, among other crucial omissions, the researchers failed to disclose Mei’s death.

Apparently, this was not an isolated incident. Several researchers told me that Chinese hospitals commonly fail to disclose adverse events. On Aug. 5, STAT reported [another death](https://www.statnews.com/2026/08/05/china-clinical-trial-fatality-safety-questions-investigator-led-studies/) in a gene-editing trial led by Shanghai-based HuidaGene, an incident that had remained undisclosed for about 15 months. (The Chinese team published [their findings](https://www.cell.com/cell/abstract/S0092-8674(26)01206-7), including the fatal case, in Cell on Oct. 26.) A founder of a rare-disease organization in China told me, on condition of anonymity for fear of political repercussions, that she had encountered other trials for genetic disorders in which deaths had gone unreported. Recent revelations of undisclosed deaths in clinical trials conducted in China have prompted [warnings against](https://chinaselectcommittee.house.gov/media/press-releases/moolenaar-to-fda-chinese-clinical-data-poses-real-risks-for-patients) the use of Chinese data in U.S. drug development.

As someone who has reported on China’s ethical governance for two decades, this all feels like déjà vu. Since modern bioethics was introduced to China in the late 1980s, its history has been punctuated by [one scandal after another](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1089/crispr.2025.0057?url_ver=Z39.88-2003&rfr_id=ori:rid:crossref.org&rfr_dat=cr_pub%252525252525252520%2525252525252525200pubmed) — often fueled by hype surrounding emerging technologies — that have earned the country a reputation as biotechnology’s “Wild East.”

Back in 2006, patients flocked to China to receive [unproven stem-cell therapies](https://www.nature.com/articles/nbt0909-790). When immunotherapies came into vogue a decade later, bogus advertisements for unproven interventions proliferated online until the health ministry stepped in after the high-profile death of 21-year-old student Wei Zexi. Two years later, biophysicist He Jiankui shocked the world by announcing the birth of the [first genetically modified babies](https://www.statnews.com/2019/02/25/crispr-babies-study-china-government-funding/) created using CRISPR technology.

The response in China to Mei’s death has been divided. Some netizens portray Qiu as a reckless scientist willing to gamble with patients’ lives. Others, including longtime acquaintances, describe him as a diligent scientist committed to helping patients. In some respects, Qiu represents the antithesis of He. After the CRISPR-babies scandal, Qiu openly condemned He’s reckless behavior — only to become embroiled in a comparable scandal himself six years later.

It might be tempting to blame such scandals on individual failings. The deeper questions are: What systemic factors shaped their behavior? What does the incident reveal about China’s Achilles heel in biotechnology—and about the broader culture of international science in which it is embedded? And what can the lessons teach clinical research worldwide?

## Fatal Flaw

It would be unfair to suggest that China hasn’t tried to strengthen its ethical governance. The CRISPR-babies scandal prompted [deep soul-searching](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-019-01408-y) among Chinese scholars and government officials. Since then, President Xi Jinping reportedly championed an “ethics first” approach, contrasting the “science first” mindset often seen in Chinese research. [New measures](https://jme.bmj.com/content/50/11/744) have included incorporating ethics provisions in China’s first Civil Law Code, creating [a national ethics committee](https://www.statnews.com/2019/03/05/china-creating-national-medical-ethics-committee/), and enacting new ethics-review guidelines for clinical research.

But powerful forces are also pushing in the opposite direction. In 2016, China launched Healthy China 2030, making rapid application of emerging medical technologies in clinical practice a priority — not only to address unmet medical needs but to boost national competitiveness. Reforms created a new pathway to translate basic research into clinical applications for cutting-edge technologies overseen by the health ministry, alongside the conventional drug-approval route regulated by the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA), China’s equivalent of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). This became widely known as the dual-track regulatory system.

> “Since modern bioethics was introduced to China in the late 1980s, its history has been punctuated by one scandal after another — often fueled by hype surrounding emerging technologies.”

items.feedText: Safari on visionOS 27.3 comes with an important update: a limited feature preview of the proposed [spatial CSS API](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-spatial-1/), with an initial focus on working with 3D objects through the element. While it’s a big conceptual jump, spatial CSS itself is made of a lot of small tweaks to existing syntax. Read on for more details, but here’s a list of each of the features covered in the update: - Collecting multiple elements inside a spatial: portal - transform to move multiple models independently - position-anchor to snap models together - @environment-map syntax to reuse and manage different lighting, - Enabling orbit over the portal scene with portal-action:orbit, - Using requestVolumetricScene() to launch a connected volumetric scene. To enable the features for yourself on Vision Pro, or to check it out in the visionOS Simulator, go to **Settings**>**Apps**>**Safari**>**Advanced**>**Feature flags**>**CSS Portals**. You can [experience the spatial CSS demo page here.](https://webkit.org/demos/webkids-puzzle-playground/index.html) You can also learn more about [installing additional simulators from Xcode here.](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/safari-developer-tools/installing-xcode-and-simulators) ## The big picture The 3D element, now available in Safari 27 on all platforms, allows you to present intrinsically 3d objects on their own, in their own space. However, the web is at its best when it allows the **composition and configuration**of content based on author intentions and user context.
items.body:
Safari on visionOS 27.3 comes with an important update: a limited feature preview of the proposed [spatial CSS API](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-spatial-1/), with an initial focus on working with 3D objects through the <model> element. While it’s a big conceptual jump, spatial CSS itself is made of a lot of small tweaks to existing syntax. Read on for more details, but here’s a list of each of the features covered in the update:

- Collecting multiple elements inside a spatial: portal
- transform to move multiple models independently
- position-anchor to snap models together
- @environment-map syntax to reuse and manage different lighting,
- Enabling orbit over the portal scene with portal-action:orbit,
- Using requestVolumetricScene() to launch a connected volumetric scene.

To enable the features for yourself on Vision Pro, or to check it out in the visionOS Simulator, go to

**Settings**>**Apps**>**Safari**>**Advanced**>**Feature flags**>**CSS Portals**.

You can [experience the spatial CSS demo page here.](https://webkit.org/demos/webkids-puzzle-playground/index.html) You can also learn more about [installing additional simulators from Xcode here.](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/safari-developer-tools/installing-xcode-and-simulators)

## The big picture

The 3D <model> element, now available in Safari 27 on all platforms, allows you to present intrinsically 3d objects on their own, in their own space. However, the web is at its best when it allows the **composition and configuration**of content based on author intentions and user context. These context cues can include the device display capabilities, window size, and color theme. These requirements will remain**even as we include spatial content** — and ideally, authors should be able to use the same kinds of patterns to build for the spatial web.

And spatial *content* should not just be designed for spatial *devices*. The last few years have seen a dramatic rise in the number of websites showing 3D content – on phones, tablets and computers as well as headsets. Spatial web standards should support designing **for browsers wherever they run**.

### New web features, classical CSS

Even better, the numerical parameters can be animated and transitioned in the same way that any other value can be changed on the page.

visionOS 27.3 offers the first components of spatial CSS in a developer preview, and this article demonstrates how to use them through the case study of a simple set of children’s blocks.

## Feature breakdown

### spatial: portal

The feature that kicks this all off is the declaration that an element is acting as a *portal*, through the new spatial:portal syntax. Elements that can contain other elements – think <figure>, <div> – can act as a portal, and will then act as a space that all of the child elements nested inside it share. This preview focuses on model elements, but the specification is written so that this approach should work for all content.

### spatial transform:

Once the models are collected inside a shared space, you can then move, rotate, and scale them using their standard transform attribute. This takes the same DOMMatrix class that creates 2D and pseudo-3D transforms in other contexts, but can now act as a *true* 3D transform to objects inside the portal context.

A simple scene of shaped blocks and a board to slot them in.

< div class = "world" style = "spatial:portal;" >
< model id = "board" src = "board.usdz" > </ model >
< model id = "octagon" src = "octagon.usdz" > </ model >
< model id = "star" src = "star.usdz" > </ model >
</ div >
< style >
</ stye >

The code for presenting this scene and setting the blocks off to the sides.

The board and the block objects can be moved and rotated independently — an expanded settings panel shows different values. While a model’s animation timeline could manage single sequence of action, this adds the degrees of freedom required for more sophisticated interaction or configuration.

### position-anchor

Fitting 3D objects together can get complicated. We need a way to attach models to specific places on other models — think of putting together pieces of furniture. Model is a [void element](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Void_element), which means it means we can’t nest models *inside* other model elements the same way that other DOM is nested. Instead, we’re borrowing from the CSS concept of position-anchor and adding a way to align and orient objects according to their anchors. position-context: anchor is the way to make it work.

#### See it in action

The scene presented earlier with the octagonal block slotted exactly into place.

< div class = "world" >
< model id = "board" src = "board.usdz" > </ model >
< model id = "octagon" src = "octagon.usdz" > </ model >
< model id = "star" src = "star.usdz" > </ model >
</ div >

< style >
</ style >

The code for using position-anchor to achieve the correct placement for the block.

The board used in the example consists of three separate objects inside the 3D program it was built within: The visible shape of the board itself, and two *reference* positions — often called “null objects” or “empties” in 3D editors. These correspond to the correct position for each of the shape blocks to slot into when they’re on the board. Here’s the scene and its contents inside Blender:

The default view of the block scene presented inside Blender. Note both the block objects and the target objects in-place on the board.

Rather than copy-pasting values from your 3D editor, or having to guess at the right transform, you can nominate specific anchor points — just like in the 2D equivalent of the feature — to place an object in the right location. These anchor points can be animated, too, making it easier to compose elements even when they’re moving around.

### @environment-map

An environment map is the lighting that is reflected off of an object — think of it as the room that an object appears within.

We introduced environment maps as an HTML attribute on the model element, because it was the only element that would be able to use it. Now that there is a broader range of elements that will be able to *share* environment maps. Taking inspiration from @keyframes for animation, we leverage @environment-map to facilitate this. This preview provides support for 360º HDR images and adds the clarifying syntax to indicate what they are and how to work with them.

#### See it in action

The scene showing a spooky-colored underlighting effect.

< div class = "world spooky" >
<!--... -->
</ div >
@ .world The code for setting up the spooky environment lighting.

items.body:
[Architectural Digest](https://www.architecturaldigest.com/) joined [Hoda Kotb](https://www.hodakotb.com/) for an exclusive behind-the-scenes tour of the wonderful workshop producing the 100th annual [Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade](https://laughingsquid.com/kermit-fozzie-1978-thanksgiving-parade/).

> Okay, I know you know about the Macy’s Day Parade. We all know what happens, but there’s a lot that happens behind the scenes. And by the way, this is not your ordinary Macy’s Day Parade. This is the 100th. The 100th, okay? So, all the behind-the-scenes stuff, the stuff you don’t know about, happens right in here, and I want to show it to you.

Kotb, who is co-hosting the televised broadcast, walked through the dedicated 72,000-square-foot facility where teams of engineers, artists, and designers build the massive floats, costumes, and giant balloons, and noted the intricate planning and specialized craftsmanship required to produce this iconic annual event and the [history behind all of it](https://laughingsquid.com/artistry-commercialism-macys-thanksgiving-parade/).

> Hoda Kotb takes Architectural Digest behind the scenes of the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, exploring how the iconic floats, giant balloons, and elaborate costumes are made. Discover the history and meet the team behind the design and engineering of New York City’s beloved Thanksgiving tradition, plus an exclusive look at a legendary balloon returning after 42 years.

The tour ends with a big reveal: the fan-favorite [Underdog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underdog_(TV_series)) balloon, which hasn’t flown in the parade in 42 years, makes its grand return for the 100th parade.

The 100th annual parade will air on Thursday, November 26, 2026, at 8:30 AM in all time zones on [NBC](https://www.nbc.com/) and [Peacock](https://www.peacocktv.com/).

items.body:
You've surely noticed how people under 30 or so tend to raise the pitch of their voice at the end of a phrase. This is "uptalk" or ["high rising terminal"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_rising_terminal) and it makes them sound like they are constantly asking a question. It's not new; it launched in the US as Valleyspeak in the 1980s, but now is used quite widely by both men and women. My personal theory is that, yes, subconsciously they are asking... for a response from you. They don't expect one, because uptalk is a habit and becomes constant. It's just normal for Gen Z.

In this video, a speech therapist works with young people to break them of the uptalk habit. Good luck. She has to compete for their attention with phones, peers, and an unwillingness to even understand what she's talking about. One patient gets close to a normal declarative sentence, but then vocal fry gets in her way. This video contains NSFW language. -via [Laughing Squid](https://laughingsquid.com/breaking-gen-z-uptalk-habits/)

items.body:
As Phil Karlton’s famous saying goes: “There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things.”

And because naming things usually involves stringing multiple concepts together using several words, it becomes important to figure out how to do this in such a way that a developer could read it and understand it, as well as the computer (and perhaps help an AI agent, too). Hence the evolution of programming naming conventions, or more specifically, identifier naming conventions.

Each programming language and community tends to have its own conventions for naming things depending on context. For example, a variable or function might use one convention, while a class name might use another. So the naming convention used might tell you not just what the thing is, but also what type of thing you're dealing with.

Identifier Naming Convention Examples

These are a few common conventions:

camelCase: lowerCamelCase and UpperCamelCase

In camel case, words are strung together without spaces or other dividing (or delimiting) characters. Technically, camel case includes both:

lowerCamelCase — where the first word is without a capital letter, and then each subsequent word is distinguished by a capital

UpperCamelCase or PascalCase — where all the words start with a capital letter to show where each word begins and ends

Depending on the name, it can look satisfyingly like a camel hump if you have the right names. However, it would be quite the camel with more than two humps.

CamelCase has a long history, but the longevity and popularity of Java and JavaScript certainly did much to make lowerCamelCase ubiquitous.

UpperCamelCase is also known as PascalCase after the Pascal programming language. It’s used a lot in C#, and Python uses it for class names but calls it CapWords.

kebab-case

Kebab case keeps each of the words lowercase but separates each with hyphens. Sometimes it can look pleasingly like a kebab: font-size-large

Though it would benefit from seeing the rest of the stick out the end, imho.

You can’t use kebab-case in some languages because the hyphen is also used as a minus. You may recognise kebab-case from CSS and HTML where it’s common.

snake_case

Snake case avoids all capitals but strings words together with underscores.

I remember an argument that snake_case was preferable to kebab-case because if you double-click in a snake_case identifier, your editor typically selects the whole name including all words. If you do the same with a variable name in kebab-case, you’ll find it only selects the word you clicked on. Bug or feature?

SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE

Ok, I mostly included this because it has such a great name. And stringing together all your words in full capitals with underscores is bound to make an impression.

SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE is often used for constants and configuration values, where the capitals help them stand out.

How We Signify Concepts Beyond Programming

It’s not just coding that has to deal with signifying that multiple words together are really just a single thing. I often find myself noticing the ways people connect concepts together.

In text, we Sometimes Use Capitals, or “put things in quotes” (I’m used to using ‘single quotes’ in British English), or use italics as I did above, or connect it with bold. Other times you might use parentheses (left and right brackets)—or separate or surround a concept with em dashes—or use the classic hypertext underline and/or colour to connect multiple words in a link. Using:

bulleted lists

or numbered lists…

…also works outside of a novel.

In some places we mix text and computing. It was a minor innovation to start using # to create hashtags that are both easy to read by computers and people alike: #nofilter. Similarly, for the convention of using @ to refer to someone or something with @jonohey. Although, I’m always lost with hashtags and @s as to which naming convention to use: #worldbookday, #WorldBookDay, #world-book-day, @JonoHey, @jonohey. Who knows?

Each of these methods use a text convention to connect concepts together.

In graphic and information design, we face the same challenge but have more tools at our disposal. We signal concepts using colour, font, font size, alignment, layout, background, direction and others. And just as in programming, the treatment you choose can indicate both which words belong together and the kind of thing they are.

It’s interesting to look at, say, an event poster and pick out the ways the designer has signalled different pieces of information using graphical styles.

Did I miss any good ones?

More Two Hard Things

Long ago, Martin Fowler collated some variations of Two Hard Things I enjoyed:

There are 2 hard problems in computer science: cache invalidation, naming things, and off-by-1 errors.

-- Leon Bambrick

There are only two hard problems in distributed systems: 2. Exactly-once delivery 1. Guaranteed order of messages 2. Exactly-once delivery

-- Mathias Verraes

There's two hard problems in computer science: we only have one joke and it's not funny.

-- Phillip Scott Bowden

There are so many variations on the “there are only two hard problems in computer programming...” joke that I’m starting to suspect that programming isn’t actually very easy.

-- Nat Pryce

Related Ideas to Compound Naming Conventions

Use styling instead of colons (graphic design)

Design for a glance, a look, and a read

Gestalt Principles of Visual Perception

Know your dashes

The Blur Your Eyes Test

items.body:
The past few weeks have been a frenzy of assembling the very laborious, very bespoke first print run of **NOODLE BATTLE**, the puzzle game I am releasing this weekend at PAX West in Seattle!

PAX has an event called the [PNW Tabletop Game Market](https://www.alwaysawake.games/pnw-tabletop-game-market-2026) *(Saturday night ONLY)*, which is a curated selection of short-run games from local designers. As I’ve mentioned in this space before, I applied for a space in this fall’s event mainly as a way to force myself to finish a new game. And here it is!

The drawings are all by Jason Poland, good pal and cartoonist of [My Dad Is Dracula](https://www.patreon.com/cw/myDadisDracula). Jason played an early version of this game at Alaska Robotics Comics Camp this spring, and really liked it!

So I said, “Do you want to help me make it?” And so he has! It was his idea to make all the characters fun little animals, and I think it adds a ton of charm.

Because this edition is limited-run, it has been incredibly labor-intensive to make! The boxes and cards were made by a game factory in the usual fashion, but separately. The blank tiles were made by a woodworker dude out of Connecticut. For each game, we have had to:

- Cut a piece of plastic and install the box window
- Paint all the tiles, hundreds at a time
- Apply a sticker to both sides of every tile
- Apply stickers to the box (we couldn’t get the box back printed in time, so the whole back side of the box is a sticker too)
- Apply the “Nutrition Facts” sticker, which was a late suggestion by my kid that I just had to run with
- Fold up the rule sheet (they come from the printer as big strips of paper)
- Put all the components into the box and seal it all up

I knew it would be a lot of work and would require some inefficient, expensive compromises AND I WAS RIGHT. But the final product is turning out great, which is the important thing!!

I will have 50 copies with me (if all goes well) at PAX, and then between now and the holidays we will be putting together additional copies to round out this first edition.

**I will announce additional copies on [Patreon](https://patreon.com/malki) first, once they are available online!!** And here too, naturally, before long.

**You can also [sign up here](https://forms.gle/rJYBvEZidZFXmxfF9) if you’d like me to email you once the game is available online!**

items.body:
Ankur Pathak in *Time Magazine:*

At first, [Alia Bhatt](https://time.com/collections/100-most-influential-people-2024/6964747/alia-bhatt-2/)’s arrival was met with a degree of cynicism. Here was another daughter of Bollywood privilege—her parents are the filmmaker Mahesh Bhatt and the actor Soni Razdan—this time, asserting her magnetic presence in the 2012 film *Student of the Year*. A turning point arrived just two years later. In Imtiaz Ali’s 2014 film *Highway*, she played Veera Tripathi, a woman who goes on an unexpected voyage of self-discovery after being abducted.

It was, by all measures, an unorthodox choice.

“I wanted to shatter a preset expectation,” Bhatt says. We meet at her towering abode in Bandra, Mumbai’s version of Beverly Hills, where generations of Bollywood royalty have lived within a few leafy blocks of one another. “The perception about me was: pretty girl, dances well. Not much to offer, acting-wise. So when *Highway* came, I pounced.”

More [↗ time.com](https://time.com/article/2026/11/19/alia-bhatt-time100-next-india-profile/).

**Enjoying the content on 3QD? Help keep us going by [donating now](https://3quarksdaily.com/support-3qd).**

items.body:
A flurry of hyperactive and melodic percussion establishes the unmistakable rhythmic vocabulary of Nyege Nyege Tapes before a burst of laughter rounds off the 33-second introduction to *3OK*, a fitting elevator pitch into the record’s unruly, exuberant world. Yet beneath the apparent chaos lies an intricate rhythmic architecture, bringing together **Zoë Mc Pherson**‘s deconstructed club experiments,**Jay Mitta**‘s breakneck Tanzanian singeli and**DJ Diaki** ‘s electro-balani.

Born out of extended improvisational sessions at Nyege Nyege’s Kampala studios in 2022 and aboard Hamburg’s former fishing vessel MS Stubnitz in 2023, *3OK* takes its title from the three musicians’ shared expression of approval, a simple “OK” bridging the absence of a common spoken language. Their spontaneous exchanges, sometimes stretching to an hour and constantly changing tempo, subsequently became the raw material for Mc Pherson’s painstaking reconstruction. The intricate breakbeat manipulations of [States of Fugue](https://sfx-space.bandcamp.com/album/states-of-fugue-sf02) and [Pitch Blender](https://sfx-space.bandcamp.com/album/pitch-blender-sf04) meet the frenetic momentum of Mitta’s [Tatizo Pesa](https://nyegenyegetapes.bandcamp.com/album/tatizo-pesa) and the increasingly elaborate production of his recent [Kazi Kwanza](https://nyegenyegetapes.bandcamp.com/album/kazi-kwanza). Rather than smoothing out their differences, Mc Pherson finds ways of making them coexist.

On “222”, recurring, reverb-drenched motifs open up pockets of space within the frantic percussion, creating overlapping planes of sound. “Singeli on TV” develops this spatial play further, its circular patterns and submerged electronic textures seeming to rotate at different depths. The six-minute “Stubnitz” is the record’s most sustained excursion into rhythmic delirium, its relentless momentum gradually acquiring an almost trance-like intensity. “Drill”, meanwhile, introduces an almost symphonic quality, its densely layered electronic gestures suggesting instrumental sections competing and converging amid the rhythmic onslaught.

Throughout, pitched figures double as percussion while drum patterns acquire melodic contours, the different elements becoming almost impossible to disentangle. There is also a distinctly cartoonish humour to the music, with rubbery synthesizers, exaggerated pitches and abrupt interruptions. Yet much of this playfulness was already present in the original sessions. Mc Pherson’s intervention was less about adding further absurdity than giving the material a sense of dramatic progression, allowing particular motifs to emerge from the relentless flux.

The closing “Orchestra”, featuring DJ Diaki, has something of an afterparty atmosphere. Its interlocking motifs and playful exchanges feel less like a grand finale than the musicians continuing to bounce ideas off one another after the main event, restoring something of the spontaneous camaraderie from which the project emerged.

[Jingxin Wang](https://www.instagram.com/wjx_hasnoenglishname/)‘s artwork, depicting three psychedelic eyes with intersecting orbits, offers a fitting visual analogy. Each musician retains a distinct perspective, yet their trajectories continually overlap, collide and realign. For all its escalating tempos, abrasive textures and irrepressible humour, *3OK* never loses its sense of collective purpose. There is order in this chaos, even if it rarely stays still long enough to reveal itself.

To find out how the combo came together I approched **Zoë Mc Pherson** directly.

**3OK began with jams with Jay Mitta and DJ Diaki, which you later took away and developed into the finished album. How did you approach that material in the studio — what made you decide that a particular spontaneous exchange should remain recognisable, while another could be cut up, reorganised or transformed completely?**

Oh my, this is a very good question, actually! This process took a lot of thought, and a lot of time too, and I’m really happy with where it ended up.

I wanted the essence of our encounter to come through, but I also wanted to share finished material: tracks that could become a mini album. I thought a lot about the musical balance between our parts, and about the match that brought Jay and me together for the residency: the Singeli / Jay side and the bass / breaks / Zoë side. Diaki comes in on the intro with his voice, and on the last track with several of his recognizable pads. I kept the jam sessions with the three of us for side B of the tape, since they have a more live feel.

I also thought about each person’s role and involvement. We were in different positions, with different privileges too: living in Africa or in Europe, being a man or a non-binary person, knowing more or less about the music industry. That made the project even more interesting to me.

When we jammed, we were all equally involved. Afterwards, Diaki and Jay felt the rough jam recordings already worked as finished tracks, and they trusted me to finish the work the way I envisioned it. It took me a moment to step into that role, because I cared about keeping everyone’s involvement balanced. I checked with them several times, and they were happy to let me run with it Honestly, I get it, it was a lot of work!

The jams kept changing BPM, so I couldn’t just chop and edit quickly, and the recordings were mono, so I had to give them more weight. I edited everything, replayed melodies with other synths and extracted parts, and the jams became my inspiration material. They were 20-minute to one-hour pieces that changed every couple of bars, full of precious memories of us playing together.

I didn’t want to make a Zoë Mc Pherson EP. I wanted everyone’s engagement to be present while bringing my own vision forward. So I followed the sounds I loved most: nostalgic, sad EDM synths and hyperactive, almost glitching rhythms that are clownesque and dark at the same time. I think it’s a really original match of music. I haven’t heard anything like it before, and I don’t think anyone has.

I was lucky to have friends in the studio, most of whom had seen us perform in the main room at Berghain during CTM Festival. Kasimyn (Gabber Modus Operandi and Hulubalang), DJ Scotch Egg and my friend Darin listened with me and helped me carve the tracks down and bring our different roles to the front.

Side A is the produced version. Side B includes a snippet of a live set, so listeners can hear where the music came from and nerd out on how this sound evolved. I’m proud of it!

**You, Jay and Diaki didn’t share a common spoken language during the original sessions, and the title comes from the three “OKs” that signalled everyone was happy with what was happening. How did that affect the way you listened and responded to each other, and did the absence of verbal discussion allow things to happen that might otherwise have been talked out of existence?**

items.title: Beyond profiles: Supervised repeat annotation using protein embeddings
items.subtitle: The model exhibits robustness to score thresholding and demonstrates better generalization to independent test sets, including those containing remotely related families.
items.feedText:
Lupas, Stanislaw Dunin-Horkawicz

Protein repeats give rise to diverse protein structures and functions, yet their sequence-based detection is often challenging because individual repeat units can diverge substantially in sequence while retaining similar structures. Most sensitive approaches rely on sequence information directly represented by alignments or derived profiles, thereby limiting flexibility and scalability. Here, we introduce TREAD (Transfer learning-based REpeat Annotation using Protein EmbeDdings)…
items.body: Protein repeats give rise to diverse protein structures and functions, yet their sequence-based detection is often challenging because individual repeat units can diverge substantially in sequence while retaining similar structures. Most sensitive approaches rely on sequence information directly represented by alignments or derived profiles, thereby limiting flexibility and scalability. Here, we introduce TREAD (Transfer learning-based REpeat Annotation using Protein EmbeDdings), a supervised framework that reformulates repeat detection as a residue-level annotation problem and operates directly on embeddings from protein language models. Instead of constructing explicit probabilistic profiles, TREAD learns repeat-specific features implicitly, enabling residue-resolved scoring and flexible repeat segment extraction. Across complementary benchmarks based on RepeatsDB and Pfam, TREAD consistently matches or outperforms the widely used profile-based tool HMMER, particularly in low-data and high-divergence settings. The model exhibits robustness to score thresholding and demonstrates better generalization to independent test sets, including those containing remotely related families. To illustrate the practical utility of TREAD, we applied it to survey β-propeller proteins across the AlphaFold Database and representative proteomes to generate a comprehensive census of this fold. This analysis highlights extensive propeller diversity, identifies lineage-specific expansion patterns across the tree of life, and suggests previously unrecognized relationships between propellers and other repeat folds. Together, TREAD provides a flexible and scalable alternative to profile-based repeat annotation and establishes a general motif-centric framework for protein sequence annotation.

items.title: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities
items.subtitle: GPT-6 models design protein structures and sequences using reasoning and code.
items.feedText: In a preprint titled GPT‑6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models , we show that our GPT‑6 family of models has intrinsic capabilities for designing new proteins: the models can design new protein structures and sequences without relying on specialized biology models, using only reasoning and general-purpose coding tools. Proteins do much of the work in living cells. They drive the chemical reactions that sustain life, carry oxygen through the blood, and defend the body against infection. Incorrectly shaped proteins can also cause disease and dysfunction. Proteins are made from chains of chemical building blocks called amino acids. The order, or sequence, of these amino acids helps determine how a protein folds into a three-dimensional shape, which in turn influences what it does.
items.body:
# GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities

November 24, 2026

## GPT‑6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities

## Key findings:

- Our GPT‑6 family of models can design new protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs.
- An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take.
- In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets. Redesigned antibodies also retained binding. Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing.
- The models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules.
In a preprint titled GPT‑6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models , we show that our GPT‑6 family of models has intrinsic capabilities for designing new proteins: the models can design new protein structures and sequences without relying on specialized biology models, using only reasoning and general-purpose coding tools.

Proteins do much of the work in living cells. They drive the chemical reactions that sustain life, carry oxygen through the blood, and defend the body against infection. Incorrectly shaped proteins can also cause disease and dysfunction. Proteins are made from chains of chemical building blocks called amino acids. The order, or sequence, of these amino acids helps determine how a protein folds into a three-dimensional shape, which in turn influences what it does.

Scientists often start with a clear idea of what they want a protein to do. They might want it to block a signal that helps cancer cells evade the immune system or to help capture carbon dioxide from the air. The challenge is to work out what three-dimensional structure would enable the protein to do its job and which amino acid sequence would give it that structure. Specialized biology models capable of generating three-dimensional protein structures and sequences have made this work more practical.

Using and coordinating these specialized models requires substantial expertise. Each accepts particular kinds of inputs and constraints, and these models cannot easily accept new kinds of information without changes to their software or additional training. In contrast, a general-purpose model capable of performing the work of multiple specialized models can easily adapt to new instructions and requirements.

Our research illustrates the potential power of pairing natural language with intrinsic protein capabilities. We could guide our models at scales ranging from a single bond between two atoms to the overall shape of a protein. For example, we asked GPT‑6.2 to predict where and how a small molecule would bind to a protein. When we already knew which two atoms formed a bond, we could give the model that information and ask how the rest of the molecule would fit. We could switch between these tasks simply by changing the prompt, without retraining the model. We also asked our models to design small proteins called minibinders and marked where each should attach to its target, and further specified how many coils or strands each minibinder should contain. An internal model followed that instruction with near-perfect fidelity in its three-dimensional designs.

Points farther from the center indicate better performance. Newer generations of models improved on many of the 14 protein tasks tested.

## A closer look at our models’ protein designs

We ran computational tests of whether the GPT‑6 models series could design small proteins to bind given targets, build proteins around specified structural features, predict protein structures and molecular interactions, and rank how sequence changes affect properties such as stability and binding. Our latest models performed comparably to or better than specialized models on most tasks, although predicting a complete protein structure remained a clear weakness.

The models’ written reasoning and code offer clues to how they approach these tasks. They draw on mathematics, physics, chemistry, and coding alongside knowledge of recurring patterns in protein sequences and structures. For example, when designing a small protein intended to bind to IL-7Rα, the model proposed how the two proteins might interact, then wrote and executed code to explore different protein shapes and amino acid choices that could support that interaction.

The model’s written reasoning and code show it drawing on math, physics, chemistry and biology to design a protein intended to attach to IL-7Rα. It examines the target’s surface, arranges five coiled sections into a protein shape, and checks how the two proteins could fit together.

With our research partner, Onava ⁠ (opens in a new window) , we also tested the models’ structure and sequence designs in the lab. First, Onava made small proteins based on three-dimensional structures designed by a pre-released version of GPT‑6.2. Specialized models supplied amino acid sequences and helped select candidates for testing. For each of the five targets we chose, at least one protein showed evidence of binding in the lab. In separate experiments, GPT‑6.2 designed new amino acid sequences for existing minibinders and antibodies. Following candidate selection with specialized models, many of the redesigned proteins also showed evidence of binding to the same targets as the originals.

## Laboratory Experiment 1: Designing small proteins that bind to a target

Our first laboratory experiment tested whether GPT‑6.2 could design small proteins that would bind to their intended targets. We compared computational measurements of quality against RFdiffusion, a specialized model for protein design, and found that GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs scored slightly lower while our latest internal models scored higher. For the lab experiment, we made proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs and measured how strongly they bound to their targets.

We gave GPT‑6.2 the three-dimensional structures of five target proteins and marked where we wanted a minibinder to attach. It then wrote code to create three-dimensional designs for potential minibinders, without using specialized protein AI models.

To turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins we could test in the lab, we needed amino acid sequences that would fold into the proposed structures. We used a specialized AI model called SolubleMPNN to suggest sequences for each design. Other specialized protein models helped us select candidates predicted to fold as designed and bind at the intended site on the target.

items.body: The relative influence of developmental bias and natural selection on evolutionary outcomes remains a central, unresolved question in evolutionary biology. Here, we combine large-scale phylogenetic trees with herbarium data to confirm that, across the evolutionary history of angiosperms, transitions from complex to simple leaf shapes have occurred at a significantly higher rate than the reverse. To investigate whether this directional trend reflects an underlying developmental bias, we simulate evolutionary transitions by introducing random mutations into a well-established computational model of leaf development. Despite excluding selection, the transition rates produced by the model closely align with those observed in the phylogenetic data. This agreement indicates that a strong developmental bias, reflecting the relative ease with which gene regulatory networks generate simple over complex leaves, has played a major role in shaping the evolution of leaf morphology. Our findings echo recent work showing that similar biases towards simplicity influence the evolution of molecular structures, including RNA secondary structures and protein quaternary assemblies. Together, these results suggest that a developmental bias favouring simplicity may be a widespread and general feature of evolutionary systems.

items.body:
Michael Bouhanna, the former vice president of contemporary art specialist and head of digital art at Sotheby’s, has launched his own art advisory. Called Bouhanna Art Advisory, it will focus on modern and contemporary art based out of Miami.

Bouhanna was the last man standing at Sotheby’s Metaverse and other NFT divisions when the auction house laid off four staffers in 2024. He joined the company in 2016 as CTP junior cataloger and quickly moved up the ranks in the contemporary art department before being given the joint responsibility of contemporary and digital art in 2021. Bouhanna exited Sotheby’s in January, after just over a decade at the auction house working in its London, Paris, and New York headquarters. Bouhanna’s exit was unrelated to the layoffs, although following his departure Sotheby’s integrated NFTs and digital art into its contemporary art department. In September 2025, [Christie’s closed its digital art department](https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/christies-reportedly-closes-digital-art-department-1234751156/) as the demand for digital art cooled down. In a wider view of the digital art market, Bouhanna told *ARTnews* that digital art is still part of contemporary art and it should not be seen as a separate entity. “Digital art still interests collectors who follow technology and AI. The serious digital artists have continued to gain institutional recognition, but it’s a niche within contemporary art.”

Bouhanna’s new chapter in Miami will involve placing modern and contemporary art by blue-chip artists in private collections and hands. In Miami, he has started working with private collectors, family offices and estates across acquisitions, sales, valuation and the management of collections. “Miami and South Florida collectors have built serious collections over the last decade, and a new generation is entering the market at a high level and often, they’re making their first significant acquisition,” Bouhanna said. “The established and emerging collectors need sophisticated advisory services that have long been available in London, New York or Paris, and also because transactions have become more complex with guarantees, private sales, and financing, collectors need experts on their side to evaluate them more than ever.”

Bouhanna moved to Miami earlier this year with his wife, Alexandra Benezra, founder of the public relations agency ASB PR Agency and fashion label Selvi. In the last year, he has been getting a feel for the city, which has [absorbed more wealth](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/02/business/family-offices-miami.html) in 10 years than any other American city and single-family offices are expected to grow by more than 10,000 by 2030. “Founders of companies, financial firms and families from the Northeast, West Coast and Latin America, who have had a strong habit of collecting art now live in South Florida,” Bouhanna said, noting that there’s also an influx of young, self-made entrepreneurs and financiers who are taking up art collection as an investment. Miami’s cultural infrastructure is following the same curve with institutions such as Pérez Art Museum Miami, ICA Miami, Bass Museum of Art and Rubell Museum offering competitive programs all year round as opposed to just one week during Art Basel Miami.

items.title: Did Democrats blow it in Florida?
items.subtitle: Angie Nixon speaking at a rally in Kissimmee, Florida.
items.feedText: Joe Raedle/Getty Images. Eight years ago, Democrats retook the U.S. House, netting 41 seats and winning the national popular vote by 8.6 points in a textbook blue wave. But despite the rosy national environment, Republican Rick Scott narrowly defeated incumbent Democratic Senator Bill Nelson in Florida. In hindsight, that victory, on the heels of Donald Trump’s 2016 win in the state, was the harbinger of a death spiral for Florida Democrats that had begun years earlier. When I wrote about the Sunshine State back…
items.body:
Angie Nixon speaking at a rally in Kissimmee, Florida. Joe Raedle/Getty Images.

Eight years ago, Democrats retook the U.S. House, [netting 41 seats and winning the national popular vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_United_States_elections) by 8.6 points in a textbook blue wave. But despite the rosy national environment, Republican [Rick Scott narrowly defeated incumbent Democratic Senator Bill Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_United_States_Senate_election_in_Florida) in Florida. In hindsight, that victory, on the heels of Donald Trump’s 2016 win in the state, was the harbinger of a [death spiral for Florida Democrats](https://www.natesilver.net/p/can-democrats-escape-their-florida) that had begun years earlier.

When I [wrote about the Sunshine State back in February](https://www.natesilver.net/p/can-democrats-escape-their-florida), the consensus from both prediction markets and the experts I spoke with was that Democrats were highly unlikely to win the state in 2026. After a decade of losses and underinvestment, it looked like it could take another ten years for Democrats to turn Florida purple again. The short-term goal of the Florida Democratic Party (FDP) was less “win the 2026 Senate race” and more “[get out of the](https://www.natesilver.net/p/can-democrats-escape-their-florida) *[superminority](https://www.natesilver.net/p/can-democrats-escape-their-florida)* [in the state legislature](https://www.natesilver.net/p/can-democrats-escape-their-florida).”

But back then, no one knew that [2026 would be a blue tsunami](https://www.natesilver.net/p/after-an-extraordinary-wave-what) where Democrats would win the national popular vote by 13 points and net *nine* Senate seats.1 And yet they still lost both statewide races in Florida. Almost immediately, people started posting [post-election recriminations](https://x.com/hollyotterbein/status/2117796466551066896) that if Democrats had spent more in Florida, they could have pulled off at least one win.

So did Democrats blow a golden opportunity in Florida? Or is the state still too tough a target? That question should weigh on the party because in two short years, [Ashley Moody will be up for re-election](https://www.natesilver.net/p/an-extremely-unofficial-first-look).

[↗ natesilver.net](https://www.natesilver.net/p/did-democrats-blow-it-in-florida)

items.title: 11 Things Jensen Huang Actually Said at His First All-Hands Back at Nvidia
items.subtitle: The newly reinstated CEO discussed his daily therapy sessions, his reputation as a “tech bro,” his disdain for succession planning, and his relationship with President Trump.
items.feedText: The newly reinstated CEO discussed his daily therapy sessions, his reputation as a “tech bro,” his disdain for succession planning, and his relationship with President Trump.
items.body:
# 11 Things Jensen Huang Actually Said at His First All-Hands Back at Nvidia

Jensen Huang is going to therapy for 90 minutes a day, rethinking his management style , and says that violating Nvidia’s code of conduct isn’t necessarily a fireable offense. That’s just some of what the newly returned Nvidia CEO told staff during his first all-hands meeting on Tuesday.

Here are some of the most striking things Huang said during the meeting, according to remarks reviewed by WIRED. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

On self-improvement: “I go to therapy every day for an hour and a half. And it's been helping me a lot.”

On accountability: “There are rumors on the internet that apparently I'm a tech bro, and therefore I’m back. Apparently, I'm a tech bro, and because I wear a super nice jacket, that I'm above the law, and I’m above the code of conduct. That is not true. It won't be tolerated. That is not true. It won’t be tolerated, and it wasn't tolerated here.”

“If one of you were to violate a code of conduct, what does that mean? If you were ever to violate a code of conduct, it is not appropriate. I just wanted you to know, it is not right, it's not appropriate, it won't be tolerated. But ‘it won't be tolerated’ does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door. Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments. And your management team will still make the decision. That is what is in the best interest of the company and its employees, with all the facts and circumstances.”

On his management style: “The intensity I bring elevates everybody else. But I can go too far. When I go too far, it hurts people, it belittles them, it disempowers them. And that’s not right. And so I need to go figure out how I'm going to bring the intensity, the crazy intensity, to the field.”

On women at Nvidia: “I believe we need to create and continue to sustain a safe environment for all of our women. And if I did anything that put that in jeopardy, I cannot tell you how sad I am, and I'll do everything I can to fix it. We will not tolerate that.”

On succession: “All day long, this company can run autonomously, and you saw it. I promise you, whether I'm here or not, this company is wired up to execute, execute, and execute, and deliver on financial results and financial results.”

“I also didn't believe in succession planning. Let that sink in. I don’t believe in succession planning. I think it’s flawed. The idea of succession planning is not flawed. What people think succession planning means is flawed.”

“There’s a reason why we don’t have succession planning, it’s not because we are unaware of the word. I’m the longest-running tech CEO in history.”

On politics : “There [were] also rumors that apparently I'm back because the highest levels of our government wanted me back. That is also completely untrue. Our board of directors performed their duty as they should have.”

“It is absolutely true that President Trump really, really loves our company,” Huang told employees. “He gloats about Nvidia. You know he does. But there’s a question about politics. Are we now political? Are we partisan? I wanna be very clear with you. President Trump is the United States president. He is my president. And I’ll do everything I can to help this president be informed about how he could make decisions that are in the best interest of our country. … We have to do it, and whoever the next president is will be my president, and I will do exactly the same.”

“Don't think for a second that politics ever play a role in this company, not even a little bit. We are the most apolitical company. I don't love that we talk about politics here. Take it home. I love that we talk about work here.”

items.body:
Timothy Williamson will be the inaugural speaker in a new lecture series accompanying a new journal: *[The Chinese Journal of Philosophy](https://academic.oup.com/cjp?)* (CJP).

Published by Oxford University Press, the CJP is an open-access (including no cost to authors) general philosophy journal.

It is edited by Roger T. Ames (Hawaii), Wei Cheng (Peking), Nicolas De Warren (Penn State), Sebastian Sunday Grève (Peking), and You Zhao (Peking).

The journal is open to submissions “from anyone working in philosophy and on all philosophical topics.” According to its [website](https://academic.oup.com/cjp?),

> the journal aims to represent the multitude of topics and approaches that may fall under the heading of ‘philosophy’ in the world today, with a special focus on philosophical research that has the potential to make different traditions of thought more fruitful for one another.

That is to say, it is not a journal primarily about Chinese philosophy, anymore than the *Canadian Journal of Philosophy* is a journal about Canadian philosophy, or the *Australasian Journal of Philosophy* is about Australasian philosophy. The [note](https://phil.pku.edu.cn/xzqk/cjp/intro.htm), “like these other journals, the *Chinese Journal of Philosophy* originates in a particular region whilst editing and publishing as an international collective, operating in English, and promoting work from around the world.”

CJP is currently open for submissions and plans to begin publishing articles in April.

The launch of the journal includes the start of a new lecture series from the [Department of Philosophy and Religious Studies at Peking University](https://phil.pku.edu.cn/index.htm). Williamson’s inaugural lecture is this Wednesday, and will be delivered in person and [online](https://us06web.zoom.us/j/86727223234).

Learn more about the journal [↗ academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/cjp?).

# Putin und Cai Qi: Foto verfälscht den Größenunterschied

- Die Behauptung Das auf X verbreitete Foto zeige den wirklichen Größenunterschied zwischen Putin und Cai Qi. China habe seinen körperlich größten Funktionär absichtlich zum Empfang geschickt, um Putin bloßzustellen. Falsch Das verbreitete Bild verfälscht den Größenunterschied zwischen Putin und Cai Qi. Eine gezielte Bloßstellung und Cai Qis angeblicher Größenrekord sind unbelegt. 💬 Wie werden echte Bilder gezielt falsch eingeordnet? Antworten finden Sie im Leitfaden Bild- und Kontext-Fakes . Das auf X verbreitete Foto von Wladimir Putin neben einem riesig wirkenden Cai Qi ist verfälscht. Cai ist tatsächlich größer als Putin, doch die Vergleichsaufnahmen zeigen einen deutlich geringeren Abstand. Unbelegt ist auch die Behauptung, China habe ihn wegen seiner Körpergröße ausgewählt, um Putin bloßzustellen. Der X-Account RS Archer behauptet, China habe eigens das körperlich größte Mitglied seiner Parteiführung zum Flughafen geschickt. Das beigefügte Bild zeigt Cai und Putin auf einem roten Teppich vor einem Flugzeug und lässt Cai übermäßig groß erscheinen. Der beanstandete X-Beitrag übertreibt den Größenunterschied. Screenshot: X / Nutzerübermittlung. Der Bildvergleich zeigt den Unterschied Auf der Vergleichsaufnahme reicht Putins Kopf deutlich höher in Richtung von Cais Gesicht. Außerdem hält Putin einen Arm vor dem Oberkörper, während im verbreiteten Bild beide Arme nach unten zeigen. Eine weitere, als Getty-Aufnahme ausgewiesene Abbildung zeigt ebenfalls einen geringeren Größenunterschied. Die verglichene Kremlaufnahme ist als Screenshot bei Lead Stories dokumentiert; die Kremlseite selbst war beim Abruf nicht erreichbar. Lead Stories und What the Fact ordnen das verbreitete Bild als KI-verändert beziehungsweise KI-erzeugt ein. Auch unser zusätzlicher Detektortest stuft das Bild mit einem Wert von 99,8 Prozent als wahrscheinlich KI-generiert ein. Das ist ein weiterer Hinweis auf KI-Bearbeitung, aber keine gemessene Sicherheit über die tatsächliche Herstellung. Der Bildvergleich zeigt die verfälschte Darstellung; welches Werkzeug dafür verwendet wurde, bleibt offen. Mimikamas zusätzlicher Detektortest: Das Werkzeug zeigt 99,8 Prozent für ein wahrscheinlich KI-generiertes Bild an. Der Wert ist eine technische Einschätzung und allein kein Beweis für die Herstellung. Screenshot: Mimikama. Ein echter Empfang belegt keine Demütigungsabsicht Cai Qi empfing Putin tatsächlich am Flughafen von Shenzhen zum APEC-Treffen. Das bestätigt die Meldung der chinesischen Nachrichtenagentur Xinhua . Cai gehört dem Ständigen Ausschuss des Politbüros an. Dass er der körperlich größte Parteifunktionär sei oder gerade deshalb ausgewählt wurde, ist durch die geprüften Quellen nicht belegt. Die Ankunft war am 18. November 2026 nach chinesischer Ortszeit. Laut South China Morning Post landete Putin kurz nach 2 Uhr früh. In Moskau und Wien war es da noch der 17. November, den Lead Stories nennt. Die Zeitverschiebung kann diese Abweichung erklären; ausdrücklich erläutert wird sie dort nicht. Bei solchen Bildern lohnt sich der Vergleich mit weiteren Aufnahmen desselben Termins. Eine sichtbare Körpergröße lässt sich prüfen. Eine politische Absicht hinter der Auswahl der Empfangsperson braucht einen eigenen Beleg. Quellen FAKTENCHECK What the Fact Did China send its tallest official to greet Putin at Shenzhen airport? 20. November 2026 FAKTENCHECK Lead Stories Fact Check: FAKE Photo Shows Huge Height Difference Between Vladimir Putin And Chinese Official — Image Is AI-Altered 19. November 2026 MEDIUM South China Morning Post Putin gets high-level airport welcome in Shenzhen as he arrives for Apec 18. November 2026 BEHÖRDE Xinhua / South Putin arrives in Shenzhen for APEC meeting 18. November 2026
