items.body:
**Editor’s note:** This story is an edition of [Link Rot](https://www.artnews.com/t/link-rot/), a column by Shanti Escalante-De Mattei that explores the intersections of art, technology, and the internet.

During last June’s heat wave, I found myself standing outside an unassuming office building in Crown Heights, Brooklyn, baking in the sun’s glare. The Gallery, a nomadic curatorial platform, had set up an exhibition, titled “WeWork (oralmoral)”, in one of the building’s vacant office spaces. In celebration of the show’s closing the curators were screening films, some of which fall into the category of what is being called “internet cinema,” a burgeoning movement, or method, that has been in the making since late 2020.

Once inside, I wandered around the cool, unlit space, laughing at funny paintings and sculptures until it was time to find a spot on the floor for the screening. Someone in front of me was hastily scrawling the lineup of the screenings on paper with a black marker and passing them around as fast as he produced them. One passed back to me. The first film on the list was Zarina Nares’ *I am going to die (this is my sign)* (2025). The projector was fiddled with and a rectangle of white with a buffer symbol appeared on the blank wall in front of the seated crowd.

A chorus of female voices rose up, all in some general distress, and while I couldn’t see these women, by the tone, I could tell they were speaking into a front-facing camera. The chorus cut out to a single voice, which spoke over dashcam footage of a car crash: “You’re having problems at work, your boyfriend broke up with you, your parents are mad at you, everything is going wrong, your car broke down – that is a good sign. Like, that is the very best sign.”

What followed was a montage of TikTok videos featuring motivational advice. One video bled into another, linked by the formulaic hooks used by podcast bros, emotional car seat influencers, clips of celebrities’ acceptance speeches, athletes in interviews, or passionate pastors, all of which was set to music. One after another these TikToks reveal ‘the one thing that you need to learn’ in a high-speed carousel of intense emotion that feels increasingly forced as it becomes clear how many of these impassioned speeches are copies of one another.

A screening of Zarina Nares’ film *This is Your Sign, I am Going to Die* at “WeWork (oralmoral)”, an exhibition organized by The Gallery in Brooklyn, New York,

“Internet cinema isn’t necessarily about the internet or its aesthetic but about its logic, how it functions and how it makes us feel,” Zarina Nares said in a phone call. On the process of making *I am going to die,* she added that “Clearly, I watched enough advice videos for too long that I kept getting more. Once you watch so many you see the formula behind them, whether it’s a certain cadence of speaking or certain music.”

Internet cinema was first defined in a 2007 paper by Chuck Tryon titled *“New Media Studies and the New Internet Cinema.”* The technologies and formats that concerned Tryon —iPods and camera phones, software like Final Cut Pro, and home movies—are far dated, but his paper was prescient, having tapped into impulses and concerns that reflect contemporary internet cinema: a do-it-yourself ethos that blurs the line between amateur and artist; the popularization of “niche exhibition;” and a “self-reflexive style” that works “to call attention to the narrative codes and technological specs that shape cultural productions.”

Contemporary internet cinema has its roots in the COVID-era, which saw an explosion of participation in internet culture and production, that often bled out into one particular place: Dimes Square, a patch of Manhattan where Chinatown and the Lower East Side meet.

One of the most memorable dramas that played out at the time was puppeteered by a then-anonymous internet figure who went by the name Angelicism01. This figure posted creeds about extinction on Substack, and gained infamy for growing a cult-like following among young women in New York (who had never met him). With the help of various film makers, he made a three-hour long movie called *Film01* which includes fast paced montages of memes, tweets, videos of natural disasters and terrorist attacks, alongside long scenes featuring the ‘it-girls’ he had recruited. Writer Madeline Cash described *Film01* in the art publication [Spike](https://spikeartmagazine.com/articles/discourse-angelicism-film01-2023-jonestown-snoozefest-madeline-cash) as “an unsophisticated collage of localized content that mimics, rather than intervenes or questions, our digital conditions,” which ultimately did nothing more than tap “into the scene’s libidinal narcissism.”

Yet, with some distance, *Film01* has proven to be a productive experiment. One of Angelicism01’s collaborators, the filmmaker Dana Dawud, found internet footage to splice into the film, created short edits that became a part of the larger film, and remotely directed certain sequences. Dawud would go on to launch Open Secret, an international screening series of internet cinema that has since played a large part in consolidating disconnected artists and practices under the term.

At the same time that young women were running around Dimes Square at Angelicism01’s request, people were locked away at home with TikTok. More than ever, people around the world were subjecting themselves to hours and hours of scrolling on this relatively new video content platform.

“When you’re doom scrolling, there is, technically speaking, no specific author to this montage that you’re watching. So, it’s as if you’re exposed to radical experimental cinema all the time by a completely cynical industrial apparatus,” said 0nty, the co-author of “Dialogues on CoreCore & the Contemporary Online Avant-Garde” during a Zoom interview also attended by his co-author Mischa Dols. “The question is, how do you even begin to think about this problem? And I think internet cinema is an answer,” 0nty said.

0nty and Dols describe internet cinema as a method, rather than a genre or an aesthetic, which seeks to expose or comment on the way that the internet functions through editing found footage.

items.body:
Tucked away in the historic centre of Anderlecht, just a stone's throw from the Collegiate Church of Saints Peter and Guido, lies one of Brussels' lesser-known historical treasures: the Beguinage of Anderlecht. Founded in 1252, it is considered the smallest beguinage in Belgium and once provided a home to a community of just eight women.

Unlike traditional convents, beguinages offered women an opportunity to live in a religious community without taking permanent monastic vows. The beguines were typically unmarried women or widows who chose a life of prayer, work and mutual support. They followed rules of chastity and obedience but remained free to leave the community whenever they wished. This offered women a degree of independence that was relatively unusual in medieval society.

The Anderlecht beguinage consists of two modest buildings surrounding an enclosed courtyard garden with an old well. The buildings date from different periods, with sections originating in the 16th and 18th centuries. From the garden, visitors can enjoy a view of the neighbouring Gothic collegiate church.

Interestingly, the beguinage was locally nicknamed the Klaphuis, meaning 'chatterbox' in Dutch, a playful reference to the conversations that supposedly took place among its residents.

Following the French Revolution, the religious community disappeared and the buildings were converted into a hospice for disadvantaged women. They continued serving this purpose until 1928. In 1930, the complex became a local history museum, displaying archaeological finds, religious art and objects illustrating Anderlecht's past.

After decades of use as a museum, the buildings underwent an extensive restoration, completed in 2022. The restoration aimed to recover the original appearance of the complex, allowing visitors to appreciate its historic architecture. Today, the beguinage offers a rare glimpse into the everyday lives of medieval women and the history of one of Brussels' oldest communities.

Despite being surrounded by the busy streets of Anderlecht, stepping through its entrance feels like discovering a little pocket of tranquillity that has survived for almost eight centuries.

items.title: the search for a home without a fixed address, from prefabricated houses to floating dwellings
items.subtitle:
THE IDEA OF A HOME WITHOUT A FIXED ADDRESS

For decades, architects have imagined homes that can be packed up, transported, and assembled somewh…
items.feedText: From prefabricated dwellings designed for mass production to experimental houses conceived for remote landscapes, these projects explore how architecture might exist beyond the limits of a fixed site. One early expression of this ambition came from American architect and inventor Buckminster Fuller. In 1928, he developed the concept for the Dymaxion House, a prefabricated dwelling conceived for mass production and delivery as a single unit by aircraft. Its lightweight aluminum structure reflected Fuller’s intere…
items.body:
## THE IDEA OF A HOME WITHOUT A FIXED ADDRESS

For decades, architects have imagined[homes](https://www.designboom.com/tag/residential-architecture-interiors/) that can be [packed up](https://www.designboom.com/tag/portable-and-emergency-architecture/), transported, and assembled somewhere new, designing alternatives to the idea that housing must be tied to a permanent address. From [prefabricated](https://www.designboom.com/tag/prefabricated-homes-and-buildings/) dwellings designed for mass production to experimental houses conceived for [remote](https://www.designboom.com/tag/floating-architecture-and-artificial-islands/) landscapes, these projects explore how architecture might exist beyond the limits of a fixed site.

One early expression of this ambition came from American architect and inventor Buckminster Fuller. In 1928, he developed the concept for the Dymaxion House, a prefabricated dwelling conceived for mass production and delivery as a single unit by aircraft. Its lightweight [aluminum](https://www.designboom.com/tag/aluminum/) structure reflected Fuller’s interest in applying industrial manufacturing to housing. Although the project never developed into a commercially viable housing system, it proposed a home manufactured away from its eventual site and transported there for assembly.

The idea took a different form in the late 1960s with Finnish architect Matti Suuronen’s [Futuro House](https://www.designboom.com/architecture/ufo-shaped-futuro-house-radical-1960s-vision-prefab-living-market-matti-suuronen-sothebys-donaldson-california/). Designed as a portable ski cabin, the fiberglass dwelling could be dismantled and transported to remote locations, including by helicopter. Its rounded silhouette and synthetic materials reflected the period’s fascination with space exploration and technological progress.

Donaldson Futuro | image courtesy of Sotheby’s International Realty

## FROM THE HOUSE TO THE CITY

Mobility, however, does not necessarily mean moving an entire building. It can also involve designing structures that can be taken apart, reassembled, extended, or adapted as needs change. This distinction became particularly important in the work of French architect and designer Jean Prouvé, who explored industrialized construction as a way to make buildings faster and easier to assemble. In the final years of the Second World War, Prouvé developed demountable houses for people whose homes had been destroyed in eastern France. His 8×8 house used a structural system based on a central steel portal frame, with components designed for assembly and disassembly. The project responded to an urgent need for housing, but it also demonstrated how prefabrication could make construction more flexible.

[Marion Post Wolcott](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Dymaxion_House_-_LOC_8c14945v.jpg), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

## MOBILITY, NECESSITY, AND THE RIGHT TO SHELTER

Mobile and temporary architecture is not always driven by a desire for a different lifestyle. In many cases, it responds to an immediate need for shelter. Following the 1994 Rwandan genocide, Japanese architect Shigeru Ban began developing paper-tube structures for refugee accommodation, experimenting with inexpensive, readily available materials that could be used to build temporary homes.

The shelters were designed to be assembled with simple construction methods, making them suitable for situations where building resources were limited. Ban’s work brought architectural thinking into a humanitarian context, showing that even temporary structures require careful consideration of how people live, rather than simply where they sleep.

Jean Prouvé’s 6×6 Demountable House (1944) | image © Galerie Patrick Seguin

## WHEN THE SITE BEGINS TO CHANGE

Another reason to reconsider fixed construction is the instability of the environments in which buildings are placed. Rising water levels, flooding, and pressure on urban land have encouraged architects and communities to explore ways of living on or alongside water. Floating architecture changes the relationship between a structure and its site, allowing the building to respond to water. In Amsterdam, Schoonschip offers an example at the scale of a neighborhood. Developed by its residents with urban planning support from architecture studio Space&Matter, the floating community comprises 30 water plots and 46 homes. Shared infrastructure connects the dwellings, while solar panels, batteries, and a smart grid allow residents to generate and exchange electricity.

Other projects approach the same question at a smaller scale. NOA’s DeKruif House, for example, is a prefabricated timber residence conceived for a family that does not want to commit to one location. Designed to adapt to different waterfront settings, it considers how a house might respond to changing views, orientation, and surroundings. David Rule’s TinyTanic takes mobility onto the water itself, compressing basic domestic functions into a miniature houseboat designed for short journeys. While their scale and ambitions differ, both projects treat the relationship between home and location as something that can be reconsidered.

Peter Cook. Plug-in City: Maximum Pressure Area, project (Section). 1964

## RETHINKING PERMANENCE

It is easy to see the appeal of a house that can move. It opens up the possibility of taking a home somewhere new, adapting it to a different setting, or using it for a limited period of time. But moving a building does not automatically make it cheaper, greener, or easier to live in. It still needs materials, energy, water, electricity, and waste systems. A house may be able to travel, but it cannot escape the practical needs of everyday life.

These projects also raise a question about why homes are expected to stay in one place in the first place.

From prefabricated houses and temporary shelters to floating neighborhoods, architects have explored different ways of building for changing needs and surroundings. Not every structure needs to be mobile, but more buildings could be designed to adapt, come apart, or be used again rather than remain fixed forever.

The Futuro House is a good example of how this idea can come full circle. Designed to be transported and assembled in different locations, it is now a rare piece of architecture that people want to preserve. A house once imagined for life on the move has become something that must stay put. Perhaps the question is not whether we will all live in houses that travel, but whether our homes can change along with the way we live and the places we inhabit.

DeKruif House elevated among tall trees in a misty forest | rendering courtesy of NOA

round windows bring natural light into the cabin | image courtesy of [David Rule](https://www.instagram.com/davidmrule/?hl=en)

items.body:
## Art Miami and CONTEXT Art Miami Announce 2026 Exhibitors for Miami Art Week

[↗ Primärquelle: mymodernmet.com](https://mymodernmet.com/art-miami-x-context-art-miami-2026/)

This December, Miami becomes the place to be for art lovers. [Art Miami](https://www.artmiami.com/) and its sister fair, [CONTEXT Art Miami](https://www.contextartmiami.com/), have just revealed their participating artists and galleries for 2026, and the lineup doesn’t disappoint. Returning to One Herald Plaza, Dec. 1–6, the two fairs will bring together an international mix of galleries, artists, collectors, and contemporary art enthusiasts for the 36th edition of Art Miami and the 14th edition of CONTEXT.

Art Miami 2026 will feature work from galleries hailing from 25 countries, representing major art destinations including London, Paris, Berlin, Seoul, Hong Kong, Dubai, Istanbul, and Bogotá. Visitors can enjoy both modern and contemporary art, from the [modern masters](https://mymodernmet.com/what-is-modern-art-definition/) and [Pop Art icons](https://mymodernmet.com/pop-art-artists/) of the 20th century to [contemporary painting](https://mymodernmet.com/contemporary-landscape-painting/), sculpture, photography, design, and new media.

Returning exhibitors include [Allouche Gallery](https://www.allouchegallery.com/), [Ascaso Gallery](https://www.ascasogallery.com/), [Boccara Gallery](https://boccara.com/), [Ethan Cohen Gallery](https://www.ecfa.com/), and [Opera Gallery](https://www.operagallery.com/), alongside more than 20 galleries from Miami and the surrounding South Florida region. Artist [Lucy Sparrow](https://mymodernmet.com/lucy-sparrow-beginning-of-convenience/) will also return following the success of her felt candy store installation at last year’s fair. She will reveal her new installation, *The Money Laundry*, a hand-felted, interactive laundromat featuring hand-painted cash, passports, and luxury watches.

Meanwhile, CONTEXT Art Miami will once again shine a spotlight on emerging and mid-career artists. Its 14th edition will feature international galleries presenting new and recent works, solo exhibitions, curated projects, and immersive installations. Participating galleries include [Bel-Air Fine Art](https://www.belairfineart.com/en), [Hilton Contemporary](https://hiltoncontemporary.com/), [Iconic Images Gallery](https://iconicimagesgallery.com/), and [Uniquity Art Gallery](https://www.uniquityartgallery.com/), among many others.

Another major highlight across both fairs will be the celebration of artist and activist [Shepard Fairey](https://mymodernmet.com/shepard-fairey-art-miami-lifetime-visionary-award/), who will receive the 2026 Art Miami Lifetime Visionary Award. Recognized for his influential practice spanning street art, graphic design, and political activism, Fairey will be honored with a curated presentation of his work in Art Miami's VIP Lounge.

Both Art Miami and CONTEXT Art Miami run between Dec. 1–6, at One Herald Plaza in Downtown Miami. Tickets are available online at [Art Miami](https://www.artmiami.com/tickets) and [CONTEXT Art Miami](https://www.contextartmiami.com/tickets).

items.body:
In Shanghai’s Jing’an Sculpture Park, a monumental new installation by Brooklyn’s [Wade and Leta](https://wadeandleta.com/) has a clear goal: to get people up and moving in the same space. Titled “Catching Feelings,” the interactive artwork doubles as an all-ages playground with the artists’ signature sculptures and geometric forms. A central tower holds a quartet of slides, while other spinning and writhing elements are designed for more unstructured interaction.

“Catching Feelings” is one of 36 projects in the ninth edition of the Jing’an International Sculpture Project, an annual project helmed by the [UCCA Center for Contemporary Art](https://ucca.org.cn/en/). In comparison to the artists’ [earlier works](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/tags/wade-and-leta/), the bold, kinetic playground is decidedly analog, with any movement powered by the people interacting with its components rather than embedded motors or motion generated by the wind.

“We’re interested in the life and activity around our work—the behaviors it causes, the elations it brings,” the artists say in a statement. “We watched the same grandfather return with his granddaughter to play hide and seek; an 84-year-old and his partner used the space as the backdrop for their video recordings; new friends were made on our ground spinners; we even glimpsed a man in a business suit having a go on the slide.”

“Catching Feelings” is presented alongside monumental works by [Olafur Eliasson](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/tags/olafur-eliasson/), [Marshmallow Laser Feast](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/tags/marshmallow-laser-feast/), and many others on view through December 31. Find more from Wade and Leta on their [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/wadeandleta/).

Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a [Colossal Member](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/members) today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article [A Sculptural Playground in Shanghai Is Designed for Human-Powered Play](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/2026/11/wade-leta-catching-feelings-shanghai/) appeared first on [Colossal](https://www.thisiscolossal.com).

items.body:
Architect and designer [Patricia Urquiola](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/Patricia-Urquiola/) has chosen fellow multidisciplinary Laerke Ryom as her pick for Dezeen’s [20x20](https://www.dezeen.com/20x20) project, in partnership with [Kohler](https://www.studiokohler.com/home?id=paid-media_dezeen_studiokohler_Global-20x20_2026_Editorial-Series_version-1). In this [interview](https://www.dezeen.com/interviews/), Ryom discusses her innovative work and how it's rooted in Danish design traditions.

Ryom, who is based in Copenhagen, first came to many people's attention as one of the co-founders of the design community [Ukurant](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/ukurant/).

Above: Laerke Ryom, photographed by Alexander Höllsberg for [Innenkreis](https://innenkreis.com/). Top image: her work includes pieces made from wood offcuts. Photo by Heidi Lerkenfelt

Together with fellow founders [Josefine Krabbe Munck](https://www.instagram.com/crabgirlgonebad/), [Kamma Rosa Schytte](https://www.kammarosaschytte.com/) and [Kasper Kyster](https://www.instagram.com/kasperkyster/), Ryom showed her work as part of its [first exhibition at Danish design week 3 Days of Design in 2020](https://www.dezeen.com/2020/09/07/ukurant-exhibition-objects-3-days-of-design/), and Ukurant quickly became a recurring highlight of the design event.

Patricia Urquiola selected Laerke Ryom for Dezeen’s 20×20 project. Photo by Nicola Carignani

Since graduating from the Royal Academy of Fine Art in Copenhagen's master’s program in furniture and object in 2022, Ryom's tactile designs have continued to evolve, and she has worked with a range of materials and products.

For her collection Blå, she made handwoven denim upholstery out of worn-out jeans, while the [Buckle chair](https://www.fredericia.com/inspiration/laerke-ryom-life-lies-in-the-folds), made with furniture brand Fredericia, resembles a leather jacket.

"I find very interesting the way she moves naturally between furniture and textiles, starting from discarded materials and giving them a new logic through simple gestures," Urquiola said of why she chose Ryom.

"There is something light in the way she works. Her work feels open and still very much in evolution.”

This experimentation has become something of a signature for Ryom, whose latest exhibition, Raiments, [was a sleek exploration of how upholstery could almost become a furniture piece in itself](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/03/20/laerke-ryom-raiments-furniture-exhibition-copenhagen/).

To the designer, her work now is in some ways a continuation of the projects she worked on during her time at the Royal Academy.

"During my studies, I was investigating different materials and different typologies, which I actually still think I'm kind of doing – I don't see myself as limited to one material," Ryom told Dezeen.

The Raiments furniture appeared to be made purely from upholstery

While she "really strongly identifies as a furniture designer", Ryom has also designed smaller products, such as [metal bowls for the Bread & Butter exhibition](https://www.dezeen.com/2025/06/20/bread-butter-exhibition-3-days-of-design/) in Copenhagen and quilted lamps.

To her, function is always at the forefront, and Ryom believes that even details that appear to be purely decorative have a function if they tell a story.

"Even when I'm doing collectible things for galleries, I'm always thinking of the functionality of the pieces," she explained.

"Even if you can say, '[what's functional] about doing a little skirt on a chair', as on the Raiments chair, it tells a story; a story of the cover being loose, something that is its own thing, [separate] from the frame. For me, that's still a function or a means to an end."

Ryom has worked with a wide range of materials, including denim, metal and leather

Her aim is to create pieces that straddle the line between collectible and functional design; something that is artistic and yet commercial enough to someday go into production.

"I want it to be something where the distance between the categories disappears, and they become a shared thing," Ryom explained.

"That's something I think a lot about, that the collectible design and the artistic work I do should have a little sprinkle of something that you could see in production."

> The collectible design and artistic work I do should have a little sprinkle of something that you could see in production

The idea of giving beauty to everyday objects, rather than creating pieces that are purely functional or purely aesthetic, is one that has deep roots in the Scandinavian design tradition.

While Ryom's pieces might not be the pale-wood designs usually associated with Danish design – though she has worked in wood, using offcut wooden pieces to design furniture for Ukurant in 2023 – she sees herself as part of this tradition.

"Even if people don't think that what I do looks like typical Danish design, I feel like it's completely rooted and very fundamentally based on the principles of the Danish design tradition," she explained.

"I view myself as someone who is not in opposition, but who is developing or following along [with it]."

The Enfold chair has a ruched-leather cover

While her own pieces in the past have so far mostly been made in smaller quantities, Ryom sees positively on the current trend of big brands, such as [IKEA](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/ikea/) and [Disney](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/disney/), working with younger designers and mass-producing their work.

She believes it helps to spread knowledge about designers to a public that isn't always aware of the people behind the products.

"I think it's an important thing because what we see, at least here in Denmark, is that the knowledge about designers today, for the general public, is crazy small for a nation that kind of brands itself as a design nation," Ryom said.

"Talking to my parents, even with them having a designer for a daughter, they're still trying to figure out 'what is it that you actually do'?

> Inspiration can only take you so far – at some point you need to get working on it, interpret it and experiment with it

Ryom herself, meanwhile, says she sees a big difference between her current work and that of a few years ago. She thinks it comes from "starting to believe in yourself and your intuition, and getting more skilled in your craft".

But, she also consciously works on developing her ideas and taking them from the initial inspiration stage to the final product.

"Inspiration is something that I stumble upon in my everyday life, but at the same time, it only becomes interesting when I sit down and work with it," she said.

"Inspiration can only take you so far – at some point you need to get working on it, interpret it and experiment with it and investigate what the substance of the inspiration actually is."

items.body:
In a Buddhist temple in the northeast of Thailand, not far from the border with Laos, one can find the World's Only Dinosaur Pulpit.

Located in the city of Khon Kean, the fourth-largest city in Thailand and the heart of the Isan region, the pulpit can be found inside the Buddhist temple Wat That Phra Aram Luang. If you look closely, you'll notice there are dinosaur mural paintings on the walls inside the temple as well.

Having been the site of Thailand’s first dinosaur fossil discovery, Khon Kean boasts a variety of dinosaur-related sites. Dinosaur imagery is scattered throughout the entire region, giving a nod to this history. Among these references is the World's Only Dinosaur pulpit. The pulpit is shaped like a giant Phuwiangosaurus, Thailand’s native sauropod dinosaur. The dinosaur was originally discovered in the hills of Phu Wiang outside the city, and officially named in 1994 in honor of Her Royal Highness Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn.

Monks reportedly stand inside the dinosaur to give sermons at times. Wat That Phra Aram Luang temple is a stunning sight to behold on its own, resplendent with numerous golden peaks and facades painted in bright shades or red.

items.body:
## Visitors choose their favorites at the 2026 venice art biennale

The public has selected its favorites at the **[61st Venice Art Biennale](https://www.designboom.com/tag/venice-art-biennale-2026/)**, with American artist [Nick Cave](https://www.designboom.com/tag/nick-cave/) receiving the Visitors’ Lion for Best Participant and India winning Best National Participation for its pavilion,**[Geographies of Distance: Remembering Home](https://www.designboom.com/art/india-pavilion-venice-biennale-2026-craft-idea-home-alive-interview/)**. Announced by La Biennale di Venezia on November 25th, 2026, the awards reflect the preferences of visitors to In Minor Keys, curated by the late Koyo Kouoh.

Following the resignation of the International Jury, the institution introduced two Visitors’ Lions, inviting audiences to vote for the Best Participant in In Minor Keys and the Best National Participation throughout the exhibition. The decision placed public engagement at the center of this year’s awards, giving visitors a direct role in determining which artistic presentations received recognition.

National Pavilion of India, Venice Art Biennale 2026 | image by Luca Zambelli Bais

## Nick Cave receives the award for best participant

Born in Chicago in 1959, Cave receives the recognition for his participation in the main exhibition. Working across sculpture, performance, textiles, and installation, the artist has developed a practice that explores identity, material culture, race, and the possibilities of transformation. His work frequently brings together elaborate material compositions and performative gestures, creating spaces where art becomes an encounter between the body, movement, and collective experience.

Under the same sky, Ranjani Shettar | image by Jacopo Salvi

## India pavilion wins best national participation

India’s winning national participation brings together five artists: Alwar Balasubramaniam, Sumakshi Singh, Ranjani Shettar, Asim Waqif, and Skarma Sonam Tashi. Commissioned by the National Gallery of Modern Art (NGMA), Ministry of Culture, and curated by Amin Jaffer, the presentation occupied the Arsenale. Its title frames the exhibition around questions of distance and belonging, placing the idea of home at the center of a collective artistic presentation.

items.body:
Full Page Ad in Conde Nast’s Traveler magazine, March 1988 ([via](https://michaelcrichton.com/works/travels/))

I was talking to my friend Jamie about therapy a few months ago and he recommended the “Psychiatry” chapter in Michael Crichton’s 1988 memoir, [Travels](https://michaelcrichton.com/works/travels/).

Around 1971, Crichton was separated from his wife. She suggested he see a psychiatrist. “I refused,” Crichton wrote. “I didn’t think psychiatry did any good for people. It was just a lot of hand-holding.”

Then his wife gave him the name of a prominent psychiatrist at UCLA but suggested that the doctor was probably too busy to see him. Crichton took offense at the idea he wasn’t important enough to be seen, and made an appointment. (It’s a very funny chapter.)

“I now found myself in a peculiar situation,” he wrote. “I didn’t really believe in psychiatry, I didn’t want to see a psychiatrist, and I didn’t think there was anything wrong with me, but I was challenged to present myself to Dr. Norton in a fascinating way.”

After a fine performance, Dr. Norton took Crichton on as a patient.

> But I still wasn’t sure psychiatry did any good. And it was expensive, sixty dollars an hour. Anything that cost so much must surely be an indulgence. Rich lazy people went to psychiatrists.
> I decided to keep track of how much it was costing me to see Dr. Norton, and I assessed each session when it was over to determine if it had been worth the sixty dollars.
> I found Dr. Norton puzzling because he was so normal. I’d tell him my story and he’s say things like ‘Time will tell’ or ‘You can’t make an omelet without breaking eggs.’
> I thought, Sixty dollars an hour to hear you can’t make an omelette without breaking eggs? What good is this?

But Crichton enjoyed “complaining about my life” and kept going back.

On the fifth session, “three hundred dollars down the drain,” as he put it, they had a breakthrough: it turns out that Crichton was an insecure person.

> I felt amazed. Just as amazed as if he had shown me that I had a third arm coming out of my chest, an arm I had never noticed before. How could I not have noticed this before? But I never thought I was insecure. If anything, I saw myself as astoundingly confident.
> Could I really have held such an incorrect view of myself?
> Dr. Norton tried to soften the blow, and explained that many things about ourselves were difficult to see without outside help. That was the whole point of a therapist. He was an objective outsider.
> This was a new idea to me, that there might be some things about myself that I couldn’t see without outside help. But it obviously was true.
> I never kept track of how much I was spending again.

Crichton then goes on to tell a funny story about getting involved with several women and how Dr. Norton warns him that things are going to go very badly. Crichton doesn’t think so. He thinks he can handle it.

“Time will tell,” Dr. Norton says.

And it does: things go very badly for Crichton.

> “What a mess” I said.
> “Hell hath no fury like a woman scorned,” Dr. Norton said.
> By now I saw the point of these homilies. Dr. Norton was trying to get me to understand that certain rules of life had been around for a long time and that life probably wasn’t going to make an exception for me.

Crichton gets divorced, goes to a psychic, becomes totally depressed after achieving all his goals in life (it happens!), reads Ram Dass’s [Be Here Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Be_Here_Now_(book)), and starts traveling again.

But he never really talks about psychiatry again in that chapter.

So I searched around, seeing if anything came up about Crichton and psychiatry.

The first thing that surfaced was [this 1970 clip of his appearance on The Dick Cavett Show](https://www.youtube.com/watch?si=lI1aj1DSOB2ekSfJ&t=326&v=eB8NapR3_rM&feature=youtu.be) to promote his first non-fiction book, [Five Patients](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Patients):

Around [5:26,](https://www.youtube.com/watch?si=lI1aj1DSOB2ekSfJ&t=326&v=eB8NapR3_rM&feature=youtu.be) Cavett asks Crichton about psychiatry.

> Cavett: What’s happening in psychiatry these days? There’s always something peculiar going on there. The latest thing I heard about is they’re using computers as psychoanalysts.
> Crichton: There is a computer program which I put in the book because it was mostly amusing. It was done as a joke by a fellow named Weizenbaum at MIT several years ago. What he set out to do is to see if you could program a computer to interact in something approaching a conversation with a person. And he did it by a series of kind of tricks. So for example, the computer will pick up something in your sentence and play it back to you. If you mention parents it’ll pop something back, “Can you tell me more?” or “Why do you say that about [blank]?” and put in the parents. But it turns out in practice to be kind of successful, kind of frighteningly successful.
> Cavett: It sounds ludicrous to begin with. I mean, it would seem like the idea of therapy would be that the genius of the therapist would be that he treats every person as individual and finds out what this individual’s problems are and he’s unlike any other individual. But how can a machine do that?
> Crichton: That particular point is why this thing is kind of frightening the psychiatrist.
> Cavett: Because it’s succeeding?
> Crichton: Yeah!

There are at several things that are interesting to me about this clip.

- This was filmed 56 years ago.
- Crichton, seen here, is about one year away from going to therapy himself.
- Cavett sort of completely gets wrong what therapy is about, which Crichton later discovers for himself: seen through the eye of an attentive but impartial observer, your problems aren’t actually that unique at all.

But by far the most interesting is the story of MIT professor and computer scientist [Joseph Weizenbaum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Weizenbaum) himself, and how his experience ELIZA caused him [to turn against AI](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2023/jul/25/joseph-weizenbaum-inventor-eliza-chatbot-turned-against-artificial-intelligence-ai).

From [his MIT obituary](https://news.mit.edu/2008/obit-weizenbaum-0310):

items.body:
## Design Miami 2026 Preview: “Unveiling” Works From 75 International Galleries at This Year’s Miami Art Week

[↗ Primärquelle: mymodernmet.com](https://mymodernmet.com/design-miami-2026-preview/)

Brodin, “Constellation of Memory,” 2026. Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Kelley and Gavin Brodin.)

[Design Miami](https://designmiami.com/fair/miami-2026), one of the most exciting events of Miami Art Week, is back for the 22nd edition of its flagship fair. The event, devoted to contemporary collectible design, returns to the Miami Beach Convention Center with a lineup of 75 international galleries, museum-quality presentations, and a curatorial theme that celebrates the creatives behind the works on display.

The theme, *Unveiling*, calls for the viewers to truly observe each object, deciphering what inspired the artist to create them, and the surrounding stories behind their choices. These may be hiding in plain sight or several times removed from the final result, reflecting something deeply personal or rooted in the artist’s culture. *Unveiling* is then divided among four curatorial threads, each with different approaches and best represented by certain artists, techniques, and galleries.

## Design Miami is back with with a lineup of 75 international galleries and a curatorial theme that celebrates the creatives behind the works on display.

Pippin Drysdale, “Sacred Lands,” 2026. Adrian Sassoon at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Adrian Sassoon, London; photography by Robert Frith, Acorn Photo.)

First up is *Process as Aesthetic: Unveiling the Hand of the Maker*. This theme highlights the creative process, particularly the techniques, labor, and experimentation that come to determine an object’s aesthetic, regarding these steps as a vehicle for expression. This can be seen in the ceramic works of Bouke de Vries and Pippin Drysdale; Caroline Desile’s architecture-influenced *Totem 1*; Richard Haining’s *STACKED* creations, made up of thousands of pieces of salvaged New York City wood; and Man Ray’s *Optic-Topic mask*, the centerpiece of this division.

Le Corbusier, “La licorne passe sur la mer,” 1959. Boccara Gallery at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Boccara Gallery.)

Meanwhile, *Subverting Archetypes: The Familiar, Reimagined*, takes a more surrealist route, blurring the line between the familiar and the uncanny, asking viewers to reassess to what they think they know. Such is the case of a selection of 20th-century tapestries by Le Corbusier, Sonia Delaunay, and Alexander Calder. This section also features the work of Brazilian designer Lucas Recchia, who blends metal with fused glass, and a wall piece by Jaydan Moore, who turns found, silver-plated tableware into sculptural forms.

Dee Clements, “Gams,” 2026. Mindy Solomon Gallery at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: Clare Britt, courtesy of the artist and Mindy Solomon Gallery)

Prateek Jain & Gautam Seth, “Enchanted Forest,” 2025. Klove Studio at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of klove.)

Glover, “A Natural History of Dreams,” 2022. Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Duane Reed Gallery.)

*Material poetry: Unveiling material potential* explores the expectations materials carry, alongside their emotional, sensory, and imaginative possibilities. This is best represented by the work of Dutch designer Frederik Molenschot and Franco-Swedish designer Ingrid Donat, with the former approaching bronze as heavy and imposing, and the latter as luminous and weightless. Fernando Mastrangelo also touches on this with a monolithic sculpture cast from glass and sand that conceals an expandable cabinet within its architectural form.

KAMEH by Nikita Erokhin, “Beyond Reflection,” 2026. KAMEH at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Nikita Berezhnoy.)

Cure, “Color in Suspension,” 2026. Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Laura Hernandez.)

Barford, Light Sculpture “Feast,” 2026. Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of David Gill Gallery)

Finally, *Mirrors of Society and Place: Unveiling Identity, Culture, and Locality* assesses how design can convey identity, values, culture, and collective memory. After all, objects can become reflections of the societies and environments from which they emerge. For this, the fair presents a selection of mid-century Brazilian design, including works by Joaquim Tenreiro, Jorge Zalszupin, and José Zanine Caldas, while also looking their influence on contemporary creatives. Meanwhile, African artists Amber Cowan, Donté Hayes, hettler.tüllmann, Nobuhito Nishigawara, Simphiwe Mbunyuza, and Virginia Leonard Samburu present pieces inspired by Kenya’s landscapes and architecture.

Yakusha, “DOLONIA Sofa,” 2026. Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Victoria Yakusha Gallery.)

Turco, Installation View, 2026. Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Alex Turco.)

Design Miami will run on Dec. 1–6. Members, Collectors, and Press Previews will take place on Dec. 1, with a VIP Preview on the morning of Dec. 2. Public Show Days start on Dec. 2 at 1 p.m. To plan your visit and get tickets, visit [Design Miami’s website](https://designmiami.com/fair/miami-2026). To stay up to date, follow [Design Miami on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/designmiami).

items.body:
From plates of ravioli and spaghetti to bottles of chianti and sardines springing from their tins, [Kate Jenkins](https://katejenkinsstudio.co.uk/)‘ immersive art-meets-restaurant experience is something to really sink your teeth into. Known for her realistic knitted foodstuffs, the Brighton-based artist and knitwear designer presents *Kate’s Knitalian* at [Air Contemporary](https://www.air-contemporary.com/), inviting us to consider the (rather unexpected) mouthwatering possibilities of yarn.

For the opening reception, visitors were required to reserve a spot much as one would do to book a table in a traditional restaurant, including two timed sittings. Everything from wheels of salami and tortellini to tiramisù and bottles of “Pinot Stitchio” fill the delicatessen experience in a celebration of Italian cuisine.

*Kate’s Knitalian* continues through December 22 in London. And if you find yourself in Brighton, you can visit the artist’s studio, which is open daily in Arundel Place. See more on Jenkins’ [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/kjcardigan). You might also enjoy Lucy Sparrow’s *The Beginning of Convenience,* an entirely [felted supermarket](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/2026/07/lucy-sparrow-the-beginning-of-convenience/) at The Momentary in Bentonville, Arkansas.

Photo by Helena Dolby

items.body:
This year [Simon Skinner](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/simon-skinner/) was [named emerging designer of the year at the Dezeen Awards](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/11/16/discover-this-years-dezeen-awards-designers-of-the-year/). Here, he selects five projects that showcase his work.

Swedish designer Skinner set up his studio in 2020 and has rapidly become known for his sculptural furniture and installations that explore rethinking and reusing found materials.

"My practice is centred around material culture, exploring the relationship between objects, meaning and everyday life," Skinner told Dezeen.

"What connects my work is an interest in how forms carry associations and how these can be reshaped to offer new perspectives on things we know and take for granted."

Skinner finds that the things that excite him about design are also "the same things that make me suffer".

"You never quite know what’s coming next when running your own practice, but there’s also something exciting about that uncertainty," he said.

"A material or an object you’ve overlooked for years can suddenly become the starting point for a whole body of work."

Over the coming year, along with creating new collections and public installations, Skinner hopes to dedicate more time to research.

"I want to make more room for research and experimentation, and give myself time to follow an interest before knowing exactly where it might lead," he said.

"When I started researching Afro combs at [Konstfack](https://www.konstfack.se/), I became aware of how much history and symbolism an everyday tool can hold. That experience still informs how I work," he continued.

"I want to keep exploring the objects and forms we take for granted, looking at the meanings they’ve inherited and what happens when you change their material, scale or context."

Read on to find out five key projects by Dezeen Award-winning Skinner, as described by the designer:

Photo by Gustav Almestål

**[Buké](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/02/05/simon-skinner-buke-lamps/)**

"An ongoing project in which vintage glass sourced from flea markets and second-hand shops is brought together in sculptural lighting compositions.

"Drawing on the memories and associations embedded in these found objects, the work explores the relationship between material, memory and light."

Photo by Hedvig Jenning

**[Afro Combs](https://www.dezeen.com/2019/04/23/afropicks-simon-skinner-design-milan/)**

"Crafted in my studio, these combs celebrate rituals and traditions surrounding textured hair.

"Informed by historical references and personal experiences, they reimagine an everyday object through distinctive forms and symbols."

Photo by Adrian Levander

**Vanity Table**

"Extending the exploration of beauty rituals within the Syntax collection, the Vanity Table offers an alternative reading of an object associated with personal grooming."

**Upholstered furniture **

"These one-of-a-kind pieces, a daybed and an armchair, are upholstered in hand-dyed canvas in deep magenta hues.

"Combining traditional upholstery techniques with an experimental approach to colour and detail, the pieces embrace the irregularities of the dyeing process, making them an integral part of their character."

**Aluminium stool/side table **

"This piece of furniture explores our relationship to the mechanical lock. The lock is integrated into the leg, with keys used to secure the connection between the leg and the seat.

"The keys can also serve as hooks for keychains and personal belongings, inviting individual expression."

items.subtitle: The current iteration of Bolsover Castle, in the NE of Derbyshire, is not, despite its appearance, a defensive structure.

items.body:
The current iteration of Bolsover Castle, in the NE of Derbyshire, is not, despite its appearance, a defensive structure. It does look  very reminiscent of the Norman white tower at the tower of London, but it is essentially a Jacobean residence dressed up for effect. However it is clear that the western and northern approaches are up steep slopes and the "keep" looks dominant on the escarpment.

Both the earlier stone building on this site and its wooden predecessor were, in contrast, both very much defensive structures. To the east and south the approach is relatively unobstructed by natural features. When the promontory at Bolsover was fortified in the 12th century  the eastern and southern defences of both the castle and the town were enhanced by earthworks and ditches with the earthworks surmounted by a wooden palisade. Bolsover was one of only 2 planned and defended towns of the 11th/12th century in Derbyshire (Castleton is the other). It was , in effect , a plantation of people of Norman descent and those Saxons who had demonstrated their acceptance of Norman rule.

What we see on the ground  today is only about 1/3 of the original height. The most obvious earthwork and ditch remains are in the Hornscroft park next to the parish church but the earthwork defences, which also became the defences of the town, apparently had strength in depth with an outer ring of ditch and earthworks being identifiable to the east of the town at Oxcroft Lane (the area is known as Dyke Fields).  Furthermore a local road between Bolsover and the next town to the north  (Clowne) has the local name "The Ramper" (as reflected in street names such as Ramper Avenue on nearby new developments). Local understanding is that the "Ramper" derives from the "Ramparts", a further layer of defence for the town which is now long gone. On Oxcroft lane there has also been found evidence of Roman and earlier occupation.

These earthworks have long had protected status and are seen as an excellent example of medieval  town defences. Certainly  a visit to the famous castle or its historic water supply system is not complete without  a look at the real defensive  structures which pre-date it by about 300 years.

items.body:
## HUMAN POINT CHOREOGRAPHS SPACE AROUND HUMAN PRESENCE

With three decades of practice behind it, Human Point approaches the built environment as a living sequence shaped by human presence. Spanning [architecture](https://www.designboom.com/architecture/), [urban planning](https://www.designboom.com/tag/masterplans-and-urban-revitalization/), real estate development, investment strategy, engineering, and turn-key construction, the multidisciplinary practice integrates architectural vision, technical expertise, and economic thinking into a unified approach, from initial concept to completed development.

In a recent conversation with designboom, founder Loukas Fotopoulos unpacks how this directorial lens shapes the practice, treating physical space as a fluid timeline that unfolds through shifting light, evolving perspectives, and tactile materiality. This framework casts residents as active protagonists whose movement and interactions bring each environment to life in real time.

Whispering Elia project, Mykonos, Greece | all images courtesy of [Human Point](https://humanpoint.eu/)

## OPEN LABORATORY MERGING CRAFT AND DIALOGUE

Loukas Fotopoulos established his own architectural practice in 1996, continuing a family tradition of architecture. Having grown up alongside his father, architect Eleftherios Fotopoulos, in his architectural studio, he developed an early understanding of architectural thinking and practice. In 2008, his [practice](https://humanpoint.eu/) evolved into Human Point, expanding its approach beyond architecture.

Across residential, hospitality, and urban scales, the studio brings architecture, strategic development consulting, and immersive visual communication under one roof. Inside this open laboratory of ideas, every phase takes shape through continuous dialogue between creators and inhabitants.

Whispering Elia project, Mykonos, Greece

## LOUKAS FOTOPOULOS ON ARCHITECTURE AND THE HUMAN LOGIC OF VALUE

**Human Point began as an architectural practice in 1996. How has it evolved?**

**Loukas Fotopoulos (LF):** Architecture remains the foundation of everything we do. But over time, I became increasingly interested in everything that determines whether a good architectural idea becomes a good building. Design is one part of a larger process involving land, feasibility, planning, engineering, construction, financing and, ultimately, how people experience the completed project. Human Point evolved to bring these decisions together, from the earliest investment strategy through construction. We wanted to take responsibility for the entire process rather than simply contribute to one stage. For me, this is not about offering more services. It is about protecting the coherence of the original idea.

**You are both an architect and a filmmaker. How does cinema influence your architecture?**

**(LF):** Architecture is often represented through static images, although nobody experiences a building that way. We move through space in time. Light changes, views unfold, materials approach the body. There is anticipation, transition and sometimes surprise. Cinema taught me to think in sequences. In architecture, the person inhabiting the space becomes the protagonist. There is another connection. Before directing a character, you must understand that character and, in a way, love them. Architecture requires something similar. Before designing for people, you must be genuinely interested in them. An architect, particularly one involved in development, cannot remain isolated in a studio. You need to understand society, economics, politics, science, technology and culture. And you need to enjoy life: travel, meet people, observe, celebrate and sometimes simply have fun. If architecture creates places for life, you must remain curious about life itself. That curiosity often generates unexpected, playful ideas that can also carry social purpose and economic intelligence.

Whispering Ampeli project, Assos, Kefalonia, Greece

**What does human-centered architecture mean in practice?**

**(LF):** For us, human-centered is not a style. It is a method of making decisions. How will somebody actually live here? How does a space feel in the morning or at night? Where do you naturally want to sit? Where do you need privacy? How does the building respond to the seasons and its landscape? Increasingly, we apply the same questions to development. If development creates the environments in which people live, it deserves the same human consideration as architecture itself.

**Development is increasingly criticized for its impact on cities, islands and communities. Can development genuinely be human-centered?**

**(LF):** Absolutely, but not automatically. Development becomes problematic when short-term financial return is its only criterion. Yet development itself is essential. We need investment, housing, hospitality, infrastructure and the intelligent transformation of existing buildings. The question is how we do it. A carefully studied development can respect its location, respond to real needs, use resources intelligently and remain economically successful. I don’t believe architecture has to choose between human value and economic value. Good development should create both. Capital is essential, but it should work alongside architectural vision, scientific knowledge, technical expertise, social responsibility and long-term thinking.

And meaningful development opportunities should not necessarily belong only to large institutional players.

Private investors, smaller investment groups and landowners should also be able to participate in professionally structured developments when they have access to the appropriate architectural, financial and technical expertise. For that to happen, the institutional and regulatory framework should provide fair and equal conditions for participation, regardless of scale. In a sense, this is also a political position. Not against capital — we need capital and want to work with it — but in favor of profitable investment that recognizes wider social, environmental and cultural responsibilities. Private value and collective benefit do not always have to be in conflict. In fact, well-conceived development can strengthen both.

Vouliagmeni, premium residential building project, Athens Riviera, Greece

items.body:
“About Texas,” newspaper + marker, 2024

My [Friday newsletter](https://austinkleon.substack.com/p/this-is-how-we-do-it) began:

> [Molly Ivins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molly_Ivins) called Texas “the laboratory for bad government,” and that’s been the case my entire adult life. I was a 17-year-old in Ohio during the 2000 election, and since I couldn’t vote, I went around waving a copy of [Shrub: The Short But Happy Political Life of George W. Bush](https://geni.us/jzBru4C) at my family members, warning them that the whole country could become Texas. (Whenever other Americans joke that they wish Texas would go ahead and secede, I reply, “But then you’d lose your [early warning system](https://austinkleon.com/2020/12/04/art-is-an-early-warning-system/)!”) 19 summers ago, Meg and I moved to Austin so she could go to grad school. We stayed. She gave birth to a couple of native Texans during the Obama administration (I was able to become a full-time writer thanks to the Affordable Care Act), and since then we’ve been raising them in a sunny city full of friendly people and great food, all the while knowing that just five miles down the road, some of the most corrupt men in the world do their best to wreck the place. So you can imagine how it felt on Tuesday night, when a good number of those creeps were [sent packing by our fellow Texans](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/05/us/texas-democrats-statewide-sweep.html?unlocked_article_code=1.OFE.jOl1.9KtaJ39zOo9a&smid=url-share). The vibe around here is: [jubilant](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/jubilant).

items.body:
## More Than 50 Dancers Will Celebrate Our Connection to the Ocean During Miami Art Week

[↗ Primärquelle: mymodernmet.com](https://mymodernmet.com/subodh-kerkar-the-ocean-odyssey/)

As part of Miami Art Week, more than 50 dancers and members of the public will come together on Miami Beach to celebrate our deep and lasting relationship with the sea. *The Ocean Odyssey* is a new, site-specific performance by Indian artist [Subodh Kerkar](https://subodhkerkar.com/), presented in partnership with the [Andaz Miami Beach Resort & Spa](https://www.hyatt.com/andaz/en-US/miaob-andaz-miami-beach), the [Miami City Ballet](https://www.miamicityballet.org/), and its artistic director, Gonzalo García.

Kerkar describes the ocean as “a symbol of celebration of one humanity,” adding, “I celebrate the inseparability of human life and the ocean.” The artist is inviting up to 60 members of the public to join professional dancers in the performance. Together, they’ll move across the beach in a carefully choreographed sequence, creating lines and shapes—like straight lines, wavy lines, and circle formations—that are particularly striking when viewed from above. As Kerkar [explains](https://www.instagram.com/p/Df2iIwFSJRH/), “No dance experience needed: it begins as a simple walk, and from above, it becomes something extraordinary.”

*The Ocean Odyssey* will take place on Dec. 4, between 4-5 p.m., in front of Andaz Miami Beach Resort & Spa. It’s organized by [REEFLINE](https://www.thereefline.org/), a non-profit and pioneering underwater public sculpture park at Miami Beach. REEFLINE is creating a new kind of underwater reef, bringing together art, science, and technology to support marine restoration, encourage biodiversity, and help ocean ecosystems thrive.

Check out some photos from one of Kerkar’s previous performances below to get a glimpse of what to expect during Miami Art Week.

items.title: Six Artworks Under $1,000 We’d Love to Give (and Receive!) This Holiday

items.body:
There’s an unparalleled joy in watching a loved one unwrap something they both never anticipated and immediately know they’ve needed all along. These types of gifts are often the most unexpected, surprisingly personal, and typically, one of a kind.

Our partners at Joy Machine have generously curated a selection of artworks that fit this category. Priced under $1,000, [the collection](https://joymachine.art/collections/artworks-under-1k) includes pieces by an international group of artists that longtime Colossal readers will surely recognize. From playful drawings in walnut ink to uncanny kitsch sculptures, these works are perfecting for gifting this holiday season, even (especially?) if that gift is to yourself.

Seattle-based artist [Debra Broz](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/tags/debra-broz/) applies her training in ceramic conservation to a practice that involves scouring flea markets and thrift shops for ceramic figurines, breaking their forms, and reassembling the figures as surreal hybrids.

*[Collect “Boxer Horse” ($750)](https://joymachine.art/collections/debra-broz)*

Collin van der Sluijs, “White Line Sphinx Moth drawing” (2026), mixed media on paper, framed, 8.3 x 11.7 inches

Dutch artist [Collin van der Sluijs](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/tags/collin-van-der-sluijs/) is a master of several styles, with a background in graffiti and street art and a parallel interest in the delicate, impeccably detailed features of the natural world.

*[Collect “White Line Sphinx Moth drawing” ($550)](https://joymachine.art/collections/collin-van-der-sluijs)*

Stevie Shao, “Star Bull” (2025), acrylic gouache and latex paint on paper, 21 x 21 centimeters

With a deep love for the flora and fauna near her home in the Pacific Northwest, Stevie Shao creates folk art-inspired works through bold color palettes and arresting patterns.

[Collect “Star Bull” ($400)](https://joymachine.art/collections/stevie-shao)

Misato Sano, “レッツ ワークアウト！ / Let’s work out!” (2025), drawing paper, acrylic gouache, walnut ink, 11 x 14 inches (framed)

Japanese artist [Misato Sano](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/tags/misato-sano/) is best known for her cheeky wooden carvings of poodles and pugs, which she translates to two-dimensions in this playful rendition that might just make us want to get up and get moving.

*[Collect “Let’s work out” ($150)](https://joymachine.art/collections/misato-sano)*

Danym Kwon, “A Quiet Afternoon” (2026), acrylic gouache on birch plywood, 11 x 5 x 1.125 inches

Through large-scale paintings and small woodcuts, [Danym Kwon](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/tags/danym-kwon/) meditates on the mundane activities like folding laundry or strolling around the park that allow memories to emerge and be understood anew.

*[Collect “A Quiet Afternoon” ($350)](https://joymachine.art/collections/danym-kwon)*

Rachel Hayden, “Halloween in May”(2026), acrylic on panel, 8 x 10 inches

Layering acrylic paint with crisp edges that evoke paper collage, Rachel Hayden blends the patterns of a summertime picnic with the eerie colors and atmosphere of fall, perfect for the perpetually witchy pal.

*[Collect “Halloween in May” ($900)](https://joymachine.art/collections/rachel-hayden)*

Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a [Colossal Member](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/members) today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article [Six Artworks Under $1,000 We’d Love to Give (and Receive!) This Holiday](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/2026/11/six-artworks-under-1000-gift-guide/) appeared first on [Colossal](https://www.thisiscolossal.com).

items.body:
For more than a decade, buildings bearing [trees](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/trees/) have been sprouting up all over the world, from New York to Paris to Shanghai to Sydney.

It has arguably become one of the defining architectural trends of our era, taken up enthusiastically by top studios including [BIG](https://www.dezeen.com/2023/10/24/big-first-supertall-skyscraper-the-spiral-new-york-city/), [MVRDV](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/06/05/la-vallee-verte-mvrdv/), [MAD](https://www.dezeen.com/2021/09/24/mad-architects-the-star-office-building-hollywood-los-angeles/) and [Ateliers Jean Nouvel](https://www.dezeen.com/2024/11/15/jean-nouvel-philippe-starck-rosewood-sao-paulo-hotel/).

And yet, not everyone is a fan. Almost every time Dezeen publishes an arboreal structure, a volley of comments crying greenwashing and gimmickry soon follows.

So, are the haters right on this one? Or do the arguments stack up in favour of wooded buildings?

## The root of the issue

To proponents of the approach, some of the benefits of putting trees on buildings are indisputable.

"I'm totally in favor of not only trees on buildings, but any type of natural habitats on buildings wherever it's possible," said Fernando Scherner, an associate director in the nature and biodiversity team at engineering firm [Buro Happold](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/buro-happold/). "There are a few things that I think we can't even argue about anymore."

There is, Scherner told Dezeen, strong evidence that vegetation on buildings [bolsters biodiversity](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ecs2.1905). And, he says, "there's no discussion" that done right, shade and evapotranspiration from leaves can [effectively keep homes cooler](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1618866717306325) in hot weather, reducing the need for air conditioning – and therefore energy use.

But this second point gestures towards the crux of the debate about trees on buildings.

Tree-planted terraces wind around BIG's The Spiral skyscraper in New York City. Photo by Laurian Ghinitoiu

Such buildings require extra structural material to support the weight of the trees and soil, increasing the [carbon cost](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/embodied-carbon/) by more than what the trees themselves will be able to sequester. Critics therefore argue that any carbon savings from reduced energy use are a red herring, because a similar benefit could be achieved through much simpler passive cooling measures such as awnings and shutters.

"I think that criticism is entirely legitimate, particularly if carbon sequestration is being used as the main justification," said [World Green Building Council](https://worldgbc.org/) technical lead for sustainable buildings Carolina Montano Owen.

"Trees do sequester carbon, but relatively slowly compared with the upfront emissions that can arise from additional reinforced concrete or steel needed for large planters, supporting structure and associated systems."

Even Dutch architecture studio [MVRDV](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/mvrdv/), one of the most fervent incorporators of trees on buildings, [admitted in its Carbon Confessions exhibition held earlier this year](https://nos.nl/collectie/13871/artikel/2602623-tentoonstelling-laat-zien-groene-intenties-pakken-in-de-bouw-soms-niet-zo-uit) that it would take hundreds of years to offset the climate impact of its [La Serre project in Paris](https://www.mvrdv.com/projects/515/la-serre), currently under construction. MVRDV declined to contribute to this article.

## A place to grow

While the phenomenon of trees on buildings goes back hundreds of years, to the [Guinigi Tower](https://www.visittuscany.com/en/attractions/the-guinigi-tower/) in Tuscany, the undisputed poster child for the current movement stands at the other end of Italy.

Bosco Verticale in Milan is a pair of residential high-rises covered in 21,000 plants, including 800 trees up to 20 metres tall. It caused a sensation upon its completion in 2014, and was later [selected by Dezeen](https://www.dezeen.com/2025/01/20/bosco-verticale-stefano-boeri-21st-century-architecture/) as that year's most significant building in the world.

The architect behind Bosco Verticale, [Stefano Boeri](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/stefano-boeri/), has since delivered other "[vertical forests](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/vertical-forests/)" in [Eindhoven](https://www.dezeen.com/2021/10/14/trudo-vertical-forest-social-housing-stefano-boeri-eindhoven-architecture/), [Huanggang](https://www.dezeen.com/2022/01/26/stefano-boeri-vertical-forest-skyscraper-china/), [Tirana](https://www.stefanoboeriarchitetti.net/en/project/tirana-vertical-forest/) and [Utrecht](https://www.stefanoboeriarchitetti.net/en/project/wonderwoods/), with several more on the way.

As you'd expect, he is bullish about the benefits of putting trees on buildings. He points to analysis by [Arup](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/arup/), which concluded that the embodied carbon of Bosco Verticale is just one per cent greater than a comparable building with balconies of the same depth without vegetation.

Several oak trees are planted on the roof of Guinigi Tower, which was built in the late 1300s. Photo via Shutterstock

"The load of the greenery, including the soil, trees and so on, really only slightly exceeds the variable loads that, in any case, must necessarily be taken into account in the structural design of cantilevered space," he told Dezeen.

Boeri argues that changes to the construction process – such as the use of prefabrication methods or [mass timber](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/mass-timber/) – promise to cut the embodied cost further in future vertical forest projects.

Even so, Philip Oldfield, head of the [University of New South Wales](https://www.dezeen.com/schoolshows/school/university-of-new-south-wales/)’ School of Built Environment, is not convinced.

"I think the equation is pretty challenging to make the case that trees on buildings are beneficial from a greenhouse-gas emissions perspective," he told Dezeen.

Photo by Giovanni Nardi

The balconies at Bosco Verticale are embedded with trees up to 20 metres tall. Photo courtesy of Stefano Boeri Architetti

However, Oldfield points out, that's not to say that architects adorning their buildings with trees are necessarily acting in bad faith.

"I'm a fan of Bosco Verticale," he said. "I think it's a really inspiring building, but not from a carbon perspective."

"What inspires me about Bosco Verticale is it says, 'hey, look: you can have a hint of suburban lifestyle in a high-rise urban building,' which could make high-density living more attractive to a greater socio-economic spectrum, and then that may be more sustainable in the long run."

Though harder to measure than carbon, it's generally acknowledged that incorporating greenery into dense urban settings has positives for human wellbeing.

items.body:
Portraying a man walking away from a modern office tower block, as if to explore the surrounding community, 'Walking East' is an impressive painted metal sculpture placed directly onto the street without a plinth.

Its creator, French Hong Kong-based sculptor Polo Bourieau, cited the inspiration for 'Walking East' as 'les adventuriers du quotidien' (the daily adventurers), the everyday working people going about their day in the Kwun Tong industrial district.

Located next to a busy junction, the 5-metre tall statue becomes especially poignant during work opening, lunch and closing hours. Surrounded by commuters and workers, it looms large over the hordes, seemingly journeying with them as they attempt to navigate their daily lives and Kwun Tong's crowded streets.

items.body:
## yuri suzuki makes sound something to see, touch, and share

[Yuri Suzuki](https://www.designboom.com/tag/yuri-suzuki/) uses sound as a material for shaping spaces, creating encounters, and bringing people together. His practice moves between [sound](https://www.designboom.com/tag/sound-art/), technology, [sculpture](https://www.designboom.com/tag/sculpture/), and graphic design, often inviting audiences to participate. Recent public commissions explore how [artificial intelligence](https://www.designboom.com/tag/artificial-intelligence/) and machine learning can generate evolving sound environments, allowing each visitor to experience and contribute to a work in a different way. Accessibility is central to this approach: as Suzuki puts it, his projects aim to be *‘accessible to the many.’*

Music follows a similarly open-ended logic in his own creative life. Asked which track best captures his practice, the Tokyo-born artist and designer, based between London and Margate, chooses Cornelius’ The Micro Disneycal World Tour, describing it as *‘a wonderful mixture of different musical elements, almost like a melting pot of sounds and ideas.’* He is drawn to its optimism and the way its complexity remains accessible, qualities he also tries to bring into his projects. Yuri Suzuki’s listening habits move between punk, electronic music, Japanese pop, and experimental sounds. Teengenerate and Melt-Banana help him clear his head when starting a project or working through a creative block, while Donald Fagen’s New Frontier takes him back to watching MTV recordings on Betamax as a child in Tokyo. His selections also reveal a longstanding interest in the relationship between music and objects, from the playful packaging of Mark Mothersbaugh’s limited-edition cassette to Peter Saville’s iconic sleeve design for New Order’s Blue Monday.

For [designboom listens](https://www.designboom.com/tag/designboom-listens/), Suzuki shares the tracks that accompany his creative process, the memories attached to particular songs, and the sounds he imagines alongside his own work. **Read on for his selections and listen to the full playlist below.**

Yuri Suzuki by Nick Glover

## music as a melting pot of ideas

**What song best captures your creative practice?**

**[Yuri Suzuki](https://www.yurisuzuki.com/) (YS):** Cornelius — The Micro Disneycal World Tour. I think this track represents my creative practice quite well. It’s a wonderful mixture of different musical elements, almost like a melting pot of sounds and ideas. There’s a sense of optimism running through it, and despite its complexity, it feels very accessible and universal. I think these are qualities I also try to bring into my own projects.

**What is the very first track you play to clear the air and get inspired when starting a new project?**

**YS:** Teengenerate — My GTO. This is a difficult one, but I often find punk music is the best way to clear my head. Something loud, fast and direct helps wash away whatever I’ve been thinking about and gives me a fresh start. Teengenerate’s My GTO is perfect for that.

Yuri Suzuki by Mark Cocksedge

**Is there a song that instantly takes you back to a specific memory or place from your past?**

**YS:** Donald Fagen — New Frontier. My father had a Betamax videotape of MTV recordings, and this music video was on it. I remember watching it at night when I was in kindergarten. Even now, whenever I hear the song, I can immediately picture those evenings and the atmosphere of watching that video as a small child. I still listen to it quite often.

**What song is stuck in your head right now?**

**YS:** Happy End — Kaze wo Atsumete. When I was in Tokyo in August, I had the chance to meet Haruomi Hosono and have a lovely conversation with him. Perhaps because of that, I’ve found myself humming Kaze wo Atsumete by Happy End, the band he was part of in the early 1970s, quite a lot recently.

synthesizers, keyboards, and electronic instruments line the walls around Suzuki’s studio | studio images courtesy of Yuri Suzuki

**What is your ultimate 2 AM studio track, the one you secretly know every word to?**

**YS:** Jeff Mills — Gamma Player / Mark Mothersbaugh — Musik for Insomniaks. Jeff Mills’ Gamma Player is one of my favorite things to listen to late at night. There’s something about hearing it in the middle of the night that feels absolutely wonderful.

Another favorite is Mark Mothersbaugh’s Musik for Insomniaks. As the title suggests, it’s a wonderful soundtrack for listening to in the middle of the night. It was also released on CD, but the limited-edition cassette version sold in Japan was particularly special. Not only did it have different content, but it also came with playing cards inside the package. I love the whole concept, both musically and as a physical object.

OTOTNOMORI – Sound Forest | image courtesy of Yuri Suzuki

**What song do you put on when you are stuck and need a breakthrough?**

**YS:** Melt-Banana — Free the Bee. When I’m stuck, I tend to listen to punk or thrash metal. I like music with enough energy to completely blow away whatever is going on in my head. I often listen to Melt-Banana, and if I had to choose one track, it would be Free the Bee.

**What track is dominating your speakers this week, and is it influencing what you are making right now?**

**YS:** Buffalo Daughter — あ (AH). My friends in Buffalo Daughter released a new track called あ this week, so I’ve been listening to it a lot. It’s incredibly catchy and keeps playing in my head. I don’t know yet whether it’s influencing my work, but it’s certainly staying with me.

Mechanical Music Wheel | image © Chris Kidall Park

**What song helps you slow down and focus on the tiny, quiet details?**

**YS:** Róisín Murphy — Through Time. I love this track by Róisín Murphy, produced by my friend Matthew Herbert. It has such a beautiful melody and wonderful sonic textures. There’s something very calming about it, and it helps me slow down and pay attention to the smaller details in sound.

**If people were to wear headphones while experiencing your latest work, what one song should be playing?**

**YS:** Raymond Scott — Portfolio 2. I think Raymond Scott’s Portfolio 2 would be a wonderful accompaniment to Onomatopia. His sound world feels very close to the kind of imaginary sonic environments suggested by the sculptures and their visual language. Although I have also composed my own soundtrack for the project, I think this would be a lovely alternative way to experience it.

items.body: The third edition of the Sharjah Architecture Triennial (SAT03), titled Architecture Otherwise: Building Civic Infrastructure for Collective Futures, brings together practitioners exploring architecture beyond conventional building practices. During the opening week, ArchDaily's Editor-in-Chief Christele Harrouk spoke with Makram el Kadi and Ziad Jamaleddine of L.E.FT, Mohamad Nahleh, Khondaker Hasibul Kabir and Suhailey Farzana of POCAA, May al-Ibrashy of Megawra-BEC, Nathalie Harb and Mohamad Hafeda, and Hamed Bukhamseen and Ali İsmail Karimi of Civil Architecture about their contributions, which engage with spiritual practices, community-led spatial production, heritage, displacement, and material reuse. Through installations, collective research, and interventions in existing spaces, their work considers how architecture can emerge through different forms of knowledge, care, and engagement with everyday life.
